--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general prologue to a specific administrative notice regarding the publication history and editorial policies of the Royal Society's "Philosophical Transactions."</meta>

## NOTICE. <note>original: "ADVERTISEMENT"</note>
---
The Committee appointed by the *Royal Society* to oversee the publication of the *Philosophical Transactions* takes this opportunity to inform the public of several facts. It is clearly evident—from the Society's Council books and Journals as well as from repeated statements made in several previous *Transactions*—that until the forty-seventh volume, the printing of these volumes was always the individual act of the respective Secretaries. As a formal organization <note>original: "as a Body"</note>, the Society never involved itself further in their publication than by occasionally recommending that their Secretaries resume them if, due to specific circumstances, the *Transactions* had been paused <note>original: "intermitted"</note> for any length of time. This was primarily done to reassure the public that their regular meetings were continuing for the advancement of knowledge and the benefit of humanity. These were the great goals of their original founding by *Royal Charters*, which they have consistently pursued ever since.

However, as the *Society* has grown significantly in recent years and the number of scientific reports <note>original: "communications"</note> has increased, it was decided that a Committee of members should be appointed to review the papers read before them and select those most suitable for publication in future *Transactions*. This was officially put into effect on March 26, 1752. The criteria for their selection are, and will remain, the importance and uniqueness <note>original: "singularity"</note> of the subjects, or the effective way they are presented. The Committee does not claim to guarantee the accuracy of the facts or the validity of the reasoning contained in the various papers published; these must still rest on the reputation and judgment of their respective authors.

It is also necessary on this occasion to note that it is an established rule of the *Society*, which they will always follow, never to give a collective opinion as an organization...

<summary>This notice explains a major shift in the editorial policy of the Royal Society in 1752, moving from individual editorial control by Secretaries to a formal peer-review committee for the "Philosophical Transactions."</summary>
<keywords>Royal Society, Philosophical Transactions, editorial policy, scientific publishing, 1752, peer review, Royal Charters</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal disclaimer regarding the Royal Society's official stance on papers and inventions presented at its meetings.</meta>

upon a subject, either of Science <note>original: "Nature"</note> or Technology <note>original: "Art"</note>, that comes before them. And therefore the thanks, which are frequently proposed from the Chair, to be given to the authors of such papers as are read at their accustomed meetings, or to the persons through whose hands they received them, are to be considered in no other light than as a matter of courtesy <note>original: "civility"</note>, in return for the respect shown to the Society by those communications. 

The same is also to be said with regard to the various projects, inventions, and curiosities of various kinds, which are often exhibited to the Society. The authors of these, or those who exhibit them, frequently take the liberty to report, and even to certify in the public newspapers, that they have met with the highest applause and approval <note>original: "approbation"</note>. And therefore it is hoped that no regard will hereafter be paid to such reports and public notices; which in some instances have been too easily believed <note>original: "lightly credited"</note>, to the dishonor of the Society.

<summary>This page clarifies that the Royal Society's formal thanks to presenters are merely a courtesy and do not constitute an official endorsement of their scientific or technical claims.</summary>
<keywords>Royal Society, scientific protocol, public notices, endorsements, institutional reputation, 18th-century science</keywords>

# PHILOSOPHICAL TRANSACTIONS.

---

### I. *On the Bodily Tides of Viscous and Semi-elastic Spheroids, and on the Ocean Tides upon a Yielding Nucleus.*

->By G. H. DARWIN, <term>M.A.</term> <note>Master of Arts</note>, Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge.<-
->*Communicated by* J. W. L. GLAISHER, <term>M.A., F.R.S.</term> <note>Master of Arts, Fellow of the Royal Society</note><-

->Received May 14—Read May 23, 1878.<-

In a well-known investigation, Sir William Thomson <note>later known as Lord Kelvin, a pioneer in thermodynamics and physics</note> discussed the problem of the <term>bodily tides</term> <note>tides that occur within the solid or semi-solid body of a planet, rather than just in its surface oceans</note> of a <term>homogeneous</term> <note>uniform in composition</note> elastic sphere. From this study, he drew very important conclusions regarding the great rigidity of the Earth.

Now, it seems improbable that the Earth is perfectly elastic. The distortions seen in geological strata <note>layers of rock</note> show that the material constituting the Earth is somewhat plastic, at least near the surface. We also know that even the most heat-resistant metals can be made to flow under the application of sufficiently great force.

Although Sir William Thomson’s investigation has gone far to disprove the old idea that the Earth has a semi-fluid interior, geologists are still strongly impressed by the fact that enormous masses of rock are being—and have been—poured out of volcanic vents in the Earth's surface. Because of this, the belief is not yet extinct that we live on a thin shell over a sea of molten lava. Under these circumstances, it seems worthwhile to investigate the consequences of the theory that the matter making up the Earth is of a viscous <term>viscous</term> <note>having a thick, sticky consistency between a solid and a liquid, like honey or tar</note> or imperfectly elastic nature. If the interior is composed this way, then the solid crust—unless it is very thick—cannot possess enough rigidity to suppress the internal tidal surging. These hypotheses should yield results that correspond fairly well to reality. The hypothesis of imperfect elasticity will be prin—

<summary>George H. Darwin introduces his research into how the Earth deforms under tidal forces, questioning whether the planet is a perfectly rigid solid or a viscous, plastic body. He aims to reconcile Sir William Thomson's theories on Earth's stiffness with geological evidence of volcanic activity and rock deformation.</summary>

<keywords>G.H. Darwin, bodily tides, elasticity, viscosity, Earth's rigidity, geophysics, Sir William Thomson, Gabriel Lamé, geological strata, volcanism</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues George Darwin's introduction, moving from the debate about the Earth's interior to his specific mathematical approach. He explains how he will use fluid dynamics and elasticity models to test whether the Earth acts more like a solid or a thick liquid.</meta>

...principally interesting in showing how far Sir W. <term>Thomson’s</term> <note>Sir William Thomson, later known as Lord Kelvin, a pioneer in thermodynamics and physics</note> results are changed by the assumption that elasticity fails under continued pressure.

In this paper, I follow these hypotheses. It will be shown that the results are just as opposed to the idea of a highly mobile or fluid interior of the Earth as Sir W. <term>Thomson’s</term> results were.

The only evidence on Earth of a <term>bodily tide</term> <note>tides that occur within the solid or semi-solid mass of a planet rather than just its surface oceans</note> would be that the ocean tides would be lower than theory predicts. Therefore, the subject of this paper is closely connected to the theory of ocean tides.

In the first part, the <term>equilibrium tide-theory</term> <note>a model that assumes the ocean adjusts instantly to the gravitational pull of the moon and sun</note> is used to estimate how much ocean tides are reduced and how their timing is shifted by bodily tides. However, it is widely recognized that this theory is quite flawed when explaining tides that occur over short periods.

In the second part of this paper, I have therefore considered the <term>dynamical theory</term> <note>a more complex model involving the actual movement and momentum of water</note> of tides within a canal at the equator surrounding a core distorted by tides. The results are almost the same as those given by the equilibrium theory.

The first two sections of the paper adapt Sir W. <term>Thomson’s</term> work* to the current hypotheses. Since it was impossible to include his entire argument here, I fear this investigation will only be understandable to those who are already familiar with his work or are willing to accept my quotes from it as proven.

Because some readers may want to know the findings of this inquiry without studying the mathematics, I have provided a summary of the whole work in Part III. As much as possible, I have moved my comments and conclusions to that section. However, I have tried to provide enough explanation in the main text to show the direction of the argument.

I consider the case of pure <term>viscosity</term> <note>a measure of a fluid's resistance to flow; its "thickness"</note> first, because the analysis is somewhat simpler and the results can later be easily applied to the case of <term>elastico-viscosity</term> <note>the property of a material that behaves with both elastic (solid) and fluid properties</note>.

# SPHEROIDS, AND ON THE OCEAN TIDES UPON A YIELDING CORE <note>original: nucleus; here referring to the Earth's central core</note>.
2 B

$$\left. \begin{aligned} -\frac{dp}{dx} + v\nabla^2\alpha + \text{X} = 0 \\ -\frac{dp}{dy} + v\nabla^2\beta + \text{Y} = 0 \\ -\frac{dp}{dz} + v\nabla^2\gamma + \text{Z} = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \text{ . . . . . . . . . . (1)}$$

In these equations, $x, y, z$ represent the rectangular coordinates of a point within the fluid; $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ <note>the Greek letters alpha, beta, and gamma</note> are the component velocities moving parallel to those axes; $p$ is the average of the three pressures measured across planes perpendicular to the three axes respectively; X, Y, and Z are the component forces acting on the fluid, calculated per unit of volume; $v$ is the <term>coefficient of viscosity</term> <note>a measure of a fluid's resistance to flow; essentially its thickness or "stickiness"</note>; and $\nabla^2$ represents the <term>Laplacian operation</term> <note>a mathematical tool used to describe how a quantity spreads or changes through space</note> $\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2}{dz^2}$.

In addition to these, we have the <term>equation of continuity</term> <note>a mathematical rule stating that mass is neither created nor destroyed as fluid flows</note>:
$$\frac{d\alpha}{dx} + \frac{d\beta}{dy} + \frac{d\gamma}{dz} = 0$$

Also, if P, Q, R, S, T, and U are the normal and <term>tangential stresses</term> <note>forces that act parallel to a surface, like friction, rather than pushing directly against it</note> calculated in the standard way across three planes perpendicular to the axes:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} \text{P} = -p + 2v\frac{d\alpha}{dx}, \quad \text{Q} = -p + 2v\frac{d\beta}{dy}, \quad \text{R} = -p + 2v\frac{d\gamma}{dz} \\ \text{S} = v\left(\frac{d\beta}{dz} + \frac{d\gamma}{dy}\right), \quad \text{T} = v\left(\frac{d\gamma}{dx} + \frac{d\alpha}{dz}\right), \quad \text{U} = v\left(\frac{d\alpha}{dy} + \frac{d\beta}{dx}\right) \end{aligned} \right\} \text{ . . . . . (2)}$$

Now, in an <term>elastic solid</term> <note>a material that returns to its original shape after being deformed</note>, if $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the displacements (the distance a point has moved), $m - \frac{1}{3}n$ is the <term>coefficient of dilatation</term> <note>a measure of how much the volume of the material expands or contracts</note>, and $n$ is the <term>coefficient of rigidity</term> <note>the material's resistance to changing its shape</note>; and if $\delta$ <note>the Greek letter delta</note> represents the change in volume ($\delta = \frac{d\alpha}{dx} + \frac{d\beta}{dy} + \frac{d\gamma}{dz}$), then the <term>equations of equilibrium</term> <note>equations describing a state where all forces are balanced and the object is at rest</note> are:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} m\frac{d\delta}{dx} + n\nabla^2\alpha + \text{X} = 0 \\ m\frac{d\delta}{dy} + n\nabla^2\beta + \text{Y} = 0 \\ m\frac{d\delta}{dz} + n\nabla^2\gamma + \text{Z} = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \text{ . . . . . . . . . . (3)*}$$

Also:

$$\text{P} = (m-n)\delta + 2n\frac{d\alpha}{dx}, \quad \text{Q} = (m-n)\delta + 2n\frac{d\beta}{dy}, \quad \text{R} = (m-n)\delta + 2n\frac{d\gamma}{dz} \text{ . . . (4)}$$

The values for S, T, and U take the same forms as seen in equation (2), but with $n$ written instead of $v$.

Therefore, if we define $-p$ as one-third of the sum of P, Q, and R ($-p = \frac{1}{3}(\text{P} + \text{Q} + \text{R})$), we find that $p = -(m - \frac{n}{3})\delta$. Consequently, equation (3) can be rewritten as:

->$\text{P} = -\frac{m-n}{m-\frac{n}{3}} p + 2n \frac{da}{dx}, \text{Q} = \text{etc., R} = \text{etc.}$<-

Now, if we assume the elastic solid is **incompressible** <note>meaning its volume cannot be reduced by pressure</note>, so that the value *m* is infinitely large compared to *n*, then it is clear that the equations of equilibrium for an incompressible elastic solid take exactly the same form as those for the flow of a viscous fluid—with *n* simply taking the place of *v*.

Thus, every problem involving the equilibrium of an incompressible elastic solid has a direct counterpart in a problem regarding the flow of an incompressible viscous fluid, provided the effects of inertia are ignored. The solution for one can be applied to the other by simply substituting "velocities" for "displacements" and the coefficient of "viscosity" for the coefficient of "rigidity."

### *2. A sphere under the influence of internal forces.*

Sir William <term>Thomson</term> <note>Sir William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, was a preeminent physicist who calculated the age of the Earth and studied its internal heat and rigidity</note> has solved the following problem:
To find the displacement of every point within an elastic sphere that is not subject to any surface pull <note>original: traction</note>, but is slightly deformed by a balanced system of forces acting throughout its interior.

If we substitute "velocity" for "displacement" and "viscous" for "elastic," we arrive at the corresponding problem for a viscous fluid; <note>original: "mutatis mutandis"</note> with the necessary changes made, the solution remains the same.

However, we cannot determine the tides of a viscous sphere simply by making the balancing force system equal to the tide-generating influence of the sun or moon. This is because we must assume the substance of the sphere possesses the power of gravitation.

Suppose that at any given time, the equation for the free surface of the Earth (which we may call the "viscous sphere" for brevity) is $r = a + \sum_2^\infty \sigma_i$, where $\sigma_i$ is a <term>surface harmonic</term> <note>a mathematical function used to describe shapes on a sphere, such as the bulges and depressions of tides</note>. In this case, the matter—whether positive (a bulge) or negative (a hollow)—filling the space represented by the sum of those harmonics exerts a gravitational pull on every point in the interior. This attraction, combined with the gravity of a perfectly uniform sphere of radius *a*, must be added to the tide-generating influence to determine the total force within the sphere. Additionally, we are dealing with a **spheroid** <note>a sphere slightly flattened at the poles, like the Earth</note> rather than a perfect sphere. However, if we mathematically "cut" a perfect sphere of radius *a* out of the spheroid (leaving out the tidal bulges $\sum \sigma_i$), then by choosing the right actions to apply to the surface, we can reduce the tidal problem to finding the flow within a perfect sphere under the influence of: (i) the external tide-generating force of the sun or moon, and (ii) the attraction of the

ever, this solution applies to a true sphere and to the positive and negative matter filling the space $\Sigma\sigma_i$, but (iii) is also subject to certain surface forces.

Since points (i) and (ii) together constitute a "bodily force" <note>a force, like gravity, that acts throughout the entire volume of an object</note>, the problem only differs from that of Sir William <term>Thomson</term> in the fact that there are forces acting specifically on the surface of the sphere.

Now, as we are only going to consider *small* deviations from a perfect sphere <note>original: sphericity</note>, these surface actions will be minor, and an *approximation* will be permissible.

It is clear that, strictly speaking, there is a tangential action\* <note>a "sideways" or shearing force acting along the surface</note> between the layer of matter $\Sigma\sigma_i$ and the core sphere. However, by far the larger part of the action is "normal" <note>acting perpendicular to the surface</note>, and is simply the weight (either positive or negative) of the matter which lies above or below any point on the surface of the core sphere.

Thus, in order to treat the Earth as a perfect sphere, the appropriate surface action is a normal pull <note>original: traction</note> equal to $-gw\Sigma\sigma_i$, where $g$ is gravity at the surface and $w$ is the density <note>original: mass per unit volume</note> of the matter making up the Earth.

In order to show what alteration this normal surface pull will make in Sir William <term>Thomson</term>’s solution, I must now give a short account of his method of attacking the problem.

He first shows that, where a "potential function" exists, the solution of the problem may be subdivided. The complete values of the displacements $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ consist of the sum of two parts which are found in different ways. 

The first part consists of *any* values of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ which satisfy the equations throughout the sphere, without considering the conditions at the surface. 

For the second part, the bodily force is treated as non-existent and is replaced by certain surface actions. These are calculated to counteract the surface actions that resulted from the first part of the solution. Thus, the first part satisfies the condition that there is a bodily force, and the second adds the condition that the total forces at the surface are zero. 

The first part of the solution is easily found. For the second part, Sir William <term>Thomson</term> discusses the case of an elastic sphere under the action of any surface pulls, but without any bodily force acting on it. In this problem, the component surface pulls parallel to the three axes are expanded in a series of "surface harmonics" <note>mathematical functions used to represent complex shapes or distributions on the surface of a sphere</note>. He shows that the harmonic terms of any "order" have an effect on the displacements that is independent of every other order. Thus, it is only necessary to consider the typical component surface pulls $\text{A}_i, \text{B}_i, \text{C}_i$ of the order $i$.

He proves that (for an incompressible elastic solid, where the resistance to compression $m$ is infinite) this single surface pull $\text{A}_i, \text{B}_i, \text{C}_i$ produces a displacement throughout the sphere given by:

$\alpha = \frac{1}{nai^{i-1}} \left\{ \frac{a^2 - r^2}{2(2i^2 + 1)} \frac{d\Psi_{i-1}}{dx} + \frac{1}{i-1} \left[ \frac{i+2}{(2i^2 + 1)(2i + 1)} r^{2i+1} \frac{d}{dx} (\Psi_{i-1} r^{-2i+1}) + \frac{1}{2i(2i + 1)} \frac{d\Phi_{i+1}}{dx} + \text{A}_i r^i \right] \right\} (5)\dagger$

Furthermore, we must include in the internal force both the external disturbing force and the gravitational attraction of the spheroid's matter upon itself.

Now, from the forms of equations (5) and (6), it is obvious that the tractions corresponding to the first part of the solution and the traction $-gw\Sigma\sigma_i$ produce entirely independent effects. Therefore, we only need to add the terms arising from the normal traction $-gw\Sigma\sigma_i$ to the complete solution of Sir W. <term>THOMSON</term>’s problem of the elastic sphere. Finally, we must transition from the elastic problem to the viscous one by substituting viscosity ($v$) for the shear modulus ($n$), and velocities for displacements.

I will now proceed to find the state of internal flow in the viscous sphere that results from a normal traction at every point of the sphere's surface, as given by the surface harmonic <note>a mathematical function used to describe patterns on the surface of a sphere</note> $S_i$.

In order to use formulas (5) and (6), it is first necessary to express the component tractions $\frac{x}{a} S_i, \frac{y}{a} S_i, \frac{z}{a} S_i$ as surface harmonics.

If $V_i$ is a solid harmonic, then:

$$\frac{d}{dx}(r^{-2i-1}V_i) = -(2i+1)r^{-(2i+3)}xV_i + r^{-(2i+1)}\frac{dV_i}{dx}$$

So that:

$$xV_i = \frac{1}{2i+1} \left\{ r^2 \frac{dV_i}{dx} - r^{2i+3} \frac{d}{dx}(r^{-2i-1}V_i) \right\}$$

Therefore:

$$\frac{x}{a} S_i = \frac{1}{2i+1} \left\{ \left[ r^{-i+1} \frac{d}{dx}(r^i S_i) \right] - \left[ r^{i+2} \frac{d}{dx}(r^{-i-1} S_i) \right] \right\}$$

The quantities within the brackets [ ] are independent of $r$ and are surface harmonics of orders $i-1$ and $i+1$ respectively. We now have $\frac{x}{a} S_i$ expressed as the sum of two surface harmonics $A_{i-1}, A_{i+1}$, where

We have now learned how to include the surface action within the potential calculation. If $W_i$ represents the potential of the external disturbing influence, then the *effective* potential per unit volume at a point within the sphere—now considered free of surface action and of mutual gravitation—is:
$W_i - \frac{2gw(i-1)}{2i+1} \left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^i \sigma_i = r^i T_i$ (let us assume).

The complete solution to our problem is then found by substituting $r^i T_i$ in place of $W_i$ in <term>Thomson</term>'s <note>Lord Kelvin's</note> solution (8).*

However, in order to apply this solution to the case of the Earth, it will be convenient to use polar coordinates. For this purpose, let $w r^i S_i$ represent $W_i$. Let $r$ be the radius vector; $\theta$ be the colatitude <note>the angle down from the North Pole, rather than up from the equator</note>; and $\phi$ be the longitude. Let $\rho, \varpi, \text{ and } \nu$ be the velocities in the radial direction, along the meridian, and perpendicular to the meridian, respectively. The expressions for $\rho, \varpi, \text{ and } \nu$ will be exactly the same as those for $\alpha, \beta, \text{ and } \gamma$ in equation (8), except that for $\frac{d}{dx}$ we must substitute $\frac{d}{dr}$; for $\frac{d}{dy}$, we must substitute $\frac{d}{r \sin \theta d\phi}$; and for $\frac{d}{dz}$, we must substitute $\frac{d}{r d\theta}$.

Then, after some mathematical simplifications, we have:

$$
\left.
\begin{aligned}
\rho &= \frac{i^2(i+2)a^2 - i(i^2-1)r^2}{2(i-1)[2(i+1)^2+1]v} r^{i-1} T_i \\
\varpi &= \frac{i(i+2)a^2 - (i-1)(i+3)r^2}{2(i-1)[2(i+1)^2+1]v} r^{i-1} \frac{dT_i}{d\theta} \\
\nu &= \frac{i(i+2)a^2 - (i-1)(i+3)r^2}{2(i-1)[2(i+1)^2+1]v} \frac{r^{i-1}}{\sin \theta} \frac{dT_i}{d\phi}
\end{aligned}
\right\} \dots \dots (10)\dagger
$$

where $T_i = w \left( S_i - 2g \frac{i-1}{2i+1} \frac{\sigma_i}{a^i} \right)$.

These equations for $\rho, \varpi, \text{ and } \nu$ provide us with the state of internal flow corresponding to the external disturbing potential $r^i S_i$, including the effects of the mutual gravitation of the matter that makes up the spheroid.

### *3. The shape of the free surface at any time.*

If $\rho'$ is the surface value of $\rho$ <note>$\rho$ represents the rate of displacement</note>, then
->$\rho' = \frac{i(2i+1)}{2(i-1)[2(i+1)^2+1]} \frac{a^{i+1}}{v} T_i$<-

Consequently, after a short interval of time $\delta t$, the equation for the bounding surface of the spheroid becomes $r = a + \sigma_i + \rho' \delta t$. During this same interval, $\sigma_i$ has become $\frac{d\sigma_i}{dt} \delta t$, which gives us:
->$\frac{d\sigma_i}{dt} = \rho' = \frac{i(2i+1)}{2(i-1)[2(i+1)^2+1]} \frac{wa^{i+1}}{v} S_i - \frac{i}{2(i+1)^2+1} \frac{gwa}{v} \sigma_i$<-
or
->$\frac{d\sigma_i}{dt} + \frac{i}{2(i+1)^2+1} \frac{gwa}{v} \sigma_i = \frac{i(2i+1)}{2(i-1)[2(i+1)^2+1]} \frac{wa^{i+1}}{v} S_i$ . . . . (11)<-

This differential equation shows the way in which the surface changes under the influence of the external potential $r^i S_i$.

If $S_i$ is not a function of time, and if $s_i$ is the value of $\sigma_i$ when $t=0$, then:
->$\sigma_i = \frac{2i+1}{2(i-1)} \frac{a^i S_i}{g} \left[ 1 - \exp \left( \frac{-gwait}{[2(i+1)^2+1]v} \right) \right] + s_i \exp \left( \frac{-gwait}{[2(i+1)^2+1]v} \right)$ . . (12)<note>original: I write "exp." for "$e$ to the power of."</note><-

When $t$ is infinite:
->$\sigma_i = \frac{2i+1}{2(i-1)} \frac{a^i S_i}{g}$ . . . . . . . . . (13)<-

At this point, the flow stops because the fluid has taken the shape it would have assumed if it were not viscous at all. This result, naturally, agrees with the equilibrium theory of tides <note>The "equilibrium theory" assumes the water or fluid responds instantly to gravity and centrifugal force, staying in perfect balance.</note>.

If $S_i$ is zero, the equation shows how the inequalities <term>inequalities</term> <note>original: "inequalities"; here meaning physical irregularities or deviations from a smooth sphere, like mountains or basins.</note> on the surface of a viscous globe would gradually subside under the influence of gravity alone. We can see that this change happens much more slowly if $i$ is large; that is to say, small-scale irregularities disappear much more slowly than wide-spread, large-scale ones. Might this solution provide some insight into the laws governing geological subsidence and upheaval? <note>Darwin is suggesting that the Earth's internal viscosity might explain why certain geological features persist for so long or change slowly over millions of years.</note>

Assume that the earth is rotating with an angular velocity $\omega$ <note>$\omega$ (omega) represents the speed of rotation.</note> about the $z$-axis, but at the moment we begin our observation, the axis of symmetry is tilted toward the $z$-axis at an angle $\alpha$ in the $xy$ plane. -> $r = a \left\{ 1 + \frac{5m}{4} \left( \frac{1}{3} - [\cos \alpha \cos \theta + \sin \alpha \sin \theta \cos \phi]^2 \right) \right\}$ <-

where $m$ is the ratio of centrifugal force at the equator to the force of gravity, and is therefore equal to $\frac{\omega^2 a}{g}$.

Then, by setting the value of $i=2$ in equation (12) and removing the sub-scripts for S, $s$, and $\sigma$, we find $s = \frac{5ma}{4} \left( \frac{1}{3} - [\quad]^2 \right)$.

We can imagine the earth to be at rest if we apply a "potential" <note>In physics, a potential is a mathematical way to describe forces like gravity or centrifugal force acting on a body.</note>:

-> $w r^2 \text{S} = \frac{1}{2} \omega^2 w r^2 \left( \frac{1}{3} - \cos^2 \theta \right)$ <-

so that

-> $\text{S} = \frac{1}{2} \omega^2 \left( \frac{1}{3} - \cos^2 \theta \right)$ <-

Using equation (12), we have:

-> $\sigma = \frac{5a^2 \text{S}}{2g} \left[ 1 - \exp \left( - \frac{2wg a t}{19v} \right) \right] + s \ \exp \left( - \frac{2wg a t}{19v} \right)$ <-

Then, by substituting the values for S and $s$, and letting $\kappa = \frac{2wg a}{19v}$ <note>$\kappa$ (kappa) here represents a constant related to the Earth's viscosity and gravity.</note>:

-> $\sigma = \frac{5ma}{4} \left\{ \left( \frac{1}{3} - \cos^2 \theta \right) [1 - \exp(-\kappa t)] + \left( \frac{1}{3} - [\cos \alpha \cos \theta + \sin \alpha \sin \theta \cos \phi]^2 \right) \exp(-\kappa t) \right\}$ <-

Now, calculating the trigonometric parts:

-> $[1 - \exp(-\kappa t)] \cos^2 \theta + \exp(-\kappa t) (\cos \alpha \cos \theta + \sin \alpha \sin \theta \cos \phi)^2$ <-
-> $= \cos^2 \theta [1 - \sin^2 \alpha \ \exp(-\kappa t)] + \sin^2 \alpha \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 \phi \ \exp(-\kappa t)$ <-
-> $+ 2 \sin \alpha \cos \alpha \sin \theta \cos \theta \cos \phi \ \exp(-\kappa t)$. <-

Therefore, the Cartesian equation <note>An equation using $x, y, z$ coordinates rather than polar coordinates ($r, \theta, \phi$).</note> for the spheroid at time $t$ is:

-> $\frac{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}{1 + \frac{5m}{6}} = a^2 - \frac{5m}{2} \{ z^2 (1 - \sin^2 \alpha \ \exp(-\kappa t)) + x^2 \sin^2 \alpha \ \exp(-\kappa t) + 2xz \sin \alpha \cos \alpha \ \exp(-\kappa t) \}$ <-

### 5. Bodily tides in a viscous earth.*

The only case of interest where the external potential $S_i$ is a function of time is when it is a <term>surface harmonic</term> <note>a mathematical function used to describe patterns on the surface of a sphere</note> of the second order and repeats periodically over time. This provides the solution to the tidal problem. Furthermore, since we are only interested in cases where the motion has reached a permanently periodic state, we can set aside the "exponential terms" <note>mathematical terms that describe temporary changes that eventually fade away</note> in the solution.

Let $S_2 = S \cos (vt + \eta)$. Following the notation used by <term>THOMSON</term> <note>Sir William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, a dominant figure in 19th-century physics</note>,† let $\frac{2g}{5a} = \mathfrak{g}$, and $\frac{19\upsilon}{5wa^2} = \mathfrak{r}$; and therefore $\frac{2gwa}{19\upsilon} = \frac{\mathfrak{g}}{\mathfrak{r}}$.

Then, by setting $i = 2$ in equation (11) and omitting the <term>suffix</term> <note>subscript</note> of $\sigma$ for brevity, we have:

->$$\frac{d\sigma}{dt} + \frac{\mathfrak{g}}{\mathfrak{r}} \sigma = \frac{a}{\mathfrak{r}} S \cos (vt + \eta) \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ (14)$$<-

It is evident that $\sigma$ must take the form $A \cos (vt + B)$, and therefore:

->$$A \{ -v\mathfrak{r} \sin (vt + B) + \mathfrak{g} \cos (vt + B) \} = aS \cos (vt + \eta)$$<-

# ON SPHEROIDS, AND ON THE OCEAN TIDES UPON A YIELDING NUCLEUS.

Or, if we set $\tan \epsilon = \frac{v \upsilon}{\mathfrak{g}}$,
<note>Here, $v$ represents frequency or speed, and $\upsilon$ (represented in the math as $v$) represents the coefficient of viscosity—how much the material resists flowing.</note>

->$\text{A} \mathfrak{g} \sec \epsilon \cos (v t + \text{B} + \epsilon) = a \text{S} \cos (v t + \eta)$,<-

From this, we find that $\text{A} = \frac{a}{\mathfrak{g}} \text{S} \cos \epsilon$, and $\text{B} = \eta - \epsilon$.
Therefore, the solution for equation (14) is:

->$\sigma = \frac{a}{\mathfrak{g}} \text{S} \cos \epsilon \cos (v t + \eta - \epsilon)$ . . . . . . . . (15)<-

Where $\tan \epsilon = \frac{v \upsilon}{\mathfrak{g}} = \frac{19 v \upsilon}{2 g a w}$.

If the globe were a perfect fluid, and if the equilibrium theory of tides <note>a theory assuming the ocean is always in a state of balance with the gravitational pull of the moon or sun</note> were true, then according to equation (13), we would have:

->$\sigma = \frac{5 a}{2 g} \cdot a \text{S} \cos (v t + \eta) = \frac{\text{S} a}{\mathfrak{g}} \cos (v t + \eta)$.<-

Thus, we can see that the tides of a viscous <note>thick or sticky</note> sphere, when compared to the equilibrium tides of a fluid sphere, follow the ratio of $\cos \epsilon$ to 1. Additionally, there is a time lag <note>original: "retardation in time"</note> of $\frac{\epsilon}{v}$.

A similar investigation applies to the general case where the gravitational influence <note>disturbing potential</note> is $w r^i \text{S}_i \cos (v t + \eta)$. The same solution will be found to hold, except that we now define $\tan \epsilon$ as $\frac{2(i+1)^2+1}{i} \cdot \frac{v \upsilon}{g a w}$, and in place of $\mathfrak{g}$ we use $\frac{2(i-1)g}{(2i+1)a}$.

### 6. Reduction of ocean tides according to the equilibrium theory.

Suppose now that there is a shallow ocean resting on this viscous core <note>nucleus</note>. Let us find how the movement of the core itself affects the ocean tides according to the equilibrium theory, while ignoring the gravity exerted by the water itself.

The gravitational potential at a point outside the core is:

->$g \frac{a^2}{r} + \frac{3}{5} g \left( \frac{a}{r} \right)^2 \sigma + r^2 \text{S} \cos (v t + \eta)$,<-

If we set this equal to a constant value, we find the shape that the ocean must take. Let $r = a + u$ be the equation for the surface of the ocean <note>where $a$ is the average radius and $u$ is the height of the tide</note>. By substituting this for $r$ in the potential formula, ignoring $u$ in the smaller terms, and setting the whole equation to a constant, we find:

->$-g u + \frac{3}{5} g \sigma + a^2 \text{S} \cos (v t + \eta) = 0$<-

or

->$u = \frac{3}{5} \sigma + \frac{a^2}{g} \text{S} \cos (v t + \eta)$.<-

# MR. DARWIN ON THE BODILY TIDES OF VISCOUS AND SEMI-ELASTIC

But the rise and fall of the tide relative to the nucleus <note>nucleus: the solid or semi-solid main body of the planet</note> is given by $u-\sigma$, and

$$u-\sigma = \frac{a^2 \text{S}}{g} \cos (vt+\eta) - \frac{2}{5} \sigma$$
$$= \frac{2}{5} \frac{a \text{S}}{g} [\cos (vt+\eta) - \cos \epsilon \cos (vt+\eta-\epsilon)]$$
$$= -\frac{2}{5} \frac{a \text{S}}{g} \sin \epsilon \sin (vt+\eta-\epsilon) \text{ . . . . . . . . . . (17)}$$

Now, if the nucleus had been rigid, the rise and fall would have been given by

$$\frac{2}{5} \frac{a \text{S}}{g} \cos (vt+\eta) = \text{H} \cos (vt+\eta) \text{ suppose.}$$

Therefore

$$u-\sigma = -\text{H} \sin \epsilon \sin (vt+\eta-\epsilon) \text{ . . . . . . . . . . (18)}$$

Consequently, the apparent tides on a yielding nucleus are equal to the tides on a rigid nucleus, but reduced in the ratio of $\sin \epsilon$ to $1$; and since $-\sin (vt+\eta-\epsilon)$ $= \cos (vt+\eta+\frac{\pi}{2}-\epsilon)$, they are delayed <note>original: "retarded"</note> by $\frac{1}{v} (\epsilon - \frac{\pi}{2})$. Because $\epsilon$ is necessarily less than $\frac{\pi}{2}$, this is equivalent to an advancement <note>original: "acceleration"</note> of the time of high water equal to $\frac{1}{v} (\frac{\pi}{2} - \epsilon)$.

It is, however, worth noting that this is only an advancement of the phase relative to the nucleus, and there is an absolute delay <note>original: "retardation"</note> of phase equal to the inverse tangent of $\frac{3 \sin \epsilon \cos \epsilon}{3 + 2 \cos^2 \epsilon}$.

### *7. Semidiurnal and fortnightly tides.*

Let the $z$-axis be the earth's axis of rotation, and let the $xz$ plane be fixed within the earth; let $c$ be the moon's distance, and $m$ its mass.

Suppose the moon moves in the plane of the equator with an angular velocity <note>angular velocity: the rate at which an object rotates or orbits</note> of $\omega$ relative to the earth, and let the moon's terrestrial longitude, measured from the $xz$ plane at time $t$, be $\omega t$.

Then, at time $t$, the gravitational potential of the tide-generating force, calculated per unit of volume of the earth's mass, is:

$$-\frac{3}{2} \frac{m}{c^3} w r^2 \left\{ \frac{1}{3} - \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 (\phi - \omega t) \right\}$$

which is equal to:

$$\frac{3}{4} \frac{m}{c^3} w r^2 (\frac{1}{3} - \cos^2 \theta) + \frac{3}{4} \frac{m}{c^3} w r^2 \{ \sin^2 \theta \cos 2\phi \cos 2\omega t + \sin^2 \theta \sin 2\phi \sin 2\omega t \}.$$

The first term of this expression does not change over time. Therefore, it produces an effect on the viscous earth that will have faded away once the movement becomes steady; its only lasting effect is to slightly increase the ellipticity <term>ellipticity: the degree to which a sphere is flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator</term> of the earth's surface.

The two latter terms produce two tides. In one of these (based on the notation used previously):

->$\text{S cos } (vt + \eta) = \frac{3}{4} \frac{m}{c^3} \sin^2 \theta \cos 2\phi \cos 2\omega t,$<-

and in the second:

->$\text{S cos } (vt + \eta) = - \frac{3}{4} \frac{m}{c^3} \sin^2 \theta \sin 2\phi \cos (2\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}).$<-

Now $\epsilon$ <note>$\epsilon$: a variable representing the phase lag caused by the planet's internal friction</note>, which depends on the frequency of the potential that generates the tide, will clearly be the same for both of these tides. Therefore, each will be equal to the corresponding tides of a fluid planet <note>original: "spheroid"</note>, reduced by the same amount and subject to the same delay <note>original: "retardation"</note>. They may therefore be recombined <note>original: "recompounded"</note> into a single tide. Additionally, the height of the tide is smaller than the corresponding equilibrium tide of a fluid planet in the ratio of $\cos \epsilon$ to one.

Similarly, according to section (6), the height of the ocean tide on the deformable core is determined by the corresponding tide on a rigid core multiplied by $\sin \epsilon$, and there is an advancement <note>original: "acceleration"</note> of the relative high tide equal to $\frac{\pi}{4\omega} - \frac{\epsilon}{2\omega}$.

The case of the fortnightly tide is somewhat simpler.

If $\Omega$ represents the moon's orbital angular velocity, and $I$ represents the inclination of the orbital plane to the Earth's equator, then the portion of the tide-generating potential on which the fortnightly tide depends is:

->$\frac{9}{8} \frac{m}{c^3} w r^2 \sin^2 \text{I } (\frac{1}{3} - \cos^2 \theta) \cos 2\Omega t$<-

and we see at once from sections (5) and (6) that $\tan \epsilon = \frac{19 v \Omega}{\mathfrak{g} a w}$. The tide within the planet's body is the tide of a fluid planet multiplied by $\cos \epsilon$; the reduction of the ocean tide is given by $\sin \epsilon$; and there is a time-advancement <note>original: "acceleration"</note> of the relative high tide of $\frac{\pi}{4\Omega} - \frac{\epsilon}{2\Omega}$ or $\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\epsilon}{\pi}$ of a week.

### 8. *The tides of an elastico-viscous planet-shaped body.*

The term <term>elastico-viscous</term> <note>elastico-viscous: a property of materials that act like a springy solid in the short term but flow like a thick liquid over the long term</note> is used to indicate that the stresses required to maintain a body in a specific distorted shape decrease the longer the body is held in that position; this is undoubtedly the case with many solids. In this particular case, it is assumed that the stresses decrease in a geometric progression <note>geometric progression: here, this refers to exponential decay, where the stress drops by a consistent percentage over each interval of time</note> as time increases in an arithmetic progression <note>arithmetic progression: a sequence that increases by a steady amount, like 1, 2, 3...</note>. If, for example, a cube of the substance is distorted by a shearing stress <note>shearing stress: a force that causes layers of a material to slide past each other</note> $T$ and held in that position, then after a time $t$, the shearing stress is $\text{T } \exp(-\frac{t}{\tau})$.

# SPHEROIDS, AND THE OCEAN TIDES UPON A YIELDING NUCLEUS <note>nucleus: here, the solid or semi-solid central mass of a planet</note>

1879. D

The time **t** measures the rate at which stress diminishes; Professor Maxwell calls this the "modulus of the time of relaxation of rigidity." It is the time required for the initial stress to be reduced to $e^{-1}$ or approximately .3679 of its original value. I do not believe, however, that any real solid follows this law exactly. However, I think it is often helpful in physics to mathematically examine an ideal case that closely resembles reality, especially when we cannot determine the exact nature of that reality.

Mr. J. G. Butcher has derived the equations of motion for such an ideal substance. He based this on the idea that the elasticity of molecular groups is constantly breaking down, after which the groups rearrange themselves.* These considerations lead him to the following results for the stresses across rectangular planes at any point in the interior (using the notation from Section 1):

-> $P = (m-n)\delta + 2n(\frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt})^{-1}(\frac{d\alpha}{dx} + \frac{1}{3\mathfrak{t}}\alpha)$, $S = n(\frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt})^{-1}(\frac{d\beta}{dz} + \frac{d\gamma}{dy})$ <-

and similar expressions for Q, R, T, U; where $m - \frac{n}{3}$ is the coefficient of dilatation <note>dilatation: the change in volume per unit volume; expansion</note>, $n$ is the coefficient of rigidity, $\delta$ is the dilatation, and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the components of flow.

These expressions clearly align with the definition of elastic-viscosity mentioned above, since $\frac{dS}{dt} + \frac{S}{\mathfrak{t}} = n(\frac{d\beta}{dz} + \frac{d\gamma}{dy})$.

If the expressions for P, S, etc., are substituted into the equilibrium equations of the elementary parallelopiped <note>parallelopiped: a six-sided mathematical solid where each face is a parallelogram; here used to describe a small unit of volume</note>, we find—by using the equation of continuity $\frac{d\delta}{dt} = \frac{d\alpha}{dx} + \frac{d\beta}{dy} + \frac{d\gamma}{dz}$—that when inertia is ignored:

-> $(\frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt})^{-1} \{ [ (m - \frac{1}{3}n)\frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + m\frac{d}{dt} ] \frac{d\delta}{dx} + n\nabla^2\alpha \} + X = 0$ <-

and two similar equations.

Using the same reasoning found in Section 1, we can set $\delta = \frac{-p}{m - \frac{1}{3}n}$, and the equations become:

-> $-(\frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt})^{-1} \{ [ \frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{m}{m - \frac{1}{3}n}\frac{d}{dt} ] \frac{dp}{dx} - n\nabla^2\alpha \} + X = 0$. <-

Assuming the substance is incompressible (meaning that $m$ is infinitely large compared to $n$, and therefore the ratio $m \div (m - \frac{1}{3}n)$ is equal to one), the equations become:

-> $-\frac{dp}{dx} + n(\frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt})^{-1} \nabla^2\alpha + X = 0$ <-

and two similar equations.

# MR. DARWIN ON THE BODILY TIDES OF VISCOUS AND SEMI-ELASTIC SPHEROIDS <note>original title: "On the Bodily Tides of Viscous and Semi-Elastic Spheroids, and on the Ocean Tides upon a Yielding Nucleus"</note>

Now these equations have exactly the same form as those for the motion of a viscous fluid, except that the coefficient of viscosity $\upsilon$ is replaced by $n \left( \frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt} \right)^{-1}$. We may, therefore, immediately proceed to the differential equation (11), which describes the shape of the surface of the spheroid at any given time.

By substituting $\frac{1}{n} \left( \frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt} \right)$ for $\frac{1}{\upsilon}$ in equation (11), we obtain:

->$\left[ 1 + \frac{i}{2(i+1)^2+1} \frac{gw a}{n} \right] \frac{d\sigma_i}{dt} + \frac{i}{2(i+1)^2+1} \frac{gw a}{n \mathfrak{t}} \sigma_i = \frac{i(2i+1)}{2(i-1)[2(i+1)^2+1]} \frac{w a^{i+1}}{n} \left( \frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} + \frac{d}{dt} \right) S_i$.<-

This equation can be solved in the same manner as equation (11) was solved; however, I will limit myself to the specific case of the tidal problem, where $i=2$ and $S_2 = S \cos (\upsilon t + \eta)$. In this particular case, the equation becomes:

->$\left( 1 + \frac{2gw a}{19n} \right) \frac{d\sigma}{dt} + \frac{2gw a}{19n \mathfrak{t}} \sigma = \frac{5w a^3}{19n} \left[ \frac{1}{\mathfrak{t}} \cos (\upsilon t + \eta) - \upsilon \sin (\upsilon t + \eta) \right] S$.<-

If we set $\frac{19n}{2gw a} + 1 = \frac{1}{k}$, $\tan \psi = \upsilon \mathfrak{t}$, and $\mathfrak{g} = \frac{2g}{5a}$, this can be rewritten as:

->$\frac{d\sigma}{dt} + \frac{k}{\mathfrak{t}} \sigma = \frac{\upsilon a k}{\mathfrak{g} \sin \psi} S \cos (\upsilon t + \eta + \psi)$.<-

In the solution relevant to the tidal problem, we can ignore the exponential term <note>The exponential term represents a transient state that fades away over time, leaving only the steady-state tide.</note> and assume that $\sigma = A \cos (\upsilon t + B)$. Then, if we let $\tan \chi = \frac{\upsilon \mathfrak{t}}{k}$:

->$\frac{d\sigma}{dt} + \frac{k}{\mathfrak{t}} \sigma = \frac{A \upsilon}{\sin \chi} \cos (\upsilon t + B + \chi)$.<-

From this, it follows that $B = \eta + \psi - \chi$, and:

->$A = \frac{a}{\mathfrak{g}} k \frac{\sin \chi}{\sin \psi} = \frac{a}{\mathfrak{g}} \frac{\cos \chi}{\cos \psi}$,<-

so that:

->$\sigma = \frac{a S}{\mathfrak{g}} \frac{\cos \chi}{\cos \psi} \cos (\upsilon t + \eta + \psi - \chi)$.<-

Therefore, the bodily tide of the elastico-viscous <term>elastico-viscous: a material that acts like a solid under short-term stress but flows like a liquid over long periods</term> spheroid is equal to the equilibrium tide <term>equilibrium tide: the theoretical tide height if the earth were entirely covered by fluid and responded instantly to gravity</term> of a fluid spheroid multiplied by $\frac{\cos \chi}{\cos \psi}$, and the time of high tide is delayed by $(\chi - \psi) / \upsilon$.

The formula for $\tan \chi$ can be expressed in a more convenient form; since $\tan \psi = \upsilon \mathfrak{t}$, we have $\tan \chi = \tan \psi + \frac{19n \upsilon \mathfrak{t}}{2gw a}$.

<summary>George Darwin adapts fluid motion equations to describe how a planet made of "elastico-viscous" material responds to tidal forces. He demonstrates that these tides are smaller than those of a pure fluid and experience a specific time delay, or "lag."</summary>

# SPHEROIDS, AND ON THE OCEAN TIDES UPON A YIELDING NUCLEUS.

But $nt$ is the coefficient of viscosity, and in treating the tides of the purely viscous spheroid, we set $\tan \epsilon = \frac{19v}{2gwa} \times$ the coefficient of viscosity. Therefore, adopting the same notation here, we have $\tan \chi = \tan \psi + \tan \epsilon$.

If the modulus of relaxation $\mathfrak{t}$ <note>The "modulus of relaxation" is a measure of the time it takes for a material to lose its internal stress after being deformed.</note> is zero, while the coefficient of rigidity $n$ becomes infinite but $nt$ remains finite, the substance is purely viscous. In this case, we have $\psi = 0$ and $\chi = \epsilon$, so that the solution reduces to the case already considered. If $\mathfrak{t}$ is infinite, the substance is purely elastic, and we have $\psi = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\chi = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Since $\frac{\cos \chi}{\cos \psi} = k \frac{\sin \chi}{\sin \psi}$, it follows that:

->$\sigma = \frac{ak}{\mathfrak{g}} S \cos (vt + \eta)$.<-

But according to <term>THOMSON's</term> <note>Sir William Thomson, later known as Lord Kelvin, a pioneer in thermodynamics and geophysics.</note> notation* $\frac{19n}{2gwa} = \frac{\mathfrak{r}}{\mathfrak{g}}$, so that $\sigma = \frac{a}{\mathfrak{r} + \mathfrak{g}} S \cos (vt + \eta)$. This is the solution to <term>THOMSON's</term> problem regarding a purely elastic spheroid.

The present solution therefore encompasses both the case he considered and that of the viscous spheroid.

### 9. *Ocean tides on an elastico-viscous nucleus.*

If $r = a + u$ is the equation for the ocean spheroid, we find, as shown in section (6), that the height of the tide relative to the nucleus is given by:

->$u - \sigma = \frac{a^2}{g} S \cos (vt + \eta) - \frac{2}{5} \sigma$,<-

By substituting the current value of $\sigma$:

->$u - \sigma = \frac{2}{5} \frac{a}{\mathfrak{g}} S \left[ \cos (vt + \eta) - \frac{\cos \chi}{\cos \psi} \cos (vt + \eta + \psi - \chi) \right]$<-
->$= - \frac{2}{5} \frac{a}{\mathfrak{g}} S \frac{\sin (\chi - \psi)}{\cos \psi} \sin (vt + \eta - \chi)$.<-

If the nucleus had been rigid, the rise and fall would have been given by $\text{H} \cos (vt + \eta)$, where $\text{H} = \frac{2}{5} \frac{a}{\mathfrak{g}} S$. Therefore, on the yielding nucleus, it is given by:

<margin>* *Natural Philosophy*, § 840. <note>Refers to the classic textbook *Treatise on Natural Philosophy* by Thomson and Tait.</note></margin>

->$u - \sigma = - \text{H} \frac{\sin (\chi - \psi)}{\cos \psi} \sin (vt + \eta - \chi)$<-
->$= - \text{H} \cos \chi (\tan \chi - \tan \psi) \sin (vt + \eta - \chi)$<-
->$= - \text{H} \cos \chi \tan \epsilon \sin (vt + \eta - \chi)$.<-

He then uses these equations to calculate how much an ocean tide is reduced when it rests on a core that yields to tidal forces.</summary>

### 10. *The influence of inertia.*

In establishing these results, inertia has been neglected; I will now show that this neglect does not materially invalidate my results.<margin>\* In a future paper (presented on December 19, 1878), I will provide an approximate solution to the problem that includes the effects of inertia.</margin>

Suppose the spheroid is forced to vibrate as it would if it were a perfect fluid and if the equilibrium theory of tides were true. Then the effective forces—which, according to <term>D'ALEMBERT's principle</term>, are the equivalent of inertia—are found by multiplying the acceleration of each particle by its mass.

Inertia may then be safely neglected if the effective force on the particle with the greatest vibration amplitude is small compared to the tide-generating force acting upon it. In the case of a viscous spheroid, inertia will have considerably less effect than it would in the supposed forced oscillation.

Now, suppose we have a tide-generating potential of $wr^2 S \cos (vt + \eta)$. According to the equilibrium theory of tides, the shape of the surface is given by:

->$\sigma = \frac{5a^2}{2g} S \cos (vt + \eta);$<-

<summary>Darwin presents tidal reduction and acceleration data for a spheroid with the rigidity of iron and begins an argument justifying the neglect of inertia in his calculations. He explains that for a viscous spheroid, the forces of inertia are negligible compared to tide-generating forces.</summary>
<keywords>iron rigidity, lunar semidiurnal tide, fortnightly tide, modulus of relaxation, viscosity, inertia, D'Alembert's principle, tide-generating potential</keywords>

<meta>This page continues George Darwin's analysis of inertia's role in tidal theory, moving into a discussion of tidal yielding and Sir William Thomson's observations on the earth's rigidity.</meta>

<header>MR. DARWIN ON THE BODILY TIDES OF VISCOUS AND SEMI-ELASTIC</header>

and this function provides the proposed constrained oscillation. It is clear that the particles at the surface have the widest amplitude of oscillation. The effective force on a unit element at the surface is

->$-w \frac{d^2 \sigma}{d t^2} = \frac{5 a^2}{2 g} w v^2 S \cos (v t + \eta).$<-

But the normal disturbing force at the surface is $2 w a S \cos (v t + \eta)$. Therefore, inertia may be neglected if $\frac{5 a^2}{2 g} w v^2$ is small compared with $2 w a$, or if $\frac{5 a}{4 g} v^2$ is a small fraction. The tide with the shortest period we must address is the one where $v = 2 \omega$, so we must consider the magnitude of the fraction $4 \times \frac{5 a \omega^2}{4 g}$. If $\omega$ were the earth's true angular velocity, rather than its angular velocity relative to the moon, then $\frac{5 a \omega^2}{4 g}$ would be the ellipticity of its surface if it were homogeneous. This ellipticity is, as is well known, $\frac{1}{232}$. Hence the fraction, which serves as the criterion for the negligibility of inertia, is about $\frac{1}{58}$.

If, then, we consider that this perspective certainly exaggerates the influence of inertia, it is clear that neglecting inertia does not materially invalidate the results provided above.

### II.

### A TIDAL YIELDING OF THE EARTH'S MASS, AND THE CANAL-THEORY OF TIDES.

In the first part of this paper, the equilibrium theory was used to determine the reduction in tidal height and the shift in phase caused by bodily tides within the earth.

Sir W. Thomson remarks, regarding a supposed elastic yielding of the earth's body: "Imperfect as the comparisons between theory and observation regarding the actual height of the tides have been so far, it is almost impossible to believe that the height is in reality only two-fifths of what it would be if—as has been universally assumed in tidal theories—the earth were perfectly rigid. It seems, therefore, nearly certain, with no other evidence than that provided by the tides, that the tidal effective rigidity of the earth must be greater than that of glass."<margin>\* 'Nat. Phil.', § 843.</margin>

The equilibrium theory is quite flawed in its explanation of the semidiurnal tide, but Sir W. Thomson is of the opinion that it must provide approximately correct results for tides with long periods. It is therefore on the observed amount of the fortnightly tide that he places reliance in drawing the above conclusion. Under these

### 11. *Semidiurnal tide in an equatorial canal on a yielding nucleus.*

I shall only consider the simple case of the moon moving uniformly in the equator, and raising tide waves in a narrow shallow equatorial canal of depth $h$.

The potential of the tide-generating force, as far as concerns the present inquiry, is, with the old notation, $(\frac{r}{a})^2 \frac{\tau}{2} \sin^2 \theta \cos 2(\phi - \omega t)$, where $\tau = \frac{3}{2} \frac{ma^2}{c^3}$. This force will raise a bodily tide in the earth, whether it be elastic, plastic, or viscous. Suppose, then, that the greatest range of the bodily tide at the equator is $2\text{E}$, and that it is retarded after the passage of the moon over the meridian by an angle $\frac{\epsilon}{2}$. Then the equation to the bounding surface of the solid earth, at the time $t$, is $r = a + \text{E} \sin^2 \theta \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon]$; or with former notation $\sigma = \text{E} \sin^2 \theta \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon]$.

The whole potential $\text{V}$, at a point outside the nucleus, is the sum of the potential of the earth’s attraction, and of the potential of the tide-generating force. Therefore

->$\text{V} = g \frac{a^2}{r} + \frac{3}{5} g (\frac{r}{a})^2 \text{E} \sin^2 \theta \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon] + \frac{\tau}{2} (\frac{r}{a})^2 \sin^2 \theta \cos 2(\phi - \omega t)$<-
->$= g \frac{a^2}{r} + \{ \text{F} \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon] + \text{G} \sin [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon] \} (\frac{r}{a})^2 \sin^2 \theta$<-

where $\text{F} = \frac{3}{5} g \text{E} + \frac{\tau}{2} \cos \epsilon$, $\text{G} = \frac{\tau}{2} \sin \epsilon$.

Sir <term>George Airy</term> shows, in his article on “Tides and Waves” in the ‘Encyclopædia Metropolitana,’ that the motion of the tide-wave in a canal running round the earth is the same as though the canal were straight, and the earth at rest, while the disturbing body rotates round it. This simplification will be applicable here also.

As before stated, the canal is supposed to be equatorial, and of depth $h$.

After the canal has been developed, take the origin of rectangular coordinates in the undisturbed surface of the water, and measure $x$ along the canal in the direction of the moon’s motion, and $y$ vertically downwards.

We have now to transform the potential $\text{V}$, and the equation to the surface of the solid earth, so as to make them applicable to the supposed development. If $v$ be the velocity of the tide-wave, then $\omega a = v$; also the wave length is half the circumference of the earth’s equator, or $\pi a$; and let $m = \frac{2}{a}$. Then we have the following transformations:—

As the canal is shallow, the motion may be treated in the same way that Professor <term>STOKES</term> has treated long waves in a shallow canal where the bottom is stationary. In this method, it appears that the water particles, which are in a vertical column at any time, remain so throughout the entire motion.

->$$bhk \left\{ 1 + \frac{d\xi}{dx} - \frac{\text{E}}{h} \cos [m(x' - vt) + \epsilon] - \frac{\eta}{h} \right\}.$$<-

But this same slice, in its undisturbed condition, had a volume $bhk$. Therefore, the <term>equation of continuity</term> is:

->$$\eta = h \frac{d\xi}{dx} - \text{E} \cos [m(x' - vt) + \epsilon].$$<-

Now the <term>hydrodynamical equation of motion</term> is approximately:

->$$\frac{dp}{dx'} = \frac{dV}{dx'} - \frac{d^2\xi}{dt^2}$$<-

The difference in pressure on the two sides of the slice $PQqp$ at any depth is $\text{N}n \times \frac{dp}{dx'}$; this depends only on the difference of the depressions of the wave surface below the $x$-axis on the two sides of the slice, namely at $\text{P}$ and $p$. Thus, $\frac{dp}{dx'} = -g \frac{d\eta}{dx'}$.

By substituting for $\eta$ from the equation of continuity and observing that $\frac{d^2\xi}{dxdx'}$ is very nearly the same as $\frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2}$, we obtain the <term>equation of wave motion</term>:

->$$gh \frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2} + mg \text{ E} \sin [m(x' - vt) + \epsilon] = - \frac{dV}{dx'} + \frac{d^2\xi}{dt^2}$$<-

However,

->$$\frac{dV}{dx'} = -m \text{ F} \sin [m(x' - vt) + \epsilon] + m \text{ G} \cos [m(x' - vt) + \epsilon].$$<-

Thus,

->$$\frac{d^2\xi}{dt^2} = gh \frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2} + m \{ \text{G} \cos [m(x' - vt) + \epsilon] - (\text{F} - \text{E}g) \sin [m(x' - vt) + \epsilon] \}.$$<-

When finding the <term>integral</term> of this equation, we can omit the terms that are independent of G, F, and E, because they only represent <term>free waves</term>, which we may assume do not exist.

The approximation will also be sufficiently accurate if $x$ is substituted for $x'$ on the right-hand side.

Assume, then, that:

->$$\xi = \text{A} \cos [m(x - vt) + \epsilon] + \text{B} \sin [m(x - vt) + \epsilon].$$<-

By substituting this into the equation of motion, we find:

->$$-m^2(v^2 - gh) \{ \text{A} \cos + \text{B} \sin \} = m \{ \text{G} \cos - (\text{F} - \text{E}g) \sin \}.$$<-

In the case of seas like those existing on the earth, the <term>tide wave</term> travels faster than the <term>free wave</term>, so that $a^2\omega^2$ is greater than $gh$; therefore, the denominators of A and B are positive.

We then have—

->$\xi = \frac{a}{2(a^2\omega^2 - gh)} \left\{ \left( \frac{\tau}{2} \cos \epsilon - \frac{2}{5}g\text{E} \right) \sin - \frac{\tau}{2} \sin \epsilon \cos \right\}$<-

But the current objective is to find the motion of the <term>wave surface</term> relative to the bottom of the canal, as this will provide the tide relative to the dry land. Now, the height of the wave relative to the bottom is

->$\text{PQ} = h - \text{E} \cos [m(x - vt) + \epsilon] - \eta$<-
->$= h - h \frac{d\xi}{dx}$<-

And

->$\frac{d\xi}{dx} = \frac{1}{a^2\omega^2 - gh} \left\{ \left( \frac{\tau}{2} \cos \epsilon - \frac{2}{5}g\text{E} \right) \cos + \frac{\tau}{2} \sin \epsilon \sin \right\}$<-

Hence, returning to the sphere and substituting $a$ for $a+h$, we obtain the following equation for the relative spheroid, of which the wave surface in the <term>equatorial canal</term> forms a part—

->$r = a - \frac{h \sin^2 \theta}{a^2\omega^2 - gh} \left\{ \frac{\tau}{2} \cos 2(\phi - \omega t) - \frac{2}{5}g\text{E} \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon] \right\}$<-

However, according to the <term>equilibrium theory</term>, if V has the same form as above, namely—

->$g \frac{a^2}{r} + \frac{3}{5}g \left( \frac{r}{a} \right)^2 \text{E} \sin^2 \theta \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon] + \frac{\tau}{2} \left( \frac{r}{a} \right)^2 \sin^2 \theta \cos 2(\phi - \omega t)$<-

and if $r = a + u$ is the equation for the <term>tidal spheroid</term>, we have, as in Part I.,

->$u = \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{g} \left\{ \frac{\tau}{2} \cos 2(\phi - \omega t) + \frac{3}{5}g\text{E} \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon] \right\}$<-

and the equation for the relative tidal spheroid is

->$r = a + u - \sigma$<-
->$= a + \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{g} \left\{ \frac{\tau}{2} \cos 2(\phi - \omega t) - \frac{2}{5}g\text{E} \cos [2(\phi - \omega t) + \epsilon] \right\}$<-

Now, in either the case of the <term>dynamical theory</term> or of the <term>equilibrium theory</term>, if E is set equal to zero, we obtain the equations for the tidal spheroid on a <term>rigid nucleus</term>. A comparison of the above equations shows immediately that both the <term>reduction of tide</term> and the <term>acceleration of phase</term> are the same in one theory as they are in the other. But where the

### III.
### SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS.

In section 1, an analogy is shown between problems regarding the state of strain of incompressible elastic solids and the flow of incompressible viscous fluids when inertia is neglected; this allows the solutions of one class of problems to be applied to the other. Sir W. <term>THOMSON</term>'s problem concerning the bodily tides of an elastic sphere is then adapted to provide the bodily tides of a viscous spheroid. This adaptation is made somewhat complex by the necessity of introducing the effects of the mutual gravitation of the parts of the spheroid.

The solution is only applicable where the disturbing potential can be expanded as a series of solid harmonics, and it appears that each harmonic term in the potential then acts as if all the others did not exist; consequently, it is only necessary to consider a typical term in the potential.

In section 3, an equation is found that gives the form of the free surface of the spheroid at any time, under the action of any disturbing potential that satisfies the condition of expansibility. By setting the disturbing potential to zero, the law is found which governs the subsidence of inequalities on the surface of the spheroid under the influence of mutual gravitation alone. If the form of the surface is expressed as a series of surface harmonics, it appears that any harmonic diminishes in geometrical progression as the time increases in arithmetical progression, and harmonics of higher orders subside much more slowly than those of lower orders. Common sense, indeed, would suggest that widespread inequalities must subside much more quickly than "wrinkles," but only analysis could provide the law connecting the speed of the subsidence with the magnitude of the inequality.*

---

<margin>*</margin> On this point, Lord <term>RAYLEIGH</term> remarks that if we consider the problem in two dimensions and imagine a number of parallel ridges where the distance between them is $\lambda$, then—with inertia being neglected—the elements on which the time of subsidence depends are $gw$ (force per unit mass due to weight), $v$ (the coefficient of viscosity), and $\lambda$. Thus, the time T must take the form:
->T = $(gw)^x v^y \lambda^z$.<-
The dimensions of $gw$, $v$, and $\lambda$ are respectively ML$^{-2}$T$^{-2}$, ML$^{-1}$T$^{-1}$, and L; hence:
->$x + y = 0$<-
->$-2x - y + z = 0$<-
->$-2x - y = 1$,<-
->And $x = -1$, $y = 1$, $z = -1$, so that T varies as $\frac{v}{gw\lambda}$.<-
If we apply this to a sphere, then when $i$ (the order of harmonics) is great, $\lambda$ is comparable to $\frac{a}{i}$;
so that T varies as $\frac{vi}{gwa}$.

MR. DARWIN ON THE BODILY TIDES OF VISCOUS AND SEMI-ELASTIC

I hope at some future time to try whether it will not be possible to shed some light on the formation of parallel mountain chains and the direction of faults by means of this equation. Probably the best way of doing this will be to transform the surface harmonics, which occur here, into BESSEL'S functions.

In section 4, the rate is considered at which a spheroid would adjust itself to a new form of equilibrium when its axis of rotation has separated from its axis of figure; the law is established which was assumed in a previous paper.*

In section 5, I pass to the case where the disturbing potential is a solid harmonic of the second degree, multiplied by a simple time harmonic. This is the case to be considered for the problem of a tidally distorted spheroid. A remarkably simple law is found connecting the viscosity, the height of the tide, and the amount of tidal lag; it is shown that if $v$ is the speed of the tide, and if $\tan \epsilon$ varies according to both the coefficient of viscosity and $v$, then the height of the bodily tide is equal to that of the equilibrium tide of a perfectly fluid spheroid multiplied by $\cos \epsilon$, and the tide lags by a time equal to $\frac{\epsilon}{v}$.

It is then shown (section 6) that in the equilibrium theory, the *ocean* tides on the yielding nucleus will be equal in height to the ocean tides on a rigid nucleus multiplied by $\sin \epsilon$, and that there will be an acceleration of the time of high water equal to $\frac{\pi}{2v} - \frac{\epsilon}{v}$.

The tables in section 7 give the results of the application of the preceding theories to the lunar semidiurnal and fortnightly tides for various degrees of viscosity. A comparison of the numbers in the first columns with the viscosity of pitch at near the freezing temperature (namely, about $1\cdot3 \times 10^8$, as found by me), when it is hard, apparently solid, and brittle, shows how enormously stiff the earth must be to resist the tidally deforming influence of the moon. For unless the viscosity were very much larger than that of pitch, the viscous sphere would behave essentially like a perfect fluid, and the ocean tides would be quite insignificant. It follows, therefore, that no very considerable portion of the interior of the earth can even remotely approach the fluid state.

This does not, however, seem to be conclusive against the existence of bodily tides in the earth of the kind here considered; for although (as remarked by Sir W. <term>THOMSON</term>) a very great hydrostatic pressure probably has a tendency to impart rigidity to a substance, yet the very high temperature which must exist in the earth at a small depth would tend to induce a sort of viscosity—at least if we judge by the behavior of materials at the earth's surface.

In section 8, the theory of the tides of an imperfectly elastic spheroid is developed. The kind of imperfection of elasticity considered is where the forces required to maintain the body in any strained configuration diminish in geometrical progression as the time increases in arithmetical progression. There can be no doubt that all bodies *do* possess an imperfection in their elasticity of this general nature, but the exact law

# SPHEROIDS, AND ON THE OCEAN TIDES UPON A YIELDING NUCLEUS.

The assumption made here has not, as far as I am aware, any experimental justification; its adoption was due more to mathematical necessity than to any other reason.

It would, of course, have been much more interesting if it had been possible to represent the mechanical properties of solid matter more exactly. One of the most important of these is that form of resistance to relative displacement to which the term "plasticity" has been specifically assigned. This form of resistance is such that there is a change in the law of resistance to the relative motion of the parts once the forces tending to cause flow have reached a certain definite intensity. This idea was established, I believe, by Messrs. <term>Tresca</term> and <term>St. Vénant</term> through a long course of experiments on the punching and squeezing of metals;<note>"On the Flow of Solid Bodies," Memoirs of Foreign Scientists, volumes 18 and 20, p. 75 and p. 137. See also 'Comptes Rendus,' volumes 66, 68, and Liouville's Journal, 2nd series, xiii., p. 379, and xvi., p. 308, for papers on this subject.</note> and they speak of a solid being reduced to a state of fluidity by stresses of a given magnitude. This theory introduces a discontinuity, since it must be determined which parts of the body are reduced to a state of fluidity and which are not. But apart from this difficulty, there is another which is almost insurmountable: the fact that the differential equations of flow are non-linear.

The hope of introducing this form of resistance must be abandoned, and the investigation must be confined to including those two other continuous laws of resistance to relative displacement—elasticity and viscosity.

As stated above, the law of elastico-viscosity assumed in this paper does not have an experimental foundation. Indeed, <term>Kohlrausch</term>'s experiments on glass<note><term>Poggendorff</term> Annals, vol. 119, p. 337.</note> show that elasticity degrades rapidly at first and then tends to reach a final condition, from which it does not seem to vary for an almost indefinite time. However, glass is one of the most perfectly elastic substances known, and, in light of <term>Tresca</term>'s experiments, it seems probable that experiments with lead would have produced very different results. It seems, moreover, hardly reasonable to suppose that the materials of the earth possess much mechanical similarity to glass. Notwithstanding all these objections, I believe that the results of this investigation into the tides of an ideal elastico-viscous sphere are worthy of attention.

There are two constants which determine the nature of this ideal solid: first, the coefficient of rigidity at the instant immediately after the body has been placed in its strained configuration; and second, "the modulus of the time of relaxation of rigidity," which is the time it takes for the force required to retain the body in its strained configuration to fall away to 0.368 of its initial value.

In this section, it is shown that the equations of flow of this incompressible elastico-viscous body have the same mathematical form as those for a purely viscous body; thus, the solutions already achieved are easily adapted to the new hypothesis.

The only case where the problem is completely worked out is when the disturbing

# MR. DARWIN ON THE BODILY TIDES OF VISCOUS AND SEMI-ELASTIC SPHERES

The gravitational potential takes the form appropriate for solving the tidal problem. The rules for the reduction of the bodily tide <note>tides within the Earth's solid or semi-solid mass</note>, its lagging, the reduction of the ocean tide, and the ocean tide's acceleration are somewhat more complex than in the case of pure viscosity <note>original: "viscosity" refers here to a thick, fluid-like consistency</note>. The reader is referred to Section 8 for the full statement of those laws. It is also shown that by choosing the right values for the two constants, the solutions can be used to provide results for either a purely viscous sphere or a purely elastic one.

The tables provide the results for the twice-daily <note>original: semidiurnal</note> and bi-weekly <note>original: fortnightly</note> tides based on this theory for spheroids that have the stiffness of glass or iron—the two cases previously studied by <term>Sir William Thomson</term> <note>also known as Lord Kelvin, a foundational figure in thermodynamics and physics</note>. Because it is only possible to estimate the amount of bodily tide by observing how much the ocean tide is reduced, I have not listed the specific heights and delays of the bodily tide itself.

It appears that if the "time of relaxation" <note>the time it takes for the material's internal stress to subside</note> of the Earth's stiffness is about one-quarter of the tidal period, then the reduction of the ocean tide is not much different from what it would be if the sphere were perfectly elastic. However, the amount of tidal acceleration <note>the shift in timing</note> still remains significant. A similar observation can be made regarding the acceleration of the tide when pure viscosity approaches the state of rigidity. This leads me to believe that one of the most promising ways to detect these tides within the Earth would be to determine the timing of the maximum and minimum points in a long-period tide, such as the bi-weekly tide at a high latitude.

In Section 10, it is shown that the effects of inertia <note>the tendency of the matter to keep moving</note>, which had been neglected when determining the laws of tidal movements, are not large enough to materially affect the accuracy of the results.

This is because it is a form that holds more potential energy than the oblate spheroidal form <note>a sphere flattened at the poles</note>, which is also a balanced shape.

In the first part of this paper, I use the equilibrium theory <note>a model of tides that assumes the ocean adjusts instantly to the gravitational pull of the moon and sun</note> to discuss ocean tides. In the second part, I consider what the tides would be in a shallow canal running around the equator if the Earth's solid core <note>original: "nucleus"</note> also shifted due to tidal forces at the same time. The reasons for performing this investigation are provided at the start of that section. In Section 11, it is shown that the height of the tide relative to the core maintains the same proportion to the tide on a perfectly rigid core as it does in the equilibrium theory, and the shift in timing <note>original: "phase"</note> is also the same. However, where one theory predicts high tide, the other predicts low tide.

The main practical result of this paper can be summarized by saying that it strongly confirms the view that the Earth possesses very great effective rigidity <note>stiffness or resistance to deformation</note>. But its primary value is that it serves as a necessary first chapter for investigating the precession <note>the slow, wobbling change in the orientation of Earth's axis</note> of imperfectly elastic spheroids, which I will address in a future paper. I believe I shall be able to show there, using an entirely different argument, that the tides within the Earth's body are likely extremely small at the present time.

### APPENDIX.

->November 7, 1878.<-

*On the observed height and timing of the bi-weekly ocean tide.*

In the following note, I attempt to follow through on the suggestion regarding the fortnightly <note>bi-weekly, occurring every 14 days</note> tide made in the previous paper.

The reports of the Tidal Committee of the British Association for 1872 and 1876 contain the simplified data <note>original: "reductions"</note> of tidal observations from several stations. These are organized into a series of "harmonic tides," which match the theoretical mathematical components of the tidal forces generated by the moon and sun. The tide we are concerned with here is the bi-weekly declinational tide <note>a tide caused by the moon's changing angle (declination) relative to the Earth's equator</note>.

The heights of the tides at various times are all expressed by the formula $R \cos(nt - \epsilon)$, where $R$ is half the total range of the tide in English feet, $n$ is the "speed" or frequency of the tide, and $\epsilon$ is the delay in timing <note>original: "retardation of phase"</note>. Consequently, $\epsilon$ divided by $n$ represents the "lag" of the tide.

In their current form, these observations do not seem to follow any obvious pattern <note>original: "present any semblance of law"</note>. However, once we rearrange them, we will be able to determine if they are truly useful for the specific point we are investigating.

According to the <term>equilibrium theory</term> <note>a theoretical model that assumes the ocean responds instantly to the gravitational pull of the moon and sun</note>, the mathematical formula for the bi-weekly tide of an ocean covering the entire Earth is:

->$\frac{3}{10} \frac{\tau}{\mathfrak{g}} a \sin^2 i (\frac{1}{3} - \cos^2 \theta) \cos 2\Omega t.$<-

In this formula:
* $\tau = \frac{3m}{2c^3}$
* $\mathfrak{g} = \frac{2g}{5a}$
* $a =$ the Earth's radius
* $i =$ the average tilt <note>original: "obliquity"</note> of the Earth's axis relative to the moon's orbit during that bi-weekly period
* $\theta =$ the <term>colatitude</term> <note>the angle measured from the North Pole (90° minus the latitude)</note> of the observation site.

If we set the tilt $i$ at 23° 28' (the tilt of the Earth's orbit) and the Earth's radius $a$ at 20.9 million feet, we find that:

->$\frac{3}{10} \frac{\tau}{\mathfrak{g}} a \sin^2 i = 0.207$ foot.<-

Therefore, the bi-weekly tide should be calculated as:

->$0.207 (\frac{1}{3} - \sin^2 (\text{latitude})) \cos 2\Omega t.$<-

In <term>Thomson's</term> <note>Sir William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin</note> corrected equilibrium theory, the second part of the formula should be:

->$\frac{1 + \mathfrak{E}}{3} - \sin^2 (\text{latitude})$<-

Where $\mathfrak{E}$ is a specific mathematical value (a definite integral) that depends on the distribution of land and water, but which has not yet been calculated.

The latitude where the bi-weekly <note>original: "fortnightly"</note> tide vanishes <note>original: "evanescent"</note> is 36° 15' if $\mathfrak{E}$ is zero. If we keep in mind that $\mathfrak{E}$ may be a negative value, it is clear that the observations at Cat Island (latitude 30° 23') were taken too close to this critical latitude to be reliable for determining the true bi-weekly tide. It is also almost impossible to believe that the observations at Toulon show a real tide of this category <note>original: "denomination"</note>, because the Mediterranean must be considered a practically closed sea. Therefore, the observations from Cat Island and Toulon will be set aside.

The first step to be applied to the observations above is obviously to divide each value of **R** <note>the tidal range</note> by $[\frac{1}{3} - \sin^2(\text{latitude})]$. The following are the factors used to adjust the values of **R**:

These factors will be applied to the values of **R** in the table previously provided.

The next point to consider is the "phase" <note>the timing of the peak</note> of the tide. The formula we have provided shows that the bi-weekly tide consists of an alternating deformation of the ocean level into an <term>oblate</term> <note>flattened at the poles, like an orange</note> and <term>prolate</term> <note>elongated at the poles, like a football</note> spheroid of revolution. This assumes the tide is layered over a perfect sphere rather than an oblate nucleus <note>the solid, slightly flattened body of the Earth</note>.

When $t$ (time) is zero, the spheroid is oblate, and this may be called high tide; when $t = \frac{\pi}{2\Omega}$, it may be called low tide. It follows, therefore, that north of latitude 36° 15', high tide is actually low water, and the reverse is true <note>original: "vice-versâ"</note>; but south of this latitude, the tide and water levels align. However, the formulas used in tidal data adjustments always refer to *high water*. Therefore, to find the delay <note>original: "retardation"</note> of the tide, we must subtract 180° from all the phase values ($\epsilon$) for places north of 36° 15'—that is to say (since Cat Island was rejected) for all locations except Karachi.

For Karachi, we may observe that any delay $\epsilon$ may be viewed as a delay of $\epsilon - 2\pi$, which, if negative, represents an acceleration of the tide. If $2\pi - \epsilon$ is less than 180°, this appears to be the more correct way to look at it.
