We will consider R' <note>the adjusted tidal range</note> first.

From these twelve values, we find that the average R' = 0.203, with a <term>probable error</term> of ±0.068.

The value of R' is almost exactly what theory predicts (namely, 0.207). However, the very large probable error makes the result so uncertain that we can only state that the results do not disprove a reduction in the bi-weekly <note>original: "fortnightly"</note> tide.

Regarding the phase <note>represented by $\eta$</note>, it will be observed that there are eight cases of early tides <note>original: "accelerated"</note> compared to four cases of late tides <note>original: "retarded"</note>. Two of the late tides occurred at Hartlepool. Regarding this station, <term>Sir William Thomson</term> <note>the physicist later known as Lord Kelvin</note> says in the report: "The agreement between the results deduced from these long-period tides is hardly consistent enough to be satisfactory, though some of the quantities are within reasonable limits."

It is worth noting, in passing, that Cat Island shows a late tide, while Toulon shows an early one.

If we treat these changes in phase the same way we treated R', we find an average early arrival (acceleration) of phase of 7.85°. However, the probable error is several times larger than the result itself. In fact, with so few and such inconsistent observations, the <term>method of least squares</term> <note>a mathematical way to find the best fit for a set of data</note> is useless here.

The cases of late phase certainly show considerably more inconsistency than those of early phase. If we take the average of the cases with an early phase, we find an acceleration of 48°, which corresponds in time to an early arrival of 1 day and 20 hours.

Now, three out of four years of observations show an early tide at Liverpool; all three years show an early arrival at Karachi; the Hartlepool observations are not of very much value; while the single year of early arrival at Brest may be balanced against the single year of late arrival at Ramsgate. If we then ask ourselves whether an early or late arrival is more probable, I think the answer must favor acceleration. If so, there seem to be some indications of a <term>viscous yielding</term> <note>the Earth's interior flowing or deforming slowly like a thick fluid</note> of the Earth's mass. It must be admitted, however, that the evidence is exceedingly uncertain.

It does not seem to be noticed in the tidal reports that among the "<term>Helmholtz compound shallow-water tides</term>" <note>complex tidal waves produced when primary tides interact in shallow water</note> there are several which have the same period, or very nearly the same period, as the true bi-weekly tide based on the moon's position <note>original: "fortnightly declinational tide"</note>. # SPHEROIDS, AND ON THE OCEAN TIDES UPON A YIELDING NUCLEUS.

<center>->F 2<-</center>

If we represent (as in the report) the Earth's rotation as $\gamma$ and the moon's mean motion as $\sigma$, then we find that the following speeds will combine to create shallow-water tides <note>tides produced by the interaction of primary tidal waves in shallow coastal areas</note> that are indistinguishable from the true bi-weekly <note>original: "fortnightly"</note> tide: namely, $2(\gamma - \sigma)$ and $2\gamma$, as well as $\gamma - 2\sigma$ and $\gamma$. Additionally, there are four combinations of the elliptic tides <note>tides caused by the elliptical shape of the moon's orbit</note> which produce the same period of compound tide, if we ignore the motion of the moon's <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in the moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth</note>. It therefore seems quite possible that at certain observation stations, the true bi-weekly tide might be masked or have its timing <note>original: "phase"</note> significantly affected by these compound tides. This is perhaps the explanation for the great irregularity found in the phases.

A series of observations on an oceanic island near the Equator—or even better, far to the north or south—would be of immense value in resolving this point.

### II. *On the Spectra of Non-Metals—The Spectrum of Oxygen.*
### *By* ARTHUR SCHUSTER, *Ph.D., F.R.A.S.* <note>original: "F.R.A.S." stands for Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society.</note>
### *Communicated by* J. CLERK MAXWELL, *F.R.S., Professor of Experimental Physics in the University of Cambridge.* <note>original: "F.R.S." stands for Fellow of the Royal Society.</note>

->Received April 25—Read May 16, 1878.<-

---

->[PLATE 1.]<-

#### *1. Introductory.*

The many unexplained phenomena regarding how electricity passes through gases will likely occupy the attention of experimental physicists for some time to come. It is best to approach this subject from as many different angles as possible. One of our most powerful research tools is the spectroscope <note>An instrument used to measure the properties of light, specifically to identify materials by the "fingerprint" of colors they emit.</note>. However, before it can be used for this study, we must determine the chemical origin of the different spectra we observe in vacuum tubes. We must also discuss how these spectra are likely to change under different conditions.

A specific investigation must be conducted for each gas. We have to study the effects of various impurities, the influence of the electrodes, and the impact of the glass—which, in the tubes typically used, is significantly heated by the electric spark. To make the investigation complete, we must vary the pressure, the internal diameter <term>bore</term> of the vacuum tube, and the strength of the spark as much as possible.

I have chosen oxygen as my first subject of investigation. Although the physicists Julius Plücker and Adolph Wüllner accurately described the phenomena seen in oxygen tubes as far as their experiments allowed, this paper contains much new information and will place older facts on a firmer foundation. When I first began this work, I intended to study gases in groups and analyze their mixtures. However, as this current investigation has required nearly a year of continuous work and is complete on its own, I trust it is worthy of publication. For now, I must limit myself to a purely spectroscopic perspective. Because several of the observations I will record relate directly to the general theory of "double spectra," I should briefly mention what we know about that subject.

#### *2. Multiple Spectra.*

We can roughly divide all known spectra into three types or "orders": continuous spectra, line spectra, and—standing between them—spectra of <term>fluted bands</term> <note>Also called "channelled spaces"; these appear as groups of lines that look like the grooves (fluting) on a column, often fading out at one edge.</note>.

<summary>In this introduction, Arthur Schuster outlines his intent to systematically study the light spectra of oxygen using a spectroscope to better understand how electricity interacts with gases. He categorizes light spectra into three distinct types: continuous, line, and fluted bands.</summary>

<keywords>spectroscopy, oxygen, vacuum tubes, Arthur Schuster, J. Clerk Maxwell, electricity in gases, fluted bands, line spectra, physics history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Arthur Schuster's 1878 report on the spectrum of oxygen, moving from the introduction into a theoretical discussion of how continuous spectra are formed.</meta>

# DR. A. SCHUSTER ON THE SPECTRA OF METALLOIDS.

*Continuous spectra.*—During the first years of spectrum analysis, it was generally supposed that a continuous spectrum <note>A continuous spectrum is a rainbow-like band of light where the colors bleed into each other without gaps, unlike a "line spectrum" which shows distinct, separated lines of color.</note> was characteristic of either a solid or a liquid body. However, as our experimental knowledge gradually increased, it was found that the fact of a substance being in its solid, liquid, or gaseous state only indirectly influenced the type <note>original: "order"</note> of the spectrum produced. It was believed at first that a chemical compound always showed the spectrum of its individual molecules; in other words, that the vibrations of the molecules were made up of the vibrations of the component atoms. If we accept this theory, then, of course, we have only one explanation for the different types of spectra: the influence of one molecule on another. According to this view, the state of matter <term>state of aggregation</term> must be the direct cause of the change in the spectrum. 

Since the work of Mitscherlich <note>Eilhard Mitscherlich (1794–1863), a German chemist famous for discovering that different substances with similar crystal structures often have similar chemical compositions.</note>, however, it has gradually been recognized that a combination of atoms changes the spectrum entirely. This change is not slight, but fundamental. The whole vibrating system seems to have been altered; at present, in the vast majority of cases, there is no hope that we may consider the vibrations of a molecule to be only the slightly disturbed vibrations of its atoms. We now have a second cause for a change in the different types of spectra. We no longer need to look at a continuous spectrum as a line spectrum disturbed by the shocks of other molecules; instead, we may explain it by the changes that have taken place within the individual molecule itself.

According to this view, liquid and solid bodies generally give continuous spectra, not because they are liquid or solid, but because in these states the molecules have a more complicated structure than in the gaseous state. Experiment must decide between the two theories: the theory of molecular disturbance and the theory of molecular structure. I think that the facts are decidedly in favor of the latter theory. Mr. Lockyer’s <note>Sir Norman Lockyer (1836–1920), a British scientist who discovered the element helium and was a pioneer in using the spectroscope to study the sun.</note> investigations have shown that most bodies give us a continuous spectrum as a gas before they condense, and many do so at a temperature considerably above their boiling point. Mr. Lockyer has rightly concluded from these facts that the grouping of atoms <term>atomic aggregation</term> within the molecules is the cause of the different types of spectra. 

If we observe the changes in a spectrum that gradually take place while heating or cooling a vapor, we find that the continuous spectrum is produced, not by a widening of the existing colored bands, but by a direct replacement. This replacement is sometimes sudden and sometimes gradual, leaving no doubt in the observer’s mind that they are dealing with two distinct vibrating systems, rather than simply one system being disturbed. I do not, of course, mean to say that the impacts of other molecules have no observable influence. If the hydrogen lines widen through increased pressure, it is very likely that the alteration is produced by molecular impacts; but the change from a line spectrum to a continuous spectrum is, as a rule, quite different from the change that takes place with hydrogen. According to the theory of molecular grouping, it seems quite possible that a liquid could give the same spectrum as its vapor, and this indeed seems to be true in some cases.

I shall show that we can obtain a continuous spectrum of oxygen, not by an

It is not easy to see how this can be due to any other cause than the one which I have advocated.*

## *Channelled space spectra.*
Standing between line spectra and continuous spectra, we have, as I already mentioned, spectra of fluted bands or channelled spaces <note>Now more commonly known as "band spectra," these are characteristic of molecules. They look like a series of colorful stripes that are bright on one side and fade out on the other.</note>. Such spectra, when seen in spectroscopes of low power, appear as a rule to be made up of bands which have a sharp boundary on one side and gradually fade away on the other. When seen with a more perfect instrument, each band seems to be made up of a number of lines of nearly equal intensity, which gradually come nearer and nearer together as we approach the sharp edge, and finally fuse together. The sharp edge is the limit toward which the lines gradually approach. This edge is sometimes towards the red and sometimes towards the blue end of the spectrum.

There is another class of channelled space spectra which, though never accurately described or measured, is, as I have reason to believe, by no means uncommon. These spectra appear, in instruments of low power, as made up of bands covering—

---

> \* Since the above was written, Professor <term>STOKES</term> <note>Sir George Gabriel Stokes (1819–1903), a physicist and mathematician who made major contributions to fluid dynamics and optics.</note> has suggested to me a way by which the continuous spectrum might be produced, and which differs from the one described above as that of molecular impacts.
>
> We have reason to believe that the mere motion of matter through the <term>ether</term> <note>In the 19th century, scientists believed a substance called "luminiferous ether" filled all space and carried light waves.</note> is insufficient to produce vibrations. There must be two portions of matter exerting forces on each other in order for the ether to be thrown into agitation. In ordinary line spectra, we consider that the two portions of matter form part of the same molecule. Now, it seems possible that also two portions of different molecules should, in their rapid approach toward each other or recession from each other, cause forces in the ether which produce vibration. These latter vibrations we might expect not to take place in fixed periods, but to produce what we call a continuous spectrum. We may suppose that at the lowest temperature at which, for instance, oxygen glows, the vibrations in the ether are chiefly produced by this rapid relative motion of different molecules, while at higher temperatures the relative motions of different portions of one molecule might have the upper hand; the continuous spectrum in one case, and the line spectrum in the other, might thus be explained.
>
> I admit that there is much to be said in favor of this view, and must leave it to further experimentation to decide whether it is the one most accordant with facts or not. That the discontinuous spectra of different types <note>original: "orders"</note> (line and band spectra) are due to different molecular combinations, I consider to be pretty well established, and analogy has led me (and Mr. <term>LOCKYER</term> <note>Sir Norman Lockyer (1836–1920), an English astronomer who discovered the gas helium.</note> before me) to explain the continuous spectra by the same cause; for the change of the continuous spectrum to the line or band spectrum takes place in exactly the same way as the change of spectra of different types into each other. Analogy is not a strong guide, yet some weight may be given to it in a case like the one under discussion, where experiment so far has failed to give a decided answer. Professor <term>STOKES</term> has also suggested that the continuous spectrum which comes out under high pressures may really be only the continuous spectrum of low temperatures. At such pressures, the discharge of an <term>induction coil</term> <note>An early electrical transformer used to produce high-voltage pulses from a low-voltage supply.</note> consists of a bright and essentially instantaneous spark, followed by an apparently continuous discharge for which the spark appears to open a path; and it is possible that the line spectrum may really belong to the spark, and the continuous background to the continuous discharge. Professor <term>STOKES</term> has suggested an experiment with a rotating mirror <note>A device used to observe very fast electrical or light phenomena by "spreading" the light out over time.</note> to decide the point—an experiment which I hope to be able to make before long.—Note added December 1, 1878.

Such are the bands that appear at the negative pole of oxygen tubes. With high dispersion, I was able to resolve these bands into a series of lines. Their appearance, under these circumstances, is represented in Plate 1, figs. 1 and 2.

It seems remarkable that most substances should, under certain conditions, give spectra which in character resemble each other so nearly as these channelled space spectra; and the idea seems natural, and almost necessary, that such a similarity of spectra should be produced by a similarity in molecular structure. We know that certain substances giving line spectra show, when they combine with others, spectra of fluted bands; and this seems to me to lead to a necessary explanation of double spectra—the one which indeed has been adopted by most experimentalists. They hold that when a spectrum suddenly changes from a line spectrum to a band spectrum, we are dealing with a molecular combination either of the molecules of the same substance or of different substances.

*Line spectra.*—The appearance of these spectra is too well known to need any description. Until lately, line spectra have avoided the many difficulties which beset their related categories <note>original: "brethren of different orders"</note>, but at last they could no longer resist the invasion. It gradually appeared that lines which are prominent at one temperature may be comparatively weak at another. This fact is sometimes exaggerated to such a degree that all the lines which form the spectrum of lower temperature disappear completely at higher temperatures, while the lines of higher temperature are not to be seen at lower temperatures. Oxygen, which is a typical gas for every difficulty in spectroscopy, is a case in point. Oxygen seems to have two perfectly distinct line spectra, each of which generally appears by itself and unmixed with a trace of the other spectrum.

Let us for a moment consider how we may explain these facts without having recourse to molecular combinations. We have to assume that, when the vibrations of a molecule are small, they take place in a series of periods, and consequently show lines in the spectroscope at places corresponding to these periods. Now imagine the temperature to be raised. We must assume that, as the intensity of vibration increases, other periods come into play which rapidly increase in intensity, while those which were prominent at first gradually disappear, so that, after a while, a different set of vibrations is formed. I do not know that there is any fact which could be brought <note>original: "adduced"</note> against such an explanation, nor do I think that the explanation is theoretically impossible. Yet the passage of one line spectrum into the other resembles so very closely the passage of a band spectrum into that of a line spectrum, that one feels inclined to refer both phenomena to the same cause. In the case of oxygen, for instance, one line spectrum appears under precisely the same circumstances as the band spectrum of nitrogen, and it changes into the other line spectrum almost identically in the same way as the band spectrum of nitrogen changes into the line spectrum.

# DR. A. SCHUSTER ON THE SPECTRA OF METALLOIDS.

The homogeneity of the phenomena seen in vacuum tubes is greatly increased if we consider the one-line spectrum of oxygen as the representative of the band spectrum of nitrogen, and I shall therefore consider it as such. I have called the spectrum the compound line spectrum of oxygen because, according to the theory of molecular combination, it would be due to a more complicated molecular structure than the other (the elementary) line spectrum. I should add, however, that I am not at all certain that the two line spectra must necessarily be explained in the same way as the line and band spectra. I have found it necessary, for the sake of clarity, to explain the results of the investigation in the language of a definite theory. It will be easy for anyone to separate the two. The fact that nearly all lines which appear at low temperatures only are lines which widen easily seems to be suggestive.

*Spectra of the negative pole.*—It has long been known that in many gases the glow surrounding the negative electrode has a different color from the remainder of the discharge. This color appears generally more blue to the eye than that of the positive discharge, and this fact was the cause that a certain blueness was often associated with the idea of negative electricity. When examined with the spectroscope, it is found that the negative glow has a spectrum of its own, different, of course, in different gases. Here, also, I think, it will be found simpler to assume that a definite molecular combination is formed at the negative pole than to suppose that external forces peculiar to the pole modify the period of vibration. The following experiments seem to me to support strongly, if not to prove, this view. When the pressure is very small, the spectrum of the negative pole is seen throughout the tube.<note>GOLDSTEIN, ‘Berliner Monatsberichte,’ May, 1876.</note> In vacuum tubes of the form usually employed for purposes of spectrum analysis, it is easy to obtain a state of exhaustion in which they show the spectrum of the negative pole throughout that half of the tube which contains the negative electrode (which I shall call the negative half), and also in the capillary part, but not in that half of the tube which contains the positive electrode (which I shall call the positive half). The experiments are assumed to be made at that stage.

*Experiment 1.*—Allow the spark to pass for some time in one direction; the spectrum of the negative pole is seen in the negative half and in the capillary part only. Now reverse the current suddenly, and the spectrum will now be seen at first throughout the tube, but will gradually disappear in the positive half, so that finally the same permanent state as before is established, and the spectrum is only seen in the negative half and capillary part.

*Experiment 2.*—In order to show that it is the reversal, and not the interruption of the current which produces the appearance of the spectrum in the positive half, break the current and make contact the same way: no change can be observed.

*Experiment 3.*—But if, after the spark has passed some time, you break the contact and wait a little time, say one minute, so as to allow any compounds which might

*Experiment 4.*—Establish and break contact very rapidly, constantly changing the direction of the current; after a short time, once the effect of the initial connection has passed, a stable state will be established for each current in either direction. In this case, the spectrum characteristic of the negative glow is seen only surrounding the negative electrode; however, I believe the glow itself is not as well-developed in this instance.

*Experiment 5.*—After alternating the current quickly, as in Experiment 4, wait a short while and then establish contact in either direction. The spectrum of the negative pole will initially be seen throughout the tube and then gradually fade away in the positive half.

These experiments work as well in nitrogen as they do in oxygen. Experiments 4 and 5 somewhat weaken the argument. However, I have obtained other results by suddenly reversing the current, which require further investigation. Without claiming to provide a complete explanation for these experiments, they seem to prove that the spectrum of the negative pole can appear away from the pole itself and must, therefore, be due to secondary causes. I have proven elsewhere that a simple difference in temperature cannot explain the creation of the spectrum at the negative pole.<note>Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, vol. iii, p. 57.</note> I must quote a passage here from <term>FARADAY’S</term> “Experimental Researches.” After referring to an explanation suggesting that the so-called <term>unipolarity</term> in the conduction of soap and similar substances depends on secondary chemical phenomena occurring at the poles, he says:

> “Probably the effects called effects of unipolarity, and the peculiar differences between the positive and negative surfaces when discharging into air, gases, or other dielectrics, which have already been mentioned, may be closely related to each other.”<note>“Experimental Researches,” Series XIII, 1636.</note>

### 3. *Description of Apparatus.*

When investigating the spectra of pure gases, it is essential to avoid all traces of carbon impurities. Rubber tubing, as well as any joint requiring the use of grease, paraffin, etc., cannot be used. I am not saying that such joints always ruin an experiment, but when determining whether a specific spectrum is caused by an impurity, every possible source of contamination must be eliminated. These precautions are absolutely necessary to obtain a pure spectrum of oxygen. I have examined many tubes from various makers that were supposed to be filled with pure oxygen, but I have found only one tube that did not show the spectrum of <term>carbonic oxide</term>. This spectrum has been described by various

By taking the necessary precautions, I have succeeded in filling a great number of tubes that show no trace of the presence of any carbon compound. I have used a SPRENGEL pump with an air trap, such as is sold by Mr. J. J. HICKS. The connection between the pump and the vacuum tube is made by means of a ball-and-socket joint. The fall tube of the pump ends at its upper extremity in a hemispherical socket. A hollow sphere is ground together with this socket so as to fit perfectly into it. The inner part of the sphere communicates with the pump by means of a small hole and ends on the other side in a glass tube. I have always fused my vacuum tubes directly to this tube. For ordinary purposes, the sphere is slightly covered with grease and fitted into the socket. A small quantity of mercury poured on the top will then make the joint perfectly tight. I have avoided even this trace of grease throughout nearly the entire investigation. Mercury alone will run through the joint as the air is exhausted, but I find that concentrated sulfuric acid, although it runs through the joint, will do so only very slowly; so if care is taken to refill the sulfuric acid from time to time, the joint will remain perfectly tight. Such a joint allows great freedom of motion, which is a great convenience, as the spectroscopic examination is always best carried out while the tube is attached to the pump.

The vacuum tubes used were, as a rule, of the form shown in the accompanying woodcut (Fig. 1); that is, they had the shape of an ordinary PLÜCKER tube, to one end of which a tube of hard glass (*a*) was fused. On the other side, it ended in a tube (*b*), which was fused to the air pump. The hard-glass tube was filled with a substance that gave off oxygen when heated. Potassium permanganate, potassium chlorate, and mercury oxide were used to eliminate any lines that might be due to the substance from which the oxygen was prepared. It is necessary to subject all these substances to preliminary heating to free them beforehand, as much as possible, from moisture, which is always attached to them. I find potassium permanganate to be the most convenient substance and have only used the others in test experiments. I have used capillary tubes of different bores, and I think that some of the contradictory statements made by different observers are simply due to the fact that the term "capillary tube" is rather vague and includes tubes of diameters different enough to affect the spectrum. When the light is weak, Figure 2 is a convenient form of tube; *e d* is the capillary part, and the collimator of the spectroscope is placed parallel to it, so as to receive the light from the whole length of the tube. <image-desc>A scientific diagram of a glass vacuum tube apparatus labeled Fig. 2. It consists of several interconnected glass chambers and tubes. A horizontal tube labeled 'b' leads into a vertical chamber, which connects via a narrow capillary tube labeled 'e' and 'd' to another vertical chamber. The following was the usual way of preparing tubes for experiment:—A plug of clean asbestos was introduced into the tube *c*, separating the hard-glass tube *a* from the <term>PLÜCKER’S</term> tube. This plug prevents any solid substance from being physically carried into the <term>PLÜCKER’S</term> tube. As the asbestos had been subjected beforehand to a considerable temperature, no gas could be given out by it; but to prevent any possibility of error, some tubes were filled without the asbestos, and showed not the least difference which could be traced to the asbestos. Permanganate of potash, which had been heated in a test tube until the crystals were disintegrated and fell into powder, was next introduced into the tube *a*, which was then drawn out at the blow-pipe. The tube *b* was then fused to the sphere of the ball-and-socket joint. The joint was rendered air-tight by means of sulfuric acid, and the tube was ready for exhaustion. There was now no danger of any carbon compounds, except such as were unavoidably attached to the glass tube; and I found, indeed, that the tube had sometimes to be filled and exhausted ten times before the spectrum of pure oxygen appeared. It is not very easy to get rid of all traces of moisture, but by continued exhaustion it is not impossible.

One of the difficulties in the investigation of the spectrum of oxygen consists in the oxidation of the electrodes. It is necessary to work while the tube is attached to the pump, so that it can always be refilled. If this is not done, the oxygen combines with the electrodes, and a vacuum is soon established which does not conduct electricity.

I have eliminated the effects of the electrodes by using different metals, such as aluminium, platinum, silver, brass, and iridium. Only in the case of aluminium did I observe lines which could be traced to the electrodes. When the vacuum is very high, a spectrum is sometimes faintly seen which can be easily obtained from aluminium and which I believe is due to aluminium oxide. The spectrum, however, is unpredictable in its appearance; and as aluminium electrodes were used in the great majority of experiments, it is quite possible that an effect from electrodes of other metals exists but escaped my notice.

Any possible effect from the glass was eliminated by using tubes of different widths. I have finally seen all the lines or bands which I attribute to oxygen in a glass receiver six inches in diameter. The electrodes were about one inch apart, and no part of the spark was within two and a half inches of the glass.

### 4. *Measurements.*

It is important to vary both the dispersive and magnifying power of the instrument. Some of the phenomena are best seen under small dispersion, others under large dispersion. I have examined the various spectra of oxygen with flint-glass prisms of 55° refracting angle, using any number from one up to seven. Whenever measurements are to be made, it is best to use as large a dispersion as possible. Some of the measurements I shall provide were made with a dispersion of seven prisms. During the investigation, however, I obtained from Mr. <term>HILGER</term> in London two very heavy flint-glass prisms (specific gravity 5) of 62° each. These prisms contain much lead; they are yellow and, therefore, can only be conveniently used up to about the solar line G. The dispersive power of each is fully equal to that of two ordinary flint-glass prisms of the same refracting angle. Each prism under minimum deviation separated the D lines by an angular distance of 52 seconds. The focal length of the observing telescope was 17.4 inches. The micrometer screw of the eyepiece with which the measurements were made had 100 turns to the inch. The distance between the two D lines when both prisms were used was 0.88, taking one turn of the screw as the unit. Most of the measurements were made with these prisms.

During the spring of 1872, I published an investigation on the spectrum of nitrogen (Proc. Roy. Soc., xx., 484), in which I showed that when nitrogen is heated with sodium in a vacuum tube, the nitrogen bands disappear and a line spectrum appears in my tubes. When measured with the instruments at my disposal, this was found to agree fairly well with the line spectrum of nitrogen. <term>SALET</term> has since shown that the reason the bands disappeared in my experiments must be found in the absorption of nitrogen by sodium under the influence of the electric spark. The lines I saw were actually due to metallic sodium. In order to avoid any similar error, I have carried my measurements to a degree of accuracy which makes any confusion between the lines of different substances quite impossible.

<summary>Schuster details how he eliminated interference from electrodes and glass in his oxygen experiments and describes the high-precision prisms used for his measurements. He also corrects a previous finding regarding nitrogen, noting that observed lines were actually sodium due to absorption.</summary>
<keywords>spectroscopy, oxygen, aluminium electrodes, flint-glass prisms, Hilger, D lines, nitrogen, sodium, Salet, dispersion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Schuster’s discussion on experimental methodology, specifically addressing the standards and mathematical formulas used for measuring wavelengths in his spectroscopic observations.</meta>

DR. A. SCHUSTER ON THE SPECTRA OF METALLOIDS.

No measurements are of any value unless they are given in <term>wave-lengths</term>. It has been suggested to use the air lines as reference lines, between which we might interpolate any known line. It seems to me that a much better choice might be made. The air lines are not spread evenly through the spectrum; they are by no means sharp under high dispersion, and their wave-lengths have only been obtained by interpolation. I do not think that these possess the required degree of accuracy to be used again as reference lines. It should be our endeavor to make our measurements as consistent as possible, and as long as Ångström’s solar maps are the standard work for wave-length measurements, we should refer all our measurements to those maps. Thalèn has adopted this plan in his excellent series of measurements, but the method which he used presents serious difficulties when the light to be examined is weak.

I have used the bright lines of metals present in the sun as reference lines, the wave-lengths of which can therefore be directly found on Ångström’s map. The lines of iron are very useful in this respect.

The <term>interpolation formula</term> which is usually employed is based on the fact that the difference in refractive indices of two lines varies nearly as the difference between the inverse squares of the wave-lengths. If reference lines can be found sufficiently close, the formula works quite well; but I find that for the dispersion which I have used, the formula is no longer applicable when the distance between the reference lines is about ten times the distance between the two sodium lines. As it is not always possible to find good reference lines within that distance, I have generally used three reference lines and taken the inverse fourth powers of the wave-lengths into account. I am not quite certain that even then the errors of interpolation did not, in some cases, slightly exceed the errors of observation. The reason why the ordinary interpolation formula cannot be used does not lie so much in the fact that the law of the inverse square does not hold accurately for refractive indices (although this, of course, is also true), but that, except in automatic spectroscopes, our measurements are not proportional to refractive indices.

It is difficult to say to what degree of accuracy measurements are made, yet I trust that, except for the weakest lines, the error of my measurements will seldom be found to exceed 0.5 x<sup>th</sup> metre.

After these remarks, I pass to the description of the various spectra of oxygen. I distinguish four such spectra. At the lowest temperature at which oxygen becomes luminous, it gives a continuous spectrum. As the temperature is raised, the continuous spectrum changes successively into two line spectra, which, as I have already mentioned, I call the <term>compound line spectrum</term> and the <term>elementary line spectrum</term>. It is one of the principal objects of this paper to show that these two line spectra, which have been much confused with each other, have a separate existence, and that the generation of one involves the destruction of the other. The fourth spectrum is that which is seen at the negative pole.

### 5. *The Continuous Spectrum of Oxygen.*

WÜLLNER (Pogg. Ann., 137, p. 350) has shown that when the pressure in his vacuum tube is gradually increased, the background begins to be illuminated at a pressure of 280 mm. This illumination, according to him, first extends from the solar line E to a point about halfway between F and G. As the pressure was increased, the continuous spectrum extended further towards both sides, but primarily towards the blue. I do not know whether this continuous illumination of the background is due to the same cause as the continuous spectrum which is seen under the circumstances I am about to describe. There is nothing contrary to known facts in the assumption that the vibration of the gas, though primarily taking place in certain definite periods, can be disturbed by mutual impacts in such a way that a slight mixture of vibrations of all periods is produced, which increases as the pressure increases. In any case, if this is the cause of the continuous spectrum seen under great pressure, it has nothing to do with the continuous spectrum that appears by a reduction of temperature, which is not the background to bright lines but forms the whole visible spectrum. The following facts seem to prove to me that oxygen, at the lowest temperature at which it is luminous, gives a continuous spectrum:

1. The wide part of a <term>GEISSLER tube</term> filled with pure oxygen generally shines with a faint yellow light; when analyzed by the prism, this yellow light gives a continuous spectrum.

2. *Experiment 6.*—A spark was passed through oxygen gas at atmospheric pressure. The maximum striking distance of the coil was about one inch. No jar was included in the circuit. The poles were about 4 mm apart. A lens concentrated the image of the spark on the slit of the spectroscope. Under these circumstances, the elementary line spectrum of oxygen, which is the spectrum commonly observed at atmospheric pressure, is seen. But when the break of the induction coil was put out of adjustment so that the spark decreased considerably in strength, it took on a yellow color, and the spectrum was perfectly continuous. The phenomena were very striking when I held the wheel of the break in my hand while looking through the spectroscope. A slight turn would change the line spectrum into a continuous spectrum, and vice versa. When the line spectrum was seen, the spark was considerably stronger and the poles became red hot. When the continuous spectrum was seen, the poles were not sufficiently heated to become luminous. The maximum intensity of the light was in the yellowish-green and decreased on either side.

I attach some importance to this experiment, as I think the sudden conversion of the line spectrum into a continuous spectrum cannot be explained by any other hypothesis than that of molecular combination.

3. An interesting observation by BECQUEREL, which he describes in a footnote (‘La Lumière,’ vol. i., page 196), bears on this point. He says that an excess of oxygen in the oxyhydrogen flame makes itself visible by a yellow streak of light.

It is reasonable to suppose that M. BECQUEREL heated up the oxygen to a sufficiently high temperature in the oxyhydrogen flame to render it luminous. That this is possible appears from an experiment made by PLÜCKER, who, working with an excess of hydrogen in the oxyhydrogen flame, saw the lines of hydrogen in his spectroscope.

I have already stated that I do not know whether the continuous background which is seen at higher pressure when the line spectrum appears has its origin in a separate cause, or whether it has to be brought into connection with the continuous spectrum of low temperature. The following experiment may assist those who wish to form an opinion on the matter:

Mr. LOCKYER has made use of the fact that when a spark is taken between metallic poles, and a lens is used to form an image of the spark on the slit of the spectroscope, the lines of the metals do not stretch across the field, but are confined to the neighborhood of the poles. As the pressure is decreased, some of the lines decrease rapidly in length, and finally disappear, while the effect on others is barely perceptible. I find that when oxygen is the gas through which the spark strikes, the lines of the gas as well as the metallic lines seem to stretch away from the poles and fade away towards the middle. The center of the field is taken up by the second line spectrum, which I have called the compound line spectrum. Here is what happens:

*Experiment 7.*—At atmospheric pressure the lines of the elementary line spectrum were seen to stretch across the field; the continuous spectrum illuminating the background was strongest in the green. As the pressure was decreased the compound lines appeared much broadened, and at the same time a dark streak was seen to pass through the continuous spectrum in the center of the spark. This means that at that pressure the continuous spectrum is chiefly confined to the electrodes. As the pressure was decreased to about half an atmosphere, the continuous spectrum only occupied a narrow band adjoining the electrodes. The compound lines came out strong in the center of the field and were better defined. At still lower pressures the lines of oxygen separated in the middle of the field, as the continuous spectrum had done before; and the continuous spectrum now seemed to be gradually absorbed into the electrodes, and finally disappeared altogether. Gradually the oxygen lines became shorter and shorter until they could no more be distinguished from the metallic lines. The center of the field was now entirely occupied by the compound line spectrum. It is necessary to add that it appears conclusively from the experiments of WÜLLNER, as well as my own, that the continuous spectrum is really due to oxygen and not to the metallic poles. The reason why there should be a difference

### 6. *The Elementary Line Spectrum.*

This is the spectrum seen when a strong spark passes through oxygen at atmospheric pressure. It can be seen at all pressures in vacuum tubes when a Leyden jar and air break are introduced into the circuit. <term>Plücker</term> provides a drawing of the lines in his paper on "Double Spectra" (Phil. Trans., 1865); however, he does not provide his measurements. <term>Huggins</term> gives measurements of the oxygen lines as seen at atmospheric pressure, but these are referred to an arbitrary scale, and some of the weaker lines are invisible at atmospheric pressure due to the continuous background. <term>Thalèn</term> gives the wavelengths of the air lines.

When the spark is captured in air, however, the oxygen lines are weak compared to the nitrogen lines, so that even some strong oxygen lines do not appear in <term>Thalèn’s</term> list. In their latest paper on the spectra of metalloids, Messrs. <term>Ångström</term> and <term>Thalèn</term> provided a drawing of the oxygen lines.

This drawing is quite complete, but the numbers obtained by measurement are not given separately, so we are dependent on the accuracy of the engraver, which cannot be relied upon to any great extent. As far as can be judged from the map, <term>Thalèn’s</term> measurements agree fairly well with mine. <term>Salet</term> also has provided some measurements, but the small dispersion he used did not enable him to obtain great accuracy. There are two weak lines on <term>Ångström</term> and <term>Thalèn’s</term> map ($\lambda=5163$ and $\lambda=4964$) which I have never been able to see, although I have been constantly looking for them. On the other hand, I see a number of weak lines not included in that map. Most of them are listed by <term>Salet</term>. Some of these lines have a different appearance than the oxygen lines; they are not as well defined and are sometimes bands. This may lead some observers to think they are due to impurities. Greatly struck by the difference in appearance between these lines and the ordinary oxygen lines, I have paid some attention to them; however, I find they appear with electrodes of many different metals and cannot be caused by the glass, as I have seen them in the six-inch diameter receiver I mentioned earlier. I have finally concluded that we have no evidence for rejecting them. I have attempted to represent the relative intensities of the oxygen lines in the spectrum marked A on Plate 1. The intensities were carefully estimated, but, of course, they cannot be greatly relied upon except regarding the relative intensity within a group. It seems hardly possible to compare the intensity of a yellow line to a blue one. The following table contains my measurements. I have not carried them beyond the group of lines near the solar line G. Photography will perform this work much better in the extreme violet than I could have.

### 7. *The Compound Line—Spectrum of Oxygen.*

In one of his early papers (*Pogg. Ann.*, 107), <term>Plücker</term> describes the spectrum of oxygen as consisting of four lines with the following wavelengths:
->6150<-
->5328<-
->5185<-
->4367<-

In his later drawing of the oxygen spectrum (*Phil. Trans.*, 1865), he includes a great many lines of which these four are a part. <term>Wüllner</term> states that these four lines are always the first to appear in oxygen tubes. <term>Ångström</term> and <term>Thalèn</term> do not include these lines; <term>Huggins</term> does not include them; <term>Salet</term> does not include them. <term>Plücker</term> and <term>Wüllner</term> are the only observers who experimented under the conditions in which the lines appear, and they seem to assume that they form part of the ordinary line spectrum of oxygen; yet when the ordinary line spectrum is at its brightest, these lines are completely invisible, and when these lines are brightest, no trace of the ordinary line spectrum can be detected. I must repeat that these lines appear equally well regardless of how the oxygen is prepared. <term>Wüllner</term> prepared his gas by electrolysis and saw the lines; I prepared my gas, as already mentioned, in three different ways. When I began this work, I was under the impression that these lines must be due to impurities; however, after spending a great deal of time trying to trace their origin, I am certain that they are produced by pure oxygen. I have seen the lines almost daily for many months and in at least 30 different tubes.

The appearance of an oxygen tube when a spark passes through it while it undergoes gradual exhaustion is as follows:

*Experiment 8.*—At first, the spark has a yellow color, and the spectrum is perfectly continuous. Almost immediately, however, four lines are seen in the capillary section above the continuous spectrum. One of these lines is in the red, two are in the green, and one is in the blue. The discharge still passes as a narrow spark throughout the length of the tube. In the wide section, the spectrum remains continuous and extends further toward the red and blue ends than in the capillary section. It seems as if the four lines had taken some of the energy from the continuous spectrum. As the pressure decreases, these lines increase considerably in strength; the spark spreads out in the wide section of the tube, and the intensity of the continuous spectrum is therefore significantly diminished, although it still remains a prominent part of the spectrum in the capillary section. When the pressure is low, the continuous spectrum decreases in intensity. At the same time, the negative glow, with its own characteristic spectrum, gradually extends through the negative half of the tube into the capillary section. The continuous spectrum has now entirely disappeared; the bands of the negative pole and the four lines stand out against a perfectly black background. It is under these conditions that the change from the compound line spectrum to the

elementary line spectrum is best studied. I find that simply inserting a Leyden jar makes hardly any difference; the jar does not seem to be charged at all. If, in addition to the jar, we insert a movable air break—which can be opened or closed at will while looking through the spectroscope—we will be able to see two perfectly distinct spectra alternately. If the air break is closed, only the four lines of the compound spectrum are visible; if the air break is opened, these four lines will disappear entirely, and the elementary line spectrum will appear. We have as much right to consider the two line spectra of oxygen as two distinct spectra as we do in the case of the two spectra of nitrogen, as the transformation occurs under exactly the same circumstances.

There are two reasons why the existence of a separate line spectrum of oxygen might have escaped the notice of previous observers. The blue line of the compound line spectrum is very near a bright line of the elementary line spectrum and cannot be distinguished from it unless high dispersive power is used—and even then, only when special attention is paid to the line.

To an observer looking at this line with low power, it would seem as if, upon the introduction of the air break, other lines spring up to its right and left which are brighter than the blue line being observed. However, the observer would notice that the blue line itself has disappeared and has been replaced by another line that is slightly more refrangible and of about the same brightness.

Again, in tubes with a rather wide capillary bore, such as those with the dimensions given on page 43 under heading B, it is impossible to completely get rid of the lines of the compound line spectrum. The effect of the jar and air break is only to widen the lines considerably, not to extinguish them. If the pressure in a tube is high, these lines widen significantly and finally fuse together to form a continuous spectrum. This has been well described by <term>WÜLLNER</term>, who likened the lines in this respect to hydrogen lines. Observations regarding the disappearance of these lines must, therefore, be made under low pressure when the continuous spectrum has vanished; the phenomenon is then very striking. If a spark is passed through oxygen at atmospheric pressure, a strong but blurry red line is seen, nearly coinciding with the red line of the compound spectrum. I admit I have not been able to determine with certainty whether the two lines are identical or not. The compound line spectrum widens considerably with increased pressure, primarily toward the less refrangible side. At first sight, the atmospheric line is decidedly less refrangible than the line of the compound line spectrum, and the measurements of the line in the atmosphere by <term>THALÈN</term> and <term>HUGGINS</term> give a wave-length significantly larger than the one I obtained for the line of the compound spectrum. Yet, if one accounts for a one-sided widening—so that the line is compared with the edge of the atmospheric band rather than its center—I am inclined to think that the two may prove to be identical. ### 8. *The Spectrum of the Negative Pole.*

This spectrum was first accurately described by <term>WÜLLNER</term>.* When examined, as he did, with low dispersive power, it seems to consist of four distinct, unshaded bands; but, as I have already said, I was able to resolve the bands into separate lines. In this case, I have also taken great care to show that the spectrum is actually due to pure oxygen, and not to impurities in the gas, the nature of the electrode, or the influence of the glass. It is interesting to note that in Experiment 6 (page 47), when the spectrum of the spark at atmospheric pressure was continuous, a purple point was seen on the negative electrode which produced the spectrum of the negative pole. The peculiar circumstances that favor the production of this spectrum always exist at the negative pole and are independent of the mode of discharge.

### III. *Electrodynamic Qualities of Metals.—Part VII. Effects of Stress on the Magnetization of Iron, Nickel, and Cobalt.*

### By Professor Sir WILLIAM THOMSON, F.R.S.

->Received May 9—Read May 23, 1878.<-

---

->[PLATES 2–13.]<-

---

->§§ 198 and 199.<-

198. In a preliminary notice of investigations regarding the effects of stress on inductive magnetization in soft iron, communicated to the Royal Society on June 10, 1875, I described experiments that provided a complete explanation of the seeming anomalies mentioned in §§ 194 and 195, <margin>* Phil. Trans. for 1876, p. 710 (Read May 27, 1875).</margin> which had at first been so perplexing. These experiments showed that the decrease of magnetism in a soft iron wire, which I had found was produced by a pull while the wire was under the influence of a constant magnetizing force, was to be observed only when the magnetizing force exceeded a certain critical value. When the magnetizing force was below that critical value, the effect of the pull was to increase the magnetism—a result which I later found had been previously obtained by VILLARI. <margin>† POGGENDORFF'S 'Annalen,' 1868; also WIEDEMANN'S 'Galvanismus,' vol. ii., § 499.</margin> I found the critical value of the magnetizing force to be about twenty-four times the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic force at Glasgow. Therefore, the magnetizing force which I had used in my first experiment, which (§ 183) was nearly 300 times the vertical component of the Earth's force, must have been about twelve times as great as the critical value. Furthermore (and most puzzling), I found the absolute amount of the effects of the pull to be actually greater with the small magnetizing force of the Earth than the opposite effects of the 300-fold greater magnetizing force of my early experiments. Thus, the effect of the Earth's force was not only in the correct direction, but was of a large enough amount to account for the seeming anomalies which had at first been so perplexing; and in reviewing the details of the old observations, I find all the anomalies are quite explained. One of them, the one particularly mentioned in § 195, is still interesting. The alternate increase of the residual magnetism when the weight was "on" and decrease of it when it was "off," with the weight of 14 lbs., corresponded to the normal effect on residual magnetism in soft iron. The 8 percent elongation produced when the 28 lbs. was hung on was undoubtedly accompanied by a shaking out of almost all the residual magnetism, and an inductive magnetization in the opposite direction by the vertical component of

<summary>Sir William Thomson explains how mechanical stress affects the magnetization of soft iron, noting a "critical value" of magnetizing force that determines whether a pull increases or decreases magnetism. Further experimental investigation is necessary to explain the *greater* magnitude of the effect—which was the same in kind as those observed before the stretching by 28 pounds—that the wire showed after it had been stretched by this weight.

199. The experiments indicated in my preliminary notice of June 10, 1875, were the beginning of an extensive series of investigations by <term>Mr. Andrew Gray</term> and <term>Mr. Thomas Gray</term>, which have been continued with little interruption from that time until now, and which are still ongoing, with the general objective of investigating the effects of longitudinal and transverse stress upon the magnetization of different qualities of iron and steel, and of nickel and cobalt. A separate series of investigations was made nearly two years ago by <term>Mr. Donald Macfarlane</term> on the effects of torsion on the magnetization of soft iron, revealing some very remarkable results, which are also included in this paper (§§ 223–229, below).

*§§ 200–212. Investigation by the Ballistic\* method, of the change of Magnetization produced in a specimen of exceedingly soft Iron Wire, by the application and removal of pulling force.*

200. The wire used in these experiments was specially prepared for this investigation by <term>Messrs. Richard Johnson and Nephew, Manchester</term>. It was of No. 22 <term>Birmingham wire gauge</term>; its weight per meter was 3.47 grams, and its diameter was 0.075 centimeters. A steel piano wire of the same gauge would bear about 230 pounds applied and removed without consequently undergoing any permanent change of quality. This iron wire was so soft that, after it was stretched by a scale-pan weighing 1 pound (which from then on was kept always hanging on it), an additional weight of 14 pounds applied and removed gave a permanent elongation of 0.4 percent, and 4 pounds more gave it a further permanent elongation of 1.6 percent (making a total of 2 percent permanent elongation produced by 18 pounds applied and removed, while the permanent weight of 1 pound was always attached). The weight of 18 pounds was applied and removed several times on the 14th of May without producing any more permanent elongation than the 1.6 percent observed after the first application and removal. For nine months after that day, no weight of more than 14 pounds (in addition to the permanent 1 pound) was ever applied to the wire, and electromagnetic experiments were conducted on it daily, with little interruption, with applications and removals of 14 pounds, and sometimes 7 pounds. During all this time, the length of the wire (about 4 meters) remained practically constant for the same weight, and the wire experienced regular elastic elongations

201. The accompanying diagram (I.) shows the arrangement of the apparatus by which the results were obtained. The wire, W, experimented on was attached to a fixed support near the ceiling of the laboratory and hung vertically downward, passing along the common axis of the magnetizing and induction coils, F, and was kept stretched by the scale-pan, D, which, as stated above, weighed exactly 1 lb. The coils, F, were supported on a clamp attached to the wire at their lower end, as shown in the drawing; and thus, as the length of the induction coil was small compared with the total length of the wire, the motion of the wire relative to the induction coil due to the stretching produced by the applied stress was largely avoided. The magnetizing coil was 86 centimeters long and was composed of two layers of silk-covered copper wire. The inner layer contained 26.7 meters of wire, of No. 23 B.W.G., arranged in a solenoid* of 960 turns; the outer layer, 24.3 meters of No. 20 wire, arranged in a solenoid of 728 turns. The resistance per meter of these wires was .0673 and .0522 ohm respectively, and the total resistance of the coil after it was wound was 3.134 ohms. The total length of the induction coil, which was contained within the magnetizing coil, was 31.5 centimeters. It was made up of two layers of silk-covered copper wire, of No. 29 B.W.G., laid on in 1439 turns. The wire thus coiled on was 10 meters long and had a resistance of .184 ohm per meter, and the total resistance of the coil, including 1 meter of electrodes, was 2.204 ohms.

<margin>* The common use of the word "helix" in this sense is completely illogical. The idea of a helix is not essential, but accidental, and in no practical case is it of any consequence whether it is a right-handed or a left-handed helix. There is nothing of helical quality in a cylindrical tube composed of two metals in two parts of its circumference, with the junctions of these metals kept at unequal temperatures. The thermoelectric current around the circumference of the solenoid produces the type of magnetizing influence which is commonly produced by a helix, and constitutes precisely the arrangement which <term>Ampère</term> called a solenoid. It is only because the ordinary helix, with an electric current flowing through it, produces more or less approximately (very approximately indeed in the case of a helix with many turns) the same effect, that it is available for electromagnetic uses. It seems desirable, therefore, to take advantage of <term>Ampère’s</term> original word "solenoid," and, except in cases in which the helical quality is taken into account, to give up the name "helix." The electromagnetic solenoid may also be called a bar electromagnet without a soft iron core.</margin>

The magnetizing coil was wound on the outside of a compound tube, made up of two tubes of thin brass of different diameters, placed one within the other with their axes coincident; the external diameter of the inner tube was less than the internal diameter of the outer by about 3 millimeters. The induction coil, which was wound on a thin copper tube just fitting the wire experimented on, was enclosed within the inner brass tube in such a position that its ends were at equal distances from the extremities of the magnetizing coil. This slide was designed to allow the battery strength to be raised continuously from 0 to nearly 1 cell, and from 1 cell to nearly 2 cells, and so on. This wire, which was 64 meters in length and had a resistance of 0.67 ohm, was stretched for convenience alternately from one side of a large board to the other, in the manner shown in the diagram. Thus, with the number of cells and arrangement of connections shown in the diagram, when the slider was brought as close as possible to C, the current flowing was very nearly that of 3 cells; when the slider made contact at any other point on the wire, the current flowing through the magnetizing coil was less than that of 3 cells by an amount depending on the distance of the slider from C along the wire.

Thus, the full range of the galvanometer scale was available for measuring the deflections produced by the stronger currents used, without the necessity of shifting the zero point of the scale using a magnet. In these experiments, the battery galvanometer was initially placed for convenience in the circuit between the commutator K and the coils F, and a reversing key was used to keep the current through it always in the same direction, but it was afterwards moved to the position in the circuit shown in the diagram and the reversing key was removed. (referred to in this paper as the ballistic galvanometer), the "throw" of which, as observed on a scale placed 120 centimeters (or 2400 of its own divisions) from the mirror, measured the strength of the induced current. This galvanometer was placed within a case of thin sheet copper, and the entire apparatus was enclosed within a glass bell jar to protect it from the effects of air currents.

205. The experimental procedure was similar to that described in Part VI, § 186 (Transactions for 1876, p. 697). One observer took the readings of the ballistic galvanometer and applied or interrupted the circuit of the magnetizing current; while a second observer, at the command of the first, applied or removed the weight and noted the elongations or contractions of the wire, as shown by the pointer and scale described above. The results were entered into the register using the system followed in my previous experiments, according to which **+M** denoted that the current was applied in such a direction as to cause the image on the scale of the ballistic galvanometer to move toward the right (toward increasing numbers); **-M** indicated that the current was applied in the opposite direction; **B** signaled that the current was stopped; **Z** was the zero point of the ballistic galvanometer scale; "**On**" referred to the application of the weight; and "**Off**" referred to its removal. The polarity of the magnetization produced in the wire by **+M** was the same as that shown by the wire when under the influence of the vertical component of the earth's magnetic force alone. Consequently, a deflection of the image on the scale toward the right, produced by a change in the magnetic condition of the wire after it had been thus magnetized, indicated an increase in its magnetization, and a deflection to the left indicated a decrease in its magnetization. I shall call the magnetization produced by **+M** "positive magnetization," and that produced by **-M** "negative magnetization." Therefore, a deflection of the ballistic image toward the right indicates an increase in positive magnetization, and a deflection toward the left indicates a decrease in positive magnetization or an increase in negative magnetization.

206. The conclusions of the preliminary notice of June 17, 1876, and the statements of § 198, are proved by the following table of results, obtained by a very careful repetition of the experiments mentioned in that notice. The first column of results in the table lists the operations in the order in which they were performed; the second gives the deflections of the image on the scale of the ballistic galvanometer obtained after each operation; and the third column gives the battery strengths. Throughout the experiments, cold water was kept flowing from cistern B through the channel between the coils to vessel H to prevent the coils and wire from heating due to the passage of the magnetizing current. The amount of elongation and contraction of the wire caused by the application and removal of the 14-pound weight was constant throughout the experiments. Each experiment began with zero current, and the 14-pound weight was applied and removed until equal and opposite effects were obtained by the "on" and "off" actions; the same process was followed after each increase of the magnetizing current. The table contains only the results obtained for each step after this stable state had been reached.

210. The curves in Diagram III were drawn by taking the mean effect for each temperature of $+M$ and $-M$ for 14 lbs. "on" or "off" as the ordinates, and the corresponding current strengths as the abscissas; they therefore show approximately the effect that would have been produced by "on" or "off" had the wire not been affected by the magnetizing force of the earth.

By comparing the curve for cold water with the curve for hot water, we see that when the wire is at a temperature of $100^\circ$ C., the average maximum effect of "on" or "off" is less than at the ordinary temperature of cold water by about 8 percent of the effect in the latter case. Furthermore, when the <term>VILLARI critical value</term> has been exceeded, the constant value toward which the effect of "on" or "off" approaches is lower for the higher temperature than for the lower—in this case, by about 30 percent of the amount of the effect at the lower temperature. The two curves also cross one another at a point above the line of abscissas, thus showing a higher critical value of the magnetizing force for the higher temperature than for the lower.

211. The curves of Diagrams IV and V show, at both temperatures, the average effect for each strength of magnetizing current when applying and removing stresses of 7 lbs. and 21 lbs., respectively.

A comparison of these curves with the average curves for 14 lbs. "on" and "off" (Section II above) shows:

(1.) That the effect at both temperatures of applying and removing the stress is greater with 14 lbs. than with 7 lbs., and much greater with 21 lbs. than with 14 lbs.; the maxima at the ordinary temperature in these three cases are 31, 35, and 54, respectively.

(2.) That the <term>VILLARI critical value</term> is much greater for 7 lbs. "on" and "off" than for 14 lbs., and is also greater for 21 lbs. than for 14 lbs., though by a smaller difference.

(3.) The difference between the maximum effects of "on" or "off" for the high and low temperatures is greater for 7 lbs. than for either 14 lbs. or 21 lbs., and appears to be greater for 21 lbs. than for 14 lbs.

### §§ 214-222. *Preliminary investigation by the direct Magnetometric Method of the effects of transverse stress on the Magnetization of an Iron Tube.*

214. In order to qualitatively test the initial effects of transverse stress on the magnetization of iron, experiments were performed on a smooth gun barrel, reported to be made of fairly soft iron. The barrel was fitted at its muzzle with a piston working in a watertight manner within a Bramah stuffing box. It was wrapped in a magnetizing coil of silk-covered copper wire, separated from the barrel by a copper tube, and contained an induction coil so that the <term>ballistic method</term> could be used if deemed advisable. The barrel was then fixed rigidly to a stone pier in the laboratory, with its breech end resting on a large block of stone which formed the base of the pier. On a shelf, also attached to the pier and at a convenient distance due magnetic west of the barrel's axis, a small reflecting magnetometer was placed with its needle level with the top of the barrel. A <term>dead-beat galvanometer</term>, with a resistance of only a small fraction of an ohm, was used to measure the magnetizing current. After the barrel was filled with water, it was subjected to hydrostatic pressure applied by a weighted lever; the lever itself was counterbalanced by a weight attached to a cord passing over a pulley above. The pressure (neglecting the friction of the piston in its collar) was measured by the amount of the applied weight and the leverage ratio. The effects of applying and removing the pressure were measured by the deflections of the galvanometer needle, read on a scale of half-millimeters placed at a distance of one meter from the mirror.

215. The first experiments, conducted after the apparatus was operational, revealed the remarkable result that the effects of transverse stress on the magnetization of iron are, in quality, the opposite of those of longitudinal stress. That is to say, when the magnetizing force is less than a certain critical value, the effect of applying transverse stress is to diminish induced magnetization, and removing it increases it; however, when this critical value has been exceeded, the effect of applying transverse stress is to increase induced magnetization, and removing it diminishes it.

The curves (1) of Diagram VII show (following the style of Diagram II above) the effect for both $+M$ and $-M$ on the magnetometer needle when placed on a level

217. The magnetometer needle was placed on a level with the top of the barrel and at a distance of two meters from its axis. Experiments were then made to find the total magnetization produced by different strengths of magnetizing current, and the effects on it of ten successive applications and removals of a hydrostatic pressure of 1000 lbs. per square inch while the current was still flowing. Experiments were also made to find the total residual magnetism after the removal of the magnetizing current—when the tube was left solely under the influence of the earth's vertical magnetic force—and the effect on it of ten successive applications and removals of the same hydrostatic pressure while the bar was still under this magnetizing influence. The general character of the results of these experiments is difficult to describe in words but can be seen by inspecting Diagram VIII, in which the curves marked A show the total magnetization, and those marked B show the residual magnetization. The abscissas of these curves are proportional to the magnetizing forces and the ordinates to the observed magnetization; however, they have inadvertently been drawn so that their negative ordinates show magnetization of the same polarity as that produced by the inductive influence of the earth's vertical force, and their positive ordinates show magnetization of the opposite polarity. The solid lines in each set of curves show the magnetization before, and the dotted lines show it after, ten "on" and "off" applications of a pressure of 1000 lbs. per square inch.

-> \* The length of the barrel and of the magnetizing coil was about 90 centimeters. <-

# SIR WILLIAM THOMSON ON THE

The results in these experiments were obtained by beginning with a *negative* magnetizing current (meaning one opposed to the earth's magnetizing force) of about 700 divisions on the battery galvanometer scale. This current was gradually diminished to zero and then increased until a *positive* current of 700 divisions (using 20 cells) was reached. This process was then exactly reversed. The results may be examined in the order they were obtained by starting at the left-hand ends of curves A and B and moving to the right along the thinner lines, then returning to the left along the thicker lines.

218. The magnetometer was found in this position to be too far from the barrel to accurately show the residual magnetism; accordingly, its distance from the barrel was reduced to one meter, and the effects of residual magnetism alone were observed. These are shown by the curves marked B' on Diagram VIII'. The method and order of the experiment were the same as described in § 217. The explanation of Diagram VIII, curves B, also applies to Diagram VIII', except that in the latter, the directions of the ordinates are reversed from the former; thus, in VIII', positive ordinates indicate positive magnetization, and negative ordinates indicate negative magnetization (see § 205).

219. Beginning at the extreme left of the curves marked B' on Diagram VIII' and following the arrows, it will be seen that the residual magnetism remains nearly constant in amount until the magnetizing current has been diminished to about 300 divisions. At that point, it begins to take a greater negative value and continues to do so until the current is reduced to 50 divisions, when it begins to slowly diminish. After the reversal of the current, the full residual magnetism diminishes with great rapidity, passing through zero at about 15 divisions of positive current. It then becomes positive, maintaining nearly the same rate of change for some distance beyond zero. After a positive current of 150 divisions is reached, the full residual magnetism increases very slowly, and the curve becomes asymptotic toward a value of about 440. The curve showing the residual magnetism after ten cycles of "on" and "off" has characteristics similar to those for the full residual magnetism; however, the increase on the left side of zero at about 300 divisions of negative current is more pronounced.

The general character of the return curves is similar to what has just been described. It should be noted, however, that the zero point of the current in each of them is passed by a much greater margin before the zero point of magnetization is reached. This difference between the outgoing and returning curves would be eliminated, and the curves from left to right and right to left in the diagram would be perfectly symmetrical around the zero of the magnetizing current, if the influence of the earth's magnetic force were removed. I intend to return to this subject with a modification of the experimental setup to allow the residual magnetism to be observed without any influence from magnetizing force along the length of the tube; rather than, as is the case here, having the tube always under the magnetizing action of the vertical component of the earth's magnetic force when the electromagnetic current is not flowing.

ELECTRODYNAMIC QUALITIES OF METALS.

Turning the current on and off ten times was not enough to remove the effect of the powerful magnetizing force of the current, nor did it allow the barrel to take on the magnetization caused by the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic force. In fact, these actions only reduced the residual magnetism in the curves—both from left to right and from right to left—by about 100 divisions, out of total residuals ranging from 230 to 440. It is interesting to see, by comparing the right-hand ends of the curves with the left-hand ends, how much stronger the residual magnetism is when helped by the vertical magnetic force of the Earth compared to when it is opposed by it.

220. A comparison between the results of the effects of longitudinal and transverse pull shows that an <term>aeolotropic</term> property (having different magnetic inductive susceptibility in different directions) is temporarily developed in soft iron by aeolotropic stress (that is, by stress that does not consist of equal positive or negative pressure in all directions). The results show that with low magnetizing forces, negative pressure <note>tension</note> perpendicular to one set of parallel planes of soft iron produces an increase in magnetic susceptibility in the direction of the pressure and a decrease in susceptibility in all directions at right angles to it. The effects of positive pressure <note>compression</note> have not yet been tested experimentally, but it is certain that they will be opposite to the effects of negative pressure. Independent of experiment, we may also infer that the effects of an infinitely small positive pressure perpendicular to one set of parallel planes, and an infinitely small negative pressure of an equal amount perpendicular to a set of parallel planes at right angles to them, must be equal and opposite in the directions of these pressures. Therefore, this must leave the magnetic susceptibility unchanged in the directions angled at 45° to them. This is exactly the stress experienced in a twisted wire with a circular section; the amount of stress is zero at the axis of the wire and elsewhere is in simple proportion to the distance from the axis. The directions of the positive and negative pressures at any point in the material are two lines on the tangent plane of the cylindrical surface passing through it, coaxial with the boundary of the wire, and angled at 45° to the perpendicular plane section. Hence, when the torsion is infinitely small, the magnetic susceptibility of the wire in the direction of its length must be unchanged. If finite amounts of torsion produce any change in magnetic susceptibility, the amount of this change must ultimately (for very small torsions) vary inversely with the square of the amount of torsion. This is evident because whatever effect is produced must be independent of the direction of the torsion, as there is no helical quality in longitudinal magnetization.

221. In <term>WIEDEMANN’S</term> ‘Galvanismus’ (vol. II, §§ 476–498), an abstract is given of research on this subject by <term>MATTEUCCI</term>, <term>WERTHEIM</term>, and <term>EDMUND BECQUEREL</term>.* One main result of all these investigations is that torsion in either direction reduces the temporary inductive longitudinal magnetization of soft iron.

222. Nearly two years ago, I started a series of experiments on this subject.

chiefly for the purpose of finding the influence of torsion upon the longitudinal magnetization of soft iron wire subjected to different amounts of pulling force.
