### §§ 223–229. *Experiments on the effect of torsion and stretching in altering the induced Magnetism of a very soft Iron Wire, subjected to various amounts of constant pull.*

223.—*Description of Apparatus.*—In Diagram IX (facing § 201 above), AB is a soft iron wire, gauge No. 22, 81 centimeters long, to the ends of which were soldered pieces of No. 16 copper wire; the upper piece, AD, about 5 meters in length, was attached to the ceiling of the room with an arrangement for raising or lowering it through a small space; the lower piece, BC, about 50 centimeters long, had a scale-pan attached to its lower end for holding the stretching weight.

E is a small mirror magnetometer—the mirror being 1 centimeter in diameter, carrying a magnet 8 millimeters in length and suspended at N by a single silk fiber 10 centimeters long—and I is a lens close to the mirror; F is a paraffin lamp; and GH is a scale (bent into a circular arc with E at the center), on which an image is formed of a fine wire placed in front of the lamp flame at E.

L and M are two edges at right angles to one another, fixed to the stand carrying the magnetometer and just in contact with the wire: their use is to ensure that the wire is maintained in the same position relative to the center of the magnet.

K is an arm soldered to the copper wire, BC, for applying torsion to the wire, and immediately below it is a circle divided at intervals of 45° 20′, with small holes at each division for inserting pegs to keep the arm twisted at any angle while readings are being taken.

A similar arm was soldered to the copper wire AD at O, the two ends of which were in contact with two vertical guides, thus confining the twist to the portion of wire between K and O.

The distance of the wire from the center of the magnetometer needle was 8.2 centimeters; the distance of the scale from the mirror was 157 centimeters; one division of the scale equaled 0.5 millimeters.

The experiments represented in Diagrams No. X to No. XXIX were made in this way:—

After removing the wire to a distance from the magnetometer, the zero reading of the latter was taken; the wire was placed in position, a stretching weight was put in the scale-pan, and the reading on the torsion circle was noted when the wire was free from torsional stress; torsion was then applied by turning the lower end of the wire 20° at a time up to 320°, and the reading on the magnetometer scale was taken at each step.

225. From the curves, it can be seen that the extent of the effect of torsion in reducing magnetization is not greatly influenced by differences in pull between 10 lbs. and 20 lbs., but that it is greatly reduced by an increase in the pull above 20 lbs. For the sake of simplicity and consistency in the comparison, consider the amount of reduction in magnetization caused by the first application of torsion in the negative direction, across the whole range from +50° to -200° on the torsion scale (the abscissas of the curves).

With pulls ranging from 10 lbs. to 20 lbs., we find various amounts between 180 and 230 magnetometer scale divisions. The seemingly irregular differences between these amounts showed no consistent dependence on the amount of pull, but instead appeared to depend upon the previous condition of the wire. However, when the weight exceeded 20 lbs., there appeared to be a somewhat regular decrease in the effect of torsion as the pull increased, as shown in the following table:

# SIR WILLIAM THOMSON ON THE

226. One very interesting feature common to all the diagrams—and shown to some degree even by the exceptional ones 9, 10, 12, and 14—shows that the effect of twisting the wire first in one direction and then in the other, and then releasing it from <term>torsive force</term>, was in every case to leave it with less magnetization than it had at the beginning.

227. These exceptional diagrams and the later continuation of the operations through a second positive <term>torsion</term> and a second negative torsion (represented in the latter halves of the curves in Diagrams XXIV to XXIX) show the general character of the effect of continued, periodic applications of positive and negative torsion through equal angles on both sides of zero.

In every case, there is a lagging of quality, showing a residual effect from previously acting causes. For example, beginning with a wire that had been reduced to a normal condition by having the weight added and removed and being left to itself for twenty-four hours, we found on the 24th of August that the magnetization fell from a normal value of 685 down to 550 as a result of twisting it to $+260^\circ$, then to $-260^\circ$, and then to zero torsion. The second application of positive and negative torsion further reduced the magnetization to 534. It is curious to find that torsion not only diminishes the magnetization temporarily, but that it also leaves such a large permanent reduction. Whether this permanence is absolute over time or not is an interesting question to be solved by leaving a wire that has been treated this way completely undisturbed from day to day, month to month, year to year, or even century to century. It seems, however, that only a slight mechanical disturbance is enough to shake out the reduction of magnetization left at the end of each of these experiments.

228. The general lagging of effect is shown by the fact that in every ascending branch, the curve is lower than in the immediately preceding descending branch. The dotted latter halves of the long curves in Diagrams XXIV to XXIX show—by the intersections of their convex portions near the zero—that if the experiment were continued long enough, the history of the variation of magnetization would in every case be represented by a curve like the one in the attached sketch.

The author notes that while this reduction persists over time in a quiescent state, it is easily removed by mechanical vibration.</summary>

229. A very interesting discovery of WIEDEMANN’S (‘Galvanismus,’ §§ 491 and 498) seemed, at first sight, to find its explanation in the aeolotropic difference of magnetic susceptibility which I have found to be induced by aeolotropic stress in soft iron. The phenomenon consists of the development of longitudinal magnetization by twisting a wire through which a magnetic galvanic current is maintained lengthwise. The attached double diagram, copied from WIEDEMANN’S book,* describes the change of

->*fig.1.* &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *fig.2.*<-

<image-desc>Two side-by-side diagrams of vertical cylinders (wires) under torsion. Fig. 1 shows a cylinder with a downward arrow at the top and internal magnetic molecules aligned in a right-handed spiral. Fig. 2 shows a cylinder with an upward arrow at the top and internal magnetic molecules aligned in a left-handed spiral. The molecules are marked with 'n' and 's' to indicate polarity.</image-desc>

ideal magnetic molecules which would represent the actually observed effect. This effect is that the end of the wire where the current enters becomes a true north pole when the twist given to it is right-handed (or like that of an ordinary screw). If this effect were due to greater susceptibility in one direction than in another, the direction of greatest susceptibility would be the direction sloping at 45°, upwards to the right in the front of the right-hand diagram; that is to say, it would be the direction of positive pull in the stressed material. But the exceedingly intense magnetization caused by the circular lines of force around the cylinder, produced by currents of such strength as WIEDEMANN may be supposed to have used, must in all probability have been above the critical degree of magnetization at which the effect of pull becomes reversed. Therefore, in all probability, the direction of least susceptibility in these actual circumstances must have been that of positive pull. Hence, it seems almost impossible to accept the explanation of WIEDEMANN’S result by aeolotropic magnetic susceptibility in these circumstances.† The true explanation is not easily guessed, for another cause, also contrary to WIEDEMANN’S result, is at work. The electric conductivity of the iron is probably lowest in the direction of the positive pull and greatest in the direction of the negative pull in the stressed material.‡ This aeolotropic quality in

### §§ 230–240. *On the effects of longitudinal stress on the Magnetization of Nickel and Cobalt.*

§ 230. Through the kindness of <term>Mr. JOSEPH WHARTON</term> of Philadelphia, USA, I was able to continue my experiments with malleable and cast bars of nickel, and of cast cobalt.

<note>Note added July 8, 1879: A qualitative analysis of one of <term>Mr. WHARTON'S</term> nickel bars, performed in the Chemical Laboratory of Glasgow University by <term>Mr. DONALD MACKENZIE</term>, showed that the bar was not absolutely pure nickel, but contained some carbonaceous matter and also a trace of iron. The amount of the latter, however, was very small and probably did not significantly affect the results of the experiments described below.</note>

The apparatus used in the preliminary experiments and its arrangement are shown in the attached diagram (XXX.). Each end of the rod being tested was inserted into a ferrule-shaped clamp, C (also shown separately in plan and elevation view), the outer surface of which was conical and threaded.

The clamp, which had three longitudinal slits, was then made to grasp the rod tightly by means of a conical nut working around it. This allowed for the application of a great amount of longitudinal pull without much danger of the clamps pulling away from the rod. One of the clamps was then hung from a pin in a strong cross-beam of a frame, so that the bar hung vertically downward.

A copper wire rope, R, connected the other clamp to a point near the end of a long, heavy lever. This lever turned on a fulcrum at that end, formed by a knife-edge pressing upward against a brass plate that formed a bridge between two strong, rigid uprights attached to the floor of the room. A heavy lead weight was hung on the lever and could be slid along it to apply different amounts of stress. The lever was graduated, and the effect of its own weight was measured so that the applied stress could be read at any time. When the bar was in position but not under stress, the lever rested on a support high enough to allow the wire rope R to be slack; the lever was then gently removed from this support when the pulling stress was applied.

232. In Table I, it is stated that when the iron bar was placed in position, the image on the scale of the magnetometer was driven off the scale in the negative direction. A controlling magnet, 15 centimeters long, placed at right angles to the <term>magnetic meridian</term> in a horizontal line passing through the center of the needle, was used to bring the image to division 769 on the scale. When the closer end of this magnet was at a distance of 23 centimeters from the needle, the image rested at division 323 on the scale; and when the magnet was brought 6 centimeters closer to the needle, it rested at division 773 on the scale. Hence, taking the tangent of the angle of deflection as equal to the angle itself, we may calculate the deflection caused by bringing the iron bar of Table I into position as 1369 scale divisions, which may be taken as measuring the magnetism of the bar.<note>The method of calculation is as follows:—Let A denote the deflection produced by placing the bar in position; D and D' the readings with the controlling magnet introduced, with its center at the distances r and r' from the magnet; a the half-length of the magnet; and B a constant depending on the controlling magnet; then we have,

-> D = A + B / (r-a)^2 - B / (r+a)^2 = A + 4Bar / (r^2-a^2)^2 <-

and similarly

-> D' = A + 4Bar' / (r'^2-a^2)^2 <-

Eliminating B between these two equations, and solving for A, we get

-> A = (D+D')/2 - (D-D')/2 * [r'(r^2-a^2)^2 + r(r'^2-a^2)^2] / [r(r^2-a^2)^2 - r'(r'^2-a^2)^2] <-

233. Passing now to the nickel bar of Table II, we see that when the bar was placed in position, it showed 10 divisions of positive magnetism (or magnetism of the same polarity as that induced by the Earth). The application of 146 lbs of pull gave it 29 divisions, and the removal of this pull gave 10 divisions of additional magnetism; that is, both "on" and "off" increased the magnetism. A second application of the pull gave a decrease of 5, and removal an increase of 6 divisions. The rest of the procedure was similar to that followed in the case of the soft iron, and with the exception of the first result after the bar was placed in the clamps, the effect of "on" was always to *diminish* the magnetism of the bar, and of "off" to *increase* it.

After the bar was placed in the clamps, the effect of the successive operations was, on the whole, to gradually increase the total magnetization of the bar from the value 10 to the value 155, at which it stood when the experiment was concluded.

234. From Table III, we see that the bar of cast cobalt, when placed in position, had its true north pole down and gave a deflection of 392 divisions. Ten "ons" and "offs" with 136 lbs diminished this deflection by 85 divisions. The effect of "on" was then to *increase* the magnetism by 15 divisions, and of "off" to *diminish* it by the same amount; that is to say, "on" increased the magnetism of the bar, and "off" diminished it. A few blows of a mallet reversed this magnetism and caused the bar to give a deflection of 90 divisions in the opposite direction. The effect of "on" was, as with the nickel bar, to diminish the magnetism, and of "off" to increase it, the effect of 146 lbs being 25 divisions of the magnetometer scale, and of 174 lbs being 29 divisions. The bar broke before the effect of the application of 249 lbs could be observed. After the reversal of the magnetism by tapping the bar while under the influence of the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic force, there was very little gradual change in the magnetization of the bar.

235. The effect of longitudinal stress on the magnetization of nickel when magnetized by a current flowing in a coil surrounding the bar formed the subject of the next series of investigations. The magnetizing coil was 54 centimeters long, and consisted of six layers of silk-covered copper wire of No. 22 B.W.G., each layer forming a solenoid containing 10.7 turns per centimeter. The resistance of the coil when cool was 7.2 ohms, and the resistance of the electrodes 0.3 of an ohm. In this experiment the magnetometer was placed at a distance of 40 centimeters from the axis of the bar, and on a level with its lower end; and in order that the deflection due to the total magnetization of the bar might be conveniently measured, the directive force on the magnetometer needle was increased by placing behind it, in the magnetic meridian, a bar magnet, with its true north pole turned towards the north. As in the previous experiments with iron and steel, —M indicates that the electromagnetic field was opposite in polarity to that of the earth, and +M that its polarity was the same as that of the earth. The dead-beat galvanometer used in the experiments on the effects of transverse stress on the magnetization of an iron tube was again employed to measure the strength of the magnetizing current.

236. The results of a series of these experiments are given in Table IV. It will be seen from that table that the effects of the application and removal of stress were respectively to diminish and to increase the induced magnetization, and that, as in the case of soft iron, this effect reached a maximum with a certain strength of magnetizing current, after which it slowly diminished. In this experiment the critical value of the magnetizing force corresponding to what has been called above, in the account of experiments in soft iron, the <term>VILLARI critical value</term>, was not reached.

237. The preceding table shows that the effect of applying a pull was to diminish, and removing a pull to increase, the magnetism of the bar, whether induced or residual; and that a series of these operations *increased* on the whole the magnetism induced by + M or — M, but diminished on the whole the residual magnetism after B <note>B likely refers to the "break" or cessation of the magnetizing current</note>. Furthermore, as stated above, the effect of applying or removing the load on the induced magnetism of the bar increases up to a certain point, and then diminishes as the magnetizing force is increased from zero upward; while, on the other hand, the effect of applying or removing the load on the residual magnetism continues to increase as the residual magnetism is increased, and, as does the residual magnetism itself, approaches more and more to a certain constant value.

to approach. It was found more convenient to continue the experiment with a smaller bar of nickel, kindly lent for the purpose by Professor <term>TAIT</term>. This (which was a square bar 45.7 centimeters long and 0.30 centimeter thick) was placed within a coil wound on a thin copper tube of just sufficient internal diameter to admit the bar. The coil contained six layers of silk-covered copper wire, of No. 22 B.W.G., each layer forming a solenoid 42.7 centimeters long, containing 10.7 turns per centimeter. The total resistance of the coil when cool was 4.33 ohms. The resistance of the electrodes was, as before, 0.3 of an ohm. The magnetometer needle was in this case placed on a level with the upper end of the bar, and at a distance of 25 centimeters from the axis of the bar, and of 108 centimeters from the scale of half millimeters on which the readings were observed. The stress was not applied by means of the lever, but a weight of 14 lbs. was placed on a pan attached to the bar. This pan, which weighed 1 lb., was left hanging on the bar during the whole experiment.

239. In their general character the results are precisely similar to those shown in Table IV. A maximum effect of 20 divisions was obtained when the magnetizing force was 194 divisions of the battery galvanometer scale, or that due to about 4 cells. As the magnetizing force was increased beyond this value the effects obtained gradually diminished, and seemed to reach zero when the magnetizing force was about 1000 divisions, or that due to about 40 cells. The results at this point could not, because of variations of the magnetizing force due to heating of the coil, be relied on as being accurate.

<note>Note added June 4, 1879.—This result has not been confirmed by experiments lately made with improved apparatus in which the effects of the heating of the magnetizing coil, formerly a great source of trouble, were to a great extent prevented. No sign of a neutral point was found, although battery powers of from 5 to 79 tray cells were employed for the purpose of magnetizing the nickel bar, which was the actual bar formerly experimented on.</note>

240. An experiment was then made to find whether this critical value could, as in the case of the soft iron tube, be obtained with a smaller degree of magnetizing force when the magnetometer was placed on a level with a point between the middle and end of the bar. Accordingly, the magnetometer was lowered 10 centimeters, and brought to a distance of 10 centimeters from the axis of the bar. The scale was left in its former position, and thus the distance of the mirror from it was increased to 123 centimeters. The directive force on the needle was also increased to 6.08 times that due to the horizontal component of the earth’s magnetic force. The maximum effect of the application and removal of stress was obtained with a magnetizing force of 50 scale-divisions, or that due to 1 cell. And the critical value was found without difficulty to be 428 divisions of the battery galvanometer scale, or the current due to 10 cells. Beyond that point the effect of “on” and “off” were respectively to increase and to diminish the induced magnetization of the bar, the effect with 707 divisions, or 20 cells, being about 3 1/2 divisions of the scale.

### §§ 241–244. *Experiment by the direct Magnetometric Method on the effects of longitudinal stress on the Magnetization of Iron Wire.*

241. In this experiment, the magnetizing coil described above (§ 201) was used. The total length of the wire (which was a piece of Messrs. <term>JOHNSON and Nephew</term>’s very soft iron wire, and cut from the same hank as that used in the former experiments) was 97 centimeters. As only the soldered fastenings of the wire projected beyond the ends of the coil, the magnetometer needle was placed level with the top of the coil, and at a distance from its axis of 25 centimeters; the distance from the mirror to the scale of the magnetometer was 108 centimeters.

242. This experiment confirmed in all essential points the results obtained by the ballistic method in the experiments described above (§§ 200–212). The effects of applying and removing a weight of 14 pounds were respectively *to increase* and *to diminish* by 31 divisions the magnetism induced in the wire by the vertical component of the earth’s magnetic force. The amount of this induced magnetism, when only the pan was hanging on the wire, was also 31 divisions. Hence, the application and removal of the 14 pounds alternately doubled the magnetization induced by the earth’s force and then reduced it to its previous amount.

When the magnetizing current was 4.25 divisions of the battery-galvanometer scale, the application and removal of pull produced no effect, thus showing that the influence of the earth’s magnetizing force was exactly counterbalanced by that due to the current. The maximum effect of applying and removing stress was obtained when the magnetizing force was about 50 divisions (one cell gave 70 divisions). The <term>VILLARI critical value</term> was obtained with 215 divisions of magnetizing current, or 50 times the magnetizing force which balanced the influence of the earth’s magnetic force. This is a much greater number than that obtained by the ballistic method; that it is so is no doubt due to the fact that the induction-coil then used was much shorter than the magnetizing coil, and was placed with the center of its length coinciding with that of the magnetizing coil. With the highest strength of current (567 divisions) the effect of “on” and “off” was 8.5 divisions, and the effects were, as in the former experiments, increasing very slowly.

243. The value in absolute units of the vertical component of the earth’s magnetic force was calculated from the value of the magnetizing current which balanced it, and the total resistance of the coil electrodes and battery, which were all measured for the purpose with great exactness. As before, the electromotive force of one tray cell was taken as one volt, or 10⁸ on the <term>C. G. S. system of units</term>. The total resistance with one cell in circuit was 3.503 ohms, the number of turns per centimeter in the coil 19.628, and the fraction of the cell which gave a magnetizing force which just balanced the earth was .0607 of that due to one cell. Hence we have vertical component $=\frac{4\pi \times \cdot0607 \times 10^8 \times 19\cdot628}{3\cdot503 \times 10^9} = \cdot429$, which must be very nearly its true value at Glasgow. (Compare with § 207 above.)

->DIRECTION OF THE LINES OF PRESSURE INSIDE THE RADIOMETER.<-

387. Although the general character of the reactions which cause repulsion under the influence of radiation is now understood, much light may be thrown on the subject by an experimental examination of the direction and strength of the lines of pressure inside the case of a radiometer on which light is allowed to fall. Radiation will pass almost unimpeded through a very thin, colorless, and transparent substance such as mica, but molecular pressure or stress is arrested by such a body (232). By introducing fixed or movable screens in various parts of the case of a radiometer, the direction of pressure can be determined at will, and its force can be modified in many ways, while all the other conditions of the experiment remain unchanged.

In this Part, I propose to give the results of a long series of experiments on the action of thin mica screens in modifying the movements of the fly of a radiometer; I shall examine the action of the residual gas, the action of the sides of the glass case, and the applicability of the information so afforded to the construction of instruments of greatly increased sensitivity for the purposes of research and illustration; and I shall also describe other experiments which have been tried from

time to time during the last few years—experiments which at the time were isolated in their bearings, but which now fit into their places.

388. My first experiments were directed to determine whether the lines of pressure could be deflected from their path by a thin plate of mica fixed on the fly of an ordinary radiometer. A two-disk radiometer was made, having flat roasted mica disks, coated with lampblack on one side (fig. 1, *a*). The lampblack surface is represented in

<image-desc>Two circular diagrams labeled Fig. 1 and Fig. 2. Fig. 1 shows a radiometer fly with two vanes; one vane has a secondary mica screen (b) placed in front of the lampblacked surface (a), with arrows indicating the direction of rotation and a point (c) where pressure is deflected. Fig. 2 shows a similar fly where the blacked disk is guarded on both sides by mica screens.</image-desc>

->Fig. 1.<- ->Fig. 2.<-

the figure by a row of dots close to the surface. In front of the black surface, and separated from it by a space of 1 millimeter, is fixed a thin disk of clear mica, *b*, about 1 millimeter larger in diameter than the blacked disk. When properly exhausted and exposed to the radiation from a candle, the normal direction of movement would be opposite to that shown by the arrows, assuming no screen were present. The screen has, however, changed the direction; the pressure, instead of reacting between the black surfaces and the sides of the glass case facing them, is deflected back, as shown at *c*, and the result is rapid rotation in the direction shown by the arrows, with the black side now approaching the light.

389. To test this action more completely, another thin mica disk was fixed on the plain side of the blacked disk, the latter being now guarded on each side, as in fig. 2. The effect of this is to cause an almost total loss of sensitivity, the fly now only moving very slowly in full sunshine.

390. Two explanations of the screen's action in fig. 1 suggest themselves. According to one, the radiation passes through the clear mica screen and generates molecular disturbance on the black surface. Because the screen prevents the direction of greatest stress from exerting itself between the black surface and the glass bulb, it is reflected back in the direction of the arrow, *c*, and produces negative rotation. Another view of the action is this: the radiation falling on the compound fly warms it in proportion to the amount absorbed. Molecular pressure is exerted on that side which is most easily warmed, and which most readily transfers its heat to the adjacent gaseous molecules. The roasted mica, *a*, coated on the inner side with lampblack, meets these conditions better than the clear mica; it warms up as a whole and gives up its heat to the gaseous molecules on the outside, because there they are free to carry off the heat. This side, therefore, becomes the driving surface.

This view is rendered less probable when referring to the behavior to a standard light

He proposes two theories for this effect, involving either the reflection of molecular stress or the differential heating of the mica surfaces.</summary>

...of the clear disks and fall on the black, the black disk immediately retreats, while the clear disk remains stationary for a moment and then approaches the light. The reason why the clear disk does not immediately move toward the light in proportion to the movement of the black disk away from the light seems to be that the slight friction between the upper needle point and cup initially opposes such movement.

Another explanation has frequently occurred to me, which, however, I offer with hesitation. This is that when radiation first falls on a black surface, the repulsion is produced not by the chain of molecular impacts between the black surface and the solid body facing it, but by the reaction between the black surface and the layer of normally moving gaseous molecules near it; these form a resisting cushion for the extra-active molecules to react against and press back the black surface. This cushion of inactive molecules is, as it were, rapidly eaten into by the active molecules, until in a very short space of time the pressure spans across from one surface to the other.

If the candle is allowed to shine on the plain side of the black disk, no movement takes place at first. Very soon both disks move in the same direction away from the candle, with the speed of the clear disk gradually increasing over that of the blackened disk.

When, by tapping, the disks are moved to about 1 mm apart, as in position B, the sensitivity is nearly at its maximum, and the rotation is in the negative direction, the same as in the radiometer shown in fig. 1.

The speed of rotation in the positions between B and C gradually diminishes as the plates approach the latter position; and in position C, the plates being about 7 mm apart, the sensitivity has vanished, with no rotation taking place even in strong light.

393. I am now able to decide between the two hypotheses advanced in paragraph 390. The result obtained when the screen is close to the blackened surface (fig. 4, A), in which the speed was considerably less than when they were 1 mm apart, shows that the negative rotation obtained in these positions is not due to a molecular disturbance generated on the plain side of the blackened disk and reacting directly between that and the glass case (the second hypothesis). Instead, it is caused by the warming of the blackened surface by radiation falling directly on it through the clear screen, and the backward deflection of the lines of molecular pressure generated there. At 1 mm apart, enough of this pressure is deflected to produce good negative rotation; at shorter distances, much of the force is consumed in molecular movement back and forth between the disks, while at greater distances, the negative rotation due to the reflected force is more or less counterbalanced by the positive rotation due to the molecular impacts exerted directly between the blackened surface and the glass bulb.

The cause of the maximum positive rotation taking place when the clear screen is close to the plain side of the blackened disk is that, in this position, the difference in temperature between the outer sides of the compound disk is greatest.

395. The explanation of these movements is not difficult. At position C, when the vanes are not screened, the molecular pressure reacts equally on each side between the bright aluminium and the glass bulb, and no movement takes place. When the mica screen is put in position A, it offers an obstruction to the lines of pressure between the inner half of one side of the aluminium plate and the side of the bulb, while the corresponding pressure is free to act on the other face. In position B, the same occurs, but more of the aluminium plate is obscured by the mica screen. Hence, in each position, the balance of pressure is exerted on the unscreened face of the plate, which retreats from the light, the available force being greater in position B than in position A.

396. The screens were put into position A, and the whole bulb was heated with a spirit lamp. Strong negative rotation took place (the screened side retreating); this continued for 2.5 minutes; the fly then changed its direction and rotated positively, continuing slowly for 12 minutes.

When the screens were in position B, the same phenomena occurred upon heating the bulb and allowing it to cool: the first negative rotation was very rapid and lasted 3 minutes, and the succeeding positive rotation was slower and lasted 13 minutes. The negative rotation lasts while the glass bulb is giving heat to the fly; when the

406. The metal cups used in these experiments were now lampblacked on the inside, and their speed compared with what it had been when they were bright, as in fig. 11, A. It was increased from 35 to 75 revolutions per minute. A mica disk, lampblacked on the inside, was now fixed close to the concave side of the cup, and the speed rose from 75 to 150 revolutions per minute. Had the blacked mica screens been some distance from the cups, this doubling of the speed would have been easily understood, as the screens would have acted as additional driving vanes to the radiometer; but being close to the cup they can only act by absorbing and radiating back the heat given out from the bright concave surface of the cups, and thereby increasing the difference between the temperature of the black convex and bright mica surfaces.

407. The experiments described so far have been with mica screens. Since mica is a poor conductor and radiator of heat, I next tried replacing it with aluminium to see if the employment of a good conductor as a screen made any radical change in the phenomena. A radiometer was constructed like the one shown in fig. 8, with the exception that the screens as well as the cups were of aluminium, and the outsides of the cups were coated with lampblack, as in fig. 7, E. The diameters of the cups and the disks were the same.

The experiments were tried with the screens in the same positions as are shown in fig. 8, so I will refer to that figure in illustrating the results. The screens could not be positioned closer than 4 millimeters to the black convex surfaces (intermediate in position between C and D, fig. 8), so I could not ascertain if there was a point of neutrality; in this position the speed was at the rate of 6 per minute in the positive direction. In position G, the screens being as close as possible to the concave surfaces of the cups, the positive rotation was at the rate of 120 revolutions a minute; and at any intermediate point between these two extreme positions the speed, in the positive direction, was proportionally intermediate between 6 and 120.

Making allowance for the increased sensitivity communicated to the cups by blacking their convex surfaces, these results agree fairly well with those illustrated in fig. 8, and prove that the action of the screens is almost entirely one of mechanical obstruction, and does not depend on their special power of conducting, absorbing, or radiating heat.

408. The cup-shape of the vanes is also not the simplest form with which to investigate these reactions. A careful examination of the results obtained in the foregoing experiments with screens, throws much light on the physics of the

410. The screen was put into position 13 $a$, B, touching the convex side of the vane, and the pumping was continued. 411. The screens were now replaced in position B, touching the convex side of the vanes, and pumping was continued. Before the movement ceased, the vanes acted as if, in revolving, they came successively under the influence of a strong attractive force. Each vane moved quickly up to the spot of warm glass opposite the candle, then hesitated, and passed with difficulty. This hesitation became more and more decided, until at last a vane refused to pass the dead center; it then swung back and the fly settled equidistant from the candle.

413. The exhaustion was now increased to 0.18 **M**, and the following observations were recorded:

->Fig. 13 $c$.<-

<image-desc>Four diagrams labeled A, E, F, and B showing a curved vane (hemi-cylinder) and a flat screen in different relative positions. Arrows indicate the direction of rotation or potential movement. Below the diagrams is the caption "Exhaustion 0.18 M."</image-desc>

414. From these observations, which are consistent with several hundred experiments conducted at different distances and pressures, the following laws can be identified.
*a.* When the screen touches the concave surface of the vanes, the rotation is always positive. It begins at a low exhaustion, increases in speed until the rarefaction is so high that an ordinary radiometer would start to lose sensitivity, and afterwards remains at about the same speed up to the highest rarefaction yet achieved.
*b.* At any rarefaction after 87 **M**, there is a neutral position for the screen. When it is on the concave side of this neutral position, the direction of rotation is positive; when it is on the convex side of the neutral position, the direction of rotation is negative. The rotation speed increases as the vanes are moved further from this neutral position on either side.
*c.* The position of this neutral point varies with the degree of exhaustion. Thus, at 12 **M**, the screens must be 3 mm from the convex side; at 0.18 **M**, they must be 13 mm from the convex side. The higher the exhaustion, the greater the distance must be between the convex side of the hemi-cylinders and the screens.

It should be recalled that in this position, when the exhaustion is 117 **M**, the fly rotates positively (409), and at an exhaustion of 0.18 **M**, the fly rotates negatively (414).

->Fig. 14.<-

<image-desc>Two circular diagrams labeled A and B, representing a radiometer bulb in cross-section. Diagram A is labeled "Exhaustion 117 M." and shows a vane with lines of force, some reaching the glass wall (solid lines) and some not (dotted lines). I have already shown (312) that when thin aluminium vanes are exposed to candlelight, the metal becomes equally warm throughout, and a layer of molecular pressure is generated at its surface. The thickness of this layer of pressure, or the length of the lines of force of repulsion, varies with the degree of exhaustion, becoming longer as the exhaustion increases. The lines of force radiate from every part of the warm metal; since they are strongest in a direction normal to the surface, it will be convenient only to recognize these in a discussion of their action. The force of repulsion is also greater the closer the repelled body is to the generating or driving surface, and the force diminishes rapidly as the distance increases, according to a law which has not yet been accurately determined,* but which does not appear to be the law of "inverse squares." It will also simplify matters if the interfering action caused by the pressure generated by the warm glass bulb is neglected.

In fig. 14, A, the exhaustion is low (117 **M**), and I assume the thickness of the layer of pressure extends to a distance of 10 millimeters from the surface of the aluminium vane. The lines in the diagram are represented as extending for that length from the hemi-cylinder in directions normal to the surface. Where the lines of force extend from the fly to the glass case, as at *a* to *b* and *c* to *d*, pressure is exerted along the line, and repulsion follows; these are represented by black radial lines. But where the lines of force do not reach the glass, as shown by dotted lines, no pressure is exerted. In the position and under the conditions shown in fig. 14, A, the rotation must be in the direction of the arrow or positive, as the pressure in the positive direction exerted by the lines of force between *a* and *b* more than counterbalances that in the negative direction exerted by the lines between *c* and *d*. Inasmuch as some active lines of force are cut off by the screen, an increase of the distance between the screen and the convex surface of the vane will allow more rays of force to become active, and will increase the speed in the positive direction.

The positive pressure between *a* and *b* is now outweighed by the negative pressure between *c* and *d*, and rotation is therefore produced in the direction of the arrow, or negatively. If we imagine the arm carrying the screens to be rotated on the axis, it will be seen that as one screen leaves the convex side of the vane, more of the positive rays of force are rendered active, while negative rays are cut off by the lower screen. Hence, as the screens are moved around, the fly will gradually rotate less strongly in the negative direction; it will become neutral when the screens are in such a position that the opposing forces balance; and ultimately it will rotate positively. This is what experiments prove to be the case (413).

I have tested this explanation by comparing it with all the phenomena obtained with movable screens in various positions and at different pressures, as described in paragraphs 391 to 413, and in no case does it fail. There is, therefore, a high probability that it is true.

The adjustable indicator, being very small in diameter compared to the other parts of the apparatus and being easily placed in any part of the bulb, was expected to provide information regarding the intensity and direction of the lines of pressure when a candle was brought near the bulb.

It will be impossible within reasonable limits to give more than a few general results that I have obtained with this apparatus. Experiments have been tried:—

*a.* With the screen in different positions relative to the hemi-cylinder;
*b.* With the indicator in different parts of the bulb;

These four conditions have been varied in numerous ways, and each time experiments have been tried both with and without an alteration in some or all of the other conditions. Although much time has been spent on this method of experiment, it will be understood that, with such a vast number of possible combinations, only a few of the most obvious can be thoroughly investigated.

However, from the general indications given by the exploring fly, I have concluded that the force is not reflected in the sense that light is reflected; instead, it is merely deflected from a surface it strikes, as would be the case with a <term>molar wind</term> <note>A term referring to the movement of a mass of gas as a whole, rather than the random movement of individual molecules.</note>.

<summary>William Crookes uses an "exploring fly" (indicator) to map molecular pressure within a vacuum bulb, testing whether the force reflects like light or deflects like wind. His observations of rotation at various positions suggest that the force is deflected by screens rather than reflected.</summary>

### ACTION OF HEAT APPLIED INSIDE THE RADIOMETER.

425. In a previous paper, it was shown that phenomena which were weak and contradictory when caused by radiation outside the bulb became strong and consistent when the radiation was applied internally using an electrically heated wire (336 to 384). It was hoped that some of the more obscure phenomena shown by the deep cups with movable screens in front (400, *and following*) might be intensified if set in action by a hot wire.

426. In the first experiment, the mica screen was adjusted to the position shown in fig. 8 A, or as close as possible to the convex surfaces of the cups. The rarefaction was brought to 12 **M**. ### THE TURBINE RADIOMETER.

434. Experiments conducted with the apparatus described in a previous paper (336, 345, 354)—where thin mica vanes, inclined at an angle of 45° to the horizontal plane, form the fly of the radiometer—show that this design of fly has advantages in cases where the incident radiation falls on the instrument at an angle; and the favorably-

The presented radiometers, when tested with hot metal rings applied at the equator and at the poles (sections 298 to 305), showed that the action of radiation was in some cases entirely different, depending on whether it fell on the vanes horizontally or nearly vertically. The experiments just described with the sloping adjustable cup (section 432) demonstrate even more clearly the significant difference in rotation speed caused by a small change in the angle presented by the vanes to the direction of pressure. These experiments were, however, conducted with a somewhat complex apparatus. A simpler form of instrument, which takes full advantage of the unique properties of sloping vanes, was exhibited before the Royal Society on April 5, 1876, under the name of the turbine radiometer.

->Fig. 20.<-

<image-desc>A scientific diagram of a turbine radiometer (Fig. 20). It consists of a glass bulb containing a vertical spindle with several small, circular vanes attached at an angle, resembling a turbine or windmill. Below the main bulb is a detail drawing labeled 'A' showing a cross-section of a vane and the direction of molecular pressure indicated by an arrow.</image-desc>

In the earlier radiometers of this kind, the vanes were made of mica, blackened on both sides and inclined at an angle like the sails of a windmill, instead of being positioned in a vertical plane. These are not sensitive to horizontal radiation, but move readily in one direction or the other when a candle is held above or below them. If only one side of each vane is blackened, the fly becomes more sensitive to radiation falling on the blackened side, but is not sensitive when radiation strikes the other side. In the ordinary form of radiometer, the number of disks making up the fly is limited to six or eight, as a greater number causes interference with one another and obstructs the incident light. In the turbine form of fly, there is no such difficulty; the number of vanes may be increased considerably without overcrowding, and with a corresponding advantage. 

The action of the vanes is evident. Fig. 20 shows the turbine vanes; light falling from above generates molecular pressure between the surface of the vanes and the top of the evacuated bulb. This pressure, acting as shown at A, drives the fly around in the direction of the arrow. A vertical light provides the strongest action, but rotation occurs regardless of the angle of incidence, provided the light is caught by one surface more than by the other. If a finger or any warm substance touches the top of the bulb, generating pressure from the inner surface of the evacuated bulb, the fly is strongly driven around in the direction shown in Fig. 20, A.

435. Dropping ether on the top of the bulb to chill it causes rapid negative rotation. If the radiometer is floated in a container of ice-cold water and exposed to the air of a warm room above, it rotates rapidly in the positive direction. In this state, it acts as a heat engine and continues to do so until the rotating fly has equalized the temperature of the upper and lower portions of the bulb.

By reversing the cycle of operations—by floating the radiometer in hot water and cooling the upper portion of the bulb—the fly instantly revolves in the negative direction.<note>Radiometers working in this manner were exhibited, with appropriate descriptions, at the meeting of the Royal Society on April 5, 1876.</note>

436. The turbine fly mounted vertically works just as well horizontally. In this configuration, it is supported on a double-pointed needle, operating horizontally in glass caps. Some care is needed in balancing the vanes; otherwise, one side tends to fall to the lowest point, making it difficult to start the movement initially. This *windmill* form is very sensitive to radiation falling on it parallel to its axis of rotation, and it has the unique quality of continuing its movement in any position. Once started, it may be turned around, upside down, or on either side without interfering with the rotation of the fly, as long as the sloping vanes catch the light.

If mica vanes are used in the turbine radiometer, they should be oval, with the arms of the support passing through the minor axis. This ensures that when viewed from the direction in which the light should fall on them, they appear circular.

Spiral flies made of mica are much more sensitive than those made of aluminium, but they are less easy to make. A very sensitive spiral radiometer may be made by threading flat mica disks on a thin aluminium wire. In all these instruments, the blackened surfaces must make an angle with the inner surface of the glass tube, or there will be no tangential action of the molecular pressure.

440. The following experiments were tried with an aluminium spiral radiometer exhausted to the most sensitive point. It was completely immersed in water at 20° C., and when quite still, it was suddenly plunged into water at 60° C. A rapid negative* movement took place, continuing for a few minutes; the fly then became still. When it was quiet in the hot water, the radiometer was suddenly plunged into cold water (20° C.). A rapid positive movement took place, stopping when the temperature was uniform.

The radiometer was now heated with a lamp over the upper half of the tube; the spiral immediately rotated positively and continued to do so until it was quite cold. Heat applied in a similar manner to the lower half of the radiometer case caused the spiral to rotate rapidly in the negative direction. While it was rotating negatively, a lighted candle was brought near; the fly stopped and then turned positively, resuming its negative rotation when the candle was removed and continuing it until the tube and fly were cold. When only the lower half of the radiometer was immersed in hot water, while the upper half was allowed to remain cool by radiation to the air, the negative rotation of the fly continued at an almost uniform speed, not coming to rest until the water was nearly cold.

These positive and negative movements of the spiral fly under the influence of partially applied heat are in strict accordance with the explanation already given: that when the glass case is heated, its inner surface becomes the generating surface for the molecular pressure. This pressure then acts as if it were a <term>molar wind</term>, repelling whatever happens to be within the sphere of its action (218, postscript).

I was interested to determine whether the substitution of another kind of surface for that of polished glass would have any effect on the motion of the fly. A radiometer was accordingly constructed with a four-vaned mica fly, the disks being blackened on one side. The case of the radiometer was made so that it could easily be opened and sealed again when a change of contents had to be made. Around the inner surface of the case, an equatorial band of aluminium was fixed, slightly wider than the diameter of the disks on the fly and coated with lampblack on the inner side. The increased speed in these experiments must not be entirely attributed to the fact that the blackened aluminum band presents a better reacting surface for the rebounding molecules than the polished glass does. In the first place, the introduction of the metal band slightly diminished the distance between the fly and the reacting surface; and in the second place, the rays from the candle not only shone on the fly, but also on the opposite half-cylinder of black aluminum, and warming it, converted it into a driving surface. Each of these actions would cause an increase of speed in the fly; but added together, they could only account for a part of the jump from 8.5 to 40 revolutions. The diameter was only slightly reduced, and it has been shown that a much greater reduction of diameter (437) only had the power to add 50 percent to the speed. The effect that the light of the candle shining on the blackened half-cylinder would have on the speed was determined by placing the candle in such a position that it would illuminate the inner half of the aluminum band, while its direct action on the fly was blocked by screens. The driving action of the pressure from the cylinder was shown in this way to be equal to only about 13.5 revolutions a minute.

### ROTATION OF THE CASE OF THE RADIOMETER.

442. Assuming the existence of pressure acting between the fly and the case of the radiometer, it follows that if one is held fast, the other must move. Usually, the bulb is fixed and the fly rotates; but if the conditions are changed and the fly is fixed while the globe is free to move, the latter must rotate. On March 30, 1876, I presented to the Royal Society an experiment in which this was shown to be the case. I quote the following opening sentence from the short note on this experiment which was published at the time\*:— "During the discussion following the reading of Professor <term>REYNOLDS'S</term> and Dr. <term>SCHUSTER'S</term> papers at the last meeting of the Royal Society, I mentioned an experiment related to the observations of Dr. <term>SCHUSTER</term>. I have since tried this in a modified form, and as the results are very clear and appear intended to shed light on many disputed points in the theory of these obscure actions, I venture to bring a description of the experiment and to show the apparatus at work before the Society."

The experiment was as follows: A radiometer was used, the fly of which carried a magnetized needle. The radiometer was floated in water, and four candles were brought near it. The fly immediately rotated, carrying the magnetic needle around with it. A powerful magnet was held over it, which arrested the rotation of the fly; then, the glass envelope rotated in the opposite direction to that in which the fly had been moving, with the rotation continuing as long as the candles were burning.

443. I have tried numerous forms of radiometer in an effort to determine the best kind for showing this rotation of the envelope. Turbines with pith or metal flies, arranged to rotate when floated on hot or cold water, did not give good results; nor did any variety of radiometers with metallic cup flies. By far the most sensitive form is one in which the fly carries four silver-flake mica disks, lamp-blacked on both sides. Over the glass cap carrying the fly, another fly moves stiffly, carrying four other disks made of clear mica. A reference to fig. 4, par. 392, will explain the arrangement, it being understood that the instrument now described has four vanes instead of two, and the opaque mica disks are blacked on both sides instead of on one side. The arms carrying the clear mica screens also carry a magnetic needle. By tapping the instrument, the screens can be brought close to the black vanes on either side. When exposed to light, rapid rotation is produced, as the exposed side of the lamp-blacked vanes is repelled. By altering the position of the screens so as to obscure one or the other black surface, rotation can be produced in either direction. By increasing the distance between the screens and the blacked mica, the rotation is made slower; and by putting the screens midway between the vanes, rotation ceases. Reference to par. 392 shows that the present results entirely confirm those given there. Lead shots are sealed in the lower part of the case to act as ballast and keep it upright when in water.

---

->\* Proc. Roy. Soc., No. 168, March 30, 1876.<-

444. The radiometer was floated in water contained in a large beaker, and a cover was placed over it to prevent interference from air currents. The screens were brought close to one side of the vanes, and the whole apparatus was exposed to sunlight. The force of repulsion immediately overcame the power of the magnet, and the compound fly rotated rapidly. A strong magnet was then brought near the bulb, the motion of the fly was stopped, and immediately the bulb rotated in the opposite direction, making about 6 revolutions a minute. The force of rotation was so strong that when the cover was removed and a paper arrow 3 feet long was glued to the top of the bulb, this paper pointer was swung around the room 3 times a minute as long as the sunshine lasted. When the screens were moved to the other side of the vanes, rotation occurred just as well, but in the opposite direction.

445. The radiometer was brought into a dark room, and four candles were placed nearby while the outside control magnet was in position. The bulb rotated about 3 times a minute. When its speed was uniform, the control magnet was removed, releasing the fly, which then revolved under the influence of the internal pressure, with the case and the vanes moving in opposite directions. After the bulb had made one-third of a revolution, it stopped and moved back for about the same distance. Then it stopped again and made one-third of a revolution in the original direction. These oscillations continued for a considerable time; they seemed to get gradually smaller and smaller, but I did not observe that they stopped altogether. The motion of the bulb in the opposite direction to the fly was always more rapid than when it moved with the fly. The movement of the fly continued at a uniform speed as long as the experiment lasted.

446. It would seem that this oscillatory movement was due in whole or in part to internal friction, either from the steel point on the glass socket or from the vanes against the residual gas, or from both these causes combined. To determine what power this friction possessed, the candles were removed, and as soon as the whole instrument had come to rest, a bar magnet was moved alternately from one side of the radiometer to the other, so as to cause the fly to rotate as if it had been exposed to light. The fly rotated rapidly, and the internal friction carried the glass envelope around in the same direction at the rate of about 1 revolution in 3 minutes, in opposition to the friction of the water against its sides.

447. The rotation of the envelope while the fly was fixed by a magnet was also achieved in another manner. Oblique mica vanes were fixed around the inner horizontal circumference of the bulb, and the movable fly, which carried a small magnet, was furnished with metallic vanes positioned favorably (273), so that molecular pressure acting between them and the envelope should cause the fly to rotate. Inside the fly, coiled around the supporting glass stem but not in contact with the fly, was a platinum wire spiral, the ends of which were connected with thicker wires passing through and sealed into the glass bulb. By connecting these terminals with a battery, the spiral was heated to a glow, and the heat warming the metallic fly caused pressure to be exerted between the fly and the outer envelope, producing rapid rotation. The

The whole instrument was floated in water, and one of the outer terminal wires was made to dip into a mercury cup at the bottom of the water, while the other terminal dipped into a ring-shaped trough of mercury surrounding the upper part of the bulb. Battery wires were connected to the two mercury cups, at which point the fly rotated rapidly. Upon stopping the movement of the fly using a magnet, the bulb was seen to rotate in the opposite direction. The movement, however, was weak and could only be maintained for any length of time with difficulty, due to the friction of the platinum wires in the mercury cups. Having demonstrated the fact of rotation, further experiments seemed unnecessary.

448. As the fixed vanes in the apparatus just described appeared to act in a very decisive manner, further experiments were attempted in this direction, as it was thought that the results might shed more light on the theory of the movement.

A radiometer was fitted with a fly, the four vanes of which were cut from thin transparent mica and were mounted symmetrically with the axis of rotation, though they were not positioned in a favorable orientation. At the side of the bulb, in a vertical plane, a plate of mica was fastened in such a position that each clear vane would pass it during rotation, clearing it by about a millimeter. The mica screen was cut away in the center to allow the vanes to pass, as shown in Figure 23. The screen is a double one, formed of two plates of mica about a millimeter apart; the outer surface of one was blackened with lampblack, while the other was clear. When a candle was brought near and the light was allowed to shine on the clear side of the mica screen, no effect was produced. If the light is shaded so that it only shines on the clear mica vanes, there is still no action; but if the light shines on the blackened side of the mica screen, the fly rotates rapidly, as if it were being blown around by a wind coming from the black surface, and it continues to move as long as the light remains nearby.

A similar instrument contained a mica screen blackened on both sides. The fly carried four bright aluminum cups (318). When the light of a candle was shaded from the blackened mica screen and allowed to shine only on the cups, the fly rotated positively, with the convex sides moving away from the light. ### THE OTHEOSCOPE.

450. The experiments on the rotation of the envelope (442 to 447) show that the surface generating the molecular pressure does not need to be the one that rotates. The apparatus shown in fig. 23, as well as the one described in a previous paper (360), proves that it is advantageous to have the driving surface stationary. In the radiometer, the surface that produces the molecular disturbance is mounted on a fly and is itself driven backward by the excess of pressure between it and the sides of the containing vessel. Considering the radiometer as a heat engine, it is seen to be imperfect in many respects. The black or driving surface, which corresponds to the *heater* of the engine, is also part of the moving fly; therefore, it is restricted in terms of weight, material, and surface area. It must be of the lightest possible construction, or friction will significantly interfere with its movement. It must not have too much surface area, or it will be too heavy. Furthermore, it must be a very poor conductor of heat so as to retain the excess of pressure on one side. Again,

<summary>This page details experiments where rotation is achieved using stationary mica partitions and flat, symmetrical vanes, demonstrating that the driving surface of a radiometer does not need to be the part that rotates. Crookes introduces the "Otheoscope" as a more efficient heat engine that separates the stationary driving surface from the moving fly.</summary>

the part corresponding to the *cooler* of the engine (the side of the glass bulb) allows for very little modification. It must almost necessarily be made of glass—one of the worst materials for this purpose; it is required to be of one particular shape; and it cannot be brought very near the driving surface.

451. To get the best results, the *heater* should be stationary; it could then be made of the most suitable material, with a sufficient surface area, and of the most efficient shape, regardless of its weight. The moving portion should be the *cooler*; it should be as near as possible to the *heater*, and of the most suitable size, shape, and weight for utilizing the force striking it. The *heater*, or driving surface, acts as if a molecular wind* were blowing from it (276), mainly in a direction perpendicular to the surface (312). By having a large heater and making it from a good conductor, such as silver, gold, or copper, a very faint amount of incoming radiation would be enough to produce motion.

In April 1877, I sent a preliminary note to the Royal Society regarding a new instrument I had made in accordance with these findings. As it was fundamentally different in its construction and operation from the radiometer, I proposed to identify it by the distinctive name <term>Otheoscope</term> ($\dot{\omega}\theta\acute{\epsilon}\omega$, I propel). While the radiometer allows for very few modifications, an instrument like the otheoscope is capable of an almost endless variety of forms. The glass envelope is an essential part of the radiometer's mechanism, without which the fly would not move; but in the otheoscope, the glass vessel simply acts to maintain the necessary level of rarefaction. If you carried a radiometer to a point in space where the atmospheric pressure is equal to, say, 1 mm of mercury, and removed the glass bulb, the fly would not move, no matter how strong the incoming radiation; but if you placed the otheoscope in the same conditions, it would move just as well without the case as with it.

452. The instrument described in a former paper (360), and repeated here with some alterations (425, fig. 17), fulfills the essential conditions of the otheoscope; by letting light shine on the blackened mica plate instead of heating it with the platinum wire and battery, the vanes can be made to rotate well.

An instrument of this kind was made, omitting the electrical portion so as to work entirely by radiation. It is shown in fig. 25, A. A mica plate, *a a*, is firmly attached to the support *c*, and is coated with lampblack on the upper side; a fly, *b b*, with polished aluminum vanes set at an angle of 45°, is supported by a glass cap on a needle point passing through *a a*, so that while rotating, the lower edge is about a millimeter from the mica plate. Light shining on the black surface creates molecular pressure, which reacts against the sloping vanes and drives them around.

The vanes are as numerous as can be conveniently assembled. Another version consists of suspending aluminum cups on the fly, angled at 45° with the concave side facing downward, as shown in figure 18, number 4 (432). This design also proved to be very sensitive.

453. Since the pressure is exerted primarily at right angles to the driving surface, it was thought that power was lost due to the tangential action of the pressure in the previously mentioned <term>otheoscope</term> design. Other instruments were therefore constructed with a driving surface made of thick copper, divided into 16 equal sections by radial lines that stop just before the center. Each of the 16 sectors is then bent to form a 45° angle with the original plane of the disk. This driving wheel is coated with lampblack and fixed to the support in the center of the bulb. Directly above it, suspended on a needle point, is another disk cut into sectors and bent at the exact same angle as the lower disk. Because the upper and lower sectors face each other in parallel planes, a force acting at right angles to the driving surface will also strike the movable fly at right angles, driving it around more directly. Experience shows that this design provides an advantage.

These otheoscopes are very sensitive to externally applied heat. If those shown in figure 25 are warmed at the top, above the movable fly, the fly is driven in the negative direction; the pressure acting on the vanes from above produces a rotation opposite to that produced when pressure acts from below.

If the lower part of the case is warmed, no movement is seen at first; gradually,

454. It was suggested by Professor <term>STOKES</term> that a disk might be made to revolve on its axis, and the following instrument was made in accordance with the design proposed. The disk is horizontal, mounted like the fly of a radiometer, and for the sake of lightness is made of mica, blackened on the upper side. The edge is in a radial direction, and the plane of the plate is inclined at about 45° to the horizon, in the same direction for all of them. When exposed to the light of a candle, the rotation is against the edge, the same as in the instruments last described.

The upper part of the mica disk in one of these otheoscopes was divided into sectors, each of which was painted with one of the component colors of white light. When exposed to sunshine, the speed was so great that it caused the colors to blend together into a neutral gray.

### THICKNESS OF THE LAYER OF MOLECULAR PRESSURE.

455. While experimenting with the otheoscope, it was found that, for a given exhaustion, the closer the reacting surfaces were to each other, the greater the speed obtained. This was in accordance with previous results (437). In a note on the theory of the radiometer, which I had the honor of communicating to the Royal Society in November 1876,* I briefly described a piece of apparatus by which I was able to measure the thickness of the layer of molecular pressure generated when radiation struck a blackened surface, enclosed in an atmosphere whose rarefaction could be varied at will.

The apparatus, which is represented in fig. 27 (plan and elevation), consists of a torsion balance fitted with a glass suspending fiber and reflecting mirror, as already

460. An examination of these tables and diagrams shows that the law governing the increase of force as the distance between the disks decreases does not remain uniform at all levels of rarefaction. At the lowest levels of exhaustion, the mean free path of the molecules of the thinned gas is less than 1 millimetre, which is shown by the force of repulsion decreasing rapidly as the distance increases. At levels of exhaustion higher than 9 millimetres, this condition changes; and as the gauge approaches barometric height, the pressure tends to become uniform over considerable distances. This occurs because the mean path of the molecules is now comparable to the greatest distance separating the surfaces between which they act. As the distance between the disks increases, the tangential action between them and the sides of the glass becomes more significant, tending to interfere with and increase the direct pressure between the two surfaces.

<summary>This page analyzes experimental data showing how the force of radiation repulsion changes at very high vacuum levels, noting that the "mean free path" of gas molecules affects how pressure is distributed between surfaces. The results indicate that as exhaustion increases, the repulsion becomes more uniform over greater distances because molecules travel further before colliding.</summary>

MR. W. CROOKES ON REPULSION RESULTING FROM RADIATION.

### REPULSION AT ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE.

461. The attraction or repulsion exerted between surfaces at atmospheric pressure or low levels of exhaustion has always shown contradictions. The air currents caused by the heating of the glass casing, and those generated inside by the heating of the movable indicator, were enough to completely or partially neutralize any repulsion caused by true molecular pressure. It was thought that by using special arrangements, the effect of air currents might be separated from that of molecular pressure, and the following apparatus was accordingly set up.

It consists of a torsion balance, similar to the one last used (455, fig. 27), but instead of the adjustable mica screen and blackened disk, the experimental end of the

->Fig. 31.<-

<image-desc>A technical diagram labeled Fig. 31 showing a torsion beam apparatus. It includes a vertical glass tube containing a mica disk (a) suspended near a shallow cup (b) and a wire spiral (c) with terminals passing through the glass.</image-desc>

torsion beam was arranged as shown in fig. 31. *a* is a clear mica disk suspended on the end of the torsion beam; *b* is a shallow cup of platinum, blackened on the convex side; *c* is a platinum wire spiral, connected with thicker platinum terminals passing hermetically through the glass. By heating the spiral, the platinum cup is warmed, and the approach or retreat of the disk *a* is measured by an index ray of light reflected onto a screen in the usual manner.

The strength of the electric current used to heat the spiral is kept constant by the system of resistance coils and galvanometer described in a previous paper (359). Two <term>LECLANCHÉ</term> cells, providing a fairly constant current, were used to heat the spiral; the heat never reached a red glow. The scale was kept 3 feet from the mirror.

462. The apparatus was exhausted to dry it and then filled with dry air which had passed through a tube packed with phosphorus pentoxide <note>phosphoric anhydride</note>. The disk was adjusted so that it just barely did not touch the platinum cup.

When the spiral was heated, the disk was immediately attracted to the cup. The mica disk was now put at different distances from the cup. Upon heating the spiral, strong attraction always took place; the disk rushed across to the cup, rebounded from it, and rapidly settled in close contact. A wet finger <note>Wetted to avoid static electricity caused by friction.</note> placed on the opposite side to the cup, after it had cooled down, drew the disk away.

463. Exhaustion was now carried out, with observations being taken at intervals. The control magnet was moved so as to let the disk lightly touch the cup; the scale was moved until the index ray of light stood at —140. The magnet then brought the torsion beam back until the index ray of light stood in the center of the scale, at zero. As now adjusted, the mica disk is several millimetres from the cup, and can move

464. *Pressure: 260 millimeters.*—When the current is turned on, the light ray index moves to +2; it then swings back to -140, the disk touching the cup and being held there for some time after contact is broken.

465. *Pressure: 240 millimeters.*—Upon making contact, the movements of the index are the same as at 260; however, the first movement is +3 divisions.

466. *Pressure: 210 millimeters.*—The same as above, but the first movement is +4.

467. *Pressure: 160 millimeters.*—Upon making contact, the first movement of the index is +4.5° repulsion. It then swings back to -139, the plate just failing to touch the cup by one division. There was no permanent attraction, as in previous cases, but the beam swung quite freely.

468. *Pressure: 125 millimeters.*—The index moved +6° (repulsion) upon making contact; it then returned to -136° (attraction), falling 4 degrees short of making contact.

469. *Pressure: 110 millimeters.*—When contact was made, the first movement was +9 (repulsion); the return movement was to -135° (attraction), or 5 degrees short of contact.

470. *Pressure: 90 millimeters.*—The first movement was +15 (repulsion); the return movement was -131°, or 9 degrees short of contact.

471. *Pressure: 60 millimeters.*—The first movement was +22 (repulsion); the return movement was to -115, or 25 degrees short of contact.

472. *Pressure: 55 millimeters.*—The first movement of the index upon heating the spiral was +34 (repulsion); the return swing was to -94.

473. *Pressure: 15 millimeters.*—Upon heating the spiral, the light ray index showed repulsion, going to +145. It then oscillated slightly back and forth but did not show any attraction.

474. *Pressure: 10 millimeters.*—As soon as battery contact was made, strong repulsion followed; the light ray index went off the scale (above 250°), and the mica disk was driven against the side of the tube and remained there. Because of this, no further experiments could be tried effectively with this apparatus.

Between each of the latter experiments, the index took a long time to return to zero due to the mass of heated metal inside, which had to become completely cold.

475. Fig. 32 shows the results of the above experiments represented as curves. The attraction, which is very strong at pressures between atmospheric and 210 millimeters, begins to decline after that level of exhaustion is passed, until it disappears at 15 millimeters. At the same time, the repulsion, which begins to be apparent at 250 millimeters, increases as the attraction diminishes. It is probable that the attraction is the effect of air currents caused by the continuous heating of the surface in front of the mica disk. If the primary action of the molecular pressure—which I assume is nearly instantaneous—could be further separated from the more slowly acting air currents, we would succeed in obtaining a clear repulsion at even higher pressures.

The index light ray and the scale were the same as before.

Tested in air (at a pressure of 745 mm), there were 10 divisions of repulsion with no subsequent attraction, showing that the water and glass screens prevented the bulb from heating.

### MEASUREMENT OF THE FORCE OF REPULSION.

479. The following experiments were undertaken with the goal of obtaining measurements of the actual amounts of force exerted by radiation in causing repulsion.

A horizontal torsion balance was used, similar in construction to the one described in a previous paper <note>Philosophical Transactions, 1876, Vol. 166, part II, p. 371.</note> (209, 210, 211). A somewhat stiffer torsion fiber was used, and the part corresponding to the pan of the balance was a clear mica disk 16 millimeters in diameter. A similar disk was fastened to the tube in which the beam oscillated, in such a position that when in equilibrium the pan would be 1 millimeter above the fixed disk. This fixed disk was blackened with lampblack on the upper surface and had beneath it a thin platinum spiral connected with terminals sealed in and passing through the glass, as in apparatus figure 31 (461). When this spiral is heated by an electric current, the blackened mica disk fixed above it becomes heated, and the molecular pressure generated between it and the mica pan causes the latter to rise. The glass thread attached to the beam is now twisted by means of the graduated circle, and the number of degrees through which the thread must be twisted, in order to bring the beam back to equilibrium, is noted. This provides a measurement of the pressure exerted in torsional degrees. To convert these degrees into grains, it is only necessary to determine how many degrees the glass thread must be twisted in order to balance a known weight placed on the pan. A piece of iron weighing 0.01 grain was used, and it was found that to restore the beam to equilibrium with this weight on the pan, 3 complete revolutions and 34.5° additional, or 1114.5 degrees of torsion, were required. Since the force with which the glass fiber tends to untwist itself is directly proportional to the number of degrees through which it has been twisted, the value in grains of any number of torsional degrees is easily calculated. A ray of light reflected from a mirror in the center of the beam is used as an indicator, being brought to a definite mark on a scale for the zero point.

The battery power was kept constant by the means already described (359, 461).

480. In the following table, the degrees of exhaustion are given in millionths of an atmosphere, and the force of repulsion is given in fractions of a grain, calculated from the degrees of torsion.

481. In figure 33 these results are plotted as a curve, taking the abscissas in units of the hundred-thousandth of a grain, and the ordinates in millionths of an atmosphere. 482. In the Proceedings of the Royal Society for November 16, 1876, <note>Vol. 25, p. 305.</note> I gave a similar curve of the variation of the force of repulsion in air at different degrees of exhaustion. The source of radiation was a candle, and the body repelled was blackened mica. In that curve the maximum action is very near 40 millionths of an atmosphere, rising slowly and sinking rapidly.

483.
