In this case also the maximum action occurred close upon an exhaustion of 40 millionths of an atmosphere, increasing slowly and dying away rapidly.

484. In the same paper (paragraph 383) <note>In the same place, p. 316.</note> I have given a third curve of the variation of the action of a candle on a blackened mica surface in an air vacuum. Observations are wanting between 59 and 14 millionths of an atmosphere, but by continuing the curve passing through the other points, it is seen that here, likewise, the maximum would not be far from 40 millionths of an atmosphere.

In concluding this series of papers “On Repulsion resulting from Radiation,” it is a pleasure for me to state that during the six years they have been in progress, I have been materially aided by my assistant, Mr. C. H. <term>GIMINGHAM</term>, whose extraordinary mechanical dexterity and skill in glass manipulation have been called into service almost daily.

### THE INDUCTION CURRENT THROUGH RAREFIED GASES. DARK SPACE AROUND THE NEGATIVE POLE.

486. When the spark from a high-quality induction coil passes through a glass tube containing a rarefied gas, certain phenomena are observed that vary greatly with the type of gas and the degree of exhaustion. There is one appearance, however, that is constant in all the gases I have examined, and within very wide limits of pressure: namely, the well-known dark space around the negative pole. I have long been impressed with the idea that this dark space coating the pole was in some way related to the layer of molecular pressure causing movement in the radiometer, and the following experiments were conducted with the goal of testing this hypothesis.

The bulb, being full of dry air and connected with the SPRENGEL pump, was exhausted. 487. At a pressure of 20 millimeters of mercury, a soft velvety halo of violet light began to form on the edges of the disk; as the exhaustion continued, this glow flickered over different parts of the surface, until at a pressure of 15 millimeters it remained steady all over the front of the disk.

Plate 14, fig. 2, shows the appearance at a pressure between 15 and 20 millimeters: *a* shows the glow creeping over the disk as the exhaustion increases; *b* is the appearance on the mica side of the disk; and *c* shows the edge of the disk. By close examination from the side, it can be seen that the glow and the metal are not in contact, but are separated by a very minute interval.

At a pressure of 7.5 millimeters, the glow is thicker, and the black space is easily visible. At 1.6 millimeters, the appearance is as shown in Plate 14, fig. 3. The dark space is half a millimeter in thickness, and the glow is very bright. As the exhaustion continues, the appearance around the negative disk goes through the stages shown in Plate 14, figs. 4, 5, 6, and 7, with the glow diminishing in intensity and the dark space widening out; the outline is still distinctly shown. Plate 14, fig. 7, shows the appearance at a pressure of .078 millimeters, with the thickness of the dark space being 8 millimeters.

488. At any particular pressure, the dark space separating the glow from the metal disk can be slightly altered by varying the power of the contact breaker. When it is adjusted to increase the intensity of the spark, the dark space slightly contracts, and when the intensity of the spark is diminished, the dark space slightly expands; the variation in size is about 1 millimeter. For the same intensity of spark and degree of exhaustion, the dark space is always uniform in size.

489. Another bulb was now made of a different construction to determine if the size of the dark space varied with the distance separating the poles. Each pole consisted of a flat metal disk, one being fixed and the other capable of sliding along a glass tube fitting loosely into a wider tube. By tapping the tube, the adjustable pole can be brought close to the fixed pole or removed some distance from it; contact between the disk and the outer loop is always preserved by wires in the sliding tubes. <note>The device of making one of the poles of a vacuum tube adjustable so as to alter the distance between the two poles has already been adopted by Mr. SPOTTISWOODE. Experiments with such a tube are described by Messrs. DE LA RUE and MÜLLER in the Phil. Trans. for 1878, p. 163.</note>

As the exhaustion continued, the observed phenomena were similar to those already described. It was found that the dimensions and thickness of the dark space did not vary, regardless of the distance separating the fixed and sliding poles.

Air was let in and exhaustion was restarted several times. At the same level of exhaustion, the dimensions of the dark space were always the same. It is indeed easy to determine the degree of exhaustion by measuring the thickness of the dark space. On afterwards measuring the pressure in the usual way, the agreement is close enough for ordinary observations.

When only one pole of the coil is connected to one pole of the tube, the same sized dark space is seen around the pole as when both poles are connected, but the light is faint, and the room needs to be darkened for accurate observations.

491. The sliding pole was now removed; one half was coated with lampblack <note>A fine black pigment made from soot</note> as shown in Fig. 8, and it was replaced. Exhaustion was restarted, and at a suitable pressure, the coil was attached. The dark space around the pole was now seen to have lost its uniform thickness; it was 1 mm thick over the metallic half and 1.5 mm thick over the lampblack half. As exhaustion continued, the dark space became larger, with the space over the lampblack maintaining roughly the same proportional excess over that of the bare metal. As the exhaustion increased, the size of the dark space over the platinum expanded slightly more than that over the bare metal.

494. At a pressure of 1.5 mm, the dark spheroid surrounded the platinum spiral at a distance of 4.5 mm. Heating the spiral with the battery caused the dark space to expand considerably, but the amount of expansion could not be accurately seen because its outline became very indistinct after it had expanded to about a 7 mm semi-diameter.

495. The poles *c* and *d* were connected with the induction coil, with the spiral *a b* still attached to the 3 <term>Grove's cells</term>. The whole tube was filled with light, and I then made battery contact with the spiral, heating it to redness. No space could be seen around the hot wire, and no change was observed in the illumination of the tube.

496. Hydrogen gas was now passed into the tube, and after several cycles of exhausting and refilling with hydrogen, the following experiments were tried: the spiral *a b* was always the negative pole of the induction coil and was also connected with the 3-cell <term>Grove's battery</term>.

At a pressure of 5 mm, the dark spheroid extended 1.75 mm from the pole. On making the pole red hot, the dark space expanded to 2.5 mm in thickness.

At a pressure of 3.75 mm, the dark spheroid was 2.25 mm from the pole, expanding to 3.75 mm when the pole was heated.

At a pressure of 2.75 mm, the expansion of the dark space upon heating the pole was from 4 mm to 6.5 mm.

The phenomena in hydrogen are therefore similar to those in air, but the dark space around the negative pole is larger for the same degree of exhaustion.

497. Carbonic acid <note>Carbon dioxide (CO2)</note> was then passed into the tube, and after several fillings and exhaustions, the following experiments were tried:—

At a pressure considerably less than that at which the dark space would appear in air or hydrogen, there was no appearance of it in carbonic acid.

At a pressure of 4 mm, the dark space was 0.75 mm thick. At a pressure of 0.62 mm, its thickness was 2.5 mm, and at a pressure of 0.27 mm, its thickness was 4 mm. Heating the negative pole caused expansion of the spheroid, but not to as great an extent as if the gas had been air or hydrogen.

->ILLUMINATION OF LINES OF MOLECULAR PRESSURE.<-

498. These experiments appear to prove three things:—

*a.* Applying an intense electrical excitation to a disk of metal produces a molecular disturbance which affects the surface of the disk and the surrounding gas.

<summary>William Crookes demonstrates that heating the negative pole in a vacuum tube causes the surrounding dark space to expand. He also compares the behavior of the dark space in air, hydrogen, and carbonic acid, noting that hydrogen produces a larger dark space at similar pressures.</summary>
<keywords>William Crookes, dark space, dark spheroid, vacuum tube, molecular pressure, induction coil, Grove's cells, hydrogen, carbonic acid, platinum spiral</keywords>

--- Page 185 ---
<meta>This page continues William Crookes's investigation into the physical properties of the "dark space" (molecular disturbance) in vacuum tubes, following his observations of how the dark spheroid expands when the negative pole is heated in hydrogen at various pressures.</meta>

<header>MOLECULAR PRESSURE, AND THE TRAJECTORY OF MOLECULES.</header>
<sig>T 2</sig>

When the gas is dense, the disturbance extends only a short distance from the metal; but as the vacuum increases, the layer of molecular disturbance increases in thickness. In air at a pressure of 0.078 mm, this molecular disturbance extends for at least 8 mm from the surface of the disk, forming an oblate spheroid around it. If the pole had been a point, the spheroid would have become a sphere 16 mm in diameter.

*b.* The diameter of this dark space varies with the level of exhaustion; with the kind of gas in which it is produced; with the temperature of the negative pole; and, to a lesser degree, with the intensity of the spark. For equal degrees of exhaustion, it is greatest in hydrogen and least in carbonic acid when compared with air.

*c.* The shape and size of this dark space do not vary with the distance separating the poles; nor, except very slightly, with alterations in battery power or the intensity of the spark. When the power is high, the brilliance of the unoccupied parts of the tube overpowers the dark space, making it difficult to observe; but on careful scrutiny, it can still be seen unchanged in size. It does not alter even when it is scarcely visible with a very faint spark. Upon still further reduction of the power, it fades away entirely, but without changing its form.

499. I consider myself justified, therefore, in assuming that if the molecular disturbance communicated to the surrounding gas by the metal were further reduced in intensity, the spheroid would still remain the same size for the same pressure, even if invisible. If, instead of exciting the disturbance in the metal pole by electrical means, I achieve the same result by heating it to a red heat, the spheroid of molecular disturbance in the surrounding gas would probably still exist; and if the disturbance is produced only by allowing light to shine on the metal plate, we may still imagine the molecular disturbance extending around the plate, although vastly reduced in intensity.

500. The vibrations communicated by the induction spark to a metal plate are undoubtedly different in kind as well as in intensity from those caused by heating the plate. This is because the electrical excitement induces luminosity in the gas, even though the metal pole is only slightly heated, while heating the metal to a bright red heat in the absence of electrical excitement from the induction coil causes no luminosity in the surrounding gas.

501. Numerous experiments have been tried with the object of seeing if this *visible* layer of molecular disturbance was the same as the invisible layer of molecular pressure or stress, the investigation of which has been the subject of many papers presented to the Royal Society <note>Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, Vol. 164, p. 501; Vol. 165, p. 519; Vol. 166, p. 325; Vol. 166, p. 355; Vol. 169, p. 243; Vol. 170, p. 87.</note>. Small <term>exploring flies</term> <note>Small, light vanes used to detect molecular movement, similar to a radiometer.</note>—similar to the one described in a previous paper (417) <note>Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, Vol. 170, p. 103.</note>—were moved around in various parts of the bulb, both inside and outside the spheroid. However, the results were very contradictory and were difficult to obtain at all, owing to the electrification of the fly.

<summary>Crookes describes how the "dark space" or layer of molecular disturbance around a negative pole depends on gas pressure and type but remains constant in size regardless of electrical intensity. He suggests that these disturbances also exist invisibly when metal is heated or exposed to light, though experiments using "exploring flies" were hindered by static electricity.</summary>

### ELECTRICAL RADIOMETERS.

502. Successful observations were ultimately obtained by making radiometers with metallic vanes in the following manner:

The needle point on which the fly rotates is connected with a copper wire, *a*, *fig. 10*, passing down the central tube and attached to the platinum terminal, *b*, sealed through the glass. The other terminal, *c*, passes through the top of the bulb and is made of aluminium wire inside. The vanes are made of aluminium, lampblacked on one side, and connected by aluminium arms to a hard steel cup; the entire fly is therefore in metallic connection with the lower terminal.

->Fig. 10.<-

<image-desc>A technical diagram labeled Fig. 10 showing a vacuum bulb containing a radiometer fly with four vanes. A central vertical support is labeled 'a'. A wire 'c' enters from the top of the bulb, and a terminal 'b' is at the bottom. The fly is mounted on a central pivot.</image-desc>

503. At a moderately low pressure, with the coil attached and the fly acting as the negative pole, a faint halo appears on the bright side of the vanes, and there is a tendency toward negative rotation. As the exhaustion continues, the dark space appears and gradually widens. The space on the black side is nearly double the thickness of the space on the bright side, but it is fainter (491). Upon exhausting the bulb still more, the dark space widens until it forms a large, irregularly shaped oval around each vane. While the dimensions of this oval are small, the fly does not move definitely in one direction or the other; however, when the dark space on the lampblacked side has grown until its luminous boundary touches the glass, positive rotation begins and continues with increasing speed as the exhaustion increases. Because the difference in size between the dark spaces on each side of the vanes is small, the space from the bright side soon strikes the glass, which prevents the positive rotation from reaching a high speed.

504. Another instrument was therefore made similar to the one last described, but with one side of each metallic vane covered with a thin piece of mica. It was connected with the coil, and experiments were conducted as the exhaustion proceeded.

At a pressure of 4.5 millimeters, a halo with a velvety violet appearance forms on the metallic side of only two of the vanes, while the others remain dark. The movement has a negative tendency.

<summary>William Crookes describes the construction of an electrical radiometer with aluminium vanes and details how the expansion of the "dark space" around these vanes triggers rotation as vacuum levels increase. He observes that rotation becomes most pronounced when the dark space boundary makes contact with the glass bulb.</summary>

<keywords>electrical radiometer, William Crookes, aluminium vanes, lampblack, dark space, vacuum exhaustion, mica, negative pole, positive rotation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues William Crookes's experimental observations on the behavior of radiometer vanes under electrical discharge at various levels of vacuum, specifically focusing on the transition between negative and positive rotation and the visual phenomena of the "dark space."</meta>

At a pressure of 1.4 millimeters, the bright velvety light has spread over the metallic sides of all four vanes. When the screw of the induction coil is adjusted to produce a faint spark, the movement is negative. If a <term>Leyden jar</term> is added to the circuit, or the contact screw is turned to produce strong sparks, the movement is positive. Inserting the jar makes the halo fainter. The ideal pressure for negative rotation is 1.14 millimeters.

When the pressure is 0.51 millimeters, the dark space on the metallic side extends nearly to the glass, and the entire interior of the bulb is luminous; the rotation is now always positive when using the coil. Inserting a piece of wet string into the circuit causes the vanes to move in a negative direction.

As the exhaustion proceeds, the dark space widens and flattens itself against the glass, and the positive rotation speeds up until its maximum is reached. Exhaustion beyond that point causes the speed to decrease, but I cannot produce negative rotation again by any amount of further exhaustion.

505. Two radiometers of this type were constructed and sealed: one at a pressure of 0.19 millimeters, showing good positive rotation, and the other at a pressure of 1.14 millimeters, showing negative rotation. Connecting the two in series—that is to say, connecting the vanes forming the negative pole of one with the positive pole of the other—and passing the induction current through them caused both to rotate at the same time, one positively and the other negatively.

506. The vanes of the radiometer were now made of <term>aluminum cups</term> (334) positioned favorably toward the side of the glass. They were almost hemispherical and bright on both sides. The other parts of the radiometer remained as before.

When the exhaustion is low and the induction coil is connected, the fly rotates negatively. This is caused by electrified air rushing off the edges of the cups and driving them around like the well-known <term>electrical fly</term> <note>Also known as Hamilton's fly, a device that rotates due to the reaction from ions discharging from its points.</note>. Luminosity appears on the cups at a pressure of 3.5 millimeters, and as the exhaustion proceeds, it spreads over each side and is separated by a dark space. This space widens while maintaining the shape of the cup as much as possible, passing through the various appearances shown in Plate 14, figure 11, *a, b, c, d,* and *e*. The luminous boundary of the dark space is concentrated at the concave side of the cup, forming a luminous center, and widens out at the convex side. As soon as the luminous boundary of the dark space reaches the side of the glass, positive rotation begins. As the exhaustion continues, the dark space becomes flattened against the glass, and the rotation becomes more rapid. At higher levels of exhaustion, the dark spaces—which surround each cup in the form of an irregular ellipsoid pulled in at the cup's focus—touch one another. They now act as if they were solid elastic bodies and become flattened out along the lines where they meet (as the distance between two cups is not large enough for complete ellipsoids to form). This creates broad longitudinal lines of light running down the bulb between each pair of cups, while the rest of the bulb is comparatively dark. These lines are closer to the concave side than the convex side and rotate with the fly.

507. The line of reasoning followed in paragraphs 498, 499, and 500 is therefore seen

# MR. W. CROOKES ON THE ILLUMINATION OF LINES OF

to be well supported by experiment, and it justifies the theory that the induction spark actually illuminates the lines of molecular pressure caused by the electrical excitement of the negative pole. The thickness of the dark space is the measure of the length of the path between successive collisions of the molecules. The extra velocity with which the molecules rebound from the excited negative pole pushes back the more slowly moving molecules that are advancing toward the pole. The conflict occurs at the boundary of the dark space, where the luminous margin provides evidence of the energy of the discharge. When the exhaustion is high enough that the length of the path between successive collisions is greater than the distance between the fly <note>the rotating vane assembly of the radiometer</note> and the glass, the swiftly moving, rebounding molecules spend their energy, either partially or entirely, on the sides of the vessel, and a production of light accompanies this sudden halt in velocity.

->CONVERGENCE OF MOLECULAR RAYS TO A FOCUS.<-

508. In the sixth part of my researches on "Repulsion resulting from Radiation," which was presented to the Royal Society last June, I gave in paragraph 415 a theoretical explanation of the movement of radiometer flies with curved surfaces, based on the assumption that the lines of molecular pressure acted in a direction normal <note>perpendicular</note> to the surface. In the figures illustrating this theory (fig. 14, A and B, paragraphs 415 and 416), I drew the lines of pressure radiating outward from the convex surface and predicted that they would converge to a focus and then diverge at the concave surface. These figures were drawn long before the experiments just described were started, and it is a confirmation almost amounting to absolute proof that the theory was correct to see how well those old drawings represent the actual lines of pressure as illuminated by the induction spark.

509. The convergence of the lines of force to a focus required a closer investigation than was possible when the cup was in rapid rotation. Therefore, a bulb was constructed similar in general character to the electrical radiometers just described, but with the cup-shaped negative pole fixed in place instead of being movable. I proceeded with the exhaustion, and the successive appearances noted were like those shown in fig. 11. As the exhaustion continued further, the dark space spread out even more, and the focus of light converging from the concave side fell on the luminous boundary. Inside this focus, the rays can be seen converging and are violet in color. Outside the line bounding the dark space, the rays diverge from the focus and are a lighter color than those inside; the entire appearance is strikingly similar to the rays of the sun reflected from a concave mirror through a foggy atmosphere.

At the part of the bulb where the rays strike, a faint spot of greenish-yellow light is observed, sharp in outline. 511. This phosphorescent light only appears at its full intensity when the dark space surrounding the negative pole extends to the surface of the bulb. At lower vacuum levels, it can be detected if specifically sought for outside the luminous boundary of the dark space, but it is faint and not easily noticeable. The color depends on the kind of glass used. Most of my apparatus are made of soft German glass, and this gives a phosphorescent light of a greenish-yellow color. English glass phosphoresces with a blue color; uranium glass becomes green; a diamond became brilliantly blue.

512. The greenish-yellow phosphorescence of the soft German glass only occurs under the influence of the discharge from the negative pole.* <note>While this paper was being printed, my attention was drawn to two Memoirs by Mr. <term>Eugen Goldstein</term>, communicated to the Berlin Royal Academy of Sciences on May 4, 1876, and November 23, 1876, in which some of the results announced in this paper were anticipated. Referring to the green phosphorescent light, Mr. <term>Goldstein</term> writes:

"The author has specifically examined the green light which appears in tubes of common glass at certain degrees of pressure and intensity of the discharge. The luminosity of the sides of the tube is not a phenomenon of fluorescence but of phosphorescence, and can change from green to orange.

"The negative light which produces this phosphorescence is, as was already assumed by <term>Hittorf</term>, a straight-line radiation which extends from the negative pole into the surrounding space. Still, there are essential differences between the diffusion of this remarkable motion and the similarly straight-line movement of light; some of these differences are presented here.

"<term>Hittorf</term> observed that a body placed between the side of the glass and a point-like cathode throws a shadow in the phosphorescent light of the latter.

"Well-defined, though not very sharp, shadows of small objects may be obtained not merely from a point-like or linear negative pole, but also from extended negative surfaces placed at a small distance from the opaque object.

"A surface which merely radiates light, such as a glowing body, throws a scarcely visible, expanded partial shadow under similar conditions.

"The negative light is therefore a straight-line radiation, which propagates primarily in a manner almost perpendicular to the producing surface.

When the exhaustion reaches 0.15 **M**, the spark has difficulty passing, and the green light appears only in occasional flashes, and then only in patches across the tube. At 0.06 **M**, the vacuum is almost non-conducting, and a spark can only be forced through by increasing the strength of the coil and carefully insulating the tube and the wires leading to it. Beyond that level of exhaustion, nothing can be observed.

513. It is difficult to experiment at these high vacuum levels. After the induction spark has been forced through several times, gas is released from the metallic poles or from the surface of the glass; conduction through the remaining gas then begins, and light starts to appear. Further exhaustion reduces the conductivity again. The greatest care must be taken to keep the conducting wires away from the tube except exactly where they touch the terminals; they should be well-insulated, and no metal should come near the tube. Despite all these precautions, however, it is difficult to prevent a spark from passing through the side of the tube, which immediately ruins the vacuum.

515. Upon exhaustion, when the hemicylinder *a* is made the negative pole through the wire *c*, the usual phenomena are observed. The dark space gradually increases in size, and as it spreads from the concave surface toward the center, it forms a denser and more luminous glow of light. 516. It is difficult to fix the exact focal point, but it gradually moves up from 11 millimetres to about 19 millimetres.

->NATURE OF THE GREEN PHOSPHORESCENT LIGHT.<-

519. Other differences are observed. The focus of the green phosphorescent light remains at the center of curvature, appearing independent of the degree of exhaustion, provided the vacuum is sufficient to make it visible; while the bluish focus of light lengthens as the exhaustion increases. The green focus cannot be seen within the body of the tube, but only where the projection causing it strikes the glass; while the concentration of light first observed is only visible in the space within the tube and produces no special effect when it touches the sides.

The bluish focus at low exhaustions, proceeding from the negative hemicylinder, is only seen when the pole *d* is positive, with no light being seen on the concave side. When the exhaustion is high and the green phosphorescent focus is bright, it makes little difference whether the positive pole is above the concave surface at *d*, or below it at *e* or *f*; in either case, the projection from the concave surface of *a* is visibly focused on the phosphorescent surface of the glass (526, 527, 549).

520. Spectrum observations show another difference that is equally decisive. When the luminosity observed at the focus of the hemicylinder at a low exhaustion (for example, 100 M) is examined in the spectroscope, it shows the lines caused by the residual gas, whether it be nitrogen, hydrogen, or carbonic acid; but when the exhaustion is at a very high point (for example, 1 M), the blue light has disappeared, and no lines are detected in the green phosphorescence, regardless of the gas whose residue causes it. The spectrum of the greenish-yellow light, which so beautifully illuminates the tube, is continuous, with most of the red and the higher blue rays being absent.

521. The green phosphorescence begins at a lower exhaustion in hydrogen than it does in air, and the phenomena known to be caused by hydrogen gas also disappear sooner than in the corresponding case with air. In all gases, however, when a high exhaustion is reached, the subsequent phenomena are identical.

522. The viscosity of a gas is almost as persistent a characteristic of its identity as its spectrum. For many years, I have been conducting research into the variations of viscosity of different gases at high exhaustions. In the *Proceedings of the Royal Society* for November 16th, 1876,\* I provided a diagram in a preliminary note showing the variation of viscosity of air, hydrogen, and other gases at exhaustions varying from 250 M to 0.1 M. A comparison of the findings on that diagram with the data given in the present paper will show that when the

In the diagram just mentioned, the variation in the force of repulsion is also provided. This is seen to decline rapidly and almost disappear along with the <term>viscosity</term>; the phosphorescent phenomena become more brilliant as these special characteristics of the gas vanish.

### PROJECTION OF MOLECULAR SHADOWS.

524. In ordinary <term>vacuum tubes</term>, illuminated by the <term>induction current</term>, the luminous phenomena follow the tube through any number of curves and angles; a hollow spiral becomes illuminated just as well as if the tube were a straight line. This is not the case, however, for the phenomena of <term>green phosphorescence</term> observed at these high exhaustion levels. The <term>molecular ray</term> that gives rise to green light absolutely refuses to turn a corner and radiates from the <term>negative pole</term> in straight lines, casting strong and sharply defined shadows\* of anything that happens to be in its path. In a **U** tube with poles at each end, one leg will be bright green and the other almost dark, with the light being cut off sharply by the bend of the glass and a shadow projected onto the curve. I can detect no trace of <term>polarization</term> in the green phosphorescent light on the surface of the glass, except, of course, when it emerges at an angle through the side of the glass tube.

525. The projection from the <term>negative pole</term> of a shadow, made visible by a sharply defined image on the side of the glass, seemed worthy of closer examination. A tube was accordingly made, as shown in fig. 13. In the center, dividing the tube into nearly equal parts, is a screen of thin mica, *a a*, loosely fitting into a groove blown around the tube. A flat plate of <term>uranium glass</term>, *b*, about half a millimeter thick, is riveted to the mica on one side. *c* is a star-shaped piece of <term>aluminum foil</term> attached to a <term>platinum terminal</term>, and *d* is a similar star made of mica. At each end of the tube are two terminals, *e* and *h*, which are flat aluminum disks, and *f* and *g* are aluminum points.

Experiments were carried out with this apparatus during the exhaustion process. When the exhaustion is moderate (say 1 or 2 millimeters), showing stratifications and the ordinary phenomena of <term>vacuum tubes</term>, the luminosity extends from one pole to the other. 529. If the aluminium star is made the positive pole, and any of the others the negative pole, it casts an enlarged and somewhat distorted image of itself all over the upper part of the tube. This image is not sharply defined.

The sharpness of the shadows cast by the negative pole is slightly affected by the intensity of the current; when the spark is very strong, the shadow widens out a little.

530. I have already proposed the theory that the thickness of the dark space surrounding the negative pole is the measure of the mean length of the path of the gaseous molecules between successive collisions (507). The electrified molecules are projected from the negative pole with enormous velocity, which varies, however, with the degree of exhaustion and the intensity of the induction current (498). In the dark space, they are few in number in comparison to what they are at the luminous boundary. When the exhaustion is so high that the mean path of the molecules stretches right across the tube, their velocity is suddenly checked by the glass walls, and the production of light is the consequence of this sudden arrest of velocity. The light actually proceeds from the glass and is caused by fluorescence or phosphorescence in or on its surface, and not by an emission of light by the molecules themselves crowding together and striking each other on the surface of the glass. Had this been the case—had the molecules themselves been the lamps—they would shine equally well regardless of the arresting surface, and their light would have shown the spectral characteristics of the gas whose residue they constituted. But no light is caused by a mica or quartz screen, however near it may be brought to the negative pole; and generally speaking, the more fluorescent the material of the screen, the better the luminosity.

531. The theory best supported by experiment, and the one which although new is not at all improbable in the present state of our knowledge respecting molecules, is that the greenish-yellow phosphorescence of the glass is caused by the direct impact of the molecules on the surface of the glass. The shadows are not optical but *molecular* shadows, though they are revealed by an ordinary illuminating effect. The sharpness of the shadow, when projected from a wide pole, proves them to be molecular. Had the projection from the negative pole radiated in all directions, in the same way that light radiates from a luminous disk, the shadows would not be perfectly sharp, but would be surrounded by a penumbra. However, being projected material molecules in the same electrical state, they do not cross each other but travel on in slightly divergent paths, giving perfectly sharp shadows with no penumbrae.

532. It was suggested by Professor <term>STOKES</term>, as an alternative to the above theory,

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the causes of phosphorescence in vacuum tubes, moving from observations of shadows to a theoretical discussion on whether the effect is caused by molecular impact or ultraviolet radiation.</meta>

# MR. W. CROOKES ON THE ILLUMINATION OF LINES OF

that the phosphorescence of the glass might possibly be excited—as we have previously known phosphorescence to be excited—by radiation, instead of being excited by the actual impact of individual molecules against the molecules of the glass. The difficulty with this hypothesis was: where could the radiation come from? The sharpness of the shadows rules out the idea that it originates in the immediate vicinity of the negative electrode, which is far from being a mere point. It might, however, be supposed that the incandescent molecules were projected with such enormous velocity from the negative electrode that the space around it remained relatively clear; that there were relatively few molecules within this space, but that, adjacent to the glass, there was a thin layer of them densely packed. Thus, if the molecules are thought of as lamps emitting not the green light observed, but the invisible ultraviolet radiation capable of exciting green phosphorescence, it is possible that the absence of phosphorescence within the sharply defined shadows could be explained by the absence of that thin, overlying phosphorogenic layer.

->PHOSPHORESCENCE OF THIN FILMS.<-

533. An experiment was suggested by Professor <term>STOKES</term> which seemed designed to be decisive, or nearly decisive, in choosing between these different views. If the phosphorescence were really produced by impact, it must be confined to a layer of almost infinitesimal thinness. However, if it were produced by radiation from a thin layer of densely packed gaseous molecules glowing with phosphorogenic light, the fluorescence should extend a measurable distance into the glass. Furthermore, if an extremely thin film of glass were used (thin enough to show the colors of thin plates) and placed in front of a thicker plate of phosphorescent glass, the full amount of fluorescence should not be triggered on it. Instead, some of the phosphorogenic rays would likely pass through, and the thin film should not cast a black shadow. By using very thin films of different glasses, as well as thin plates of quartz, the result would be more conclusively shown, for it is unlikely that thin layers of all these materials possess a metallic-like opacity to phosphorogenic rays.

534. To experiment on these points, an apparatus was constructed in the following manner: In the center of a tube, equipped with flat aluminum terminals, *d* and *e*, a plate of uranium glass, *a*, is supported. About half a millimeter to one side is a film of uranium glass, *b*, and on the other side is a similar film of German glass, *c*. The two films are thin enough to show brilliant colors of thin plates when viewed by

535. When the tube is evacuated to within a few millionths of an atmosphere, and the pole *d* is made negative, the uranium film *b* casts a strong shadow on the uranium plate *a*. No phosphorescence can be detected on the part of the plate that is beneath the films, but where the plate is uncovered, it shines with its characteristic greenish light.

536. Upon making contact with the coil, the film *b* flashes out suddenly over its entire surface with a yellowish-green phosphorescence, which instantly disappears except at the part where it is attached to the aluminum support at its back. The plate does not seem to become phosphorescent quite so suddenly, but the phosphorescence remains permanent as long as the coil is kept running.

537. When the contact hammer of the coil is adjusted so as to make the spark excessively faint, the thin film remains more luminous than the plate; but if the screw is turned to produce an intense spark, the luminosity of the film sinks, and that of the uncovered part of the plate increases; the plate is now three or four times brighter than the film.

538. If an intense spark is used and the contact is made and broken suddenly, so as to send one spark at a time through the tube, only the film becomes visible, flashing out with a brilliant yellowish-green light, while the plate—even in its uncovered part—remains dark.

539. Exactly similar phenomena take place if the pole *e* is made negative, so as to experiment with the film of German glass, *c*. The only difference is in the color of the phosphorescent light, which is much yellower with German glass than with uranium glass. In other tubes, English glass, which phosphoresces with a bluish light, has been found to behave in the same way. A very thin film of quartz casts a perfectly opaque shadow, but it does not become phosphorescent. The same thing occurs with mica.

540. These experiments are conclusive evidence against the theory that phosphorescence is caused by the radiation of phosphor-producing (phosphorogenic) ultraviolet light from a thin layer of arrested molecules at the surface of the glass; if this were the cause, the film could under no circumstances be brighter than the plate.

The momentary phosphorescence of the film, and its rapid fading, prove more than this. The molecular bombardment is too much for the thin film. It responds to it at first, but immediately becomes heated by the impacts and then ceases to be luminous, except where it is attached to the aluminum support, which conducts the heat away. The plate, however, withstands the heating without getting hot enough to lose its power of phosphorescing. The experiment demonstrates for the first time the transfer over a finite distance, from molecule to molecule, of even that short-period vibration on which phosphorescence depends; furthermore, it experimentally exhibits the decay of phosphorescence by its transformation into a disturbance of a longer period, which is quickly propagated from molecule to molecule and carried away as heat.

it is not the same line of molecules which forms the curved line *c c*. The action of the magnetic force is to twist all the trajectories of the molecules around in a direction at an angle to their normal path, and to a greater extent as they are nearer the magnet; the direction of the twist is that of the electric current passing around the electro-magnet. The line *c c* is therefore not the line *b b* twisted out of its place, but is another line, *e e*, which is bent around from *e* to *c* by the magnet, while the line *b b* passes away somewhat in the direction *f f*.

554. These phenomena of magnetic deflection are obtained with permanent magnets as well as with electro-magnets. A copper wire helix without the iron core acts like an electro-magnet, though more weakly, when an electric current is passed through it. The shadows used in the experiments with the tubes and bulbs already described are easily deflected by bringing a magnet near.

556. Another apparatus was accordingly made to test this point, and also to obtain a more definite relation between the dimensions of the dark space around the negative pole, the start of the green phosphorescence, and the magnetic deflection under varying conditions of pressure in different gases.

I have spoken of shadows being deflected by the magnet as a convenient way of describing the observed phenomena; but it will be understood that what is really deflected is the path of the molecules driven from the negative pole, and their impact on the phosphorescent surface causes light. The shadows are the result of a physical obstacle in the path of the molecules.

In the apparatus now about to be described, a ray of light was used instead of a shadow. Figure 19 shows the arrangement.

557. The magnet used is a compound horseshoe magnet capable of supporting about 5 pounds. It is placed underneath the negative pole, as shown in figure 18 at N S. The experiments already attempted with the straight electromagnet show that the molecular ray is deflected in a spiral to the right or to the left, according to the pole presented to it. When two opposite poles, as in a horseshoe magnet, are placed in a line with the normal direction of movement of the molecules, one tends to twist it spirally to the right, and the other to the left (figure 20, A, B). The resulting

->Fig. 20.<-

<image-desc>A scientific diagram labeled Fig. 20, showing two scenarios, A and B. Each scenario depicts a horseshoe magnet with poles labeled S and N. direction is that the ray is bent in a curve, up or down, along a plane at right angles to the plane of the magnet and the line joining the poles, depending on whether the North pole is to the right or to the left. The magnet is arranged so that it can be put in position or moved away as often as necessary, with the certainty of always being replaced in exactly the same position.

The first observations were taken with air at different pressures. Exhaustion = 411.7 millionths of an atmosphere. The thickness of the dark space in front of the negative pole, measured along the scale *e*, is 6.5 millimeters. The bulb is filled with blue and violet light; no green phosphorescence is visible.

558. Exhaustion = 161.8 M (millionths of an atmosphere). Thickness of dark space = 8.5 millimeters. Some green phosphorescence is seen near the negative pole, but no projection of an image is yet seen on the screen *d*.

559. Exhaustion = 102.6 M. Thickness of dark space = 12 millimeters. A spot of green light is now seen projected on the scale *d*, bright in the center and shading off at the edges. The spot is about 5.5 millimeters in diameter. The center of the spot, with the magnet removed, is at 18.3 millimeters on the scale. Upon placing the magnet in position, the spot of light is bent vertically down to 5 millimeters on the scale, a distance of 13.3 millimeters.

The magnet would easily bend the light much more if brought nearer, but it was not considered advisable to create a greater deflection for fear that the light would move off the scale in other gases.

576. These experiments prove several important points. In paragraph 559, when working with an air vacuum, it is recorded that the spot of green light is visible on the screen at a pressure of 102.6 M when the thickness of the dark space is only 12 millimeters from the pole. Assuming, as I do, that this is a measure of the <term>free path</term> <note>the distance a molecule travels before colliding with another</note> of the molecules before collision, it follows that some of the molecules, sufficient to cause green phosphorescence on the screen, are projected the whole distance from the pole to the screen, or 102 millimeters, without being stopped by collisions. It is probable that this would have occurred at an even lower exhaustion; for on reference to paragraph 566, it is seen that the green spot was detected on the screen when the mean path in <term>carbonic acid</term> <note>carbon dioxide</note> was 8.5 millimeters, and it was seen with hydrogen (paragraph 570) when the mean path was only 7 millimeters.

577. If we suppose the magnet is permanently in position, and thus exerting a uniform downward pull on the molecules, it is seen that their trajectory is much curved at low exhaustions and gets flatter as the exhaustion increases. Since a flatter trajectory corresponds to a higher velocity of the molecules, it follows that the molecules move faster the higher the exhaustion. This may arise from one of two causes: either the...

<summary>Experiments using hydrogen gas demonstrate that as vacuum exhaustion increases, the molecular trajectory flattens and velocity increases. The results suggest that molecules can travel the entire length of the tube without collision even at relatively low exhaustion levels.</summary>

# MOLECULAR PRESSURE, AND THE TRAJECTORY OF MOLECULES.
MDCCCLXXIX. Y

The initial impulse given by the negative pole is stronger, or the collisions are less frequent. I consider the latter to be the true cause. The molecules that produce the green phosphorescence must be looked upon as being in a different state from those that are stopped by frequent collisions. These collisions impede the velocity of the free molecules and allow longer time for the magnetism to act on them; and although the deflecting force of magnetism might be expected to increase with the velocity of the molecules, Professor <term>STOKES</term> has pointed out that it would have to increase as the square of the velocity in order for the deflection to be as great at high velocities as it is at low velocities.

Comparing the free molecules to cannonballs, the magnetic pull to the earth's gravity, and the electrical excitation of the negative pole to the explosion of the powder in the gun, the trajectory will be quite flat when no gravity acts, and becomes curved under the influence of gravity; it is also much more curved when the ball passes through a dense resisting medium; it is less curved when the resisting medium becomes thinner; and, from paragraph 562, it is seen that intensifying the induction spark—equivalent to increasing the charge of powder—gives greater initial velocity and therefore flattens the trajectory. The parallel is still closer if we compare the flash of light seen when the shot strikes the target with the phosphorescence produced in the glass screen by molecular impacts.

578. In carbonic acid, the mean free path of the molecules is shorter for the same degree of exhaustion than in air, and the velocity of the molecules—measured by the flatness of the trajectory under magnetic influence—is also lower than it is in air at similar pressures.

579. Although in many cases, especially at a moderate exhaustion and using a feeble spark, the image on the screen was a perfectly well-defined circle, I could detect no image of the notch cut in the negative pole. The hole in the mica was small enough to have given a good inverted image of the negative pole on the screen had it been shining by ordinary light; but because the rays are corpuscular and the particles do not cross, no image of the pole is formed, but only the image of the hole in the mica.*

580. Attempts to obtain continuous rotation of the ray of molecular light by means of a magnet have so far failed. The stream of molecules does not obey <term>AMPÈRE'S Law</term> as it would if it were a perfectly flexible conductor joining the negative and positive pole. The molecules are projected from the negative pole, but the position of the positive pole—whether in front, at the side, or even behind the negative pole—has no influence on their subsequent behavior, either in causing phosphorescence, producing mechanical effects, or in their magnetic deflection (519, 526, 527, 549). The magnet seems to give them a spiral twist, greater or less according to its power, but diminishing as the molecules get further off and independent of their direction.

---

\* With another apparatus, in which the pole and screen are nearer together and the mica with the hole in it can be moved to and fro, I have succeeded in seeing a poorly defined image of the negative pole. This only occurs at low levels of exhaustion and soon disappears, giving way to a sharp image of the hole.

<summary>Crookes explains that molecular trajectories flatten with higher velocity and lower resistance, using a ballistics analogy to describe magnetic deflection. He also notes that these molecular streams do not follow Ampère’s Law and that their behavior is determined by the negative pole regardless of the positive pole's location.</summary>

### FOCUS OF MOLECULAR HEAT OF IMPACT.

581. In the experiment described in paragraphs 536 to 540, the heating effect of the molecular bombardment is assumed to be the cause of certain phenomena. It was thought that by concentrating the molecular impacts onto one point, the heat produced might be made apparent. The experiments conducted with the apparatus shown in Figure 21 prove that this supposition is correct. A polished aluminum cup *a* is made the negative pole in a properly evacuated tube.

->Fig. 21.<-

<image-desc>A technical diagram showing two vacuum tubes, labeled A and B. Tube A shows a concave aluminum cup (a) emitting rays that converge to a sharp focal point at the top of the tube. Tube B shows the same apparatus, but the path of the rays is deflected to the side by an external influence, creating a curved path toward the glass wall.</image-desc>

The focus appears very sharp and distinct, as seen at A, and is a dark blue color. Although the light is blue in the center of the tube, when it spreads out and strikes the end of the tube, it illuminates it beautifully with a yellowish-green light. By using a magnet, the focus was deflected to the side of the tube, as shown at B, and the path of the rays was beautifully curved. On the tube, the appearance was that of a sharply defined yellowish-green oval with a dark spot in the center. To determine if heat was generated there, I touched it with my finger and immediately developed a blister. The spot where the focus fell was nearly red-hot.

582. Another apparatus was then constructed, as shown in Figure 22. A nearly hemispherical cup of polished aluminum *a* is used as one pole in a bulb, and a small aluminum disk *b* is used as the other pole. At *c*, a strip of platinum is held by a wire passing through the glass, forming another pole at *d*. The tip of the platinum strip is positioned at the center of curvature, and the entire vessel is evacuated to a very high degree. When the induction current was first turned on, with the cup acting as the negative pole, the platinum strip began to vibrate very rapidly. This soon stopped, and the platinum quickly reached a white heat; it would have melted if I had not stopped the operation of the coil.

The same phenomenon of ignition occurs if the platinum strip itself is made the positive pole.

### AN ULTRA-GASEOUS STATE OF MATTER.

585. The modern idea of the gaseous state of matter is based upon the supposition that a given space with a capacity of, say, a cubic centimeter, contains millions of millions of molecules in rapid motion in all directions, each having millions of encounters in a second. In such a case, the length of the **mean free path** of the molecules is excessively small as compared with the dimensions of the vessel, and properties are observed which constitute the ordinary gaseous state of matter, and which depend upon constant collisions. But by great rarefaction, the free path may be made so long that the hits in a given time are negligible in comparison to the misses,

<summary>William Crookes acknowledges his assistant's technical skill and introduces the concept of an "ultra-gaseous state of matter," where molecular collisions become rare due to high vacuum levels.</summary>

<keywords>C. H. Gimingham, vacuum apparatus, molecular trajectory, mean free path, ultra-gaseous state, rarefaction, kinetic theory of gases</keywords>

--- Page 210 ---
<meta>This page continues the explanation of the gaseous state, detailing how the reduction of molecules in a vessel allows them to move freely, transitioning matter into a fourth state.</meta>

# MR. W. CROOKES ON LINES OF MOLECULAR PRESSURE.

...in which case the average molecule is allowed to obey its own motions or laws without interference; and if the mean free path is comparable to the dimensions of the vessel, the properties which constitute gaseity are reduced to a minimum, and the matter becomes elevated to an ultra-gaseous or molecular state, in which the very distinct but previously hidden properties now under investigation come into play.

The phenomena in these vacuum tubes reveal to physical science a new world—a world where matter may exist in a fourth state, where the <term>corpuscular theory of light</term> may be true, and where light does not always move in straight lines, but where we can never enter, and with which we must be content to observe and experiment from the outside.

### I.—*Definition and description of the sensitive state.*

It has often been noted that the luminous column produced by electric discharges in vacuum tubes occasionally shows great sensitivity when a finger or other conductor is brought near the tube. The exact effect of this approach varies considerably depending on the circumstances of the discharge. In many instances, the luminous column is repelled; in others, and especially when the finger is brought into actual contact with the glass, the column is split. In the latter case, in addition to the light previously present, a blue haze—which usually characterizes the negative end of a discharge—often appears coming from the interior of the tube at the point where the finger rests. In some cases, the discharge is so powerfully affected that the well-known green or blue fluorescence appears on the side of the tube opposite to the point touched.

The degree of sensitivity varies between wide limits. Discharges frequently occur in which close observation is necessary to detect any trace of it, while others may be produced that are so sensitive that the magnetic action of a powerful electromagnet is hardly more noticeable than the action caused by its presence as a conductor. This condition does not appear to be confined to any particular gaseous medium or to any special form of tube; in fact, it is probable that sensitivity may be produced in almost any tube by taking suitable precautions.<note>Subsequent experiments have removed all doubt on this point. So long as the tube permits any traces of a luminous column to appear, this column can be rendered sensitive.</note> This state of sensitivity may be shown by stratified discharges, but it is more commonly associated with those which show no clear traces of stratification. It is not, however, universally present in either kind of discharge.

The state in which the discharge is affected by the presence or approach of a conductor will be called the *sensitive state*; while that in which it is not so affected will be called the *non-sensitive state*. The former is the subject of the present inquiry.

The attention of the authors of this paper was drawn to this form of vacuum discharge, partly by the striking character of the phenomena it presents and partly by their own earlier observations, which led them to connect it with an interruption or intermittence in the current. Although there are a great variety of methods by which the sensitive state can be produced, they all agree, as will presently be seen, in causing a rapid intermittence in the current. The experiments of Mr. <term>De La Rue</term> and others have furnished strong evidence for concluding that vacuum discharges are never continuous in the same sense that the flow of electricity along a metallic conductor is continuous, but that they are always disruptive and periodic with an extremely high rate of periodicity. Such being the case, it appeared desirable to subject to special examination a form of discharge in which periodicity (though much less rapid) is

<summary>The authors define the "sensitive state" of electrical discharges in vacuum tubes, where the luminous column reacts to the proximity of conductors. They argue that this state is fundamentally linked to a rapid, periodic interruption or intermittence in the electrical current.</summary>
<keywords>sensitive state, non-sensitive state, vacuum tubes, electric discharge, luminous column, fluorescence, stratification, intermittence, periodicity, De La Rue</keywords>

--- Page 213 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on vacuum discharges, specifically examining the periodicity and intermittence of the "sensitive state" as theorized by Spottiswoode and Moulton.</meta>

->ON ELECTRICAL DISCHARGES THROUGH RAREFIED GASES.<-

...produced by artificial means, where the periodicity can therefore be varied at will. Moreover, the usefulness of an investigation into the phenomena of discontinuous discharges does not depend entirely on the theory that regards all vacuum discharges as discontinuous; for, just as the mathematician is often forced to reason from the discontinuous to the continuous—from the polygon to the curve—so the physicist may eventually be better able to understand the causes of the phenomena accompanying ordinary vacuum discharges (whether these are absolutely continuous or only relatively so) by studying the phenomena that rapidly intermittent discharges present. The importance of this method is greatly increased when we consider that none of the usual phenomena of ordinary vacuum discharges is necessarily absent from or incompatible with the discontinuous discharge; and that if the theory of the discontinuous character of the ordinary vacuum discharge is correct, this method offers us the prospect of building a continuous chain of phenomena, extending from the single flash of a Leyden-jar discharge to the steadiest striated column that can be produced by a battery current.

### II.—*The sensitive state is due to a periodic intermittence in the discharge of considerable rapidity and regularity, the quantity of electricity in each individual discharge being small enough to allow the discharge to be instantaneous.*

To establish this proposition, we will first describe all the methods known to us for producing sensitive discharges, and we will show that in all cases the circumstances of the discharge make it highly probable that it is discontinuous or intermittent in the manner described above. We will then provide direct experimental evidence that such intermittence actually exists in the resulting discharge in all these cases. Finally, we will examine the cases in which we know that intermittence actually exists in non-sensitive discharges, and we will show that such intermittence does not have the required characteristics specified above, but is of a completely different type from the one we have described as the cause of sensitivity in vacuum discharges.

The simplest method of producing the sensitive state is by conducting a current from a <term>HOLTZ machine</term> or some other constant source of electricity through the exhausted tube.*

---

<note>* In describing the sensitive state as being caused by an intermittence in the discharge, the authors of this paper are discussing discharges that last for a finite time. Naturally, sensitivity was first known to them in this form; but in the course of the inquiry they have discovered, as will appear later, that each individual discharge is sensitive, and that the sensitivity of the intermittent discharge is due solely to the sensitivity of its individual members. The effect of the intermittence is only to change, through rapid repetition, the instantaneous phenomena presented by each discharge into an appearance that seems steady and continuous to the eye.</note>

Although this is by no means the only way in which the sensitive discharge can be produced, it is the most generally convenient method for experimental purposes; for that reason, it may be regarded as the typical mode of production. That the discharge within the tube should be intermittent when the supply of electricity is made intermittent by the air-spark is so obvious that it does not need discussion. Furthermore, although we cannot positively assert (without experimental evidence) that the pulses of free electricity forming the discharge pass into the tube instantaneously, it is difficult to imagine any circumstances where we would less expect the individual discharges to have a prolonged or continuous character than in this case. Here, they are caused by charges of free electricity that arrive suddenly at the terminal of the tube after leaping across the air-spark interval in the form of a disruptive discharge.

Another method of producing a discharge that shows signs of sensitivity is by using an <term>induction coil</term> in connection with a large <term>condenser</term>, such as the one described in a paper titled "On Stratified Discharges, V." When the coil is operating, a certain amount of sensitivity will usually be visible. (See Plate 16, fig. 6.) But if the coil is stopped and the current is allowed to flow from the condenser through the tube without interference from the input of the coil discharges, the discharge will be found to have lost all its sensitivity. We believe the explanation for this is that as long as the coil was operating, its pulsations produced sudden periodic increases of tension in the condenser, which caused corresponding discharges through the tube. It is probable that in these cases the periodic discharges are only superimposed upon the continuous discharges that we see upon stopping the coil—which are caused by the average tension in the condenser—so it would be more strictly accurate to say that the discharge is subject to intermittent or periodic variations of intensity than to say that the discharge itself is intermittent. However, as all the phenomena align with the assumption that the discharge is partly sensitive and partly non-sensitive, and that the sensitive portion is entirely caused by the pulsations produced by the coil, it is better to view it as a superposition of two discharges and to regard the sensitive one as intermittent.

It is not, however, always the case that the discharge from the condenser is non-sensitive when the coil is not acting. When the tension in the condenser becomes low, it is very common to find sensitivity in the discharge. This phenomenon, however, does not in any way contradict the view that sensitivity arises from intermittence; for the very last stages of the discharge from the condenser are visibly intermittent, and it is therefore not surprising that the stage immediately preceding should also be intermittent, though with a much more rapid period. That such is the true explanation of the phenomenon can also be shown directly, either by means of a rapidly revolving mirror or by placing a telephone in the circuit, as will be more fully described later.

Again, certain tubes appear to make the discharge from a continuous source sensitive without the necessity of artificially producing intermittence in the current. Such cases, however, will be found to offer no difficulties. They are merely instances of tubes which, at higher tensions of the condenser, produce the phenomenon already described as being very common when the tension is low. No doubt, if the tension in the condenser—or perhaps, more strictly speaking, if the quantity of electricity discharged (current strength)—were increased even further, the sensitivity could be made to disappear in all cases.*

Again, rapid intermittency and sensitiveness in what would otherwise be a continuous discharge may be produced by the use of a "<term>wheel-break</term>," such as is described (see Plate 15, fig. 3) in a paper "On Stratified Discharges, III." in the Proceedings of the Royal Society for February 15, 1877. This instrument consists of a wheel coated with platinum at the edge, on which a platinum spring rests. In the circumference of the wheel a number of slots are cut and filled with ebonite plugs, so as to interrupt the current. If the wheel-break is placed in the circuit of a <term>HOLTZ machine</term> when producing a luminous discharge in a vacuum-tube, and the break is operated at a considerable speed so as to cause the current to be interrupted some 400 to 2,000 times per second, the discharge becomes highly sensitive. This instrument is used as a shunt—namely, to divert the current given by the machine from the tube by permitting it to pass through a continuous metallic circuit during the time that the platinum wire rests upon the metallic portion of the circumference. In this way the current is never actually broken, and one great advantage of this arrangement is

Another method of producing a sensitive discharge is by using a very rapidly vibrating break, such as the one described in a paper "On Stratified Discharges"*

<note>
* The following is an extract from the paper in question:—
"In the stratified discharges through rarefied gases produced by an induction coil working with an ordinary contact breaker, the striae are often unsteady in position and apparently irregular in their distribution. Observations made with a revolving mirror led me to conclude that an irregular distribution of striae is not a natural property of stratification, but that its appearance is due to certain peculiarities in the current that depend largely on instrumental causes.

"Having reason to think that the defects in question were mainly due to irregularity in the ordinary contact breaker, I constructed one with a steel rod as a vibrator, which had a small independent electromagnet to maintain its action. The natural vibrations of the rods that were tested varied from 320 to 768 per second; while under the action of the battery current and electromagnet, they varied from 700 to 2500 per second, or thereabouts. The amplitudes of the vibrations were exceedingly small, in fact not exceeding 0.01 of an inch; I attribute the steadiness of the results mainly to this fact, combined with the extreme rapidity and the resulting precision of the 'make and break.'

"With a contact breaker of this kind in good working order, several phenomena were noticeable; but first and foremost was the fact that, in a large number of tubes (especially those containing hydrocarbons), the striae—instead of being sharp and flaky in form, irregular in distribution, and fluttering in position—were soft and rounded in outline, equidistant in their intervals, and steady in proportion to the regularity of the contact breaker. I believe these results are due more to the regularity than to the rapidity of the vibrations. This view is supported by the fact that although the contact breaker may change its pitch (as occasionally happens) and, in doing so, may cause a temporary disturbance in the stratification, the new pitch may produce as steady a set of striae as the first. Not only that, but frequently a strident sound is heard simultaneously with a pure note from the vibrator, indicating that contacts of two separate periods are being made; yet, when the strident sound is regular, the striae remain steady. On the other hand, any sudden change in the action of the breaker (usually indicated by a change in the sound) always corresponds to a change in the striae.

"It is difficult to describe the extreme delicacy in the action of this kind of contact breaker, or 'high break,' as it may be called. Turning a screw through only 2° or 3°—where a complete revolution raises or lowers the platinum pin by 0.025 of an inch—is enough to create or destroy the entire phenomenon. A similar turn of a screw forming one foot of the breaker's pedestal is enough to adjust or regulate the striae; even a slight pressure of the finger on the center of the mahogany stand (which appears rigid), or even on the table where the contact breaker sits, will often control their movements.

"The discharges described above are usually (though not always) those produced by breaking the contact; however, it often happens—most frequently when the strident noise is heard—that the current produced by making the contact is strong enough to cause a visible discharge. This happens with both the ordinary and the high break; but in the latter case, the double current presents a very remarkable peculiarity: the striae of one current are arranged so as to fit exactly into the intervals of the other. Furthermore, any disturbance affecting the column of striae from one current affects the other similarly in terms of absolute space, so that the double column moves, if it moves at all, as a solid or elastic mass. This fact is even more remarkable when we consider, as is easily observed with a revolving mirror, that these currents alternate not only in direction but also in time, and that no current is produced until after its predecessor has been completely extinguished. It is also worth noting that this association of striae is not destroyed even when a magnetic pole separates the two currents toward opposite sides of the tube. In that case, however, there seems to be a tendency for the

(Proceedings of the Royal Society, June 10, 1875). If such an instrument is used with an induction coil, the discharge, though often beautifully stratified, is intensely sensitive. The minimum rate at which we have produced stratified sensitive discharges in this way is 240 breaks per second.

We will now consider the direct experimental evidence that the current is intermittent in all cases in which the discharge is sensitive. This evidence is derived from the revolving mirror and the telephone. If the body of the tube containing the discharge is hidden by an opaque screen containing a narrow longitudinal slit, and the image of this slit is observed in a rapidly revolving plane mirror, a series of bright and black bands appear whenever the discharge is sensitive. This shows that there are striae from one current advancing upon the positions occupied by those of the reverse current, giving the whole column a twisted appearance. But as there is no trace, as far as my observations go, of this association of alternate discharges when produced by the ordinary break, we seem led to the conclusion that a stratified discharge, upon ceasing, leaves the gas distributed in a way that favors, during a very short interval of time, a similar stratification when another discharge occurs, whether in the same or in the opposite direction.

“The column of striae, which usually occupies a large part of the tube from the positive toward the negative terminal, has until now been described as stationary, except when disturbed by irregularities of the break. The column is, however, frequently susceptible to a general motion or ‘flow,’ either from or toward the positive pole—say, a forward or backward flow. This flow may be controlled, both in speed and in direction, by resistance introduced into the circuit or by placing the tube in a magnetic field. The resistance may be introduced in either the primary or the secondary circuit.

“When the striae are flowing, they maintain their mutual distances and do not increase or decrease in number. Usually, one or two remain permanently attached to the positive electrode; as the moving column advances or recedes, the foremost stria diminishes in brightness until, after traveling a distance less than the intervals between the two striae, it is lost in darkness. The reverse takes place at the rear of the column. As the last stria leaves its position, a new one, at first faint and shadowy, appears behind it at a distance equal to the common interval of all the others. This new stria increases in brightness until, when it has reached the position originally occupied by the last stria when the column was at rest, it becomes as bright as the others. The flow may vary greatly in speed; it may be so slow that the appearance and disappearance of the terminal striae can be watched in all their phases, or it may be so rapid that the separate striae are no longer distinguishable, and the tube appears as if illuminated with a continuous discharge. In most cases, the true character of the discharge and the direction of the flow can be easily distinguished with the help of a revolving mirror. In some tubes, especially those whose length is great compared to their diameter, the whole column does not present the same phase of flow; one portion may be at rest while another is flowing, or even two adjacent portions may flow in opposite directions. This is also seen in very wide tubes, in which the striae generally appear more mobile than in narrow ones. But in all cases, these nodes or junction-points of the flow retain their positions under similar conditions of pressure and current; it therefore seems that, under similar conditions, the column in a given tube always breaks up into similar flow-segments.

“These nodes will often disappear under the action of a magnetic pole. Thus, if the first segment, measured from the positive terminal, is stationary and the second is flowing backward (*that is*, from $-$ to $+$), a magnetic pole of suitable strength, placed at the distant end of the latter, will stop its flow, and the whole column will become stationary throughout. An increase in the strength of the magnet, or bringing it closer to the tube, will produce a general forward flow of the column.”

We have said that the telephone, as well as the revolving mirror, can be made to show that there is intermittency in the discharge in vacuum tubes as long as there is sensitivity. The evidence it gives us is as follows: When a telephone is in a circuit with a non-interrupted, non-sensitive discharge, a rushing sound is frequently, though not always, heard. In a very large number of cases, there is absolute silence. But as soon as the discharge becomes sensitive, the silence is broken by a shrill sound, or if the rushing sound we mentioned previously existed, there is a sudden change in the character of the sound, which usually becomes musical. The pitch of the note is always high and naturally varies with the circumstances of the discharge. When the air-spark is again abolished, the note stops or gives way to the rushing sound mentioned above.<note>It may reasonably be objected that this test shows only the intermittency of the current in the circuit outside the tube, and does not directly tell us anything about the discharge through the tube. But to make the nature of this evidence clear would require the theory of the sensitive discharge to be more fully developed than is possible at this early stage.</note> Occasionally, in the sensitive discharge, the rushing sound and the musical note are heard simultaneously. This may arise from rapidly succeeding periods of being interrupted and non-interrupted; however, it is not a phenomenon of any particular importance at this stage of our inquiry.<note>When the air interval is increased beyond striking distance, a silent discharge takes place across the interval; and the discharge through the tube is the same in character as that produced without an air-interval; it is also non-sensitive. Instead of the shrill whistling heard with a proper air-spark, nothing is audible in this case but a soft rushing sound. A similar result is obtained when an arc is formed across the air-spark interval, which occurs under certain circumstances that will be mentioned later.</note>

This is usually followed by what appears to be a complete stop of the discharge; it then starts again and continues to show very irregular variations throughout its entire duration. In fact, it is likely that during the period after the first outburst and the brief pause that often follows it, the state of the tube is much the same as it would be during a continuous discharge, because there is no regular pulsing. The tube is always conducting a discharge, although perhaps the resulting disturbance is more violent in one part than in another. There is no switching between a sharply defined discharge and a state of electrical emptiness. The distinction between what may be called irregularly fluctuating and periodically intermittent discharges is so important that, in the case of a fairly rapid coil discharge, it is often found that while the <term>striæ</term> in the main luminosity show very little sensitivity, the faint, ghost-like <term>striæ</term> seen extending far past the end of the <term>positive column</term> proper show great sensitivity (see Plate 16, fig. 6).* The experiments mentioned above with the <term>revolving mirror</term> show that this faint column of light is caused solely by the first outburst we spoke of; thus, such outbursts create a sensitive system, while the fluctuating discharges that follow are not sensitive. As the action of the contact-breaker becomes faster, it is found that the fluctuating part of the discharge becomes less developed, and the discharge consists more and more of the first portion only. Observation shows that as we reach even higher speeds of contact-breaker action, this becomes even more the case, and at very high speeds, the discharge is reduced to this first portion alone. Thus, we understand why a very high-speed contact-breaker produces the most intense sensitive discharges from a coil.

It will therefore be observed that all methods of producing the <term>sensitive state</term> share not only the intermittent nature of the discharge but also the short duration of the individual discharges themselves.† This has led the authors of this paper to consider brevity of duration to be as essential a feature of the individual discharges that produce the <term>sensitive state</term> as the speed or regularity of the intervals between these discharges. These latter characteristics are, in fact, more important for maintaining the <term>sensitive state</term> over a specific period of time than for actually creating it, since careful experiments fail to show any lower limit for the speed of the periodicity needed to produce such a discharge.
