<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between the intermittence of electrical discharges and their sensitivity, providing experimental evidence from Leyden jar flashes and defining new terminology to distinguish these states.</meta>

<page-num>176</page-num>
<header>MESSRS. W. SPOTTISWOODE AND J. FLETCHER MOULTON</header>

In truth, it is not impossible to produce a discharge with the characteristics of sensitivity by a single flash. If a charged Leyden jar\* (“On Stratified Discharges, IV.,” Proceedings of the Royal Society, March 22, 1877) is used with a suitable tube, the instantaneous discharge that passes through the tube when the jar is connected to it will show all the symptoms of sensitivity during its passage through the tube.

This direct evidence of the connection between the intermittence of discharge and the sensitive state will, we believe, be further supported by the agreement of the various phenomena with the theory of the sensitive state. This theory will be developed in the course of this paper and rests upon the hypothesis that the sensitive state is due to such intermittence—a hypothesis that the authors of this paper hope is sufficiently demonstrated by the experimental facts already stated.

In conclusion, the authors of this paper wish it to be understood that, in claiming intermittence as an essential part of the sensitive discharge, they do not intend to exclude all ideas of intermittence from the non-sensitive discharge. The experiments of Sir W. <term>Grove</term>,† Mr. <term>De La Rue</term>, and others, have demonstrated almost beyond doubt that there is intermittence even in the most stable and non-sensitive discharges. But such intermittence must be of an order almost incomparably higher than the kind we are discussing. Although sensitivity has been found to coexist with intermittence at the highest speeds reachable by the mechanical or chemical means mentioned above, and even in many cases to increase with the speed of intermittence, it is by no means necessary that it should continue to do so when this speed is increased—for example, several hundred or thousand times. Indeed, with the speed provided by a short and rapid air-spark, the sensitivity is not as clearly marked in its features as with a longer and slower air-spark. Nor, as will be seen, does our view require that a very great speed of intermittence should necessarily produce very great sensitivity. On the contrary, far from it being an advantage for the discharge to be divided into a very large number of small, separate discharges, it seems that the most favorable condition for the production of sensitivity is that the individual discharges should be as large (and therefore as few in number) as possible, while remaining free of the prolonged or fluctuating phases observed in the ordinary coil discharge.‡ Therefore, to avoid any misunderstanding, the terms *interrupted* and *uninterrupted* will be used to describe the condition of the currents causing the sensitive and non-sensitive states respectively, instead of the terms *intermittent* and *continuous*, which might otherwise have been adopted.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of sensitive electrical discharges, moving from the evidence of intermittence to the physical cause of sensitivity: the influence of nearby conductors on the electrical tension within the tube.</meta>

<sig>MDCCCLXXIX. 2 A</sig>

III.—*The effect produced on a sensitive discharge by the approach of a conductor is directly due to the relief its presence gives to the instantaneous electric tension within and around the tube, caused by the individual discharges as they pass through the tube.*

In the case of the sensitive or interrupted discharge, we have seen that discrete pulses of electricity pass between the terminals. It is, therefore, a likely supposition that the pulse of positive electricity leaving the positive terminal as free electricity—and consequently exercising electric induction in every direction around it—may cause that electric tension or (as Professor <term>Maxwell</term> would call it) displacement, which, as far as we know, always accompanies free electricity. Such induction would cause an electric tension on the outer surface of the glass and in the space beyond; but, because the glass is a non-conductor, it could not cause any redistribution of the electricity within it or on its surface. It is somewhat difficult to determine the effect on the space around the tube, filled as it is with the mobile and rapidly moving particles of air; however, there can be little doubt that the induction from the discharges would only cause a very slight redistribution of electricity in this part of the field. If, however, we place a conductor on or near the glass, the induction can easily cause a redistribution of electricity within the conductor. The state of the electric field near the conductor would then differ from that at any other part of the tube; and this would, in turn, react upon the discharge or upon the gaseous matter that exists inside the tube. We shall now show that the observed effect is due to such a redistribution of electricity in the conductor; we will then proceed to examine the cause of this redistribution and its <term>modus operandi</term> in producing the observed effect.

In order to demonstrate that the phenomena of sensitivity are primarily due to a redistribution of electricity in the conductor—caused by changes in the electrical condition of the interior of the tube—it is only necessary to observe that a non-conductor, no matter how highly charged, does not affect the sensitive discharge. Nor will a small conductor in contact with the tube (such as a piece of tinfoil) affect the discharge as long as it is insulated. But if the tinfoil is connected to the earth, or to a distant conducting body, it immediately produces a marked effect on the sensitive discharge.

A consideration of these experimental facts leads to the following conclusions: (1) that the effect is due to a redistribution of electricity in the conductor; and (2) that this effect is periodic. If a continuous electric state in the external body were the necessary condition, the observed effect could be produced by charged non-conductors. But as this is not the case, we must look to the ease with which the electric state changes...

<summary>This page explains that the sensitivity of electrical discharges is caused by the electric induction of discrete pulses, which creates tension that reacts with nearby conductors. Experimental evidence shows that only grounded or connected conductors—not insulated ones or non-conductors—affect the discharge, proving the effect is due to a periodic redistribution of electricity.</summary>

provided by conductors for an explanation of their effect on the sensitive discharge. This conclusion is supported by the previously stated fact that a small piece of tinfoil placed on the tube produces no effect as long as it is insulated. Such a piece of tinfoil would provide very little scope for the redistribution of electricity—at least in a way that would affect the space around it. But if it is connected by a metal connection to a distant conducting body, so that positive or negative electricity can be driven from it to a noticeable distance from the tube, the situation is different; and if this is done, it is immediately found to affect the sensitive discharge.

If, then, the effect on the sensitive discharge is caused by the ease of a redistribution of electricity within the part of the electric field occupied by the conductor, there must be a varying electric action upon it from the discharge in the tube. That this is the case may be shown by connecting a ring of tinfoil placed around the glass to the earth, and placing a telephone in the circuit between the tinfoil and the earth. As soon as the current becomes interrupted by an air-spark, a sound is heard in the telephone corresponding with the sound of the air-spark causing the interruption. This shows conclusively that at each pulsation there is an electrical redistribution within the system composed of the earth, the wire, and the tinfoil. And as this continues indefinitely without producing any charge on the tinfoil, it is clear that during the complete period of each pulsation, there must be a flow of one kind of electricity from the tinfoil, followed by its return or a similar flow of the opposite kind of electricity from the tinfoil.

Now, since this periodic redistribution is caused by the pulsations of electricity within the tube, it follows that we may regard the conductor as providing a kind of relief to the tension in the electric field around the portion of the tube with which it is in contact. The nature of its action can be shown by numerous experiments, such as the following: If, instead of connecting the tinfoil to the earth, a wire leading to the earth is placed almost in contact with it, sparks will be seen to pass, showing the state of electric tension to which the tinfoil is occasionally subjected. Furthermore, if the effect on the sensitive discharge is examined closely, it will be found to be stronger in proportion as the circumstances in which the tinfoil is placed are more favorable for providing more complete relief. As long as the wire does not touch the tinfoil or permit sparks to pass to or from it, the tinfoil is unable to affect the sensitive discharge. But if the wire is near enough for sparks to pass, the sensitive discharge will be affected, but to a decidedly lesser extent than would be the case if the wire were in actual contact with it. In the latter case, the relief it could provide would be perfect; in the former, it would be imperfect, since the sparks would not be able to perfectly equalize the potentials of the tinfoil and the wire. Again, the effect of the tinfoil when in electrical connection with the conducting body will be found to vary in proportion to the capability of the system to relieve the tension of the tinfoil. If the conducting body is large or distant, the effect will be nearly the same as though

...as if the tinfoil were joined to the earth; if, on the other hand, it is small and near to the tube, the effect will be much less. The same remarks apply to cases in which, although the tinfoil is not absolutely disconnected from the earth, its connection is electrically very imperfect. Thus, if the wire from the tinfoil is allowed to just touch the finger, it will produce less effect than if it is tightly held, and similarly for other imperfect connections. Even in the case of the telephone in circuit between the tinfoil and the earth, if the telephone is not too far from the tube, a marked diminution in loudness will be observed when the connection between the telephone and the earth is severed, so that the displaced electricity, no longer able to escape to the earth, is compelled to rearrange itself in the telephone and the wire connected with it.

There is no need to place the conducting body in actual contact with the glass in order to affect the sensitive discharge. If the body is near the tube, it will produce nearly the same effect as though it were in contact, as in Plate 15, fig. 5; if it is farther off, it will produce less; and, as in the former case, if it is large and capable of permitting displaced electricity to move to a considerable distance from the tube, it will produce a much greater effect than if the contrary were the case. In short, it may generally be stated that the completeness of the effect of a conducting body upon the sensitive discharge depends on the completeness of its capacity to permit a displacement of electricity within it (caused by the electric disturbances in the tube) without any material alteration of its potential.

Such experiments as those involving the telephone in circuit with the tinfoil and the earth may naturally suggest the idea that these effects may be due to electromagnetic and not to electrostatic induction. But careful examination refutes this supposition. In the first place, it is not necessary for the tinfoil to have any considerable length in the direction of the tube, which is presumably the direction of the current through it. A narrow ring of tinfoil around the tube will produce all the results described above. Again, if a coil of insulated wire is placed near or around the tube, no difference is produced by joining the ends of the wire. In fact, no difference in effect is observable whether the conductor is made up of insulated wire or is a mere mass of metal; the whole seems to owe its effect to being a conductor of considerable size. No form of conductor produces a greater effect than a narrow ring of tinfoil connected to the earth by a single fine copper wire perpendicular to the tube, and no conducting system could be devised more unfavorable to the production of electromagnetic inductive currents by the original current in the tube. Moreover, the effect is far too great to be attributed to electromagnetic induction in circuits so unfavorable to its action. In short, every feature of the case, upon examination, tends to make it less probable that any of the electrical phenomena in the external conducting system are due to electromagnetic induction; and the supposition has been mentioned here more to show that it has not escaped consideration than because it was thought to have any valid claims to notice.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how conductors affect sensitive electrical discharges, specifically clarifying that the intensity of the "relief-effect" depends on the conductor's capacity to redistribute electricity rather than its specific electrical potential.</meta>

<page-num>180</page-num>
<header>MESSRS. W. SPOTTISWOODE AND J. FLETCHER MOULTON</header>

The arrangement in which the tinfoil is connected to the earth is the one that provides the most complete relief to the periodic changes of electric tension produced by the periodic pulsations of electricity through the tube. And, considering that the earth may be regarded as an infinite conducting body with zero potential, it seems justifiable to use the term *complete relief* in connection with its effect. But in order to make the relief complete, it is not necessary for the potential of the relieving conductor to be zero; it is the relief to the periodic alternations of electric tension which produces the effect. If a Leyden jar is connected to the tinfoil, its effect on the sensitive discharge is the same whether it is charged or not. In short, any conductor of sufficient size connected to the tinfoil will produce the same effect as the earth, regardless of the potential at which it stands.

It is so important to establish clearly that the effect of a conductor is independent of the potential at which it stands, and is due only to the ease of redistribution of electricity which it provides, that we will refer here to an experiment which very clearly demonstrates this to be the case. Let a <term>HOLTZ machine</term> be used as the source of the current, and let an air-spark be placed at some part of the current outside the tube—say, for example, in the section between the tube and the positive terminal of the machine—and let a ring of tinfoil be placed around the tube and connected to the earth, and the relief-effect carefully noted. It will be found that no effect is produced either upon the current* or the relief-effect by connecting either of the terminals of the machine to the earth. That no effect should be produced upon the current is not surprising, as the entire effect, like all other electro-dynamic effects, must be due to the difference in the potentials of the two terminals and not to their absolute values. But it is very remarkable that the relief-effect is the same in both cases, since in one case the tinfoil is at the same potential as the positive terminal of the machine, which is at a higher potential than any other part of the whole circuit (including the tube), and in the other case it is at the same potential as the negative terminal of the machine, which is necessarily at a lower potential than any other portion of the circuit. We think no stronger proof could be given that the effect is completely independent of the potential of the relieving system.

From this follows a remarkable result, the accuracy of which is, however, fully

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "relief-effect" in electrical discharge tubes, specifically discussing how conductors of sufficient capacity act as an electrical earth regardless of their potential, provided their electrical period differs from the discharge tube's period.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
# ON ELECTRICAL DISCHARGES THROUGH RAREFIED GASES.

confirmed by experiment. It is a common occurrence in physics that when a cause with one period acts upon a subject with a different period, the result is, on average, the same as if the former remained constant at its mean value. Applying these considerations to the present case, we see that if the tinfoil is connected to a conductor whose electric state changes periodically, but whose period is not the same as that of the discharge in the tube, we may expect the effect to be the same as if it remained constant at its mean value. That is to say, it will be the same as if the tinfoil were connected to the earth (assuming the conductor has sufficient capacity), since it does not matter at what potential the relieving conductor actually stands. Thus, to whatever conductor of sufficient capacity the tinfoil is connected, the effect will be the same as if it were connected to earth, unless the conductor has an electrical period identical to that of the discharge in the tube. The effect produced by joining the tinfoil to earth therefore naturally becomes our standard effect, with which all others may be compared. We shall in future call this effect the *to-earth* or *relief-effect*.

We have said that experiments fully confirm the theoretical result that any conductor of sufficient capacity not having the same electrical period as the discharge in the tube will give the *to-earth* or *relief-effect*. And this is true. If the tinfoil is connected with either terminal of the <term>HOLTZ machine</term> when the current is obtained from it,* or to an independently working coil or to a wire carrying a current with an independent air-spark, the relief-effect will be produced exactly as if the tinfoil had been connected with earth. It must, of course, be understood that if the changes of tension in the conductor are sufficiently violent, they will of themselves produce inductive discharges in the tube, just as they would in a tube with no discharge through it, and the total effect will be the sum of the relief-effect and these inductive discharges. But allowing for these independent effects of the variations in the electric state of the conductor, we have not found any exception to the rule stated above, namely, that any conductor of sufficient capacity whose electric state does not suffer variations of a similar period to the interrupted discharge in the tube will, when connected with the tinfoil on the tube, produce the relief-effect—that is to say, the same effect as if the tinfoil had been connected with the earth.

IV.—*The relief effect (when the intermittence occurs near the positive terminal)* takes the form of either repulsion or discharge from the interior surface of the glass. These two effects are identical in nature, and the form actually assumed in a single tube depends solely on the intensity of the action that causes it.

In this section, we will assume that the air-spark, wheel-break, or other device used to cause intermittence is placed between the positive terminal of the tube and the electrical source. This being the case, even a brief examination of vacuum tubes allows us to identify two types of effects when a conductor is brought near the tube. In one case, the luminous column is repelled by the conductor; in the other, the light appears to jump toward the conductor, usually in two tongues. These tongues move toward the glass but do not necessarily touch it, appearing on either side of the point where the conductor is closest to the glass. Between these two tongues, a luminous haze appears, similar to the one that usually surrounds the negative terminal. We shall call these the *repulsion form* and the *discharge form* of the *relief effect*, respectively (Plate 16, fig. 7).

Further examination reveals that these two forms of the relief effect<note>By using the term *relief effect*, the authors of this paper mean nothing more than the effect on the luminous discharge caused by a nearby conductor whose state is such that its potential remains mostly unchanged by the electrical disturbances in the tube. No theory regarding the *method of operation* of these effects on the luminous discharge is intended by this term. It was chosen because the electrical strain in the tinfoil was *relieved* by connecting it to a larger conductor, and it has been kept because no more convenient term was found.</note> include all cases. It is common to find both forms present at once. The luminous column is not always completely interrupted; the two tongues branching from it toward the conductor are often connected at their bases by the remnants of the luminous column. This connecting segment usually shows signs of having been repelled by the conductor and, while not notable in other respects, is typically dimmer than the rest of the luminous column. The *discharge form*, again, often lacks one or more of its parts; the two tongues may be very weak, and the haze may be so faint as to be practically invisible. The intensity of the repulsion effect also varies significantly, depending, as will be seen, on all the factors involved in producing the sensitive discharge. In many cases, the sensitivity is indicated only by a slight depression of the luminous column when a finger is placed on or very near the glass; in others, the luminous column is strongly repelled even before the finger is brought near the glass. ...does not affect the truth of the statement that the effects of bringing a conductor near to the tube consist in all cases of one of the above described types or of a mixture of the two; and the doubtful cases can be shown to be cases in which the faintness of the effect creates a difficulty in recognizing their true features rather than cases in which a foreign element is present in the appearances themselves. We shall presently examine the causes which increase sensitiveness, but we wish first to examine the relationship in which the two forms of the relief effect stand to one another.

Take a tube exhibiting a sensitive discharge, and find a spot where, on contact with the finger, the discharge effect is manifested. Instead of placing the finger on the glass, commence with the finger at so great a distance from the spot that no visible effect is produced on the sensitive discharge. Now slowly approach the finger to the spot chosen on the tube. The first symptom of sensitiveness will in all cases be a slight repulsion of the luminous column; this will, on nearer approach of the finger, become more decided, and at length a slight haze will become visible between the repelled luminous column and the spot on the glass. This will, if the process be continued, rapidly develop into the ordinary discharge effect. The change from the state of greatest repulsion to that of the discharge effect is usually extremely rapid, so much so as to give rise to the idea that there is an absolute discontinuity at this point; but if care be taken to get a steady current, and the approach be very gradual, it can be shown that there is a continuous transition from the one state into the other.

A more accurate method of trying the experiment consists in fixing a piece of tinfoil or thin metal, bent to the curvature of the tube, at the end of a glass rod, and connecting it to ground by a thin wire running along the rod. If this be made to work through a socket in a stand so as to admit of complete control, it will be found that the luminous discharge may be made to pass continuously through all gradations from almost imperceptible repulsion to the discharge effect merely by diminishing the distance of the tinfoil from the tube. Actual contact is, as may easily be imagined, the most favorable arrangement for the production of the discharge effect, but it is by no means essential to it, nor is there indeed any discontinuous or even very rapid change in the effect when contact commences. The experiment fully bears out the principle previously enunciated: that the more complete the relief, the greater the effect on the sensitive column, understanding for the future that the discharge effect must rank higher than the repulsion effect, or, in other words, must be considered as an intensified form of it (Plate 16, fig. 8).

A very slight modification of the arrangement last described will serve for an experiment which yet more clearly demonstrates that the intensity of the relief effect depends on the completeness of the relief afforded to the static induction caused by the free electricity in the tube, and that for this purpose the discharge effect must be taken as an intensified form of the repulsion effect. If the tinfoil, instead of being connected to ground, be connected to any system of conductors insulated from ground, it

It will be found that by increasing the capacity of the system, we can cause the produced relief-effect to vary from slight repulsion to the full "to-earth" effect. A very striking way to demonstrate this is by taking a thin copper wire, about 18 inches or 2 feet long, and fixing its two ends to two glass rods. Coil the wire around one rod until it is completely wound, and place the other so that the end of the wire is in electrical contact with a piece of tinfoil placed on the tube at a spot where the discharge-effect is strongly evident when the tinfoil is grounded. The capacity of the system in this form is so small that it will only produce a slight repulsion. If the rod in contact with the tinfoil is now held stationary while the other is moved away, allowing the wire to uncoil as the rods separate, it will be found that the repulsion gradually increases and passes almost imperceptibly into the discharge-effect. Moving the other end of the wire away from the tube has simply had the effect of increasing the system's capacity to provide relief to the tinfoil when it is under the influence of the electricity's static induction in the tube. This, after causing the effect on the column to increase from faint to strong repulsion, further intensifies it by making it pass into the even stronger form of the discharge-effect.

There are other ways to transition continuously from the repulsion-effect to the discharge-effect; these not only support our view that the two effects are identical but also, by comparison with the results just obtained, shed light on the causes of these phenomena. If a finger is passed along a tube containing a discharge of considerable sensitiveness, it will usually be found that from the positive terminal to a certain distance from it, the discharge-effect is produced, but beyond that point, the repulsion-effect occurs. If we stop at any point where the discharge-effect is produced and vary the effect by replacing the finger with a conducting system capable of providing only imperfect relief, we shall find that the closer we are to the positive terminal, the more difficult it is to reduce the effect to mere repulsion; in other words, the relief-effect tends to take its more intense form the closer we approach the positive terminal.

A third method of causing the repulsion-effect to transition continuously into the discharge-effect is by increasing the intensity of the interruptions that make the current sensitive. If a very small air-spark is introduced into the "positive circuit" of an uninterrupted discharge, the luminous column will become slightly sensitive, but this sensitiveness will only appear in the form of the repulsion-effect. If the air-spark is increased so that the pulsations become more violent but less frequent, this sensitiveness will increase, and the relief-effect near the positive terminal will take the discharge form, while the rest of the luminous column will only show repulsion. If the air-spark is increased even further, it will be found that the limits of the discharge-effect gradually extend further and further along the tube until the entire column is capable of manifesting it; and this state of things remains until the interruptedness of the discharge becomes so great—due to the length of the air-spark and the resulting slowness of the intermittence—that the discharge

It appears, then, that we can transition continuously from the repulsion form to the discharge form of the relief-effect in any one of three ways:

(1.) By keeping the relieving system fixed at the same spot on the tube and varying the completeness of relief, while the discharge remains the same;
(2.) By keeping the relieving system constant and varying its position on the tube, while the discharge remains the same;
(3.) By keeping the relieving system constant and fixed in position, and varying how interrupted the discharge is.

It is probable that there is a fourth way: namely, by varying the quantity of the discharge, while keeping all other factors the same. The only phenomenon observed so far regarding this point is that when the condenser is allowed to run down, the discharge-effect appears where previously there had only been repulsion. This might suggest that a decrease in quantity tends to produce the discharge-effect, but it is likely that the reverse is true. The phenomenon in question is probably due to the increased interruption—the significantly longer periods between discharges—that accompanies the drop in tension in the condenser. As we have seen, this would tend to produce the discharge-effect. The importance of a slow rate of interruption in producing the discharge-effect is shown by the fact that when operating the coil with a very high-speed break, the resulting sensitive discharge only produces repulsion-effects. Conversely, when a slower break is used, the tendency of the coil discharge to produce the discharge-effect is so great that it will often appear in a luminous discharge even when the condenser and coil are used under circumstances where the size of the air-spark would suggest it should not. However, it will vanish when the coil is stopped and the condenser is allowed to work alone. This shows that its appearance was due to the pulsations of the coil being felt in the discharge; their slowness and intensity caused the discharge-effect in places where the more rapid and steady interruption of the air-spark would not have produced it. No doubt part of this effect is due to the greater intensity of the coil pulsations, but overall it tends to support the other experiments showing that the discharge-effect is closely linked to a high degree of current interruption.

It should not be assumed that all tubes produce both forms of relief-effect. According to the authors' observations, all tubes produce a repulsion-effect, but it is relatively rare to find tubes that exhibit both forms. Generally speaking, the typical effect—especially in tubes with high resistance—is a slight repulsion. A further discussion of the meaning of these forms of relief-effect will be necessary when we consider the similar phenomena that exist in ordinary vacuum discharges.

We therefore have, as has before been pointed out, a standard phenomenon at every point of a tube illuminated by a sensitive discharge: the *to-earth* or *relief-effect*. We can get other effects connected with this, and to a great extent dependent upon it, by varying the completeness of the relief afforded. These effects form a continuous series from zero up to the complete relief-effect; and this series can easily be passed through continuously by some such process as that described above, in which two glass rods and a connecting wire were used to form the relieving system. Hence, if at a point of the tube we obtain by any process an effect on the sensitive luminous column, we can at once ascertain whether it belongs to the category of relief-effects or not. If it does not, there must exist some foreign element other than the mere facility for granting electrical relief in the influences brought to bear upon the tube. We now proceed to examine these special or non-relief effects.

### V.—*On the special or non-relief effects produced on the sensitive luminous discharge by connecting it with the air-spark terminal.*

In the present section we shall at first suppose the intermittence to be caused by an interruption in the circuit between the source of electricity and the positive terminal of the tube. For convenience we shall express this fact by calling the positive terminal the *air-spark terminal*.

If we connect a wire with a piece of tinfoil placed upon the tube, and connect the wire with any independent conducting system, we shall obtain, as we have seen, more or less complete forms of the relief-effect. Both the wire and tinfoil will, in the majority of cases, repel the luminous column. But if the wire is connected with the positive terminal a sudden change takes place in the phenomenon. Instead of the luminous column being repelled by the wire, the course of the latter along the tube (supposing it partly to rest upon the tube) will be marked by a bright line of luminosity on the inner surface of the glass as though it had attracted the luminous column instead of repelling it. And the effect of the presence of the tinfoil is changed in a no less remarkable manner. Instead of the former repulsion, a tongue of luminosity will be seen apparently starting from the actual inner surface of the glass under the tinfoil and stretching toward the negative terminal of the tube, while the luminous column on the positive side of the tinfoil is usually depressed or repelled, and is often nearly severed in two. If the tinfoil is in the form of a ring around the tube the appearance of the phenomena is very striking. In many cases the luminous column extending

One thing that must be noted at this stage regarding these effects is their complete difference from what we have described as relief-effects. As we showed in a previous section, every part of a tube where a sensitive discharge passes has a standard relief-effect called the *to-earth effect*, produced by connecting it to a conducting system of virtually infinite capacity. A continuous range of relief-effects from zero up to this *to-earth effect* can be obtained by limiting the capacity of the relief system so that it can no longer be influenced by the electrical disturbances in the tube without its potential undergoing significant change. Now, if we compare the appearances described in this section with any part of this sequence, we see they are completely different. Thus, we immediately learn that these effects are not caused by the relief capacity of the system to which the tinfoil is now connected, but by some special electrical interference created by the new arrangement. Because of this difference, we shall call these effects *special* or *non-relief effects*; and it should be remembered that these effects are only obtained when we connect the tinfoil with the air-spark terminal or use an arrangement that is electrically equivalent.

If the negative terminal is the air-spark terminal, there will be an equally great contrast between the effects obtained by connecting the tinfoil to the earth and to the air-spark terminal. As before, the relief-effects can be obtained by connecting the tinfoil to any conducting system of sufficient capacity, whatever its potential, provided that its potential does not vary in the same period as the potential inside the tube. On the other hand, the special or non-relief effects can only be obtained by connecting the tinfoil with the negative terminal. However, it is not necessary to examine or contrast these effects here, as they will later be shown to follow a general rule; it is enough to state here that the contrast mentioned above exists.

### VI.—*On the nature of the electrical actions by which the relief and non-relief effects are respectively caused or accompanied.*

As we have seen, it is clear that tinfoil placed on the tube and connected to the ground affects the luminous discharge by allowing the electric forces—generated by or arising from the discharge inside the tube—to create electric displacement within the tinfoil and the system connected to it. Because it does not matter how the actual displacement is produced, we can assume, without changing the result, that a suitable electric charge is sent into the tinfoil from a source outside the tube. This charge will naturally be equal in quantity, but opposite in sign, to the charge that passes from the tinfoil to the ground. We can therefore set aside the ideas of "relief" or "non-relief" and view both states as being caused by charges sent into the tinfoil from external sources at the appropriate times. In the case of the relief-effect, it is obvious that these charges will occur at the same intervals as the electrical changes in the tube, since they are caused by them.

When considering this topic, we are immediately struck by the fact that, up to this stage of the inquiry, the non-relief-effect has only been produced by connecting the tinfoil electrically to the air-spark terminal. It is clear that the unique quality of this electricity source does not come from its high or low potential, because we have seen that potential does not affect the ability of the conducting system to influence the luminous discharge. Nor, as we have also observed, would simple fluctuations of potential in the wire produce anything other than the relief-effect, or interfere with or destroy it, unless they occurred in the same period as the pulsations in the tube. Therefore, the special effect in question must be due to the fact that the connection with the air-spark terminal interferes with the electrical state of the tinfoil in a specific way; this uniqueness must lie in the fact that the timing of the charges (and the resulting variations in potential) is such that they match the timing of the pulsations within the tube.

Now, the electrical displacement that would otherwise result in the standard relief-effect can be interfered with by intensification, by reversal, or by reduction. The last option is ruled out by the experimental fact that these special or non-relief-effects do not look like any of the relief-effects we have described, which range from zero to the full "to-ground" effect.

To choose between the remaining options, we can take a similar approach. Like the relief-effect, the special or non-relief-effect can be produced in forms other than the complete one we have already described. In that version, a piece of tinfoil placed on the tube is connected to the air-spark terminal. If, instead of resting on the tube, the tinfoil (still connected to the air-spark terminal) is attached to an insulated rod and moved toward the tube, a series of special effects is produced, ranging from zero to the complete non-relief-effect. Now, if this complete non-relief-effect were simply a stronger version of the relief-effects, we would expect to find the ordinary relief-effects—or something very close to them—at some point in this sequence of special

<summary>This page discusses the electrical mechanisms behind relief and non-relief effects, arguing that the unique non-relief effect occurs when external electric charges from an air-spark terminal synchronize with the tube's internal pulsations. The authors conclude that these effects result from the timing and nature of electrical displacement rather than simple potential levels.</summary>

effects. But such is not the case. From the beginning to the end, the special effects are completely different from the relief-effects, showing clearly that the special effects cannot be caused by a change in the intensity of the same kind of electrical pulses that produce the relief-effects, but must be due to pulses of an opposite character.

This is, of course, not the only proof that the electrical pulses producing the two effects are of opposite kinds. In fact, an examination of the appearances of the two effects is almost enough to convince the observer that it is impossible for one to be a mere heightening of the other, so fundamental is the difference, especially in their more distinct forms. But the proof given above is the simplest and most direct experimental proof, and it is sufficient at the present stage, even when taken alone. It will, however, be subsequently found that there is strong confirmation of the correctness of this view.

We conclude, therefore, that the electrical displacements in the tinfoil caused by joining it with the air-spark terminal have the same period but are opposite in character to those which produce the relief-effect. But it is evident—taking the positive terminal to be the air-spark terminal—that the former consist of periodic pulsations of positive electricity at the moments when the air-spark passes.<note>If it is necessary to provide experimental proof for a conclusion so obvious, it is sufficient to connect this portion of the circuit to the ground, placing a telephone in the circuit; the air-spark note will clearly be heard, showing that there are periodic variations of potential accompanying each spark.</note> Therefore, in the case of the non-relief-effect, the tinfoil receives a pulse of positive electricity each time a spark passes. This must be, as we have seen, of the opposite character to that which causes the relief-effect. Hence, for every pulsation coming from the air-spark, there corresponds in the case of the relief-effect a pulsation of negative electricity to the tinfoil; that is to say, a pulsation of positive electricity *from* the tinfoil.

This conclusion is exactly what we might have expected on the assumption that when the positive is the air-spark terminal, the positive electricity passes intermittently through the tube in pulses of the same period as the air-spark. If each time the air-spark passed there were a sudden charging-up of the positive terminal and the portion of the circuit metallically connected to it, causing a sudden discharge of positive electricity into and through the tube, this positive electricity—on reaching the part near to the tinfoil—would, by its induction, tend to drive away positive electricity from the tinfoil and to attract negative electricity to it. This is what we find to be the case, and similar reasoning will apply to the case when the negative is the air-spark terminal. Therefore, we shall assume that in the relief-effect there is a pulse from the tinfoil of the same character as the excess of electricity within the part of the tube opposite to it. Or, as it may be more simply stated, there is a pulse of electricity to the tinfoil of the opposite character to the electricity which is discharged from the air-spark terminal; and that in the non-relief-effect, there is a pulse to the tinfoil of the same kind as the electricity which is discharged from that terminal.

<summary>The authors demonstrate that relief and non-relief effects are produced by electrical pulses of opposite characters, determined by whether the tinfoil receives a charge similar to or opposite of the air-spark terminal. This is explained through the principle of induction, where a discharge in the tube attracts an opposite charge to the nearby tinfoil during the relief effect.</summary>
<keywords>electrical pulses, relief-effect, non-relief-effect, air-spark terminal, tinfoil, induction, potential variations, positive electricity, negative electricity</keywords>

--- Page 236 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of electrical discharges in vacuum tubes, specifically discussing the relationship between the timing of pulses and the phenomena of intermittence and sensitivity.</meta>

<page-num>190</page-num>
<header>MESSRS. W. SPOTTISWOODE AND J. FLETCHER MOULTON</header>

The first happens at the moment that the electricity in the tube passes the spot where the tinfoil is located; the second coincides with the charging of the terminal which leads to the discharge, and is therefore most intense at the moment of discharge. And, further, we have the experimental fact that under ordinary circumstances these effects are of a diametrically opposite nature.

This is, perhaps, the most suitable place for explaining the connection between intermittence and sensitivity in vacuum discharges. The effects observed in sensitive discharges have been traced in the preceding part of the paper to the effect of static induction from the free electricity that passes into the tube at each pulse. Now, in order that this static induction outside the tube may be strong, it is clearly necessary that the quantity of free electricity within the tube while the discharge is passing should be great. In other words, the current must pass in large pulses and not in small trickles. This is exactly what intermittence achieves. The electricity is held back until it has accumulated in large quantities, and then in one pulse it bursts into and sweeps through the tube. In the so-called continuous current, also, the electricity undoubtedly passes into the tube in pulses, but as these pulses are perhaps many thousand times more numerous in any given time than is the case with the sensitive discharge, the quantity in each pulse is proportionately smaller, and is thus insufficient to produce a static induction of a magnitude capable of causing, in its turn, discharges within the tube. Hence the so-called continuous current is really a sensitive current of infinitely small sensitivity. The difference between the two is much the same as the difference between the effect of letting the excess water of a river overflow a weir every moment, and holding it back for a whole day and then suddenly releasing it.

### VII.—*Examination and interpretation of the special or non-relief effect when the positive is the air-spark terminal.*

For the purposes of this section, we shall take first the form of special or non-relief effect already described. It is a very distinct form, but by no means an unusual one, and indeed it is probable that it can be obtained in a more or less complete form in most vacuum tubes; and it possesses, as we shall see, the important property of being the typical form from which all others can be derived by modifications of known and definite kinds corresponding to peculiarities in the circumstances of the tube or the discharge.

If we place around the tube a narrow ring of tinfoil, and connect it with the positive terminal (where the air-spark is supposed to be) by a wire passing at a sufficient distance from the tube to prevent its directly affecting the luminous column, the following appearances will be noticed:—

(1.) The column which starts from the positive terminal will be found suddenly to terminate at the tinfoil ring in a bright column of small diameter

(2.) On the side of the tinfoil towards the negative end of the tube, a conical column of luminosity is seen to start from the inside of the tube immediately beneath the tinfoil, and to stretch towards the negative terminal. This cone, in fact, forms the base of the new positive column.

(3.) On examination, this luminous cone is found to be hollow, the interior having an ill-defined and hazy surface in strong contrast with the somewhat sharp and regular outline of the exterior (Plate 16, fig. 10).

Let us consider the explanation for these appearances. We know that strong pulsations of positive electricity pass to the positive terminal of the tube and the tinfoil, keeping time with the passage of the air-sparks. These pulsations, when they arrive at the terminal, are of sufficient intensity to cause a discharge to pass through the tube, and the pulsations that reach the tinfoil must be of exactly the same strength as those that go to the terminal. Such pulsations must drive off positive electricity in corresponding pulsations from the interior parts of the tube adjacent to the tinfoil. These latter pulsations are similar to the discharges that take place from the positive terminal, and they seek relief in the same manner, namely: by rushing towards the negative terminal of the tube. In this process, they form the hollow luminous cone mentioned above. These discharges of positive electricity from the inner surface of the tube leave behind them an excess of negative charge which would be held imprisoned by the positive charge in the tinfoil if that were permanent; but just as the latter was generated by the momentary charging due to the passage of the air-spark, so it is released by the relief given to such charging by the discharge through the tube. When such a discharge takes place, the negative electricity on the interior of the tube is set free, and in its turn neutralizes the positive electricity of the discharge that meets it in its passage from the positive terminal. Thus, we naturally get the termination of one positive column on the side of the tinfoil nearest to the positive terminal, and a complete discontinuity between it and the second, which starts in a hollow cone from the edge of the tinfoil nearest to the negative terminal.

To show more clearly that this is the true interpretation of the phenomena, and that the effect of the arrangement is thus to substitute for the original discharge two independent discharges occupying different parts of the tube, take two or three such rings separated from each other by spaces somewhat less than the diameter of the tube and connect them as before with the positive terminal. Each of these will be found to be the base of a hollow cone similar to that described above; and each such cone will form the base of a luminous column having all the features of a positive column, and terminating sharply behind the next tinfoil-ring or at the borders of the usual negative dark space near the negative terminal of the tube. These sectional positive columns will be small in diameter and bright, and will or will not be striated according to whether their length is sufficient to permit striæ or not. If they are not

Each behaves as though it started from the tinfoil ring at its base, while still maintaining its position relative to the sectional columns on each side of it. If a magnet is used, it deflects all these columns, but each column still moves independently and as if it had the tinfoil ring as its base. The magnet also shows, as might be expected, that the discharge through each of the columns is in the same direction; namely, the positive charge passes from the hollow cone toward the bright end of the column of which it forms the base or beginning.

Now, taking a tube in which the phase described above is clearly marked, let us gradually increase the air-spark interval to make the electrical pulsations more violent. The sharply defined head of the terminated column will be found to flatten and widen out, becoming less bright in the center until it becomes almost an annular ring of light. As the air-spark interval is increased even further, this annular ring widens and becomes less definite, until at last the column on the positive side of the tinfoil takes on something of the form of a hollow cone pointing toward the positive terminal of the tube. The base of this cone is, however, not quite close to the tinfoil, <note>The authors of this paper believe that this is always the case, but the phenomenon is complicated by the presence of a reverse current which accompanies the use of a large air-spark in the positive circuit.</note> and is formed, as stated above, by the final phase of the annular luminous ring created from the head of the terminated positive column (Plate 17, fig. 12).

If the air-spark interval is too small, these phenomena will not be obtained, but only a more or less faint suggestion of them mixed with diffused luminosity. This is not surprising, as in such cases the electrical pulsations to the outside of the glass are probably insufficient to produce discharges within it of enough intensity to satisfy the discharge from the positive terminal; therefore, we have an effect produced by the overlapping of an ordinary luminous discharge and one interrupted in the way described above. But careful examination of various tubes has convinced the authors of this paper that the forms described above are the truly typical forms of the special or non-relief effect when the positive is the air-spark terminal.

To do this satisfactorily, it is necessary to examine the various forms these effects assume as we continuously vary the intensity of the causes that give rise to them, from zero up to the highest limit practically attainable with the instruments used. This variation may, as we have seen, be made in several different ways, of which the following are the most convenient:

(1.) We may vary the air-spark from zero up to the limit of striking distance; or if the interruption of the current is achieved by other means, some equivalent mode of altering the character of such interruption may be adopted.

(2.) We may vary the distance of the tinfoil (which produces the effect upon the tube) from the greatest distance at which an effect is observable down to actual contact.

(3.) We may move the tinfoil up and down the tube so as to be at a greater or lesser distance from the air-spark terminal.

Supposing, then, the tinfoil to be in the form of a narrow ring surrounding the tube, and taking first the *non-relief effect* with the air-spark in the *positive* portion, we obtain the following results by these respective methods:

(1.) As we increase the air-spark from its initial value, zero, there appears first of all a brightening of the central portion of the positive column in the part of the tube close to the edge of the tinfoil on the same side as the positive terminal of the tube. As the air-spark is still further increased, this effect grows clearer and clearer, until it reaches its greatest perfection. Increasing the air-spark even more, the terminal stria or head of the column gets wider, or nearly the same diameter as the tube, and the brightness is greatest around its edges, so that it actually becomes annular <note>ring-shaped</note>. (1.) Increasing the air-spark from its initial value of zero produces exactly the same series of effects as those just described in section (1), with minor differences in the clarity of the various phases. (2.) Increasing the size of the ring was equivalent to decreasing the air-spark.
(3.) Moving further from the positive terminal caused a pointed termination to become annular. However, this phenomenon is generally very difficult to observe.

This similarity of effect in both cases provides the strongest possible confirmation of the correctness of the conclusions previously reached. We know that the specific effect occurring when the positive terminal serves as the air-spark terminal is caused by pulses of positive electricity passing to the tinfoil. These pulses are synchronized (*co-periodic*) with the increases in potential at the positive terminal produced by the passage of electrical charges across the air-spark gap. We find that such electrical pulses in the tinfoil produce hollow-cone discharges in the tube. These form the base of a subsequent positive column, while the original positive column stops short within the hollow cone; its discharge is apparently neutralized by the negative electricity released there. Applying this knowledge to explain the identical effects obtained by grounding the tinfoil and using the negative terminal for the air-spark, we see that we must attribute the pulses of positive electricity causing these effects to the inductive action of the negative charges. These charges rush through the tube from the negative terminal each time electricity passes across the air-spark gap. These pulses release positive electricity within the tube, which flows from the glass in its usual form of a hollow-cone discharge to neutralize the negative discharge that originally induced it. Then, the negative electricity on the inner side of the tube—released again because the original discharge was neutralized—passes from the interior of the hollow cone and continues the discharge through the tube. Consequently, it will be observed that the interior of this luminous hollow cone is considered to act as a negative terminal in both cases.

One difference between the two cases must be noted here. The positive pulses in

Both these should be produced, according to the theory, by pulses of negative electricity rushing to the tinfoil, caused in the one case by the inductive action of the positive discharge within the tube, and in the other case coming directly from the terminal of the tube which is in metallic connection with the air-spark interval.

As the air-spark was increased, the dimensions of this space also increased, until nothing was left of the luminous column within the part of the tube surrounded by the tinfoil but a very bright central line (Plate 17, fig. 14).

### IX.—*On the nature of striæ, and the artificial production of striation in the luminous (sensitive) discharge.*

We have seen that positive and negative pulses on the outside of the tube, synchronous with the discharges that pass through it, cause the interior of the tube within the tinfoil to assume the character of positive and negative terminals respectively. The negative terminals formed in this way possess all the characteristics usually belonging to terminals of such shape, but otherwise they do not give us any suggestions especially valuable for our present inquiry. With the positive terminals, however, the case is very different, as we shall proceed to show, taking as an example the special effect when the air-spark is in the positive circuit.

We have seen that the positive discharge caused by a ring of tinfoil forms a hollow cone with a sharply-defined luminous outer surface. This cone, if the nearest negative terminal is the negative terminal of the tube, passes into a column of diffused luminosity similar in all respects to the ordinary luminous column which starts from the positive terminal of a tube. But if there is another similar ring of tinfoil also connected with the positive terminal between the first ring and the negative terminal, the luminous column that starts from ring No. 1 is stopped by ring No. 2, and from this latter ring there starts a second hollow luminous cone which stretches away in its turn towards the negative terminal in a diffused luminous column as previously described. If these rings are placed at the proper distance from one another, and the size and exhaustion of the tube are suitable, the short luminous column between the rings will diminish to a hollow cone with a blunt rounded head. This head is greatly superior in brightness to any other part of the cone and stretches to a point close to or even a little within the next ring, so that it is in the middle of the space enclosed by the hazy blue inside surface of the hollow cone that starts from that ring. By using additional rings, this can be made to repeat itself until the whole luminous column is segmented into these hollow luminous cones or shells with bright rounded heads.

The theory which the authors of this paper desire to put forward is that each of these luminous cones or shells is a perfect <term>stria</term> in both function and structure. The resemblance in appearance is most striking. In the luminous shells which we have just described, there is the same convex bright outline pointing towards the negative terminal, and the same hazy blue ill-defined hollow surface turned towards the shell immediately behind or on the side toward the positive terminal of the tube; and there are the same dark intervals dividing consecutive shells as divide consecutive <term>striæ</term>. In fact, this segmented discharge presents to us all the familiar phenomena of striated discharges in which the <term>striæ</term> have rounded or conical forms. Moreover, the conical is not the only type of <term>striæ</term> which can be successfully produced in this manner. It is equally possible to form flat or annular <term>striæ</term> by proper adjustments of the air-spark interval, as explained in page 192. And as these are precisely the forms which natural

<summary>The authors argue that artificial striations can be produced by using tinfoil rings on a vacuum tube, creating segmented luminous cones that function and appear identical to natural striæ. They describe how these shells mimic the structure of natural discharges, including the convex bright heads and dark intervals.</summary>
<keywords>striæ, striation, luminous discharge, tinfoil rings, positive terminal, negative terminal, air-spark, luminous column, electrical discharge theory</keywords>

<page-num>200</page-num>
<header>MESSRS. W. SPOTTISWOODE AND J. FLETCHER MOULTON</header>

striae tend to assume when they deviate from the conical type, it may be fairly stated that all forms of natural striae can be artificially reproduced: a fact that strongly supports the identity of the two phenomena.

But these luminous shells resemble striae in more than just structure. There is also an identity of function. We know that when the positive pulses arrive at the glass, they drive off similar positive pulses from the interior of the tube, thus forming the luminous shells. Knowing, therefore, that each luminous shell signifies a positive discharge, and also that no electricity passes through the glass, it is absolutely certain that an equal amount of negative electricity must collect on the surface of the glass within the tube and must ultimately satisfy an equal amount of the original positive discharge—*that is*, the discharge coming to it from the positive terminal, or from the shell immediately on the positive side of the one we are considering, as the case may be. We have, then, a negative discharge from the side of the tube (or from the gas immediately within it) satisfying a positive discharge advancing toward it along the tube; and we find that it causes the luminosity of this discharge to stop short and end in a bright, clearly defined rounded head, which is separated by a dark space from the source of the negative discharge. 

This, then, is the function of the shell: the bright part serves as the point of departure for the positive electricity about to pass across the dark space (or the point of arrival for the negative electricity after doing so), and the hazy interior of the cone forms its point of arrival (or the point of departure for the negative electricity). As far as we know, this is the sole function of these elements of the shell. Now let us consider the case of the striated discharge. Here, too, we know that the positive electricity in the current must leave the bright head of the stria and, after passing through the dark space, arrive at the hazy interior of the next stria, while the negative electricity must take the opposite course. 

There is an absolute identity in the functions of the corresponding parts of the two structures. The only difference is that we know, from independent external evidence, that the electricity in the artificially segmented discharge does not flow continuously but in intermittent discharges. This independent evidence is absent in the case of the ordinary striated discharge. We will refer to this point again at the conclusion of this paper, but for now, we will assume what we have already stated to be highly probable: namely, that all vacuum discharges are in reality intermittent. Anyone who does not wish to admit this must treat the reasoning in this section as applicable only to those striated discharges known to be intermittent.

Returning, then, to the case of the artificially produced conical shells, the *modus operandi* of the discharge is as follows: When the pulse of positive electricity arrives at the terminal and causes the discharge into the tube, a positive discharge equal * to

that which passes into the tube moves synchronously from the interior of the tube at each ring of tinfoil, forms the bright shell or stria, and passes on to the next shell or stria; thus taking the place of the positive pulse that the ring of tinfoil there has just sent forward. The last shell passes its discharge to the negative terminal, and the first shell receives a discharge from the positive terminal. In this way, a discharge passes through the tube that is identical in quantity and character to the one that enters it from the positive terminal.

If, then, we are right in supposing that the series of artificially produced hollow shells are analogous in their structures and functions to striæ, it is not difficult to deduce, from the explanation given above, the *modus operandi* of an ordinary striated discharge. The passage of each intermittent pulse from the bright surface of a stria toward the hollow surface of the next may well be supposed, by its inductive action, to drive a similar pulse from the next stria, which in its turn drives one from the stria after that, and so on. Thus, the processes in naturally and artificially striated columns are precisely similar, except that in the case of the latter, the pulses from the several striæ are excited by induction from outside the tube, while in the case of the former, the induction is caused by the discharge itself as it passes from stria to stria. The passage of the discharge is due in both cases to an action consisting of an independent discharge from one stria to the next; and the idea of this action can perhaps be best illustrated by a line of boys crossing a brook on stepping stones, where each boy steps onto the stone that the boy in front of him has just vacated.

The truth of the preceding theory is confirmed by the fact that we obtain formations analogous to striæ not only through the positive special effect, but also through other special and relief-effects, when the electrical actions are of the kind that would lead us to expect them according to the theory presented here. Take, for example, the positive relief-effect. When the pulses passing through the tube are positive and a finger is placed on the tube, the resulting positive relief-effect consists—under certain conditions of discharge quantity and tension (notably when the discharge is produced by a small coil, as described on page 210, with the negative terminal of the tube grounded)—of a faint haze beneath the finger and a large dark space extending across the tube, stretching for some distance from the spot where the finger rests along the tube toward the positive end (Plate 18, fig. 16).<note>* If the positive terminal is grounded, the striæ will appear immediately beneath the fingers as in Plate 18, fig. 16A, which is what we would expect.</note> The end of the positive luminous column, where it meets this dark space, is bright with a sharply defined rounded outline, like the bright head of a stria, except that instead of pointing straight along the center of the tube, it is slightly angled upward toward the spot where the finger is placed. There is a positive discharge which is satisfied by a source of negative electricity, or, as we may call it, a negative terminal, located within the tube at the surface of the glass, and we find exactly the same formation appearing. The luminous positive column is separated from the negative terminal by a dark space, and its head becomes bright, rounded, and definite in outline, and takes on all the characteristics of the bright head of a stria. And the experiment may be made even more striking and instructive by placing a second finger a little on the negative side of the first. The luminosity which previously began close to the first finger and stretched away toward the negative end of the tube, becomes divided exactly as in the previous case, and the portion intercepted between the fingers resembles a stria in all respects, except that the hazy blue negative surface is imperfectly developed, being actually replaced by the haze under the first finger, which is the place where the interchange of discharges occurs. The length of the body of this stria can be varied at will by increasing or decreasing the distance between the fingers so as to leave a more or less prolonged positive column behind the bright head, but the real structure is in no way changed by this.

The unit of a striated vacuum discharge is therefore composed of the body of a stria ending in its bright surface, the dark space in front of it, and the hazy interior surface of the stria on the further side of that dark space. In this unit* we have a positive terminal, with a luminous positive column starting from it, a space across which the discharge passes non-luminously, and a negative terminal; so that in each unit we have represented all the elements of a complete discharge. And in the opinion of the authors of this paper, all striated vacuum discharges are composed of repetitions of this unit, and any phenomena connected with the negative terminal which seem to contradict this view, and to suggest a special structure of the discharge near the negative terminal unlike anything that exists in other portions of the discharge, are merely modifications due to the local circumstances of the terminal in a manner now to be explained. We are referring, of course, to the phenomena known as the negative dark space, the negative glow, and <term>CROOKES’ space</term>; and we now proceed to examine these phenomena, taking the negative glow first, as the one presenting the greatest difficulty for the theory mentioned above.

It is well known that the bright surfaces of striæ are usually convex. But this is not always the case. If a striated discharge is produced in a tube which has a bulb in the middle of its length, with a diameter considerably larger than that of the tube, it will be found that the striæ in the bulb toward the side nearest the negative terminal are concave on their bright surface, especially in that part of the bulb that rapidly narrows—

In artificially produced striæ this column can, as we have seen, be made any length; and even in the natural striæ its length varies within very wide limits.</note>

We see, then, that we can greatly modify the bright outline of a stria by changing the size and shape of the next stria—that is, the negative terminal of this unit. If we make this small, the bright surface of the next stria will curve around it and be concave; if, on the other hand, it is large—and even more so if it is hollow and partially envelops the next stria—the bright surface of the latter will be very convex. Now, if we replace this negative terminal (whose hazy, gaseous structure is easily shaped by, and probably owes its form and structure to, the discharge itself) with a fixed metallic body, we should expect significant changes in the appearance of the other parts of the unit. It is not surprising that the dark space, and the bright surface forming its other boundary, should follow the outline of the new negative terminal. If it consists of a small metallic body projecting into the tube, the general appearance would be as if the bright surface enveloped it, while remaining separated by a dark space. This is exactly what the negative glow looks like, and we believe the above is a complete explanation of its formation and function. According to this theory, this negative glow and the haze behind it (which ends in what is known as the negative dark space) is a stria turned inside out by the influence of the shape and character of the negative terminal (Plate 18, fig. 18). <note>It will undoubtedly occur to those familiar with striated discharges that there are significant differences in how striae and the negative glow behave when subjected to a magnet. But in the case of the negative glow, the lines of electric discharge whose termination it marks are fixed to the negative terminal at one end; thus, the glow can only be displaced as far as the deformation of these lines allows. In fact, the negative glow is like a *stria at anchor*. There is exactly the same difference between the behavior of the two as there is between the effect of waves on floating seaweed and seaweed growing on rocks. In this respect, the artificial striae we have been speaking of resemble the negative glow, except that they have a fixed positive terminal instead of a fixed negative terminal.</note>

First, in the case of Crookes' space, we are dealing with the passage of electricity from metal to gas or gas to metal, instead of simply the passage of electricity from one part of the gas to another. And further, we have the far more important circumstance that in both Crookes' space and the negative dark space, we have a case of a discharge in which the negative terminal of the unit is of a shape and arrangement wholly unlike that of the negative terminal of any other of the <note>These last remarks will explain a difficulty which would otherwise be felt as to why it is only in particular cases that we get any counterparts of striae from those special or relief effects which cause negative discharges within the tube. It will be seen that the authors of this paper regard each segment as constituting a separate discharge. One phenomenon observed by them, of a different kind from those of which we have been chiefly speaking, appears to strongly confirm this. If a magnet is applied to a striated column, it will be found that the column is not simply moved up or down as a whole, as would be the case if the discharge passed in direct lines from terminal to terminal, threading through the striæ in its passage. On the contrary, each stria is subjected to a rotation or deformation of exactly the same character as would be caused if the stria marked the termination of flexible currents radiating from the bright head of the stria behind it and terminating in the hazy inner surface of the stria in question. An examination of several cases has led the authors of this paper to conclude that the currents do thus radiate from the bright head of a stria to the inner surface of the next, and that there is no direct passage from one terminal of the tube to the other.

It is natural to inquire what, in this theory, is the physical structure of <term>striæ</term>. Are they merely luminous appearances (that is, <gloss>loci of maximum luminosity</gloss>), or are they aggregations of matter having a material structure? This is a question which is beyond the scope of this paper to discuss, but the most probable view, in the opinion of the authors, is that they should be regarded as <term>septa</term> <note>Partitions or membranes.</note> of complete electric porosity, having a material structure. One of the most important facts favoring this conclusion is that when striæ are formed by a coil working with a high-speed break, the striæ produced by the two currents (the make and the break) adhere persistently together in pairs as though the alternate currents found ready-made striæ that only needed a little deformation to make them available for their purposes (Plate 17, fig. 15). There are other facts tending to support this conclusion, but a complete examination of the question would carry us beyond the limits of the present paper.

A great difficulty in the way of this, and indeed of all attempted solutions of the stratification of vacuum discharges, arises from the difficulty of imagining any physical cause which could form material aggregations in the form of striæ out of the diffused and mutually repellant particles of the rarefied gas. The following theory is offered as a suggestion of a possible mode of accounting for their formation. It is known that the blue haze that surrounds the negative halo or glow is magnetic, and follows the lines of magnetic force just as would be the case if it were a mass of magnetized steel filings. Now on the present theory this haze is identical in function, and there-

Now, if we suppose that these discharges are effected by or accompanied by the convection of free electricity on particles of gas, it does not seem impossible that a positively charged particle might pass so near a negatively charged particle that they would rotate rapidly around one another, under the influence of the mutual attraction of the free electricity with which they are respectively charged. This would form an analogue to a circular current, which would behave like a magnetic particle just as the electrically laden particles in <term>CROOKES’</term> lines behave like flexible currents. In this way, we should have matter capable of mutual attraction, assuming that there is on average some directing force or factor which prevents the directions of the poles of the magnetic matter from being completely indifferent. That in some way there must be manufactured out of the gas a substance capable of mutual attraction, which when formed into the glow has a surface tension, is quite evident from Mr. <term>CROOKES’</term> experiments with the radiometer. In those experiments, he found that the particles driven off the vanes (when used as a negative terminal) did not produce rotation so long as the glow did not intersect the side of the glass vessel. This is explicable only by supposing that the glow and the vane formed a physically continuous surface kept together by mutual forces.

It may be objected to this theory that the circular currents produced by the two elements of a revolving pair would be in opposite directions, and that they would consequently represent two magnets having opposite polarity, which would neutralize one another. But there is no reason to think that the two currents would always be exactly equal; and any inequality in the currents would produce a preponderance of magnetic polarity, and the preceding remarks would apply.

It is no objection to this theory that the bright portion of the glow does not appear magnetic. Its position is fixed by its being the locus of the extremities of the <term>CROOKES’</term> lines that proceed from the fixed negative terminal, and it can only be affected by the displacement or deformation of these lines, as is found to be the case.

X.—*The passage of the discharge through the tube occupies a time which is sufficiently small in comparison with the interval between the discharges to prevent any interference between successive electrical pulses.*

We shall now revert to the phenomena of the sensitive discharge and show that all the effects of which we have spoken are due to actions whose durations are contained within the time that a single pulse takes in passing through the tube, so that these effects are not in any way due to the action of one electrical pulse on a consecutive one. In other words, the whole of the effects take place in each...
