an individual pulse, and the repetition of successive pulses only serves to make them appear to the eye as continuous phenomena.

The most valuable direct evidence of the velocity of the discharge through the tube and the independence of each discharge is obtained from the examination of the discharge by a revolving mirror. For this purpose, a revolving four-sided prism, whose sides consisted of glass coated with platinum on the upper surface and which was rotated by hand at a rate of 400 to 800 revolutions per minute, was used. It was found that this instrument was capable of showing the intermittent nature of the current when in a sensitive state, no matter how small the <term>air-spark</term>, showing that the upper limits of the speed of the pulsations when produced by the aid of an air-spark are not very high. The difficulty in increasing the speed of the pulsations arose from the tendency of the heated poles of the air-spark to produce an arc between them if they are kept too close to one another.<note>The air-spark in these experiments passed between two small platinum spheres. Perhaps a variation of the shape of the poles might produce air-sparks whose frequency would be much faster. This tendency to form an arc was most strongly marked when the air-interval was in the negative part of the circuit.</note> The revolving mirror was used in the ordinary way by placing a narrow slit upon the tube so that the image of the discharge was a bright line about one-eighth to one-sixteenth of an inch wide. On making the mirror revolve rapidly, the appearance in the mirror consisted of parallel bands that were alternately bright and black; the black bands became broader as the mirror rotated faster and as the frequency of the discharges decreased.

On trying the above experiments, it was found that the discharge could always be resolved into such black and bright bands. There was no visible broadening of the bands, showing—so far as such means of observation were capable of demonstrating it—that the discharges were instantaneous. When the air-spark was reversed, *i.e.*, moved from the positive into the negative side, a change occurred in the appearance of the bands; but it was difficult to define the essential characteristics of such a change. They seemed to consist of a slight variation in the circumstances of the discharge caused by what may be termed a lack of electrical symmetry in some portion of the circuit, rather than any change in the nature of the discharge due to a fundamental contrast in the properties of the two types of electricity. The definition seemed to be sharper when the air-spark was in the negative than when it was in the positive.

The negative end of the tube was observed first; the slit used was long enough to allow the negative pole, the <term>negative dark space</term>, and the negative end of the <term>positive column</term> to appear in the field at the same time. When the mirror was set to revolve, the black and bright bands generally appeared to extend in straight lines through the entire field, right across the negative dark space, although they grew faint and sometimes even invisible in the region of the negative dark space.

<summary>The authors use a revolving mirror to prove that electrical discharges in rarefied gases are instantaneous, intermittent pulses rather than a continuous flow. <meta>This page continues the technical analysis of electrical discharges, focusing on observations made with a revolving mirror and metal rings to determine the nature and velocity of pulsations within a vacuum tube.</meta>

<header>MESSRS. W. SPOTTISWOODE AND J. FLETCHER MOULTON</header>

When the air-spark was lengthened, not only did the black bands become broader, but, associated with the intensely bright bands, there seemed to be one or more other bright bands, much fainter in character and apparently narrower. Whether they were in fact narrower is difficult to decide, as their greater faintness would perhaps give them the appearance of being so; but if it is a fact that they were narrower, it is possible that this points to the main bright lines being broader than the image of the slit, which would show that the principal discharge occupies some little time; on the other hand, the apparent width of the bright bands may be due to irradiation. The subsidiary discharges may perhaps arise from the existence of return currents, such as are evidenced by the appearance of negative discharge at the positive pole when an air-spark of considerable size is introduced, and also by the double effects which tubes so constantly show when we try to produce the relief or non-relief-effects.

A metal ring was now put around the tube about the middle of its length, and the slit was so placed that the ring passed across it about its center. This ring was then joined successively to the air-spark and non-air-spark terminals, and to earth, and the slit examined in each case. In no instance was any crookedness found in the bright lines, although when the air-spark was in the positive, the slit sometimes included the bright termination of the positive column and a section of the hollow luminous cone which surrounds it. These observations show that there is no lack of simultaneity between the discharges caused by the relief or the non-relief-effect and the ordinary discharge in the tube; and as we know that the pulse which causes the former passes along the outside of the tube with the velocity of electrical currents in a conductor, this experiment would seem to demonstrate the existence of a velocity in the discharge within the tube of a similarly high order.

In order to further test the possibility of single pulses giving rise to the effects of which we have been speaking, the following experiment (to which reference has already been made) was tried. The terminals of a tube were connected with the outside and the inside of a small <term>Leyden jar</term>. The poles of the secondary circuit of a coil were placed so that the discharge from the coil charged the jar by leaping over intervals of considerable size (about a quarter of an inch for the negative pole and three-quarters of an inch for the positive pole), so that the make-current was excluded. When the coil was worked, there appeared a brilliant discharge caused by the jar periodically discharging itself through the tube. A slit was placed on the tube and the luminous column was examined by the revolving mirror, and it was found that the discharge was quite instantaneous, and that usually it was not followed by the next at any regular interval, but that occasionally it was multiple. The discharge was then tested for both relief and non-relief-effects, and notwithstanding the very large quantity that passed at each discharge, it gave them very markedly. The contact breaker was then worked by hand so as only to give single flashes. These were tested for sensitiveness and were found to be perfectly sensitive. Thus it appears from experiment that the whole of the relief and non-relief-effects are completed within each single pulsation,

XI.—*The discharge is produced under ordinary circumstances by the passage through the tube, from the air-spark terminal, of free electricity of the same polarity as the electricity at that terminal.*

The knowledge gained from our previous experiments regarding the difference between the effects of positive and negative pulses arriving at the outside of the tube enables us to determine the nature of the electrical disturbances within the tube; for, as we have seen, there is a complete dissimilarity between the appearances produced within the tube by the two types of pulses. Now, if we take a tube containing an ordinary sensitive discharge—where the sensitivity is produced by an air-spark—and connect tinfoil placed upon it to earth, we obtain the same type of effect regardless of where the tinfoil is placed. Thus, if the air-spark is in the positive portion of the external circuit, the effect of connecting a piece of tinfoil placed upon any part of the tube to earth will be what we may call a negative effect, showing that throughout the tube the primary and main effect is a sudden inflow of positive electricity across the section of the tube beneath the tinfoil.* This is the case even if the tinfoil is placed very close to the negative end of the tube. Thus, throughout the entire length of the tube, the charge of positive electricity passes without triggering a response from the other terminal; or, if there is a response, it must be very faint, so as not to cast any doubt on the overwhelming dominance of the original charge. If the negative terminal is the air-spark terminal, the same result is observed, except that the charge passing through the tube is of negative electricity.

It must be observed that in stating this, we do not commit ourselves to the <term>two-fluid theory</term> of electricity or to any equivalent theory. It may be that instead of a charge of negative electricity being sent through the tube in this way, what is propagated is a state of deficiency of positive electricity. Nor do we necessarily adopt any specific theory of propagation. It may be that electricity is carried on material particles of gas; it may be that it is passed from one particle to another without, or in addition to, the actual motion of the particles charged with it at any moment; or it may be propagated without the assistance of the material particles of the gas. Which

---

<note>* These remarks are strictly applicable only to cases in which the discharge in the tube would be non-sensitive without the introduction of the air-spark. Those tubes that inherently make discharges sensitive must be regarded as tubes where one or both terminals act as if an air-gap were essentially connected to them. Consequently, when using such tubes with an external air-spark, we are often in the position of using a tube with an air-spark in both the positive and negative external circuits. The phenomena in such cases are, of course, somewhat complicated, as special effects (though different in character) are obtained by connecting the tinfoil to either terminal; however, they otherwise present no theoretical difficulty and will not be mentioned further in this paper.</note>

Of these, whichever represents the actual means by which electricity is propagated through the tube must be decided by other evidence. All that is claimed as following from these experiments is that the charge passes (disruptively) from the air-spark terminal in the form of what we know as free electricity, and in such a form passes through the tube until it arrives at the other terminal and becomes neutralized by the opposite electricity that is awaiting it there. And this is shown conclusively by the identical nature of the relief-effect throughout the whole of the tube.*

The force of these arguments will become more evident if we consider certain results obtained with an arrangement that made the conditions of the two terminals of the tube electrically symmetrical, instead of permitting them to be in such radically different electric conditions as is the case when an air-spark is used.

If we take a coil giving rapid discharges of small quantity, we will obtain a sensitive discharge. If the tube is symmetrical in figure, and the terminals as nearly alike as possible, then, on examination, we will find that the sensitivity is very slight in the center of the tube and that it increases toward the ends. This is in marked contrast to the ordinary sensitive discharge described so far, which shows a sensitivity gradually decreasing through the whole length of the tube as we pass from the air-spark terminal; and, moreover, the character of the relief-effects differs in the two portions of the tube. In the portion toward the positive terminal, the effects are similar to those presented by a tube having an air-spark in the positive, while in the portion toward the negative terminal, the effects are similar to those in a tube having an air-spark in the negative. The part of the tube near the center, which shows little or no sign of sensitivity, will be called the *neutral zone*.

Nor is this the only peculiarity presented by this form of sensitive discharge. If we place a piece of tinfoil on the tube near one of the terminals and connect it with the nearer terminal, we get a marked effect, wholly different from the to-earth or relief-effect. If, on the other hand, we connect it with the more distant terminal, we get an effect which, though stronger and more marked in character, is decidedly of the type of the to-earth-effect. These peculiarities are in no way caused by the double current, as they are well marked when the break-current alone passes.

These phenomena are easily explained by the supposition that owing to the

Due to the symmetry of the electrical condition of the terminals, the arrangement is equivalent to an air-spark at both ends, meaning that the positive and negative pulses are approximately equal in quantity and rush simultaneously along the tube to meet near the center. The parts near the center will thus be continually in a state of no electric tension, and therefore there can be no relief-effect and no sensitivity. The pulse at either terminal is of the opposite sign to the pulse at the other terminal, and consequently opposite to the pulses that attempt to leave the tinfoil on the tube near that terminal. Hence, the connection of a piece of tinfoil with the more distant terminal will naturally produce the relief-effect, though in a stronger and more pronounced form. Moreover, the relief-effects in the two portions of the tube are of opposite characters, showing conclusively that the corresponding electrical pulses within the tube have opposite signs.

A slight variation of the experiment tends to confirm this view. If we connect one of the terminals to the earth, so that these discharges cannot produce electrical tension or an increase in potential there, we find at once that the neutral zone disappears. The luminous discharge then presents all the characteristics of an ordinary sensitive discharge, with the air-spark at the terminal opposite to the one that is grounded, and the sensitivity decreases in the usual manner throughout the whole length of the tube as we proceed from the air-spark terminal toward the other end of the tube. And if, instead of connecting the terminal to the earth, we connect it to a condenser of small capacity whose other surface is grounded—so as to diminish, without completely suppressing, the variations of tension—we find that an intermediate effect is produced. The neutral zone is displaced toward the terminal connected to the condenser, and the sensitivity is found to decrease as we pass from either terminal toward the neutral zone.

A striking confirmation of the correctness of this interpretation is obtained by placing a broad piece of tinfoil around the tube midway between its ends and putting a telephone in a circuit between the tinfoil and the earth. When discharges from a small coil (such as the one described above) are sent through the tube, the sound heard in the telephone will be faint; but it instantly becomes loud upon either terminal of the tube being touched with a finger. The reason is obvious. By touching one of the terminals, the discharge becomes one in which the same kind of electricity passes throughout the tube; therefore, the charge requirements of the tinfoil are all of one kind and are additive. But when both discharges enter the tube, the charge requirements of opposite ends of the tinfoil have different signs, and only the remaining balance passes through the telephone circuit.

Even more striking effects illustrating this subject were obtained by using a larger coil with a moderately exhausted tube and a contact breaker operating at a somewhat rapid rate. The luminous discharge presented the ordinary characteristics of a coil-discharge as we have just described them. When a ring of tinfoil, somewhat less than an inch in width, was placed around the tube not far from one end and connected

On placing a similar ring of tinfoil in the same position relatively to the opposite terminal, and connecting it with the terminal most distant from it, an exactly similar discharge took place at that end of the tube, and the middle portion of the tube remained dark.

The interpretation of these very striking phenomena follows readily from the theory we have stated. Indeed, the action in this case is so plain that it is easy to arrive at the interpretation of the phenomena without any reference to the theory of sensitive discharges; and the importance of these experiments for our purposes is chiefly due to the support they give to the explanations we have put forward of the hollow luminous discharge in the positive non-relief state, and the other characteristic phenomena of sensitive discharges. A positive pulse coming from the secondary circuit rushes at once to the terminal and to the tinfoil ring. At the same instant, a negative impulse rushes to the terminal nearest to the tinfoil ring and leaps into the tube. The impulse to the ring has already produced an inductive discharge into the tube of positive electricity, and this meets and satisfies the negative pulse from the terminal, leaving negative electricity predominating near the tinfoil, and this holds the positive charge in the tinfoil for a brief instant. That brief instant suffices for the next pulse from the coil (which will necessarily be of the opposite character) to come up and satisfy the positive charge, and thus set free the negative within the tube, which in its turn satisfies the positive pulse that now comes from the terminal, and then the cycle begins again.

As it has reference to the phenomena of sensitive discharges described in the earlier part of this paper, it is worth remarking that if we do not properly adjust the breadth of the tinfoil, or if the tube is not of a suitable character, we fail to get a complete absence of discharge in the intermediate portion of the tube, but we find that superposed upon the discharges as we have described them there is a somewhat feeble discharge going through the whole tube. This is precisely what we so often obtain in the case of the relief and non-relief-effects in tubes; the phenomena are there with all their characteristics, but blurred or masked by the superposition, as it were, of a further discharge which does not show the usual phenomena. It is reasonable to suppose that the cause is the same, namely: that the external actions are not of the suitable strength, or the internal conditions are not such as to permit the effect upon the discharge to exist in all its completeness.

...provoking a response from the other terminal. This method shows us that in the ordinary case of an air-spark discharge, it passes completely through the tube before this response occurs—if, in fact, it can be said to occur at all. One of the most important consequences that necessarily follows from this is that the discharges at the two terminals of the tube are entirely independent. They are primarily determined by the conditions at their own terminal, and only in a secondary degree, if at all, by the conditions existing at the opposite terminal. We shall return to this point later and demonstrate even more conclusively the complete independence of the discharge at either terminal of a tube, but it is useful to call attention here to the very important consequences that flow from this principle. Since the discharges are not identical at both terminals, the tube must contain different free charges at different times.<note>* In order to demonstrate this conclusively, a vacuum tube was enclosed in a metal canister (with wires passing to its terminals through tubes of insulating material inserted into small holes in the canister), and a telephone was placed in a circuit between the canister and the ground. When a discharge with an air spark in the external circuit was sent through the tube, a sound was heard in the telephone similar to the sound made by the air spark. By a fundamental principle of electricity, the free electricity on the surface of the canister (which escaped through the telephone to the ground) was at any instant equal to the excess of one type of electricity over the other in the space within the canister. If the discharge had been a form of conduction, as in a galvanic current, there would never have been an excess of either type of electricity, and therefore no sound would have been heard in the telephone. The existence of a sound proved there were variations in the algebraic sum of the free electricity in the tube. To show that this was not due to anything depending on the wires leading to the tube, the same experiment was repeated with a tube in which the middle section was connected to the two end portions by very narrow passages. The middle section was placed in the canister and the narrow parts passed through small holes made in its side, so that only a portion of the complete tube was within the canister. The same results were obtained with this arrangement.</note> It is therefore in no respect like a conductor, but is an independent electrical system, holding much the same position as the air vessel in a forcing pump. All the electricity that enters it leaves it again, but the truth of this can only be asserted when we consider the entire discharge from beginning to end; it may not be even approximately true during a small, finite period of time.

This independence of the discharges from the two terminals is a most important fact in analyzing the way electricity passes through <term>rarefied gases</term>. It corrects the error of seeking analogies in metallic conduction and shows that any appearance of following regular laws—such as changes in <term>potential</term> along the tube, <term>resistance</term>, etc.—must arise from the fact that the effects measured are actually average effects over a span of time that is enormously long compared with the duration of

---

Through these experiments, together with those previously described in which a telephone is placed in a circuit between the ground and a piece of tin foil on the tube, we are able to obtain direct evidence from the telephone of the intermittent nature of the discharge at the time of its actual passage through the tube. This evidence fully confirms what was previously obtained using the <term>revolving mirror</term>. It is, however, of lesser value; for although it shows conclusively that there are rapid, periodic alterations of intensity or character in the <term>induction</term> around the tube, it does not enable us to decide whether these are due to full interruptions or only to fluctuations in the discharge.

### XII.—*On unipolar discharges.*

We have seen that, because the discharge from the air-spark terminal produces its special effect without any indistinctness or confusion right up to the opposite terminal, it appears that the discharges from the two terminals are independent enough that the discharge can occur from one terminal and the free electricity can pass through the tube to the immediate vicinity of the other without triggering a specific response from that second terminal. And if each such discharge does in any way call forth a specific response from the other terminal, it must be so slight that it does not materially affect the electrical condition of the interior of the tube, or the effect which that condition produces on conducting systems outside the tube. We have also seen that this independence implies that the electricity leaves the terminal from which it starts as a result of the electric tension within that terminal, and only to a very minor degree because of the related action at the opposite terminal. Lest these should seem to be too hastily drawn conclusions, we will proceed to describe a class of phenomena which provide very important evidence of their truth.

If we take two vacuum tubes of the same general type and connect one terminal of each with one terminal of a large <term>HOLTZ machine</term>, and connect their other terminals with the second terminal of the machine—placing an <term>air-spark</term> (for example, in the positive circuit) so that the electricity has two alternative paths, one through the first tube and one through the second, with the air-spark being shared by both paths—a very remarkable phenomenon will be witnessed (Plate 19, fig. 19). If the air-spark is of a suitable size, it will be found that one of the tubes is completely traversed by the discharge, but that the other is occupied only by a luminous column extending from the positive terminal into the tube for a significant portion of its length, and gradually tapering to a point. If the air-spark does not exceed a certain limit, depending upon the "resistance" of both tubes, there will be no light at the other end of the tube, and no discharge through it. Breaking the connection with the distant terminal will produce no effect on the luminous column, nor on any portion of the discharge; this shows—as the appearance of the column itself sufficiently indicates—that the discharge is unipolar or incomplete. Slight traces of blue haze are sometimes seen at the tip of this tapering column, likely due to some negative electricity gathered from the surroundings, but not directly discharged from the opposite terminal. The discharge is, in fact, one which passes into the tube but not with sufficient force to pass through it, and which accordingly returns by the way by which it entered. We shall examine the cause of this return later; for our present purposes, it is enough to point out the fact that here we have a discharge from one pole which is unable to approach near enough to the other pole to find relief there, and

actually prefers to return the way it came rather than to pass through the tube to the other terminal. Such discharges we shall term *unipolar discharges*.

This unipolar discharge is, of course, intermittent and therefore sensitive. If we take a glass rod with a piece of tinfoil at the end, electrically connected by a wire with the positive terminal of the tube, and hold it near to but slightly beyond the end of the luminous column, we shall find the luminous column driven back; and by carefully advancing it toward the positive terminal, we can often succeed in driving the luminous column completely back and preventing any visible discharge from taking place in the tube (Plate 19, fig. 20). The explanation for this is obvious. At the moment that the charging up which causes the discharge occurs in the positive terminal, there is also a charging up in the tinfoil; through its inductive effect, this tends to prevent the advance of any free positive electricity. Thus, however rapid the pulsation, the force tending to oppose the discharge keeps exact time with it and causes the retreat of the luminous column. If the tinfoil and wire are connected to the ground, or otherwise made a relieving system, we find the usual to-earth effects produced on this unipolar discharge.

A form of these experiments, which is in some respects even more striking, is obtained by taking a tube with an intermediate terminal and connecting the intermediate and one of the end terminals with the positive terminal of the machine, and the other terminal of the tube with the negative terminal of the machine. Interpose an air-spark in the positive circuit so that it forms part of the path to both of the terminals that were connected with the positive terminal of the machine. With an air-spark of proper dimensions, it will be found that while the entire effective current passes from the positive intermediate terminal to the negative terminal, there is also seen, first, a tongue-shaped luminous column extending from the positive end terminal toward the intermediate terminal; and secondly, a similar tongue-shaped luminous column stretching out from the intermediate terminal to meet it (Plate 19, fig. 21). Or again, if we arrange two tubes as first described and connect both terminals of the second tube with the positive terminal of the machine, we shall have two positive unipolar columns as before. These two do not join; and it is clear that here we naturally have the same effect as that obtained by using the tinfoil in the former case (Plate 19, fig. 22). Each of these discharges acts repulsively on the other, and they drive each other back. If we use the tinfoil, as in the former experiment, we can drive each in turn back toward, and sometimes into, its terminal; within considerable limits, when one column is driven back, the other advances, and *vice versa*.

This experiment with the intermediate terminal shows very forcibly how the discharge from an air-spark terminal depends solely on the forces at work at the terminal itself, and has very little reference to the condition of the other terminal of the tube. We see here that the positive electricity from the intermediate terminal actually issues abundantly in a direction where there is not only no negative terminal, but actually a positive terminal, which ultimately succeeds in repelling its advance.

Similar phenomena, except for the shape of the luminous columns, are seen when the two terminals are joined to the negative terminal of the machine; but we will not dwell here on the similarities or differences between the two phenomena. The two kinds of unipolar discharge, however, are instantly distinguishable from one another, and this may be used as final proof of the correctness of the conclusions reached regarding the nature of the electric displacements that cause the relief-effects. If a piece of tinfoil is placed on a tube through which a discharge passes, and this tinfoil is electrically connected with *one* terminal of a tube of suitable resistance, it will be found that when an air-spark is introduced into the discharge, a unipolar discharge will appear in the tube whose terminal is connected with the tinfoil (Plate 20, fig. 24). If the air-spark is in the positive circuit, this will be found to be a positive unipolar discharge; if the air-spark is in the negative circuit, it will be a negative unipolar discharge. This test is made even more certain and useful by taking the wire from the tinfoil to both terminals of the auxiliary tube. The result will then be a double unipolar effect, the nature of which is much more easily recognized. This provides a very convenient test of the sign of the disruptive discharge at any part of the tube, and it has been frequently employed with great advantage in cases where the complexity of the circumstances has made it difficult to determine it directly.

The following experiment is instructive regarding unipolar discharges. If, using the arrangement described on page 214, we place a ring of tinfoil upon a tube containing a positive unipolar discharge—not very far from the further end of the tube—and connect it with the positive terminal, the discharge is at once completed and continues to pass throughout the tube (Plate 19, fig. 23). On examining it, we find that from the interior of the tube within the ring of tinfoil proceeds the usual hollow conical discharge characteristic of the non-relief state with the air-spark in the positive; this stretches in the usual way toward the negative terminal of the tube, and the luminosity that starts from the positive column reaches and stops at the limit of the dark space within this cone in the usual manner. Thus, by our tinfoil ring, we have cut the tube into two sections, each of which shows its own separate discharge; and the tension <note>In this context, tension refers to electrical potential or voltage.</note> which was insufficient to cause a discharge through the whole tube is capable of supporting the two shorter discharges. And, just as in the corresponding case in the ordinary sensitive discharge, the pulsations in the tinfoil cause positive induction discharges that are strong enough to reach the negative terminal. The relief of the tension in the tinfoil that follows the occurrence of the discharge into the tube from the positive terminal releases negative electricity from beneath the tinfoil, which satisfies the discharge from the positive terminal. Thus, the interior of the tube within the ring of tinfoil acts alternately as a positive and

We have already spoken of the results of connecting a small condenser with one of the terminals of the tube, when a coil discharge is used, so as to depress the electrical tension produced at that terminal and shift the position of the neutral zone. It is very instructive to compare these effects with the analogous effects in the case of unipolar discharges. If we join the effective terminal of the tube containing the unipolar discharge to a small condenser composed of, say, two pieces of tinfoil about three square inches in area, with a plate of mica between them, we shall see the luminous tongue slightly shorten. If, now, we connect the other side of this condenser to the earth, we see a further shortening of the column, which will often almost disappear. If we connect the terminal with a larger condenser or a Leyden jar, the discharge completely disappears. Thus, we see that the condenser or Leyden jar has, just as in the case of the coil discharges, the effect of muffling or toning down the intensity of the impulsive changes of electrical tension at the terminals and thereby lessening the violence of the discharges into the tube.

We conclude, then, from these experiments that the independence of the discharge from each terminal is so complete that we can at will cause the discharges from the two terminals to be equal in intensity but opposite in sign (as in the case of the coil) or of any required degree of inequality (as in the case of the coil with a small condenser). Or we can cause the discharge to be from one terminal only, with the other terminal acting merely receptively (as in the case of the air-spark discharge); or we can cause the discharge to pass from one terminal only and return to it, with the other terminal not taking any part in the discharge; or, finally, we can make the two terminals pour forth independent discharges of the same sign, each of which passes back through the terminal from which it came.

### XIII.—*On the state of the tube during the occurrence of the discharge.*

We have already shown that each pulsation may be considered as a separate disturbance, the effects of which have passed away before the next pulse comes. It now remains for us to ascertain what the state of the tube is during the continuance of the almost instantaneous pulse which may be considered as the unit of which the visible discharge is built up.

For the purpose of experimentally ascertaining this, it is obvious that if we employ any tests which are not themselves affected with the same periodicity as the discharge being examined, we shall get no results that speak with any degree of certainty regarding the state of the tube at the instant in question. Thus, if we listen with a telephone in circuit between the earth and a piece of tinfoil on the tube, we hear a sound identical in pitch with that of the air-spark, but this only tells us

The simplest experiment is to take two pieces of tinfoil, one near the air-spark end and one near the opposite end of the tube, and connect them with a thin wire.

In an ordinary sensitive discharge, if we place a piece of tinfoil somewhat near the air-spark terminal and connect it with a larger piece of tinfoil at a significant distance along the tube, we shall find that we have a complete relief effect at the first-mentioned spot. And if we examine the effect at the larger piece of tinfoil, we shall find indications of the non-relief effect. If we now reverse the arrangement and place the larger piece near the air-spark terminal and the smaller piece at a considerable distance from it, we shall find that while we have feeble relief effects at the larger piece, we have strongly marked non-relief effects at the other.*

Nor must it be thought that only the less definite types of relief and special effects can be produced in this way. If the pieces of tinfoil are made in the form of rings surrounding the tube, all the effects previously described can be produced in this manner. If, for instance, with a positive air-spark, a broad ring of tinfoil near the positive end of the tube is connected to a narrower ring near the opposite terminal, we shall—with a proper adjustment of the air-spark—obtain the segmentation of the luminous column and the formation of the hollow cone, just as definitely as if we had joined the narrow ring to the positive terminal of the tube. A similar effect can be produced with a negative air-spark, provided the narrower ring is the one that is nearer to the air-spark terminal.

Now, these effects can scarcely be reconciled with any theory which makes the discharge simultaneous throughout the tube. Suppose that it is so; then, if we take A to be the smaller piece of tinfoil (which we shall suppose is the nearer to the air-spark terminal) and B to be the larger piece, it is obvious that the sudden change

The tension at A is greater than that at B, since it compels B to provide it relief. But however large B might be, such relief could never be greater than what would result in making the potential at A sink to that of B; this would by no means be equivalent to connecting A to the earth, since the impulsive change at B will ordinarily be very considerable. Hence, as we achieve complete relief at A by joining it to B, it must be that B has not suffered any increase of potential at the moment that A seeks relief, and thus B is not prevented from giving A that relief which its size and distance from the spot where the free electricity is located at that instant enable it to give—a relief which, as we have seen, is for all practical purposes complete. However, it does so at the expense of receiving a pulse of electricity from A of the same type as it would receive if it were joined to the air-spark terminal, and we therefore see indications of the non-relief-effect. We see then that the discharge is progressive, and that it proceeds from the air-spark terminal. For the electric disturbance at A makes its demand for relief on B and finds B quite as capable of providing it as though no discharge had taken place, meaning the discharge has not yet reached B.

Another very instructive form of these experiments is obtained by placing a long strip of tinfoil along the tube from end to end, taking care, of course, that it is not connected with the terminals (Plate 20, fig. 25). Suppose the air-spark is in the positive; then, if the tube is sufficiently sensitive, it will be found that near the positive terminal there is the discharge relief-effect. A little further on there is repulsion, which gradually diminishes and is finally replaced by the attraction of the luminous column which, as we have seen, is an ordinary form of non-relief-effect.<note>When the air-spark is in the negative, the relief-effect usually assumes the appearance of an attraction of the luminosity to the inner surface of the tube. In reality, it is due to the luminous positive discharges from the side of the tube, as such discharges always appear (as we have seen) to start from the actual surface of the glass. The same remarks apply to the non-relief-effect when the air-spark is in the positive.</note> The portion of the tinfoil near the air-spark terminal has derived relief from the remainder because it is the first to experience the sudden change of tension, and the more distant parts receive, as a consequence, pulses of electricity sufficient to cause the non-relief-effects. If the tinfoil is divided a little beyond the part of the tube occupied by the discharge relief-effect, the positive end of the further portion will now present the discharge relief-effect; this is because, instead of being a part of the relieving system for the portion of the strip of tinfoil between it and the positive terminal, it is now the part of the further piece of tinfoil that is the first to feel the call for relief. Consequently, it is the part that derives the full benefit of the relieving system formed by the piece of tinfoil of which it forms a part. At the same time, the negative end of the nearer piece of tinfoil (which previously showed relief-effects) will show non-relief-effects, as it has to afford relief to the part nearest to the positive terminal and no longer has any more distant piece of tinfoil from which to draw supplies of positive electricity.

This experiment, then, proves that the instantaneous increase of tension arrives at the tinfoil closer to the air-spark end, which we will call A, sooner than at the other end, which we will call B. Now, what is the state of the tube at B at the moment when the rise of tension occurs at A? We have shown that it is not affected by the rise of tension at A, but we have not otherwise determined its electrical state. This is determined in the following way. Secure the piece of tinfoil B to a glass rod and use a fine wire to connect it, running the wire near the tube during its entire course so that the capacity of the system providing relief to A may depend almost exclusively on the capacity of B (Plate 20, fig. 26). Now, if we move B as far as possible from the tube while keeping the wire straight, it will be found that *the capacity of B to relieve A is diminished*. In other words, by placing B on the tube, we place it in a neighborhood where there is a rising demand for the very electricity that is driven off from A. Suppose, for example, that the air-spark is in the positive. The electricity that leaves A is positive; and hence it follows that at the part of the tube where B rests, there is a demand for positive electricity, which means there is a rising negative potential there; or in other words, the quantity of negative electricity within the tube at B must be increasing.

There would seem to be only one interpretation of this phenomenon. The negative terminal (in this case) is connected with its source of electricity during the entire interval between the pulses, and it must be pouring its electricity into the tube during all that time, thus gradually increasing the quantity of negative electricity in the tube. When the positive pulse arrives, it sweeps up all the negative electricity it encounters and rushes out at the opposite terminal, likely leaving the tube in a positive state. Indeed, this is so marked that we often see indications of a reverse current as soon as we introduce an air-spark, showing that the positive pulse is so violent that it causes over-relief. When this pulse has passed, the non-air-spark terminal—or, as we may better term it, the connected terminal—begins to pour out its electricity, undoing the effect of the pulse on the tube and gradually filling it with negative electricity until the next pulse comes.

So much then for the condition of the tube in front of the electric pulse. We must next inquire what the condition of the tube is behind the pulse during the discharge. This is much more difficult, because we can no longer use the test described above, as we cannot tell whether the reaction which clearly follows the relief-effect occurs during or after the passage of the pulse.

If, however, we put several pieces of tinfoil on the tube and connect the one nearest to the air-spark terminal to earth, placing a telephone in circuit, we shall find that the loudness of the tone is increased by connecting the other pieces of tinfoil with the first piece. This shows that their relief demands are additive, and as we know that the sign of the electricity in the relief-pulse is the same for all, and consequently that the pulse which constitutes the reaction must also necessarily be of the same sign for all, we see that the last piece must be in a condition demanding relief before the first has

According to theory, the nature of the relief required in such a case is different on opposite sides of the <term>neutral zone</term>. Therefore, it should be possible to provide complete relief to a part of the tube on one side of the <term>neutral zone</term> by connecting it with tinfoil placed on the tube at a suitable spot on the other side of the <term>neutral zone</term>. This is found to be the case, and furthermore, it is found that the two corresponding spots approach and move away from the <term>neutral zone</term> together. Moreover, if a long strip of tinfoil is placed on the tube extending from end to end, it is found that there are relief effects all along it, although of course they are of opposite types on opposite sides of the <term>neutral zone</term>, and that a very slight change is caused by connecting the strip of tinfoil to the ground, showing that the demands of the two portions of the tube are nearly complementary. And further, although the experiment is difficult to conduct in such a way as to leave no doubt as to the result, it has been observed several times that the effect of connecting a piece of tinfoil (which is connected to the ground through a telephone) near one terminal of a tube containing such a discharge with a piece near the other is to reduce the sound instead of increasing it, thus showing that the electrical requirements of the two pieces are opposite in character; and in further confirmation of this we may refer to the experiment described on page 212, which in a more marked and obvious way demonstrates the fact that the electrical requirements of pieces of tinfoil on opposite sides of the <term>neutral zone</term> are of opposite signs.

directly operates in producing the observed effects, we are brought face to face with the question: How far are our conclusions relative to these discharges applicable to the case of ordinary or uninterrupted <term>vacuum discharges</term>? Or in other words, how far are they independent of the peculiarity of the interruptedness of the discharge? In considering this most important question, it must be conceded that full weight must be given to the consideration that our investigations have been carried out by means of experiments which would, every one of them, have failed had they been applied to ordinary vacuum discharges; so that any conclusions sought to be drawn from them regarding such ordinary discharges must be received with great caution. But this would not justify us in neglecting the remarkable resemblances that exist between the two classes of discharges, or in refusing to examine the information which our knowledge of the makeup of one gives us regarding the probable makeup of the other.

As we have previously remarked, it may be stated generally that there is no phenomenon presented by ordinary vacuum discharges which may not be shown by sensitive or interrupted discharges; and conversely, there is no phenomenon presented by the latter (except such as directly depend on and are due to its sensitive and interrupted character) which is not also shown by the former. In illustration of this, we will select two important features, namely: <term>striation</term> and the terminal peculiarities. And first as to striation: every one of the many shapes presented by the <term>striae</term> of the one can be found among striae produced by the other; and, moreover, the very same element which leads to the presence or absence of striation (namely: the greater or less quantity of <term>electricity</term> discharged) in the one case leads to it also in the other. No doubt the sensitive discharge, under the conditions in which it has been studied here, is much less often striated than the non-sensitive discharge, but as the character of such a discharge is essentially variable and unsteady, it is not at all surprising that effects which are known to depend on the complete steadiness of the discharge should be those least frequently met with. And that we are right in assigning these as reasons for the tendency in interrupted discharges to be non-striated is rendered more probable by the fact that, when we compel the discharges to operate with great regularity and within the prescribed limits of quantity and of time—as, for example, in the case of the <term>high-speed break</term> or of artificially produced striation—we at once find it easy to produce the steady effects commonly observable in ordinary discharges.

Next as to the terminal peculiarities.<note>If the theory of the authors of this paper is correct, these terminal peculiarities are in reality cases of striation where the circumstances of the discharge are such as to maintain by necessity the required steadiness and uniformity of conditions. But for the present purposes, it is better to consider them separately.</note> These are, it will be admitted, common to both classes of discharges. But inasmuch as we have seen that the <term>relief-effects</term> and non-relief-effects are substantially identical with terminal peculiarities, we can now go further and say that they are shown wherever there is an instantaneous electric discharge from the space close to the surface of any fixed body. Therefore, examining either of these important features leads us to the conclusion that the essentials of the discharge of electricity through rarefied gases are the same whether the discharge is interrupted, uninterrupted, or entirely discontinuous—and perhaps alternate, as in the case last mentioned.

The simplest, and indeed the only obvious explanation for this result, is that the characteristic found to be fundamental in sensitive discharges—namely, disruptiveness—is common to both types of discharge. The difference between the two kinds should be sought in the scale on which that characteristic is displayed.<note>To this we must add the restriction that, in the case of the ordinary discharge, the discontinuous pulses in which the electricity leaves the terminals must be very minute; this condition follows naturally from the greater rapidity of intermittence in that discharge.</note> In both discharges, each terminal pours forth its electricity to satisfy its own electrical state, and only in a very secondary degree to satisfy the state of the opposite terminal. One terminal does not directly sense the electrical state of the other, as would be the case if they were connected by metal; instead, it pours forth its electricity in the form of free electricity and leaves it to wander independently in that form. If these points could be demonstrated conclusively—in other words, if it could be shown that all disruptive discharges are discontinuous, and that the appearance of continuity in an ordinary discharge is solely due to the extreme speed with which consecutive pulses follow each other, combined with the fact that each individual pulse is extremely small—a great step would be gained in our knowledge of the nature of electric discharges. Although this cannot be hoped for at present, we trust that the results recorded in this paper add considerably to the evidence in favor of these ideas, and we shall now proceed to indicate the considerations which have led us to this conclusion.

First, it is undeniable that all vacuum discharge phenomena, and especially the terminal phenomena, *can* be produced by discontinuous discharges, where each individual part is entirely independent of those preceding or following it. Thus, we may say they can be produced by single instantaneous discharges. If the circumstances are such as to produce considerable regularity in these successive discharges, they will display all the characteristic phenomena of the steady uninterrupted discharge. Consequently, the idea of a continuous discharge is not necessary to account for these effects. Furthermore, we can show that a continuous displacement of electricity from the surface of a body will fail to produce these effects, while a more rapid displacement of an equal amount will produce them. In the experiment described on page 170, it is found that if the wire on the outside of the tube comes from the *positive* terminal of the machine, the appearance inside the tube is that of a *negative* terminal, and *vice versa*. Since the action must necessarily be alternate within the tube, there must be as great a discharge of positive electricity during one part of the process as there is of negative during the other. The only difference is that one occupies only the time required for a spark to pass between the—

The passage from stria to stria must then be regarded as disruptive and discontinuous; and if this is granted, then, as striæ are only particular cases of terminals, it follows almost naturally that all discharges in rarefied air are equally so. And this consideration becomes of greater weight when we consider the intimate relation of striæ and their component parts to what we have termed the *physical unit* of a striated discharge. Such a discharge is, as we have seen, made up of repetitions of a unit consisting of the bright surface of a stria, the dark space between it and the next stria, and the hazy interior of the latter. Such a structure, then, must either be necessary for the passage of the discharge or its natural consequence. Take the hollow cone discharge produced by the positive non-relief-effect. Here we compel a positive discharge to leave the interior surface of the glass under such circumstances that an equal amount of negative electricity is left behind to satisfy the original positive discharge. This it achieves by causing the positive column to stop suddenly at a considerable interval from the place of the discharge, and to terminate in a sharply-defined bright head, which is in all respects identical with the outer surface of a stria, while for its part the negative discharge forms the hazy interior of the hollow cone. Thus, the discharge requires and compels the formation of a unit of the structure described above. It seems in the highest degree improbable that structures formed and maintained to satisfy the needs of disruptive discharges (which have to leap from one part and land on the other of the differently constituted terminal portions of the structure) should also be formed and maintained by discharges which, because of their continuous character, must be assumed to flow with the same smoothness as in a metallic current, and to remain obedient to the law that the same amount of electricity flows across every section of the circuit in the same infinitesimal portion of time.

But if we admit that the ordinary discharge is discontinuous, the rapidity of the intermittence must be very great. For if this were not the case, the individual pulsations would be of considerable magnitude and would cause a sufficient rise and fall of electric tension outside the tube to give us the phenomena of the sensitive state. discharge. There may be many discharges from each terminal into the tube within the time it takes the discharge to pass through the tube, and the alterations of tension at any point outside the glass may be infinitesimal, so as to be completely unable to produce any relief-effect within.

It may be objected that this theory assumes something like a discontinuity in the range of frequency for pulses in an electrical discharge. Either they occur at the comparatively slow period that creates the sensitive state, or at the indefinitely faster period that creates the non-sensitive state. This difficulty, however, is only parallel to the problem we encounter when an air-spark gap is enlarged beyond the striking distance; at that point, the discharge across it immediately becomes silent, and the current that passes—when conducted through the tube—is found to have all the characteristics of a continuous discharge. No one can believe that the discharge across the gap has suddenly become continuous; the real nature of the change must be that the intermittent pulses (whether carried by convection on air particles or not) have become so numerous that the average of the discharge, when measured over an extremely short period of time, is constant. The relevance of the comparison is shown by the fact that the discharge through the tube is non-sensitive.<note>In this case, as in the other, there is probably no abrupt change in the character of the discharge. No doubt much of the discharge is carried in the silent form as we approach striking distance, and the apparent discontinuity is due to the fact that the increase in the proportion so carried is very sudden as we get near that point.</note>

We have seen that the pulses in the sensitive discharge are sudden and of sufficient quantity to significantly affect the electric tension in the surrounding space. This suddenness is essential. It is to this quality that we must attribute the discharge's indifference to the potential of the body affecting it and the dependence of the effects on the change of electric state alone. If an electrified body is surrounded by air, it must naturally create an electric field around it, which will or will not change over time depending on whether the air can reach the body and carry away its free electricity. But once this electric field has been established, it is affected just as easily by a new electric force introduced suddenly into the field as if the original body were not there. The change is, for all practical purposes, the same. We do not know what material changes accompany the formation of such an electric field, but for the sake of argument, let us assume that gaseous particles are driven off until equilibrium is reached. Then, a new force suddenly introduced will send away a similar stream of particles, regardless of whether the field on which it operates has already been subjected to a similar process.

The true analogy for these effects is found in the consideration of impulsive and continuous forces in dynamics. It is a well-known principle that when calculating the effect of impulsive forces, all continuous forces—whether they are pressures, strains, external attractions, or otherwise—may be ignored. The same is true of the changes in electric tension with which we are dealing in

<summary>The authors argue that "continuous" electrical discharges are actually composed of pulses so rapid that they appear constant, similar to how silent discharges occur when a spark gap is widened. This rapid pulsing explains why sensitive discharges respond to sudden changes in electric tension rather than the static potential of surrounding objects.</summary>

the sensitive discharges. They are so sudden and yet of such considerable magnitude that, in considering the change they effect, we may proceed as though no other electrical forces were at work. Thus, if we take the case of the positive unipolar discharge, a conductor connected with the acting terminal will, if moved toward the head of the column, drive it back; this is because when the sudden rush of electricity comes to the terminal, and from it into the tube, there is an equally sudden rush of the same kind to the conductor. Each causes an impulsive change in the electric tension around itself; and as these are of a nature that nullifies one another within the tube, the column is shortened. But a <term>Leyden jar</term> charged with the same kind of electricity to a much higher potential than the source of the discharge will not drive back the column. All that it does is to set up a permanent electric field which offers no resistance whatever to the sudden impulsive electrical changes that occur in the terminal and in the space within the tube.

The authors of this paper have intentionally avoided dwelling upon any questions involving theories of the nature of electricity or the difference between positive and negative electricity, or upon other differences which have come to light during the present investigation. But it is important to observe that the difference in behavior of the two kinds of electricity is not confined to cases in which these electricities leave the terminals proper of the tube, but is equally present when they come from quasi-terminals (as in the case of the relief and non-relief-effects), or even when they form their own terminals out of gaseous materials, as in the case of striæ.

#### A.—*On the variations of form of the negative glow.*

It is obviously a matter of great importance to the theory of striæ put forward in this paper that the negative glow should be shown to be merely a stria modified by the local conditions that exist at the negative terminal of the tube. We have therefore thought it desirable to record one or two cases of special forms assumed by the negative glow under special circumstances, which have been encountered by us since the date at which this paper was originally presented to the Royal Society, and which appear to us to show very clearly that the negative glow is only a modified stria.

The first case was observed by one of the authors of this paper in a tube belonging to Mr. <term>WARREN DE LA RUE</term>, which was being experimented upon in his laboratory with a current of several thousand cells of his well-known battery. The negative terminal was in the form of a rather large ring, but the exhaustion of the tube was so thorough, and consequently the breadth of the <term>CROOKES’ space</term> was so considerable, that the negative

The column of <term>striæ</term> did not usually extend from the positive end as far as the ring. However, when the column was drawn out by the influence of a magnet and made to reach the ring fully, the column of <term>striæ</term> was immediately pushed back, forming a comparatively long dark space between the <term>stria</term> anchored on the ring and the column behind it. This sudden pushing back was repeated every time a <term>stria</term> was brought onto the ring by the magnet, and was undoubtedly due to the fact that the ring was acting as a (weak) negative pole through leakage from the air.

The tube in which this was first observed was quite long, but of only moderate diameter and a moderately good level of exhaust. The appearance of the discharge is shown in Plate 20, fig. 30. Only the <term>break current</term> <note>The "break current" is the electrical current produced in the secondary circuit of an induction coil at the moment the primary circuit is interrupted.</note> passed. The <term>luminous column</term> starting from the <term>positive terminal</term> was much smaller in diameter than the interior of the tube; consequently, it left a dark space between itself and the sides of the tube. In contrast, the portion in the half of the tube nearer to the <term>negative terminal</term> appeared to fill the tube completely. On touching the positive terminal, the discharge filled the entire tube; on touching the negative terminal, the discharge with the smaller cross-section extended through the whole length of the tube. When a small condenser was used, as described on page 211, the length of the portion occupied by each could be varied at will. It should be added that the narrow and broad discharges showed, by the nature of their <term>relief-effects</term>, that they were respectively caused by positive and negative electricity, and the part of the tube where they were seen to join was found in all cases to be the <term>neutral zone</term>. It should also be added that either column could be shortened by producing <term>relief-effects</term> near its base, as though such a proceeding delayed the discharge, just as the small condenser would do.

The cause of the difference in the two discharges is not difficult to explain. Both discharges receive some degree of relief from the inner surface of the glass even when a finger is not placed upon it. In the case of the positive discharge, this naturally results in the formation of a dark space at the surface of the glass, while in the case of the negative discharge, it leads to the formation of positive luminosity close up to the surface of the glass.

A similar difference in appearance in the two discharges has since been observed in other tubes, and it is probably not an uncommon phenomenon. It is undoubtedly analogous to what is very frequently seen in the case of a discharge with a positive <term>air-spark</term>, in which it is found that the <term>luminous column</term> is very slender and does not nearly fill the tube while the <term>air-spark</term> is small.

->C.—*On the <term>interference</term> of <term>intermittent discharges</term>.*<-

In making certain experiments with <term>intermittent discharges</term>, it happened that a discharge was sent through two tubes placed in series, but lying parallel to one another and at no great distance apart. It was observed that the discharge in one tube strongly affected the one in the other, and from this the authors were led to examine more closely the question of the <term>interference</term> of discharges which do not take place in the same tube.

For this purpose, <term>intermittent discharges</term> were sent through two parallel tubes in series, with the current passing sometimes in the same and sometimes in contrary directions through the two tubes. The two discharges were found to be greatly

On examining the nature of these effects, they seemed to follow the same law that would have prevailed if the tubes had formed one long tube that could be doubled up or bent so as to make one portion of it parallel to the other. This law is that the discharge in the portion of the tube nearer the <term>air-spark</term> tends to produce special effects on the further portion, and itself to manifest <term>relief-effects</term>. One remarkable result of this law deserves mention. When the <term>air-spark</term> is in the positive, the special effect is naturally accompanied by a <term>positive luminous discharge</term> from the inside of the glass. Accordingly, the tube through which the discharge passed last had <term>positive luminous discharge</term> throughout its entire length on the side where the other tube lay; thus, the whole luminosity in that tube appeared to be attracted toward the other discharge. This was the case whether the discharge passed in the same or opposite directions through the tubes, so that the remarkable phenomenon was presented of a <term>luminous discharge</term> (which we know behaves like a current) appearing to violently attract a discharge moving in the opposite direction. After the explanation given above, it will be understood that the phenomenon was not actually a case of two currents moving in opposite directions attracting one another, but was a case of the luminous effects of the interference of two <term>co-periodic discharges</term> through the medium of the <term>impulsive static induction</term> of the pulses that composed them.

When a discharge is an <term>intermittent discharge</term>, it can be made to pass through several tubes that are connected so as to offer alternative paths to the discharge. When this was done, it was found that these discharges affected each other either by apparent attraction or repulsion of the luminosity that accompanied them. The authors have not had time to investigate the subject further to ascertain the precise law in such cases, but they have no doubt that, upon examination, the effects could be explained by similar considerations to those found to hold in the previous case.

An extremely interesting experiment showing how <term>intermittent discharges</term> can be made to interfere in this way when they are <term>synchronous</term>, but not otherwise, was made by using two identical small coils to produce the discharges in two parallel tubes. When the <term>contact breakers</term> were made to work in unison, any effect the discharges produced on one another was steady, as would have been the case if their <term>co-periodicity</term> resulted from their being part of a single discharge, as in the previous cases. But when they were slightly out of unison, so that audible beats were produced in addition to the two notes made by the <term>contact breakers</term>, it was found that the luminosities in the tubes flickered (that is, were attracted or repelled) in synchronization with each such beat. The reason is obvious. It was only during the moments when the <term>contact breakers</term> were moving approximately in unison that the two <term>intermittent discharges</term> were sufficiently <term>synchronous</term> to interfere with one another.

# VII. *On Stresses in Rarefied Gases arising from Inequalities of Temperature.*
### *By* J. CLERK MAXWELL, *F.R.S., Professor of Experimental Physics in the University of Cambridge.*

->Received March 19—Read April 11, 1878.<-

1. In this paper, I have followed the method given in my paper "On the Dynamical Theory of Gases" (Phil. Trans., 1867, p. 49). I have shown that when temperature inequalities exist in a gas, the pressure at a given point is not the same in all directions. The difference between the maximum and minimum pressure at a point may be of considerable magnitude when the density of the gas is low enough, and when the temperature inequalities are produced by small* solid bodies at a higher or lower temperature than the vessel containing the gas.

2. The nature of this stress may be defined as follows: Let the distance from a given point, measured in a given direction, be denoted by $h$; then the space-variation of the temperature for a point moving along this line will be denoted by $\frac{d\theta}{dh}$, and the space-variation of this quantity along the same line by $\frac{d^2\theta}{dh^2}$.

There will, in general, be a particular direction of the line $h$ for which $\frac{d^2\theta}{dh^2}$ is a maximum, another for which it is a minimum, and a third for which it is a maximum-minimum. These three directions are at right angles to each other, and are the

---

<margin>
* The dimensions of the bodies must be of the same order of magnitude as a certain length $\lambda$, which may be defined as the distance traveled by a molecule with its mean velocity during the medium's time of relaxation.

The time of relaxation is the time in which stress inequalities would disappear if the rate at which they diminish were to continue constant. Hence
$$\lambda = 2 \left( \frac{2p}{\pi\rho} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{\mu}{p} = 2\mu \left( \frac{2}{\pi p \rho} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.$$

On the hypothesis that encounters between molecules resemble those between "rigid elastic" spheres, the free path of a molecule between two successive encounters has a definite meaning, and if $l$ is its mean value,
$$l = \frac{3}{2} \mu \left( \frac{\pi}{2p\rho} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{3\pi}{8} \lambda = 1 \cdot 178 \lambda.$$

So the mean path of a molecule may be taken as representing what we mean by "small."

If the force between the molecules is supposed to be a continuous function of the distance, a molecule's free path no longer has a definite meaning, and we must fall back on the quantity $\lambda$, as defined above.
</margin>

# PROFESSOR CLERK MAXWELL ON STRESSES IN RAREFIED

axes of principal stress at the given point; and the part of the stress arising from inequalities of temperature is, in each of these principal axes,

->$$3 \frac{\mu^2}{\rho \theta} \frac{d^2 \theta}{d h^2},$$<-

where $\mu$ is the coefficient of viscosity, $\rho$ is the density, and $\theta$ is the absolute temperature.

3. Now for dry air at $15^\circ$ C, $\mu = 1.9 \times 10^{-4}$ in centimeter-gram-second measure, and $\frac{3 \mu^2}{\rho \theta} = \frac{1}{p} 0.315$, where $p$ is the pressure, the unit of pressure being one dyne per square centimeter, or nearly one-millionth part of an atmosphere.

If a sphere $2a$ centimeters in diameter is T degrees Celsius hotter than the air at large distances from it, then, when there is a steady flow of heat, the temperature at a distance of $r$ centimeters from the center will be

->$$\theta = \theta_0 + \frac{\text{T}a}{r}, \text{ and } \frac{d^2 \theta}{d r^2} = \frac{2 \text{T}a}{r^3}.$$<-

Hence, at a distance of $r$ centimeters from the center of the sphere, the pressure in the direction of the radius arising from inequality of temperature will be $\frac{\text{T}a}{p r^3} 0.63$ dynes per square centimeter.

4. In Mr. <term>CROOKES</term>’ experiments the pressure, $p$, was often so small that this stress would be capable, if it existed alone, of producing rapid motion in a <term>radiometer</term>.

Indeed, if we were to consider only the normal part of the stress exerted on solid bodies immersed in the gas, most of the phenomena observed by Mr. <term>CROOKES</term> could be readily explained.

5. Let us take the case of two small bodies symmetrical with respect to the axis joining their centers of figure. If both bodies are warmer than the air at a distance from them, then, in any section perpendicular to the axis joining their centers, the point where it cuts this line will have the highest temperature, and there will be a flow of heat outward from this axis in all directions.

Hence $\frac{d^2 \theta}{d h^2}$ will be positive for the axis, and it will be a line of maximum pressure, so that the bodies will repel each other.

If both bodies are colder than the air at a distance, everything will be reversed; the axis will be a line of minimum pressure, and the bodies will attract each other.

If one body is hotter and the other colder than the air at a distance, the effect will be smaller, and it will depend on the relative sizes of the bodies and on their exact temperatures whether the action is attractive or repulsive.

6. If the bodies are two parallel disks very near to each other, the central parts will produce very little effect because, between the disks, the temperature varies uniformly, and $\frac{d^2 \theta}{d h^2} = 0$. Only near the edges will there be any stress arising from inequality of temperature in the gas.

7. If the bodies are encircled by a ring having its axis on the line joining the bodies, then the repulsion between the two bodies, when they are warmer than the air in general, may be converted into attraction by heating the ring so as to produce a flow of heat inwards toward the axis.

8. If a body in the form of a cup or bowl is warmer than the air, the distribution of temperature in the surrounding gas is similar to the distribution of electric potential near a body of the same form, which has been investigated by Sir W. <term>Thomson</term>. Near the convex surface the value of $\frac{d^2\theta}{dh^2}$ is nearly the same as if the body had been a complete sphere, namely $2T\frac{1}{a^2}$, where T is the excess of temperature, and $a$ is the radius of the sphere. Near the concave surface the variation of temperature is exceedingly small.

Hence the normal pressure will be greater on the convex surface than on the concave surface, and if we were to neglect the tangential pressures we might think this an explanation of the motion of Mr. <term>Crookes</term>’ cups.

Since the expressions for the stress are linear regarding the temperature, everything will be reversed when the cup is colder than the surrounding air.

9. In a spherical vessel, if the two polar regions are made hotter than the equatorial zone, the pressure in the direction of the axis will be greater than that parallel to the equatorial plane, and the reverse will be the case if the polar regions are made colder than the equatorial zone.

10. All such explanations of the observed phenomena must be subjected to careful criticism. They have been obtained by considering the normal stresses alone, to the exclusion of the tangential stresses, and it is much easier to give a simple explanation of the former than of the latter. If, however, we go on to calculate the forces acting on any portion of the gas by virtue of the stresses on its surface, we find that when the flow of heat is steady, these forces are in equilibrium. Mr. <term>Crookes</term> tells us that there is no molar current or wind in his radiometer vessels. It is not easy to prove this by experiment, but it is satisfactory to find that the system of stresses described here as arising from inequalities of temperature will not, when the flow of heat is steady, generate currents.

11. Consider, then, the case in which there are no currents of gas but a steady flow of heat, the condition of which is

->$\frac{d^2\theta}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dz^2} = 0.$<-

(In the absence of external forces such as gravity, and if the gas in contact with solid bodies does not slide over them, this is always a solution of the equations, and it is the only permanent solution.) In this case the equations of motion show that every particle of the gas is in equilibrium under the stresses acting on it. Hence, any finite portion of the gas is also in equilibrium; also, since the stresses are linear functions of
