the temperature, if we superimpose one system of temperatures on another, we also superimpose the corresponding systems of forces.

Now the system of temperatures due to a solid sphere of uniform temperature immersed in the gas cannot of itself give rise to any force tending to move the sphere in one direction rather than in another. Let the sphere be placed within the finite portion of gas which, as we have said, is already in equilibrium. The equilibrium will not be disturbed. We may introduce any number of spheres at different temperatures into the portion of gas, so as to form a body of any shape, heated in any manner, and when the flow of heat has become steady the whole system will be in equilibrium.

12. How, then, are we to account for the observed fact that forces act between solid bodies immersed in rarefied gases—and this, apparently, for as long as inequalities of temperature are maintained?

I think we must look for an explanation in the phenomenon discovered in the case of liquids by <term>HELMHOLTZ</term> and <term>PIOTROWSKI</term>,* and for gases by <term>KUNDT</term> and <term>WARBURG</term>,† that the fluid in contact with the surface of a solid must slide over it with a finite velocity in order to produce a finite tangential stress.

The theoretical treatment of the boundary conditions between a gas and a solid is difficult, and it becomes more difficult if we consider that the gas close to the surface is probably in an unknown state of condensation. We shall therefore accept the results obtained by <term>KUNDT</term> and <term>WARBURG</term> based on their experimental evidence.

They have found that the velocity of the gas sliding over the surface due to a given tangential stress varies inversely with the pressure.

The coefficient of sliding for air on glass was found to be G = $\frac{8}{p}$ centimeters, where $p$ is the pressure in millionths of an atmosphere. Hence, at ordinary pressures G is imperceptible, but in the vessels exhausted by Mr. <term>CROOKES</term> it may be considerable.

Hence, if close to the surface of a solid there is a tangential stress S acting on a surface parallel to that of the body in a direction $h$ parallel to that surface, there will also be a sliding of the gas in contact with the solid over its surface in the direction $h$ with a finite velocity = $\frac{\text{SG}}{\mu}$.

13. I have not attempted to enter into the calculation of the effect of this sliding motion, but it is easy to see that if we begin with the case in which there is no sliding, the immediate effect of allowing the gas to slide must be to diminish the action of all tangential stresses on the surface without affecting the normal stresses, and in the course of time to set up currents sweeping over the surfaces of solid bodies, thus completely destroying the simplicity of our first solution of the problem.

All that we know is that the more rarefied the gas and the smaller the vessel, the less the effect of the convection currents is, so that in Mr. <term>CROOKES’</term> experiments they play a very small part.

We now proceed to the calculations:—

### (1.) *Encounter between two Molecules.*

The motion of the two molecules after an encounter depends on their motion before the encounter and is capable of being determined by purely dynamical methods. If the encounter of the molecules does not cause rotation or vibration in the individual molecules, then the kinetic energy of the centers of mass of the two molecules must be the same after the encounter as it was before.

This will be true on average, even if the molecules are complex systems capable of rotation and internal vibration, provided the temperature is constant. If, however, the temperature is rising, the internal energy of the molecules is, on the whole, increasing; therefore, the energy of translation of their centers of mass must be, on average, diminishing at every encounter. The reverse will be the case if the temperature is falling.

But however important this consideration may be in the theory of specific heat and that of the conduction of heat, it has only a secondary bearing on the question of the stresses in the medium. Because it would introduce great complexity and much guesswork into our calculations, I shall suppose that the gas considered here is one whose molecules do not take up any significant amount of energy in the form of internal motion. <term>KUNDT</term> and <term>WARBURG</term>* have shown that this is the case with mercury gas.

Let the masses of the molecules be M$_1$ and M$_2$, and their velocity-components $\xi_1$, $\eta_1$, $\zeta_1$, and $\xi_2$, $\eta_2$, $\zeta_2$ respectively. Let V be the velocity of M$_1$ relative to M$_2$.

Before the encounter, let a straight line be drawn through M$_1$ parallel to V, and let a perpendicular $b$ be drawn from M$_2$ to this line. The magnitude and direction of $b$ and V will be constant as long as the motion is undisturbed.

During the encounter, the two molecules act on each other. If the force acts in the line joining their centers of mass, the product $b$V will remain constant, and if the force is a function of the distance, V and therefore $b$ will be of the same magnitude after the encounter as before it, but their directions will be turned in the plane of V and $b$ through an angle $2\theta$. This angle is a function of $b$ and V, which vanishes for values of $b$ greater than the limit of molecular action. Let the plane through V and $b$ make an angle $\phi$ with the plane through V parallel to $x$; then all values of $\phi$ are equally probable.

If $\xi_1'$ is the value of $\xi_1$ after the encounter,

From these, by the transformation of coordinates, we find:

$$\delta(\xi_1 \eta_1 + \xi_2 \eta_2) = - 3(\xi_2 - \xi_1)(\eta_2 - \eta_1) \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 \theta \text{ . . . . . . . . . . (5)}$$
$$\delta(\xi_1 \eta_1^2 + \xi_2 \eta_2^2) = - \frac{1}{2} [9(\xi_1 \eta_1^2 + \xi_2 \eta_2^2) - 3(\xi_1 \eta_2^2 + \xi_2 \eta_1^2)$$
$$- (\xi_1 + \xi_2)(6 \eta_1 \eta_2 + \text{V}^2)] \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 \theta \text{ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (6)}$$
$$\delta(\xi_1 \eta_1 \zeta_1 + \xi_2 \eta_2 \zeta_2) = - \frac{1}{2} [9(\xi_1 \eta_1 \zeta_1 + \xi_2 \eta_2 \zeta_2) - 3(\xi_1 \eta_1 \zeta_2 + \xi_1 \eta_2 \zeta_1 + \xi_1 \eta_2 \zeta_2 + \xi_2 \eta_1 \zeta_1$$
$$+ \xi_2 \eta_1 \zeta_2 + \xi_2 \eta_2 \zeta_1)] \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 \theta \text{ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (7)}$$

---

->[*Application of Spherical Harmonics to the Theory of Gases.*]<-

If we suppose the direction of the velocity of $\text{M}_1$ relative to $\text{M}_2$ to be indicated by the position of a point P on a sphere, which we may call the sphere of reference, then the direction of the relative velocity after the encounter will be indicated by a point P'. The angular distance PP' is $2\theta$, so that the point P' lies in a small circle, where every position is equally probable.

We must calculate the effect of an encounter upon certain functions of the six velocity-components of the two molecules. These six quantities may be expressed in terms of the three velocity-components of the center of mass of the two molecules (say $u, v, w$), the relative velocity of $\text{M}_1$ with respect to $\text{M}_2$ which we call V, and the two angular coordinates which indicate the direction of V. During the encounter, the quantities $u, v, w$, and V remain the same, but the angular coordinates are altered from those of P to those of P' on the sphere of reference.

Whatever the form of the function of $\xi_1, \eta_1, \zeta_1, \xi_2, \eta_2, \zeta_2$, we may consider it expressed as a series of spherical harmonics of the angular coordinates. Their coefficients are functions of $u, v, w$, and $\text{V}$, and we only have to determine the effect of the encounter upon the value of the spherical harmonics, because their coefficients do not change.

<summary>Maxwell derives mathematical formulas for the change in molecular velocity-components during encounters and proposes using spherical harmonics to analyze these interactions based on a center-of-mass coordinate system.</summary>
<keywords>James Clerk Maxwell, kinetic theory of gases, molecular encounter, spherical harmonics, velocity-components, center of mass, rarefied gases</keywords>

<header>GASES ARISING FROM INEQUALITIES OF TEMPERATURE.</header>

Let $Y^{(n)}$ be the value at $P$ of the surface harmonic of order $n$ in the series under consideration.

After an encounter, the corresponding term becomes what $Y^{(n)}$ becomes at the point $P'$. Since all positions of $P'$ in a circle centered at $P$ are equally probable, the average value of the function after the encounter must depend on the average value of the spherical harmonic in this circle.

Now, the average value of a spherical harmonic of order $n$ in a circle, where the cosine of the radius is $\mu$, is equal to the value of the harmonic at the pole of the circle multiplied by $P^{(n)}(\mu)$, the zonal harmonic of order $n$ and amplitude $\mu$.

Hence, after the encounter, $Y^{(n)}$ becomes $Y^{(n)}P^{(n)}(\mu)$. If $F_n$ is the corresponding part of the function to be considered, and $\delta F_n$ is the increment of $F_n$ resulting from the encounter, then $\delta F_n = F_n(P^{(n)}(\mu) - 1)$.

This is the average increment of $F_n$ resulting from an encounter in which $\cos 2\theta = \mu$. The rate of increment is found from this by multiplying it by the number of encounters each molecule undergoes per second in which $\mu$ lies between $\mu$ and $\mu + d\mu$, and integrating for all values of $\mu$ from $-1$ to $+1$.

In general, this operation requires knowledge of the law of force between the molecules, and also knowledge of the distribution of velocity among the molecules.

When, as in this investigation, we assume both molecules are of the same kind and take both molecules into account in the final summation, the spherical harmonics of odd orders will disappear. Thus, if we restrict our calculations to functions of no more than three dimensions, the effect of the encounters will depend on harmonics of the second order only, in which case $P^{(2)}(\mu) - 1 = \frac{3}{2}(\mu^2 - 1) = \frac{3}{2} \sin^2 2\theta$. <note>Note added May, 1879.</note>

### (2.) Number of Encounters per unit of Time.

We now leave the dynamical method and adopt the statistical method. Instead of tracing the path of a single molecule and determining the effects of each encounter on its velocity components and their combinations, we focus our attention on a specific element of volume. We trace the changes in the average values of such combinations of components for all the molecules that happen to be within it at a given instant. The problem now presented may be stated as follows: to determine the distribution of velocities among the molecules of any element of the medium, given the current velocity and the temperature of the medium in terms of the coordinates and time. The only case in which this problem has actually been solved is when the medium has reached its final state, in which the temperature is uniform and there are no currents.

Denoting by

-> $dN = f_1(\xi, \eta, \zeta, x, y, z, t)d\xi d\eta d\zeta dx dy dz$ <-

Regarding the number of molecules of type M$_1$ which, at a given instant, are within the element of volume $dxdydz$, and whose velocity components lie between the limits $\xi \pm \frac{1}{2}d\xi$, $\eta \pm \frac{1}{2}d\eta$, $\zeta \pm \frac{1}{2}d\zeta$, BOLTZMANN has shown that the function $f_1$ must satisfy the equation:

->$\frac{df_1}{dt} + \xi_1\frac{df_1}{dx} + \eta_1\frac{df_1}{dy} + \zeta_1\frac{df_1}{dz} + \text{X}\frac{df_1}{d\xi_1} + \text{Y}\frac{df_1}{d\eta_1} + \text{Z}\frac{df_1}{d\zeta_1} +$<-
->$+ \iiint d\xi_2 d\eta_2 d\zeta_2 \int bdb \int d\phi \text{V}(f_1 f_2 - f'_1 f'_2) = 0$ . . . . . (8)<-

where $f_2, f'_1, f'_2$ denote what $f$ becomes when, instead of the velocity components of M$_1$ before the encounter, we use those of M$_2$ before the encounter, and those of M$_1$ and M$_2$ after the encounter, respectively. The integration is extended to all values of $\phi$ and $b$, and of $\xi_2, \eta_2, \zeta_2$, the velocity components of the second molecule M$_2$.

In general, it is impossible to perform this integration without knowing not only the law of force between the molecules, but also the form of the functions $f_1, f_2,$ $f'_1, f'_2$, which must themselves be found by using the equation.

Therefore, the equation has so far been solved only for particular cases.

If the medium is surrounded by a surface through which no communication of energy can take place, then one solution of the equation is given by the conditions:

->$f_1 f_2 - f'_1 f'_2 = 0,$<-

and

->$\xi\frac{df}{dx} + \eta\frac{df}{dy} + \zeta\frac{df}{dz} + \text{X}\frac{df}{d\xi} + \text{Y}\frac{df}{d\eta} + \text{Z}\frac{df}{d\zeta} = 0,$<-

which give:

->$f_1 = \text{A}_1 e^{-h(2\psi_1 + \xi^2 + \eta^2 + \zeta^2)}$ . . . . . . . . . (9)<-

where $\psi_1$ is the potential of the force whose components are X$_1$, Y$_1$, Z$_1$, and A$_1$ is a constant that may be different for each kind of molecule in the medium, but $h$ is the same for all kinds of molecules.

This is the complete solution to this problem and is independent of any hypothesis regarding the manner in which the molecules act on each other during an encounter. The quantity $h$ that occurs in this expression may be determined by finding the mean value of $\xi^2$, which is $\frac{1}{2h}$. Now, in the kinetic theory of gases,

->$\rho\bar{\xi^2} = p = \text{R}\rho\theta$ . . . . . . . . . . (10)<-

where $p$ is the pressure, $\rho$ the density, $\theta$ the absolute temperature, and R a constant for a given gas. Hence:

->$\frac{1}{2h} = \text{R}\theta$ . . . . . . . . . . . (11)<-

We shall suppose, however, along with BOLTZMANN, that in a medium in which there are inequalities of temperature and of velocity

where F is a rational function of $\xi, \eta, \zeta$, which we will assume does not contain terms of more than three dimensions, and $f_0$ is the same function as in equation (9).

Now consider two groups of molecules, each defined by their velocity components, and let the two groups be distinguished by the subscripts $(_1)$ and $(_2)$. We must estimate the number of encounters of a specific kind between these two groups in a unit volume during the time $\delta t$, considering only those encounters for which the limits of $b$ and $\phi$ are $b \pm \frac{1}{2}db$ and $\phi \pm \frac{1}{2}d\phi$.

Let us first suppose that both groups consist of mere geometric points which do not interfere with each other's motion. The group $dN_1$ is moving through the group $dN_2$ with the relative velocity V, and we must find how many molecules of the first group approach a molecule of the second group in a manner which would, if the molecules acted on each other, produce an encounter of the given kind. This will be the case for every molecule of the first group which passes through the area $bdbd\phi$ in the time $\delta t$. The number of such molecules is $dN_1 \text{V} bdbd\phi \delta t$ for every molecule of the second group, so that the total number of pairs which pass each other within the given limits is

-> $\text{V} bdbd\phi d\text{N}_1 d\text{N}_2 \delta t$, <-

and if we take the time $\delta t$ as small enough, this will be the number of encounters of the real molecules in the time $\delta t$.

### (3.) Effect of the Encounters.

We have next to estimate the effect of these encounters on the average values of different functions of the velocity components. The effect of an individual encounter on these functions for the pair of molecules concerned is given in equations (3), (4), (5), (6), and (7), each of which is of the form

-> $\delta \text{P} = \text{Q} \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 \theta$ . . . . . . . . . (13) <-

where P and Q are functions of the velocity components of the two molecules. If we write $\overline{\text{P}}$ for the average value of P for the N molecules in a unit volume, then by taking the sum of the effects of the encounters—

-> $\Sigma \delta \text{P} = \text{N} \delta \overline{\text{P}}$ . . . . . . . . . . (14) <-

We thus find

-> $\frac{\delta \overline{\text{P}}}{\delta t} = \text{N} \int \! \! \int \! \! \int \! \! \int \! \! \int \! \! \int \text{Q} \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 \theta \text{V} bdbd\phi f_1 f_2 d\xi_1 d\eta_1 d\zeta_1 d\xi_2 d\eta_2 d\zeta_2$ . . . (15) <-

Now, since $\theta$ is a function of $b$ and V, the definite integral

-> $\text{V} \int_0^{2\pi} \! \! \int_0^\infty b \sin^2 \theta \cos^2 \theta db d\phi = \text{B}$ . . . . . . . (16) <-

will be a function of V only.

The experiments of <term>O. E. MEYER</term>,\* <term>KUNDT</term> and <term>WARBURG</term>,† <term>PULUJ</term>,‡ <term>Von OBERMAYER</term>,§ <term>EILHARD WIEDEMANN</term>,|| and <term>HOLMAN</term>,¶ show that the viscosity of air varies according to a lower power of the absolute temperature than the first power—probably the $0.77$ power. ->B=$\frac{p}{3\text{N}\mu}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . (19)<-

->$\frac{\delta\text{P}}{\delta t} = \frac{p}{3\mu} \iiiiiint \text{Q} f_1 f_2 d\xi_1 d\eta_1 d\zeta_1 d\xi_2 d\eta_2 d\zeta_2$ . . . . . . . . . . (20)<-

->$+ (2h)^{\frac{3}{2}} (\frac{1}{6}\alpha^3\xi^3 + \frac{1}{6}\beta^3\eta^3 + \frac{1}{6}\gamma^3\zeta^3 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha^2\beta\xi^2\eta + \frac{1}{2}\alpha^2\gamma\xi^2\zeta + \frac{1}{2}\beta^2\gamma\eta^2\zeta$<-
->$+ \frac{1}{2}\beta^2\alpha\eta^2\xi + \frac{1}{2}\gamma^2\alpha\zeta^2\xi + \frac{1}{2}\gamma^2\beta\zeta^2\eta + \alpha\beta\gamma\xi\eta\zeta)$ . . . . . . . . . . (22)<-

### (4.) *Mean Values of Combinations of $\xi, \eta, \zeta$.*

To find the mean value of any function of $\xi, \eta, \zeta$ for all the molecules in the element, we must multiply this function by $f$ and integrate with respect to $\xi, \eta$, and $\zeta$.

If the non-exponential factor of any term contains an odd power of any of the variables, the corresponding part of the integral will vanish. However, if it contains only even powers, each even power, such as $2n$, will introduce a factor

->R$^n \theta^n (2n-1)(2n-3) \dots 3 \cdot 1$<-

into the corresponding part of the integral.

First, let the function be 1; then

-> $1 = \iiint f \, d\xi \, d\eta \, d\zeta$ . . . . . . . . . . (23) <-

or

-> $1 = 1 + \frac{1}{2}(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2)$ . . . . . . . . . . (24) <-

which gives the condition

-> $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2 = 0$ . . . . . . . . . . (25) <-

Let us next find the mean value of $\xi$ in the same way, denoting the result with the symbol $\bar{\xi}$:

-> $\bar{\xi} = (R\theta)^{\frac{1}{2}} [\alpha + \frac{1}{2}(\alpha^3 + \alpha\beta^2 + \alpha\gamma^2)]$ . . . . . . . . . . (26) <-

Since in what follows we shall denote the velocity components of each molecule as $u+\xi, v+\eta, w+\zeta$, where $u, v, w$ are the velocity components of the center of mass of all the molecules within the element, it follows that the mean values of $\xi, \eta, \zeta$ are each zero. We thus obtain the equations:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} \alpha + \frac{1}{2}(\alpha^3 + \alpha\beta^2 + \alpha\gamma^2) &= 0 \\ \beta + \frac{1}{2}(\alpha^2\beta + \beta^3 + \beta\gamma) &= 0 \\ \gamma + \frac{1}{2}(\alpha^2\gamma + \beta^2\gamma + \gamma^3) &= 0 \end{aligned} \right\}$ . . . . . . . . . . (27) <-

Remembering these conditions, we find that the mean values of combinations of two, three, and four dimensions are of the forms:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} \bar{\xi^2} &= R\theta(1 + \alpha^2) \\ \bar{\xi\eta} &= R\theta\alpha\beta \end{aligned} \right\}$ . . . . . . . . . . (28) <-

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} \bar{\xi^3} &= (R\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}\alpha^3 \\ \bar{\xi\eta^2} &= (R\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}\alpha\beta^2 \\ \bar{\xi\eta\zeta} &= (R\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}\alpha\beta\gamma \end{aligned} \right\}$ . . . . . . . . . . (29) <-

### (6.) *Effect of External Forces.*

The only effect of external forces is expressed by equations of the form

->$\frac{\delta u}{\delta t} = \text{X} \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (36)$<-

The average values of $\xi$, $\eta$, $\zeta$ and their combinations are not affected by external forces.

### (7.) *Variation of Mean Values within an Element of Volume.*

We have used the symbol $\delta$ to denote the variation of any quantity within an element, arising either from encounters between molecules or from the action of external forces.

There is a third way, however, in which a variation may occur: namely, by molecules entering or leaving the element, carrying their properties with them.

We shall use the symbol $\mathfrak{d}$ to denote the actual variation within a specified element.

If MQ is the average value of any quantity for each molecule within the element, then the quantity per unit of volume is $\rho\text{Q}$. We must trace the variation of $\rho\text{Q}$.

We begin with an element of volume moving with the velocity-components U, V, W; then, by the ordinary investigation of the "equation of continuity,"

->$\frac{\mathfrak{d}}{\delta t}[\rho\text{Q}] + \frac{d}{dx}[\text{Q}(u + \xi - \text{U})] + \frac{d}{dy}[\text{Q}(v + \eta - \text{V})] + \frac{d}{dz}[\text{Q}(w + \zeta - \text{W})] = \rho\frac{\delta}{\delta t}\text{Q} \quad . \quad (37)$<-

If after performing the differentiations we make $\text{U} = u$, $\text{V} = v$, $\text{W} = w$, the equation for an element moving with the velocity $(u, v, w)$ becomes:

### (8.) *Equation of Density.*

Let us first set Q=1; then, since the mass of a molecule is constant, the equation becomes
$$\frac{\delta \rho}{\delta t} + \rho \left( \frac{du}{dx} + \frac{dv}{dy} + \frac{dw}{dz} \right) = 0 . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (39)$$
which is the standard "equation of continuity."
Eliminating the second term of the general equation (38) by means of this equation, we obtain the more convenient form—
$$\rho \frac{\delta Q}{\delta t} + \frac{d}{dx}(\rho Q \xi) + \frac{d}{dy}(\rho Q \eta) + \frac{d}{dz}(\rho Q \zeta) = \rho \frac{\delta Q}{\delta t} . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (40)$$

### (9.) *Equations of Motion.*

Setting Q=$u+\xi$, this equation becomes
$$\rho \frac{\delta u}{\delta t} + \frac{d}{dx}(\rho \xi^2) + \frac{d}{dy}(\rho \xi \eta) + \frac{d}{dz}(\rho \xi \zeta) = \rho X . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (41)$$
where any combination of the symbols $\xi, \eta, \zeta$ represents the average value of that combination.
Substituting their values as given in (28):
$$\rho \frac{\delta u}{\delta t} + R \frac{d}{dx}(\rho \theta) + R \left[ \frac{d}{dx}(\rho \theta \alpha^2) + \frac{d}{dy}(\rho \theta \alpha \beta) + \frac{d}{dz}(\rho \theta \alpha \gamma) \right] = \rho X . \quad . \quad . \quad (42)$$
which is one of the three standard equations of motion for a medium in which stresses exist.

### (13.) *Equation of Temperature.*

Adding the three equations of the form (44), and omitting terms containing small quantities of two dimensions, as well as products of differential coefficients such as $\frac{d\mu}{dx}\frac{d\theta}{dx}$, we find:

$$\frac{\delta\theta}{\delta t} = \frac{5}{2}\frac{\mu}{\rho}\left(\frac{d^2\theta}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dz^2}\right) + \frac{2}{3}\frac{\theta}{\rho}\frac{\delta\rho}{\delta t} \text{ . . . . . . . (52)}$$

We must remember that the gas considered here is one for which the ratio of the specific heats is 1.66.

### (14.) *Stresses in the Gas.*

Subtracting one-third of the sum of the three equations from (44), we obtain

-> $p\alpha^2 = -2\mu\frac{du}{dx} + \frac{2}{3}\mu\left(\frac{du}{dx} + \frac{dv}{dy} + \frac{dw}{dz}\right) + 3\frac{\mu^2}{\rho\theta}\frac{d^2\theta}{dx^2} + \frac{3}{2}\frac{\mu^2}{\rho\theta}\left(\frac{d^2\theta}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dz^2}\right) \dots$ (53) <-

This equation gives the excess of the normal pressure in $x$ above the mean hydrostatic pressure $p$. The first two terms of the second side represent the effect of viscosity in a moving fluid, and are identical to those given by Professor <term>Stokes</term> (Cambridge Transactions, vol. viii., 1845, p. 297). The last two terms represent the part of the stress that arises from inequality of temperature, which is the special subject of this paper.

There are two other equations of similar form for the normal stresses in $y$ and $z$.
The tangential stress in the plane $xy$ is given by the equation

-> $p\alpha\beta = -\mu\left(\frac{du}{dy} + \frac{dv}{dx}\right) + 3\frac{\mu^2}{\rho\theta}\frac{d^2\theta}{dxdy} \dots \dots \dots \dots$ (54) <-

There are two other equations of similar form for the tangential stresses in the planes of $yz$ and $zx$.

-> $p' = p + \frac{1}{3}\mu\left(\frac{du}{dx} + \frac{dv}{dy} + \frac{dw}{dz}\right) + \frac{9}{2}\frac{\mu^2}{\rho\theta}\left(\frac{d^2\theta}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2\theta}{dz^2}\right) \dots$ (56) <-

<meta>This page continues the analysis of gas motion equations, specifically addressing the conditions for equilibrium and steady motion when external forces are absent and considering the effects of gas slipping against solid surfaces.</meta>

<header>PROFESSOR CLERK MAXWELL ON STRESSES IN RAREFIED</header>

If there are no external forces such as gravity, then one solution of the equations is

->$u=v=w=0, p'=\text{constant},$<-

and if the boundary conditions are such that this solution is consistent with them, it will become the actual solution as soon as the initial motions, if any exist, have subsided. This will be the case if no slipping is possible between the gas and solid bodies in contact with it.

But if such slipping is possible, then wherever in the above solution there is a tangential stress in the gas at the surface of a solid or liquid, there cannot be equilibrium; instead, the gas will begin to slide over the surface until the velocity of sliding has produced a frictional resistance equal and opposite to the tangential stress. When this is the case, the motion may become steady. I have not, however, attempted to calculate the state of steady motion.

<note>I have recently applied the method of spherical harmonics, as described in the notes to sections (1) and (5), to carrying the approximations two orders higher. I expected that this would have involved the calculation of two new quantities—namely, the rates of decay of spherical harmonics of the fourth and sixth orders—but I found that, to the order of approximation required, all harmonics of the fourth and sixth orders may be neglected. Thus, the rate of decay of harmonics of the second order, the time-modulus of which is $\mu \div p$, determines the rate of decay of all functions of fewer than 6 dimensions.

The equations of motion, as given here (equation 55), contain the second derivatives of $u, v, w$ with respect to the coordinates, with the coefficient $\mu$. I find that in the more approximate expression, there is a term containing the fourth derivatives of $u, v, w$ with the coefficient $\mu^3 \div \rho p$.

The equations of motion also contain the third derivatives of $\theta$ with the coefficient $\mu^2 \div \rho \theta$. Besides these terms, there is another set consisting of the fifth derivatives of $\theta$ with the coefficient $\mu^4 \div \rho^2 p \theta$.

It appears from the investigation that the condition for the successful use of this method of approximation is that $l \frac{d}{dh}$ should be small, where $\frac{d}{dh}$ denotes differentiation with respect to a line drawn in any direction. In other words, the properties of the medium must not be significantly different at points within a distance of each other that is comparable with the "mean free path" of a molecule.—Note added June, 1879.</note>

### APPENDIX.

->(Added May, 1879.)<-

In the paper as submitted to the Royal Society, I made no attempt to express the conditions that must be satisfied by a gas in contact with a solid body; I thought it very unlikely that any equations I could write down would be a satisfactory representation of the actual conditions, especially as it is almost certain that the layer of gas nearest to a solid body is in a very different state from the rest of the gas.

One of the referees, however, pointed out that it was desirable to make the attempt and indicated several hypothetical forms of surfaces which might be tried. I have therefore added the following calculations, which are carried to the same degree of approximation as those for the interior of the gas.

It will be seen that the equations I have reached express both the fact that the gas may slide over the surface with a finite velocity—the previous investigations of which have already been mentioned\*—and the fact that this velocity and the corresponding tangential stress are affected by temperature inequalities at the surface of the solid, which give rise to a force tending to make the gas slide along the surface from colder to hotter places.

This phenomenon, to which Professor <term>Osborne Reynolds</term> has given the name <term>Thermal Transpiration</term>, was discovered entirely by him. He was the first to point out that a phenomenon of this kind was a necessary consequence of the <term>Kinetic Theory of Gases</term>, and he also subjected certain actual phenomena, of a somewhat different kind indeed, to measurement, and analyzed his measurements by a method admirably adapted to throw light on the relations between gases and solids.

It was not until after I had read Professor <term>Reynolds</term>’ paper that I began to reconsider the surface conditions of a gas, so that what I have done is simply to extend to the surface phenomena the method which I think most suitable for treating the interior of the gas. I think that this method is, in some respects, better than that adopted by Professor <term>Reynolds</term>, while I admit that his method is sufficient to establish the existence of the phenomena, though not to provide an estimate of their magnitude.

The method which I have adopted throughout is a purely statistical one. It considers the mean values of certain functions of the velocities within a given element of the medium, but it never attempts to trace the motion of a molecule, not even so far as to estimate the length of its mean path. Hence all the equations are expressed in the forms of differential calculus, in which the phenomena at a given place are connected with the spatial variations of certain quantities at that place, but in which no quantity appears which explicitly involves the condition of things at a finite distance from that place.

The particular functions of the velocities which are here considered are those of one, two, and three dimensions. These are sufficient to determine approximately the prin-

->*On the Conditions to be Satisfied by a Gas at the Surface of a Solid Body.*<-

As a first hypothesis, let us suppose the surface of the body to be a perfectly elastic, smooth, fixed surface, having the apparent shape of the solid, without any minute asperities.

In this case, every molecule which strikes the surface will have the normal component of its velocity reversed, while the other components will not be altered by impact.

The rebounding molecules will therefore move as if they had come from an imaginary portion of gas occupying the space really filled by the solid, such that the motion of every molecule close to the surface is the optical reflection in that surface of the motion of a molecule of the real gas.

In this case, we may speak of the rebounding molecules close to the surface as constituting the *reflected gas*. All directed properties of the incident gas are reflected, or, as Professor <term>LISTING</term> might say, *perverted* in the reflected gas; that is to say, the properties of the incident and the reflected gas are symmetrical with respect to the tangent plane of the surface.

The incident and reflected gas together constitute the actual gas close to the surface. The actual gas, therefore, cannot exert any stress on the surface, except in the direction of the normal, for the oblique components of stress in the incident and reflected gas will destroy one another.

Since gases can actually exert oblique stress against real surfaces, such surfaces cannot be represented as perfectly reflecting surfaces.

If a molecule, whose velocity is given in direction and magnitude, but whose line of motion is not given in position, strikes a fixed elastic sphere, its velocity after rebound may with equal probability be in any direction.

Consider, therefore, a stratum in which fixed elastic spheres are placed so far apart from one another that no one sphere is to any significant extent protected by any other sphere from the impact of molecules, and let the stratum be so deep that no molecule can pass through it without striking one or more of the spheres, and let this stratum of fixed spheres be spread over the surface of the solid we have been considering; then every molecule which comes from the gas toward the surface must strike one or more of the spheres, after which all directions of its velocity become equally probable.

When, at last, it leaves the stratum of spheres and returns into the gas, its velocity

<meta>This page continues the appendix where Maxwell examines the behavior of gas molecules at the surface of a solid, transitioning from a model of perfect reflection to a more realistic model involving "absorbed and evaporated gas" caused by surface irregularities.</meta>

<page-num>251</page-num>
<header>GASES ARISING FROM INEQUALITIES OF TEMPERATURE.</header>
<sig>2 K 2</sig>

must of course be *away from* the surface, but the probability of any particular magnitude and direction of the velocity will be the same as in a gas at rest relative to the surface.

The distribution of velocity among the molecules leaving the surface will therefore be the same as if, instead of the solid, there were a portion of gas at rest, having the temperature of the solid and a density such that the number of molecules passing from it through the surface in a given time is equal to the number of molecules of the real gas outside that strike the surface.

To distinguish the molecules which, after being entangled in the layer of spheres, later return into the surrounding gas, we shall call them, collectively, the *absorbed and evaporated gas*.

If the spheres are so close together that a significant part of the surface of each sphere in the outer layer is shielded from the direct impact of the incoming molecules by the spheres lying next to it, then if we call the point of each sphere furthest from the solid the *pole* of the sphere, a greater proportion of molecules will strike any one of the outer layer of spheres near its pole than near its equator. Furthermore, the greater the angle of incidence of the molecule, the greater the probability that it will strike a sphere near its pole.

The direction of the rebounding molecule will no longer have an equal probability in all directions; instead, there will be a greater probability of the tangential part of its velocity being in the direction of the motion before impact, and of its normal part being opposite to the normal part before impact.

The condition of the molecules leaving the surface will therefore be intermediate between that of evaporated gas and that of reflected gas, approaching most closely to evaporated gas at normal incidence and most closely to reflected gas at grazing incidence.

If the spheres, instead of being hard elastic bodies, are supposed to act on the molecules at finite though small distances, and if they are so close together that their spheres of action intersect, then the gas leaving the surface will be even more like reflected gas and less like evaporated gas.

We might also consider a surface with a great number of minute <term>asperities</term> <note>roughnesses or irregularities on a surface</note> of any given form; however, since in this case there is considerable difficulty in calculating the effect when the direction of rebound from the first impact leads to a second or third impact, I have preferred to treat the surface as something intermediate between a perfectly reflecting and a perfectly absorbing surface. In particular, I suppose that for every unit of area, a portion $f$ absorbs all the incident molecules and afterwards allows them to evaporate with velocities corresponding to those in still gas at the temperature of the solid, while a portion $1-f$ perfectly reflects all the molecules incident upon it.

We shall begin by supposing that the surface is the plane $y$ $z$, and that the gas is on that side of it where $x$ is positive.

<summary>Maxwell describes how gas molecules interact with a solid surface, proposing a model where a fraction of molecules are absorbed and re-evaporated while the remainder are reflected. He explains that surface irregularities, or asperities, cause the velocity distribution of leaving molecules to be intermediate between perfect reflection and thermal evaporation.</summary>

<header>PROFESSOR CLERK MAXWELL ON STRESSES IN RAREFIED</header>

The incident molecules are those which, close to the surface, have a negative normal component of velocity. We shall distinguish these molecules by the suffix $(_1)$. For these, and only these, $\xi_1$ is negative.

The rebounding molecules are those which have a positive $\xi$. We shall distinguish them by the suffix $(_2)$. Those which are evaporated will be further distinguished by an accent.

Symbols without any mark refer to the whole gas—incident, reflected, and evaporated—close to the surface.

The quantity of gas which is incident on a unit of surface in a unit of time is $-\rho_1 \xi_1$.

Of this quantity, the fraction $1-f$ is reflected, so that the sign of $\xi$ is reversed, and the fraction $f$ is evaporated. The mean value of $\xi$ in evaporated gas is $\xi'$, where the accent distinguishes symbols belonging to unpolarized gas at rest relative to the surface and having the temperature, $\theta'$, of the solid.

Equating the quantity of gas which is incident on the absorbing part of the surface to that which is evaporated from it, we have

-> $f \rho_1 \xi_1 + f \rho_2' \xi_2' = 0$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (60) <-

Equating the total quantity of gas which leaves the surface to the reflected and evaporated portions, we have

-> $\rho_2 \xi_2 = (f-1) \rho_1 \xi_1 + f \rho_2' \xi_2'$ . . . . . . . . . . (61) <-

If we next consider the momentum of the molecules in the direction of $y$, the momentum of the incident molecules is $\rho_1 \xi_1 \eta_1$. A fraction $(1-f)$ of this is reflected and becomes $(1-f) \rho_1 \xi_1 \eta_1$, and a fraction $f$ of it is absorbed and then evaporated, with the mean value of $\eta$ now being $-v$—namely, the velocity of the surface relative to the gas in contact with it.

The momentum of the evaporated portion in the direction of $y$ is therefore $-f \rho_2' \xi_2' v$, and this, together with the reflected portion, makes up the total momentum which is leaving the surface, or

-> $\rho_2 \xi_2 \eta_2 = (f-1) \rho_1 \xi_1 \eta_1 - f \rho_2' \xi_2' v$ . . . . . . . . . (62) <-

Eliminating $f \rho_2' \xi_2'$ between equations (61) and (62), we get

-> $(1-f) \rho_1 \xi_1 \eta_1 + \rho_2 \xi_2 \eta_2 + v [(1-f) \rho_1 \xi_1 + \rho_2 \xi_2] = 0$ . . . . . (63) <-

The values of functions of $\xi, \eta$, and $\zeta$ for the incident molecules are to be found by multiplying the expression in equation (22) by the given function and integrating with respect to $\xi$ between the limits $-\infty$ and $0$, and with respect to $\eta$ and $\zeta$ between the limits $\pm \infty$.

The values of the same functions for the molecules which are leaving the surface are to be found by integrating with respect to $\xi$ from $0$ to $\infty$.

We must remember, however, that since there is an essential discontinuity in the

<summary>Maxwell establishes the mathematical framework for calculating the movement and momentum of gas molecules as they strike and leave a solid surface. He derives equations to balance the quantity and momentum of incident, reflected, and evaporated gas molecules.</summary>

<page-num>253</page-num>
<header>GASES ARISING FROM INEQUALITIES OF TEMPERATURE.</header>

Regarding the conditions of the gas at the surface, the expression in equation (22) is a much less accurate approximation of the actual distribution of velocities in the gas close to the surface than it is in the interior of the gas. Therefore, we must consider the surface conditions we arrive at in this way to be subject to significant corrections once we discover more powerful methods of approaching the problem.

For the present, however, we consider only terms of three dimensions or less, and we find:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} \rho_1 \xi_1 = -\rho(2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(R\theta)^{\frac{1}{2}}(1 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha^2) \\ \rho_2 \xi_2 = \phantom{-}\rho(2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(R\theta)^{\frac{1}{2}}(1 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha^2) \end{aligned} \right\} \text{ . . . . . . . (64)}$$

$$\left. \begin{aligned} \rho_1 \xi_1 \eta_1 = \frac{1}{2} \rho R \theta \alpha \beta - \frac{1}{2} \rho (2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}} R \theta \alpha^2 \beta \\ \rho_2 \xi_2 \eta_2 = \frac{1}{2} \rho R \theta \alpha \beta + \frac{1}{2} \rho (2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}} R \theta \alpha^2 \beta \end{aligned} \right\} \text{ . . . . . . . (65)}$$

By substituting these expressions into equation (63) and neglecting $\alpha^2$ in comparison with one, we find:

$$(2 - f) \rho R \theta \alpha \beta + f(2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \rho R \theta \alpha^2 \beta + 2f(2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}} (1 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha^2) (R\theta)^{\frac{1}{2}} \rho v = 0 \text{ . . . (66)}$$

If we define

$$\text{G} = \frac{1}{2} \mu (2\pi)^{\frac{1}{2}} (p\rho)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \left( \frac{2}{f} - 1 \right) \text{ . . . . . . . . . . . (67)}$$

and substitute the values for $\alpha \beta$ and $\alpha^2 \beta$ as given in equations (54) and (51), and then divide by $2(p\rho)^{\frac{1}{2}}$, equation (66) becomes:

$$v - \text{G} \left( \frac{dv}{dx} - \frac{3}{2} \frac{\mu}{\rho \theta} \frac{d^2\theta}{dx dy} \right) - \frac{3}{4} \frac{\mu}{\rho \theta} \frac{d\theta}{dy} = 0 \text{ . . . . . . . . . . (68)}$$

If there is no temperature difference, this equation reduces to:

$$v = \text{G} \frac{dv}{dx} \text{ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . (69)}$$

Therefore, if the gas at a finite distance from the surface moves parallel to it, the gas in contact with the surface will slide over it with a finite velocity $v$. The movement of the gas will be almost the same as if a layer of depth G had been removed from the solid and replaced with gas, so that no slipping occurs between the new solid surface and the gas in contact with it.

The coefficient G was introduced by Helmholtz and Piotrowski as the *Gleitungs-coefficient*, or coefficient of slipping. The dimensions of G are those of a length, and its ratio to $l$, the mean free path of a molecule, is given by the equation:

$$\text{G} = \frac{2}{3} \left( \frac{2}{f} - 1 \right) l \text{ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . (70)}$$

Kundt and Warburg found that for air in contact with glass, G = $2l$, from which we find $f = \frac{1}{2}$; this means the surface acts as if it were half perfectly reflecting and half perfectly absorbent. If it were entirely absorbent, G would equal $\frac{2}{3}l$.

<summary>This page derives the "coefficient of slipping" (G), explaining how gas slides over a solid surface rather than remaining stationary at the boundary. It concludes by showing that experimental data suggests glass surfaces act as a mix of reflective and absorbent interfaces for air molecules.</summary>

# PROFESSOR CLERK MAXWELL ON STRESSES IN RAREFIED GASES

It is easy to write down the surface conditions for a surface of any shape. Let the direction-cosines of the normal $\nu$ be $l, m, n$, and let us write

$$\frac{d}{d\nu} \text{ for } l \frac{d}{dx} + m \frac{d}{dy} + n \frac{d}{dz}.$$

We then find as the surface conditions

$$\left. \begin{aligned} u - G \frac{d}{d\nu} [(1 - l^2) \ u - \ lmv - lnw] + \frac{3}{4} \frac{\mu}{\rho \theta} \left( \frac{d}{dx} - l \frac{d}{d\nu} \right) \left( \theta + 4G \frac{d\theta}{d\nu} \right) = 0 \\ v - G \frac{d}{d\nu} [(1 - m^2) v - mnw - mln] + \frac{3}{4} \frac{\mu}{\rho \theta} \left( \frac{d}{dy} - m \frac{d}{d\nu} \right) \left( \theta + 4G \frac{d\theta}{d\nu} \right) = 0 \\ w - G \frac{d}{d\nu} [(1 - n^2) w - \ nlu - nmv] + \frac{3}{4} \frac{\mu}{\rho \theta} \left( \frac{d}{dz} - n \frac{d}{d\nu} \right) \left( \theta + 4G \frac{d\theta}{d\nu} \right) = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \quad . \quad . \quad (71)$$

In each of these equations, the first term is one of the velocity components of the gas in contact with the surface, which is assumed to be fixed. The second term depends on the slipping of the gas over the surface, and the third term indicates the effect of temperature differences in the gas close to the surface; it shows that, in general, there will be a force driving the gas from colder to hotter parts of the surface.

As an illustration, let us take the case of a <term>capillary tube</term> with a circular cross-section. For the sake of simple calculation, we shall assume that the motion is so slow and the temperature varies so gradually along the tube that we may consider the temperature to be uniform throughout any single cross-section of the tube.

Taking the axis of the tube as the $z$-axis, we have the condition for <term>steady motion</term> parallel to the axis:

$$\frac{dp}{dz} - \mu \left( \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} \right) \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (72)$$

Since everything is symmetrical about the axis, if we write $r^2$ for $x^2 + y^2$, we find the solution of this equation is:

$$w = \text{A} + \frac{1}{4\mu} \frac{dp}{dz} r^2 \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (73)$$

If $Q$ denotes the quantity of gas which passes through a section of the tube per unit of time:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Q} &= 2\pi \int \rho w r dr \\ &= \pi \rho a^2 \left( \text{A} + \frac{1}{8\mu} \frac{dp}{dz} a^2 \right) \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (74) \end{aligned}$$

At the inner surface of the tube, we have $r = a$, and:

$$\begin{aligned} w &= \text{A} + \frac{1}{4\mu} \frac{dp}{dz} a^2 \\ &= \frac{\text{Q}}{\pi \rho a^2} + \frac{1}{8\mu} \frac{dp}{dz} a^2 \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad . \quad (75) \end{aligned}$$

also
->$\frac{dw}{dv} = - \frac{1}{2\mu} \frac{dp}{dz} a$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . (76)<-

The last of equations (71) may therefore be written
->$\frac{Q}{\pi \rho a^2} + \frac{1}{8\mu} (a^2 + 4Ga) \frac{dp}{dz} - \frac{3}{4} \frac{\mu}{\rho \theta} \frac{d\theta}{dz} = 0$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . (77)<-

Equation (77) provides the relationship between the quantity of gas passing through any section of the tube, the rate of pressure variation, and the rate of temperature variation along the axis of the tube.

If the pressure is uniform, there will be a flow of gas from the colder to the hotter end of the tube. Conversely, if there is no flow of gas, the pressure will increase from the colder to the hotter end of the tube.

Professor <term>OSBORNE REYNOLDS</term> identified these effects of temperature variation in a tube as a result of the <term>Kinetic Theory of Gases</term>. He gave this phenomenon the name <term>Thermal Transpiration</term>, a term chosen to be strictly analogous to <term>GRAHAM</term>'s use of the word <term>Transpiration</term>.

However, the phenomenon actually observed by Professor <term>REYNOLDS</term> in his experiments was the passage of gas through a porous plate rather than a capillary tube. As <term>GRAHAM</term> demonstrated, the passage of gases through porous plates is of an entirely different nature than the passage of gases through capillary tubes; it is more closely analogous to the flow of a gas through a small hole in a thin plate.

When the diameter of the hole and the thickness of the plate are both small compared to the length of a molecule's mean free path, then—as Sir <term>WILLIAM THOMSON</term> has shown—any molecule approaching the hole from either side is in very little danger of colliding with another molecule before it has passed completely through to the other side.

Consequently, the flow of gas in either direction through the hole occurs almost exactly as if there were a vacuum on the other side of the hole, regardless of whether the gas on the other side is of the same or a different kind.

If the gas on the two sides of the plate is of the same kind but at different temperatures, a phenomenon occurs which we may call *thermal effusion*.

Molecular velocity is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature, and the quantity of gas passing through the hole is proportional to both this velocity and the density. Therefore, more molecules will pass through the hole from whichever side has the greater product of density and the square root of temperature. This will continue until this product is equal on both sides of the hole. Thus, the condition for equilibrium is that the density must be inversely proportional to the square root of the temperature. Since pressure is the product of density and temperature, the pressure will be directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature.

<summary>Maxwell explains the relationship between temperature gradients and gas flow, distinguishing between thermal transpiration in tubes and thermal effusion through porous plates. He concludes that for gas in equilibrium across a small aperture, pressure is directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature.</summary>

<header>PROFESSOR CLERK MAXWELL ON STRESSES IN RAREFIED GASES.</header>

The theory of thermal effusion through a small hole in a thin plate is therefore very simple. It does not involve the theory of viscosity at all.

The finer the pores of a porous plate and the more rarefied the gas that effuses through it, the more closely the passage of gas through the plate corresponds to what we have called effusion, and the less it depends on the viscosity of the gas.

The coarser the pores of the plate and the denser the gas, the further the phenomenon departs from simple effusion, and the more closely it approaches transpiration through a capillary tube, which depends entirely on viscosity.

To return to the case of transpiration through a capillary tube: when the temperature is uniform,
->Q = $-\frac{\pi \rho a^4}{8 \mu} \frac{dp}{dz} (1 + 4 \frac{G}{a})$ . . . . . . . . . . (78)<-

Through experiments on glass capillary tubes, MM. <term>KUNDT</term> and <term>WARBURG</term> found* the value of G for air at different pressures and at temperatures from 17° C to 27° C to be:
->G = $\frac{8}{p}$ centimeters . . . . . . . . . . . (79)<-

where $p$ is the pressure in dynes per square centimeter, which is nearly the same as in millionths of an atmosphere. For hydrogen on glass:
->G = $\frac{15}{p}$ centimeters . . . . . . . . . . . (80)<-

* When there is no gas flow in a tube where the temperature varies from one end to the other, the pressure is greater at the hot end than at the cold end. Setting Q = 0, we have:
->$\frac{dp}{d\theta} = 6 \frac{\mu^2}{\rho \theta} \frac{1}{a^2 + 4Ga}$ . . . . . . . . . . . (81)<-

The quantity $6 \frac{\mu^2}{\rho \theta}$ is exactly double that calculated in section (3) of the introduction; in C.G.S. measure, it is $0.63 \div p$ for dry air at 15° C. Let us suppose $a = 0.01$ centimeter and the pressure is 40 millimeters of mercury; then G = $0.00016$ centimeter.

If one end of the tube is kept at 0° C and the other at 100° C, the pressure at the hot end will exceed the pressure at the cold end by about 1.2 millionths of an atmosphere.

This difference in pressure might be increased by using a tube with a smaller bore and less dense air, but the effect is so small that, although the theoretical proof of its existence seems satisfactory, verifying it experimentally would be difficult.

# VIII. Researches on the Action of Organic Substances on the Ultra-violet Rays of the Spectrum.

->By W. N. HARTLEY, *F. Inst. Chem., F.R.S.E., F.C.S., Demonstrator of Chemistry, King's College, London*; and A. K. HUNTINGTON, *F. Inst. Chem., A.R.S.M., F.C.S.*<-

->Communicated by Professor G. G. STOKES, *Sec. R.S.*<-

->Received October 10, 1878—Read January 9, 1879.<-

->[PLATES 21-34.]<-

->PART I.<-

### Method of Experimenting.—Examination of Alcohols and Fatty Acids.

In the year 1863, the late Dr. W. A. Miller described his method of examining the <term>diactinic</term> <note>transparent to ultraviolet light</note> properties of various saline solutions and organic substances. (MILLER, "On the Photographic Transparency of Various Bodies, etc.," Phil. Trans., 1863, I.)

He found that the spectrum transmitted by lenses and prisms of rock-crystal was far superior in length, as determined by sensitive photographic plates, to that obtained when lenses and prisms of glass and other materials were employed. He found particularly that the spectrum produced by passing electric sparks between silver points was very rich in photographic rays, and he ascertained how far various substances were transparent to these rays. Professor Stokes at the same time communicated results he had obtained when studying the long spectrum of the electric light by receiving the rays on a fluorescent screen. (STOKES, "On the Long Spectrum of Electric Light," Phil. Trans., 1863, I.) He discovered the fact that certain solutions showed light and dark bands which were otherwise invisible. More recently, M. Soret has studied the absorption of the ultra-violet rays of the spectrum transmitted by various substances, using for the purpose a spectroscope of his invention, which has a fluorescent eyepiece. (SORET, "Researches on the Absorption of Ultra-violet Rays by various substances," *Archives des Sciences Physiques et Naturelles*; Geneva, January, 1878.) In 1872, the apparatus of Dr. Miller was reconstructed by one of us, and certain improvements were introduced. The intention of repeating his experiments and carrying them out in a more complete manner was prompted by a desire to know what relation, if any, exists between the molecular constitution and the actinic absorption of organic substances. No encouragement to pursue this line of research was offered by the results of Dr. Miller, since he states, "I have not been

Thus, water was found to be perfectly diactinic, and ethyl alcohol more so than methyl alcohol, though less so than water. Since all the physical properties of organic substances depend on their molecular constitution, it is very probable that the photographic transparency of a substance is a delicate test of its purity; and despite the care taken in the purification of specimens, some of the experiments of Dr. <term>MILLER</term> were likely made with impure substances. In the face of this difficulty, it was thought that by observing a large number of bodies of similar constitution—many of which would be metameric substances, such as the ethereal salts of the organic acids, and homologous series of the normal alcohols and acids—evidence might be found regarding the influence of impurities and the variations in the absorption of the invisible rays caused by each increment of CH₂ in the molecule. Since, according to the research of <term>MILLER</term>, the physical state of a substance does not generally affect its absorptive power, we may avoid the difficulty of making observations on equal volumes of organic substances in a state of vapor. Instead, we can easily arrive at the maximum absorption due to a molecule of a substance by taking into account its specific volume in the liquid state and by making the thickness of the layer of liquid experimented on proportional to its specific volume, or by dissolving molecular weights of substances in solvents of known transparency.

->*The Method of Experimenting.*<-

After spending a considerable amount of time trialing the various methods of studying ultraviolet rays, the photographic method appeared to be decidedly the most satisfactory.

Rays which are very indistinct, or even quite invisible on any fluorescent screen, may be brought out clearly on a properly prepared photographic plate. It is useful, however, to have a focusing screen of uranium glass in the camera, or—what serves the purpose equally well—a glass plate coated with gelatin in which some esculin has been dissolved. To observe the spectrum by reflected light and view the visible and invisible rays simultaneously, a piece of paper soaked in a solution of esculin to which a little ammonia has been added may be used; it works even when dry.

The instruments employed were the following: 1st. An induction coil and Leyden jar for producing a continuous stream of sparks between metal points. 2nd. A collimator tube 3 feet long, carrying a pair of clips at one end for holding the points close to the slit and a quartz lens at the other. 3rd. A quartz prism placed at the angle of minimum deviation for the sodium D line. 4th. Another quartz lens and the body of a photographic camera which could be extended to 36 inches. The separate portions of this lengthy apparatus were firmly screwed down to two heavy tables to prevent the shifting of any part, since the proper adjustment of the whole takes some

This box was about 4 inches long with a hinged lid, and it was possible to place a series of three or four cells full of liquid within it through which the rays were transmitted.

These were fitted into metal frames, and pieces of quartz were attached to each end by means of screws pressing against a metal rim. ->*The Photographic Process.*<-

The original method of photographing employed by Dr. <term>MILLER</term> we have found to be defective: first, because the more refrangible end of the ultra-violet spectrum is extremely weak, if not entirely missing, when photographed on plates containing a plain iodized collodion; secondly, a wet collodion process is disadvantageous when long exposure is sometimes necessary; and thirdly, when working in a small room the ozone generated by the electric discharge acts upon wet collodion plates in such a manner that they become coated with a thick deposit of silver as soon as the developing solution is applied, the deposit being densest where the bath solution has most accumulated. Much larger and better spectra are obtained by using ordinary bromo-iodized collodion and an iron developer, but of course this process is rendered useless by the action of the ozone on the silver solution.

The extraordinary improvements made in recent years in the preparation and development of dry plates, together with the aforementioned facts, combined to recommend a dry process.

Successive trials have been made with plates coated with washed collodio-bromide emulsion, with the <term>BEECHY</term> standard dry plates, uranium plates, Mr. <term>KENNETT</term>’s and <term>WRATTEN</term> and <term>WAINWRIGHT</term>’s gelatine pellicle plates. The gelatine plates are to be preferred for two reasons: if they are wanted for the production of negatives to print from, the film is exceedingly fine and even in texture, and on the other hand, if transparencies showing absorption bands are desired they need not be varnished. The <term>BEECHY</term> plates are more sensitive to very feeble rays in a certain part of the spectrum than those coated with gelatine pellicle; this may be seen by comparing the spectra of iron photographed on these two varieties of plates. One advantage of the gelatine plates is that they photograph more of the less refrangible rays than any others we have tried, and though the lengthening of the spectrum in consequence is comparatively slight, yet it is of importance in the examination of certain colored substances, which while they transmit rays of higher refrangibility absorb the blue and violet. Such bodies are solutions of the nitrophenols and nitranilines. The exposure of the sensitive plates has been varied from 10 seconds to an hour and a half, according to circumstances, depending partly on the plates employed and the object to be attained; but it is seldom that a longer period than a minute is necessary even for the production of negatives to print from, and when photographing absorption spectra with an open slit 10 seconds will suffice.

<summary>The authors describe the transition from Dr. Miller's defective wet collodion photographic process to the use of modern dry plates, specifically favoring gelatine pellicle plates for their sensitivity and fine texture. They also note the interference caused by ozone on wet plates during long exposures and identify nickel points as providing the most useful spectrum.</summary>
<keywords>photography, ultra-violet spectrum, wet collodion, dry plates, gelatine pellicle, ozone, absorption spectra, nitrophenols, nitranilines, spectroscopy</keywords>

### *The Measurement of Bands and their Position.*

The lines of zinc, cadmium, and aluminum offer a convenient means of determining the position of absorption bands, etc., and M. <term>SORET</term> has employed them. The lines of cadmium in the ultra-violet as well as in the visible portion of the spectrum have been measured by M. <term>MASCART</term> and their wavelengths calculated. M. <term>SARASIN</term> has made use of these measurements in his determination of the refractive indices of quartz for the ordinary and extraordinary rays in the ultra-violet spectrum. ('Archives des Sciences Physiques et Naturelles;' Geneva, vol. lxi, p. 109; January, 1878.) The wavelengths for the cadmium lines in the invisible portions of the spectrum are shown in Diagram No. 1, and it will be seen that several of the following diagrams have been made according to this scale, as it is an advantage to have the metallic lines placed at intervals corresponding to their wavelengths. When nickel points instead of cadmium have been used, two strongly marked air lines below the solar line L (Plate 21, fig. 1) serve as a starting point for measurements; another air line between lines 11 and 12 also serves the same purpose. However, because the appearance of spectra as seen when photographed is different from when the lines have been mapped out according to their wavelengths, it has been considered desirable to follow the plan of M. <term>SORET</term> and lay down the spectra in some cases exactly as they appear in the photographs.

Some of the advantages derived from using photography in studying the ultra-violet rays include the following: the measurements are free from any personal error, the photographs are permanent and unmistakable records easily referred to, and the observations are made more rapidly and with much less fatigue to the eye than by any other means. Furthermore, liquids which are slightly turbid and unfit for observation with a fluorescent screen or eyepiece can be examined photographically by lengthening the exposure of the plate.

### *Absorption Caused by Films of Canada Balsam.*

It was considered very desirable to know whether Canada balsam, as used in the construction of optical apparatus, was capable of cutting off the ultra-violet rays to any considerable extent. We know, from the research of M. <term>SORET</term>, that Iceland spar is extremely transparent, as the 26th line of cadmium is distinguishable through a thickness of 65 mm of the substance. It was only necessary, then, to take a small <term>NICOL'S prism</term> and place it between the slit and the first lens. The result showed that lenses and prisms cemented with Canada balsam are utterly useless for such experiments as these, as the more refrangible rays are cut off sharply at the 12th line. Several kinds of beautifully clear and colorless optical glass, made by <term>FEIL</term> of Paris and lent to us by Mr. <term>HILGER</term>, have the same effect upon the spectrum, whether the glasses are made of lead or aluminum; they are all utterly worthless for observations on rays more refrangible than cadmium line No. 12. Fluor spar is quite transparent.

<summary>This page explains the methods for measuring ultra-violet absorption bands using cadmium and nickel lines and highlights the advantages of photography over visual observation. It also concludes that Canada balsam and certain optical glasses are unsuitable for this research because they block highly refrangible rays.</summary>

### *Examination of Organic Substances.*

After making a preliminary series of observations on the alcohols, ethereal salts, and fatty acids, we abandoned the use of silver electrodes used by Dr. <term>MILLER</term>. Instead, by the aid of other metallic spectra (referred to in diagram No. 1), we immediately investigated the comparative transparency of the quartz used for constructing cells; these cells were filled with water and with different alcohols.

It can be seen that the sides of the three quartz cells are almost completely transparent and that they are practically unchanged in this respect when filled with water.

It is clear that we do not need to fear employing the three cells in a series, or using pure water as a solvent for such substances as we may desire to examine in solution. The thickness of the liquid examined was never less than three-quarters of an inch.

Many of the following organic substances were obtained from Mr. <term>KAHLBAUM’S</term> agents; they were prepared in his factory and were afterwards carefully distilled and purified by us.

*Methyl Alcohol. Specimen No. 1.*—This was apparently perfectly pure; it had no odor or color, and it boiled at 66° C. It transmitted very few rays beyond 12 Cd <note>cadmium</note>, and it is worth noting that it yielded the same absorption spectrum both before and after distillation from quicklime prepared from pure marble. The identical specimen of methyl alcohol examined by Dr. <term>MILLER</term> was compared with this one and was found to give the same spectrum. The bottle containing it was labeled “Methyl alcohol from methyl oxalate.”

*Specimen No. 2.*—This sample was kindly furnished in a raw state by Mr. <term>JOHN WILLIAMS</term>, President of the Pharmaceutical Society. It had been prepared from oil of wintergreen. After redistillation with caustic potash and dehydration with caustic lime, it was rectified and found to boil between 66° and 66.5° C. As it possessed a faint, sweet smell, it was clearly impure, the impurity undoubtedly being a small quantity of some essential oil not capable of saponification. The somewhat longer spectrum of this substance supported the belief that a specimen of absolute purity would be nearly transparent in photographs. The specimen examined by M. <term>SORET</term> transmitted very little beyond the line 18 Cd and was therefore not of such purity as this, since only 10 mm, or about half the thickness of the liquid, was examined.

*Specimen No. 3.*—About a kilogram of methyl oxalate, beautifully crystallized and perfectly white, was decomposed by a strong soda solution, which was made from pure soda prepared from sodium. Repeated distillations from lumps of soda yielded more than 200 grams of methyl alcohol, which, as it gives a spectrum showing almost as great a transparency as water, must be regarded as absolutely pure. It boils at 66° C and has neither color, odor, nor a distinctive taste. Two photographs of this specimen are represented in the diagram; the longer spectrum resulted from the use of indium and zinc points. It shows how very nearly the alcohol approaches water in transparency.

<summary>The authors describe their methodology for testing the transparency of quartz cells and various preparations of methyl alcohol in the ultra-violet spectrum. They determine that highly purified methyl alcohol, derived from methyl oxalate, is nearly as transparent as water.</summary>

*Ethyl Alcohol. Specimen No. 1.*—This specimen was obtained from Mr. <term>KAHLBAUM</term> of Berlin. After purification, it boiled at 78.5° C. It exhibits slightly less transparency than methyl alcohol.

*Specimen No. 2.*—A sample of ordinary commercial absolute alcohol obtained from Messrs. <term>BURGOYNE and BURBIDGES</term>, boiling point 79° C. We tested two or three Winchester quarts of this liquid and used it for dissolving substances that were insoluble in water. They yielded the same spectrum as specimens Nos. 1 and 2. Several other samples we examined from the same firm were not of such great purity.

*Propyl Alcohol.*—This was carefully purified and redistilled, boiling point 97.5° C. It is a substance very difficult to dehydrate completely, but, as a trace of water does not affect its <term>diactinic</term> <note>transparent to ultra-violet rays</note> quality, this may be disregarded. A glance at the diagram shows that one cell-full of the liquid is less diactinic than ethyl alcohol, and that the absorption caused by three times the thickness of one cell is not much greater than that caused by one cell only. As the specific volumes of the three alcohols are represented by the following numbers:

| Substance | | Specific Volume |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Methyl | . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . | 40.8 |

we may examine the liquids in what are nearly molecular proportions by using layers of liquid differing in thickness in the proportions of 2, 3, and 4, according to the number of carbon atoms in the molecule. It will be seen that these three substances show a gradual increase in the absorption of the more <term>refrangible</term> <note>refractable</note> rays corresponding to the size of their molecules—or, in other words, to the number of carbon atoms they contain. The increased absorption is perfectly evident whether we use equal volumes of the liquids or thicknesses proportional to their specific volumes, from which we may conclude that one cell-full of liquid exerts nearly the maximum amount of absorption for the substance.

*Normal Octyl Alcohol.*—It has been shown that this substance is obtainable from the oil of *Heracleum Spondylium* <note>Cow Parsnip</note>. This specimen was prepared from heracleum oil by Mr. <term>KAHLBAUM</term>. After purification, it boiled at 192.5° C instead of at 198° C, the correct boiling point. One cell-full of the liquid exerts a marked degree of absorption, though, judging from the alcohols previously examined, the spectrum is very much what one might expect from a substance containing as many as eight carbon atoms.

It is worth remarking that the impure specimens of methyl and ethyl alcohols, when diluted with an equal or double volume of water, were perfectly diactinic.

*Specimen No. 2.*—Another sample similar to No. 1, obtained from Messrs. <term>HOPKIN and WILLIAMS</term>.

*Specimen No. 3.*—Prepared by us from a beautifully crystallized specimen of <term>formate of lead</term>, by decomposing the salt, after drying it at 130° C., in a current of pure dry <term>hydrogen sulfide</term>, and subsequent distillation from a further quantity of formate of lead crystals.

*Specimen No. 4.*—Consisted of two or three portions of the acid fractionally distilled during the preparation of the substance from <term>oxalic acid</term> and <term>glycerin</term>.

All these specimens were manifestly impure, for they yielded spectra in which the more refrangible rays were absorbed to a varying extent in every case, and the absorption was considerable. The acid prepared from the lead salt by means of hydrogen sulfide gives the shortest spectrum and probably contains some sulfur compound. We have been much troubled by repeated attempts to prepare pure <term>formic acid</term>. It was decided, if possible, to oxidize pure <term>methyl alcohol</term> to the acid. When <term>potassium bichromate</term> and <term>sulfuric acid</term> are used for this purpose, there is a danger of oxidizing the acid further to <term>carbonic acid</term>; and when we consider, too, that in order to oxidize 16 grams of alcohol, a liter of a solution of the bichromate salt is required, it is easily seen that the formic acid will be diluted so largely that in the process of separation by distillation the product would be destroyed—at any rate, this method was unsuccessful. The action of sulfuric acid and <term>manganic oxide</term> or <term>tartaric acid</term> does not yield a pure substance. The action of oxalic acid on <term>barium formate</term> yields a distillate which at first is different from the product of other processes in being free from a slight but peculiar odor, which it is highly probable does not belong to formic acid, but rather to some ever-present impurity. On continuing the distillation, the usual smell developed, which seems to show that heat causes a change in the formic acid. It is said by <term>LORIN</term> (*see* <term>WATTS’ ‘Dictionary of Chemistry,’</term> vol. vi.) that formic acid of 87 percent can be obtained by the dry distillation of <term>cupric formate</term>. It is quite true that a small quantity of very weak formic acid can be obtained by this process, but as soon as all the water of crystallization has been distilled off, no yield of formic acid is obtainable from the salt. The products of the action of heat on the dried salt, when maintained at a temperature of 200° in a paraffin bath, are metallic copper, carbonic acid, and water; in all probability, carbon monoxide is also formed.

The specimens of formic acid examined by <term>Dr. MILLER</term> and by <term>M. SORET</term> give much shorter spectra than ours. The formic acid examined by the latter observer absorbed all the rays beyond the 8th cadmium line, while the two better of our specimens transmit rays to a distance midway between the 12th and 17th lines (see Diagram 2), and that too through double the thickness of liquid.

*Acetic Acid.*—Two or three specimens of the <term>glacial acetic acid</term> of commerce were examined, as well as specimens carefully purified by distillation and crystallization. The spectra were the same in each case, transmitting rays just beyond 17.

### *Normal Hydrocarbons.*

Only three of these—hexane, heptane, and octane—have been examined; they were specimens kindly lent to us by Prof. <term>SCHORLEMMER</term> and were believed to be perfectly pure. Three series of photographs were taken of them, but they yielded spectra in no way corresponding to their difference in composition, from which we are inclined to believe they were impure (see Diagram No. 2).

### *Compound Ammonias.*

A series of five of these bodies was examined, with the solutions containing 33 percent of the substances in the case of ethylamine and methylamine. It is believed that, with the exception of ethylamine, they contained some impurity, since the methylamine and dimethylamine yielded shorter spectra than the ethylamine. These were commercial samples and were most probably prepared from ammonia obtained from gas-liquor. M. <term>SORET</term> has shown that commercial ammonia, even after many recrystallizations as a sulfate, still shows an absorption band due to some impurity that is constantly present; it is therefore unlikely that pure products would be obtained unless specially prepared ammonia is used for the purpose. We considered that volcanic ammonia, which is free from some of the impurities present in that made from gas-liquor, might be perfectly diactinic. Three separate samples, each measuring half a gallon, were examined, with the result that all the rays beyond 17 Cd <note>a specific line in the cadmium spectrum</note> were cut off. Even when so dilute that only one volume of ammonia was contained in 64 volumes of water, all traces of absorption had not been destroyed (see Diagram No. 5, Plate 25). This absorption is not due to nitric acid, because M. <term>SORET</term> has shown that the absorption band due to that substance occurs between 12 Cd and 17 Cd.

### *Conclusions.*

(1.) The normal alcohols of the series C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>OH are remarkable for transparency to the ultraviolet rays of the spectrum; pure methyl alcohol is nearly as transparent as water,

(2.) Normal fatty acids show a greater absorption of the more refrangible <note>rays of shorter wavelength that are more easily refracted</note> rays of the ultraviolet spectrum than normal alcohols containing the same number of carbon atoms.

(3.) There is an increased absorption of the more refrangible rays corresponding to each addition of CH₂ in the molecules of the alcohols and acids.

(4.) Like the alcohols and acids, the ethereal salts <note>esters</note> derived from them are highly transparent to ultraviolet rays and do not show absorption bands.

### PART II.

#### *Examination of Substances containing the Benzene Nucleus.*

In the examination of substances containing a closed chain of carbon atoms linked by double bonds, one fact was strikingly apparent. All these bodies are strongly adiactinic <note>opaque to ultraviolet light</note>, with the hydrocarbons being the least so; Diagram No. 2 will make this immediately clear. Professor <term>STOKES</term> has pointed out that one of these substances, salicin, in an aqueous solution (the concentration of which is not stated), shows a characteristic absorption band. Now salicin is a substance whose chemical structure is perfectly well known: it is a glucoside of saligenin,

->C₆H₁₁O₅<-
->} O<-
->C₆H₄(OH)CH₂<-

and consequently, the absorption band may be due to the saligenin. At any rate, it seemed worthwhile to dilute solutions of known concentration containing related substances such as phenol, salicylic acid, and methyl salicylate, and to determine whether any absorption bands are thus made visible. The result has revealed the fact that almost all, if not entirely all, benzene derivatives—including the hydrocarbon itself—are characterized by one or more absorption bands, which resist modification or removal by dilution to an enormous extent.

For this part of the research, it has been necessary to prepare solutions of known strength, dilute them with definite quantities of water, and photograph the various liquids obtained. These photographs have been placed on graph paper, upon which the lines of cadmium (as seen in a photograph of the metallic spectrum) have been drawn; the proportions of the substance in solution have been coordinated with the position of the absorption bands relative to the cadmium lines. A series of curves has thus been obtained, and each of these proves to be a highly characteristic feature of the substance observed. The number of photographs necessary for completing the curves varied significantly with different substances; sometimes four or five, and occasionally eighteen or twenty, were taken.

When the substance to be examined was a liquid, two cubic centimeters were measured and diluted with alcohol if necessary, or water if possible, so as to form a total volume of 100 c.c. From this solution, other more dilute ones were obtained. If the
