If the substance was a solid, 0.2 grams or 0.02 grams of the body were dissolved in alcohol or water to form a total volume of 100 ml; when it was desirable to compare a liquid substance with a solid, both were weighed and dissolved in the same manner. In this way, methyl salicylate was compared with salicylic acid and salicin.

*Benzene* (Diagram No. 6).—A very pure specimen, kindly lent to us by Professor GUTHRIE. About ten ounces of the substance had been separated from more than a gallon and a half of commercial benzene by successive crystallizations in a freezing mixture. The first noticeable feature here is the small alteration in the absorption of the rays caused by dilution with 99 volumes of alcohol. It is impossible to describe the changes noticed on repeated dilutions without reference to the diagram, but it may be well to record the proportions of alcohol to benzene in the liquids photographed.

One part of benzene was successively diluted to measure 100, 150, 190, 220, 235, 250, 375, 500, 750, 850, 1000, 1275, 1500, 2000, and 2500 times its original volume. With a dilution of 750, six absorption bands are seen. In other words, as the cell is 3/4 inch in thickness, a layer of benzene 1/1000th of an inch in thickness would show the same spectrum. As the bands are perfectly visible after a dilution of 1500 times, it follows that a film of benzene 1/2000th of an inch in thickness would show them.

*Toluene.—Methylbenzene*, BP. 111° C.—The various solutions examined contained 1/100, 1/500, 1/1000, 1/2000, 1/2500, and 1/3000 of their volume of the hydrocarbon. It is evident from Diagram No. 7 that a similarity exists between this substance and benzene, though fewer rays are transmitted by toluene, which greatly modifies the appearance of the two diagrams. The two absorption bands between <term>17 Cd</term> and <term>18 Cd</term> <note>Lines in the cadmium spark spectrum used as reference points</note> are highly characteristic.

*Ethylbenzene*, BP. 135°–6 (Diagram 8).—The solutions examined contained the following volumes of the liquid: 1/150, 1/300, 1/500, 1/1000, 1/2000, 1/3000, 1/3500, 1/4000, and 1/6000. At 1/500, a strong band of transmitted rays appears from about halfway between 18 Cd and 23 Cd and extends to 24 Cd; this widens out until, at 1/3000, it meets the narrow absorption band noticed in the previous spectrum as situated between 17 Cd and 18 Cd.

*Trimethylbenzene.—Mesitylene.*—The methyl molecules occupy the position indicated by 1–3–5, BP. 163–4° C. (Diagram No. 9). Observations were made on solutions containing 1/240, 1/500, 1/1000, 1/2000, 1/3000, 1/6000, and 1/10000 of their volume of the liquid. A transmitted band occurs between 18 Cd and 23 Cd, commencing at 1/500 dilution. At 1/2000, two narrow bands of transmitted rays occur between 17 Cd and 18 Cd.

These hydrocarbons are the least opaque to the photographic <note>ultraviolet</note> rays of the many substances containing the benzene nucleus <note>benzene ring</note> which we have examined, although compared with the substances previously treated—namely, the alcohols, fatty acids, and ethereal salts <note>esters</note>—they are significantly lacking in transparency.

The following examples provide an instance of one of the applications of this kind of work to research purposes.

Tyrosine was for some time considered by <term>BARTH</term> and other chemists to be a derivative of paroxy-benzoic acid, but more recently it has been regarded as an oxyphenyl-amido-propionic acid,

->C~6~H~4~ $\begin{cases} \text{OH} \\ \text{C}_2\text{H}_3(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH.} \end{cases}$<-

However, these views have not been confirmed by the synthesis of the substance.

If it is a derivative of paroxy-benzoic acid, it may be expected to share the peculiarities of that substance in its action on the ultra-violet rays of the spectrum.

We have accordingly examined solutions of tyrosine (see Diagram No. 26), and find that it more nearly resembles a phenol in actinic quality than an acid in which the carboxyl group replaces hydrogen in the benzene nucleus. Hence, the latter view of its constitution—which represents the oxyphenyl group as substituting hydrogen in amido-propionic acid—is more correct than the former, since it is in accordance with its optical character.

*Phlorizine* (Diagram No. 27).—It was considered interesting to examine this substance, since it is a glucoside containing the residue of phloroglucin, a body isomeric with pyrogallol, and phloretic acid, an oxyphenyl-propionic acid. It is evident that most interesting results may be anticipated from a continuation of this research, and this contribution must be accepted as rather the bare beginning of the subject than its conclusion.

The following is a summary of the chief points of interest relating to benzene and its derivatives : —

(1.) Benzene and the hydrocarbons, alcohols, acids, and amines derived from it are remarkable—first, for their powerful absorption of the more refrangible rays; second, for the absorption bands made visible by dissolving them in water or alcohol; and third, for the extraordinary intensity of these absorption bands: that is to say, their power of resisting dilution.
(2.) Isomeric bodies containing the benzene nucleus exhibit widely different spectra, because their absorption bands vary in position and in intensity.
(3.) The photographic absorption spectra can be used as a means of identifying organic substances and as a most delicate test of their purity. The curves obtained by coordinating the extent of dilution—or in other words, the quantity of substance—with the position of the rays of the spectrum transmitted by the solution, form a strongly marked and highly characteristic feature of very many substances.

### IX. *On the Microrheometer.*

->By J. B. HANNAY, F.R.S.E., F.C.S., lately Assistant Lecturer on Chemistry in Owens College, Manchester.<-

->Communicated by H. E. ROSCOE, Ph.D., Professor of Chemistry in Owens College, Manchester.<-

->Received December 11, 1878,—Read January 23, 1879.<-

---

->[PLATE 35.]<-

The examination of the phenomena regarding the flow of liquids through capillary tubes, as well as the discovery of the fact that chemical composition influenced the rate of flow, was the work of M. Poiseuille,* who, in the paper referred to, gave the results of an extended series of carefully conducted experiments. These experiments illustrated the laws regulating the rate of flow as affected by the length and diameter of the tube, the pressure acting upon the liquid, and also, within a certain range, by the temperature. His work was carefully examined, in an experimental manner, by a commission of chemists and physicists, and found to be very exact. The formula for the rate of flow which he found was—

$$Q = 1836.724 (1 + 0.0336793T + 0.0002209936T^2) \frac{HD^4}{L}$$

where—

->Q = quantity of liquid passed.<-
->T = temperature in centigrade degrees.<-
->H = pressure on liquid, measured by mercury column.<-
->D = diameter of tube.<-
->L = length of tube.<-

Poiseuille pointed out that these results are different from those obtained by other investigators, but the results of others had been obtained by using tubes of much greater diameter, so that the laws regulating the flow of liquids through capillary tubes are different from those relating to wide tubes. The most characteristic law relating to capillary tubes appears to be that the rate of flow varies directly as the pressure; and as it is also the easiest method of testing a tube, I shall only use the

---

<margin>
\* "Experimental Research on the Movement of Liquids in Tubes of Very Small Diameters," 'Annales de Chimie et de Physique' [3], vol. vii., p. 50.
</margin>

<summary>J. B. Hannay introduces the microrheometer and discusses Poiseuille's foundational research on the flow of liquids through capillary tubes, specifically the relationship between flow rate, pressure, and tube dimensions.</summary>
<keywords>microrheometer, Poiseuille, capillary tubes, liquid flow, viscosity, fluid dynamics, Owens College, pressure laws</keywords>

--- Page 322 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws of liquid flow through capillary tubes, specifically addressing the work of Poiseuille, Graham, and Guérout.</meta>

<page-num>276</page-num>

# MR. J. B. HANNAY ON THE MICRORHEOMETER.

the term "capillary" for tubes that follow this law. Poiseuille intended to apply his studies to the action of various substances within the capillary vessels of the living body; consequently, he examined substances such as alcohol, blood, and various saline solutions. Upon examining the flow rate of various mixtures of alcohol and water, it was found that a mixture of approximately equal quantities of alcohol and water required about three times as much time to pass as either pure alcohol or pure water. The mixture corresponded to a hexhydrate of alcohol, so that, in this case, Poiseuille discovered a chemical compound by purely physical means. Some results were obtained by dissolving various salts in water and finding the flow rates of the solutions; but as there appeared to be no connection between the combining weights and the rates, Poiseuille could offer no explanation for the figures. One thing can be concluded from Poiseuille's work: that the flow of a liquid through a capillary tube is very rarely comparable to its physiological action in the veins. 

It was not for many years after this that any attention was paid to the subject, until Graham,<note>Philosophical Transactions, 1861, page 373.</note> in 1861, noticing the existence of the hydrate of alcohol discovered by Poiseuille, conducted some experiments to find whether any hydrates of acids could be discovered by this method. His research showed that several acids absorbed water three molecules at a time, with each addition being marked by a further slowing of the flow, though each successive slowdown was less pronounced than the previous one. This addition to the work of Poiseuille showed that the capillary tube might become an important instrument in the hands of the chemist. 

Recently,<note>Comptes Rendus, lxxix., 1201; lxxxi., 1025.</note> M. Aug. Guérout has presented several papers on the subject to the Academy of Sciences in Paris, giving an account of some experiments on the flow rate of various alcohols. In these, he shows that the rate decreases as the molecular volume increases, but not in any definite proportion. Guérout, however, overlooks the most important factor in this kind of investigation: temperature. He experiments with all his alcohols at the same temperature, even though there is a difference of 60° between their boiling points. Now, in a substance such as water, a difference of 60° means that the flow is three times faster at the high temperature than at the low temperature; therefore, some of the alcohols which, by Guérout's method, seemed to offer the greatest resistance may actually, if compared under fair conditions, have the least friction. 

Regarding liquids, it would appear from the research of Kopp that in order to obtain chemical deductions from their physical examination, they must be examined when their vapor tensions are equal, as they then exist under somewhat comparable conditions regarding mobility and expansion. Guérout has also, in the second of these papers, determined the effect of temperature variation on the flow rate, and concludes that the rate for water varies by a constant factor with a value of 1.025. The experiments were, however, performed within a very narrow range—specifically 10° to 17°—and Guérout seems to have been unaware of the fact that his countryman, Poiseuille, carefully determined this some forty years earlier, and

<summary>This page reviews the history of capillary flow research, highlighting Poiseuille's discovery of chemical compounds via physical flow rates and subsequent studies by Graham and Guérout. The author criticizes Guérout for failing to account for temperature and boiling point differences when comparing the viscosity of different alcohols.</summary>

arrived at a different result. Graham also published a table from 0° to 70°, but Guérout does not appear to be aware of Graham's work. According to Guérout, the curve representing the effect of temperature would be a straight line, whereas the numbers provided by both Poiseuille and Graham correspond with a curve. This will be considered further on.

About four years ago, it occurred to me that since all the work done so far with the capillary tube had not properly tested its usefulness (either because it did not consider temperature or because it used percentage instead of normal solutions), a more thorough investigation of the subject might yield important results. The term "normal solutions" is used in the sense that chemists apply to it: specifically, solutions in which the molecular weight of the compound in grams is dissolved in a liter of water—or, more simply, gram-equivalents per liter. Where this could not be achieved due to the salt's insolubility, the strongest possible solution was used, and its proportional effect was calculated. 

In using Poiseuille's tube, which was also used by Graham and Guérout, I found a great deal of inconvenience. The apparatus consists of a tube bent at right angles; the horizontal lower portion is the capillary, and the vertical part consists of the measuring bulb and the tube for applying pressure. The entire unit was immersed in the liquid being tested, and alternate suction and pressure were applied to fill and empty the bulb. This requires so much of the experimental liquid that I modified the apparatus, as shown in *Plate 35, fig. 1*, by placing a receiving bulb at the other end of the capillary. 

However, even this had its disadvantages, as the pressure tube had to be placed alternately at each end; this disturbance sometimes caused dust to fall into the bulb and clog the tube. It did, however, have this advantage over Poiseuille's tube: liquids like bromine could be tested. After working for some time with that design, I finally decided to adopt the form of apparatus shown in *Plate 35, fig. 2*. It consists of a capillary tube at the bottom, to which two bulbs are attached—one for measurement and the other as a receiver. Two tubes pass up from these bulbs and end in **Y**-pieces. One of the **Y**-tubes from each side is connected to an inverted **Y**-tube, and each is also provided with a clip or stopcock. One of the inverted **Y**-pieces is connected to the pressure chamber, while the other is left open to the air. 

Through this arrangement, pressure can be applied to either side; moreover, the apparatus can be filled with any gas other than air. To introduce the experimental liquid, one only needs to disconnect one of the **Y**-tubes on the side of the measuring bulb and pour in enough liquid. A thermometer is placed between the two bulbs, with its bulb positioned at the midpoint of the entire system, thereby registering the average temperature of the experiment. In the case of some mixtures, it was found that they deposited a slight sediment over time, which clogged the tube. To prevent this, another design was created, as shown in *Plate 35, fig. 3*, where the receiving bulb is at the lower end; this allows the liquid to settle for a time so that the upper portion can be forced into the bulb free from any solid matter.

# MR. J. B. HANNAY ON THE MICRORHEOMETER.

In his earlier experiments on gases, GRAHAM gave the name "transpiration" to the passage of gases through capillary tubes, which expresses what is meant admirably; but when he came to work with liquids, he still used the term "transpiration," although the laws relating to liquids were quite different from those relating to gases. Since the term "transpiration" is not easily translatable into other languages—as it is already used in French to mean "perspiration"—I have decided to abandon that title. I will substitute the term "microrheosis" (from the Greek $\mu\iota\kappa\rho\acute{o}\varsigma$ and $\acute{\rho}\acute{\epsilon}\omega$) and call the instruments described above "microrheometers." The microrheosis of a liquid, then, is the time taken for a certain volume of liquid to pass through a tube of such dimensions that the rate of flow varies according to the pressure, using water as the standard of comparison in the meantime.

It initially seemed probable that the friction in the microrheometer might be due, in great measure, to the cohesion of the liquid. This led me to seek a method for determining the cohesion of all liquids (which has been published elsewhere),* but I soon found that the two phenomena were not comparable—in fact, cohesion had almost no effect in retarding the flow. I do not need to quote that work here, as there will be plenty of proof further on to show the real cause of the retardation. In this paper, I shall confine myself to the work I have done on saline solutions and on the substance (water) in which the salts are dissolved. The tube and measuring bulb used for these experiments had the following dimensions: the capillary tube had an average diameter of 0.0938 mm and deviated from a perfect circle by only .002. Its length was 21 mm, while the capacity of the glass bulb was 4.0530 cubic centimeters. Both the bulb and tube were made of soda glass, the expansion of which had been determined by weighing it with mercury at different temperatures, with the following results:

->Coefficient from $0^\circ$ to $50^\circ$ . . . . 0.0000252 per degree.<-
->Coefficient from $50^\circ$ to $100^\circ$ . . . . 0.0000259 per degree.<-

In these experiments, the temperature was measured by a thermometer graduated to tenths of a degree, which had been compared with a standard. The pressure of the air in the chamber was at first regulated by an air pump, but I found that I could regulate it much more accurately by blowing by mouth; this method was generally used when the pressure was not over 1 meter. In the apparatus shown in Plate 35, Fig. 2, it will be seen that during the first half of the flow, the liquid in the bulb from which it is flowing will be at a higher level than the liquid in the other bulb, thereby adding to the pressure; however, because it is below that level during the latter half of the flow, the two effects neutralize each other. The pressure was measured by a water gauge, and the temperature of the water in the column was recorded; when it differed from $15^\circ$, a correction was made either way. In using Fig. 3, Plate 35, the pressure was adjusted to account for the difference in the levels of the two bulbs.

At a temperature of $20^\circ$ and under a pressure of 1 meter of water, it was found that it took an average of 131.3 seconds to empty the bulb, based on the following 10 experiments—

->131.2 + 131.3 + 131.2 + 131.2 + 131.4 + 131.4 + 131.3 + 131.3 + 131.4 + 131.2'' ÷ 10 = 131.29''.<-

It can be seen that this method gives very consistent results, with the deviation in these experiments being only one-tenth of a second, and most likely due to personal error. The pressure was then halved—that is, only half a meter of water was used—when the following times were recorded:—

->263.0 + 262.9 + 262.8 + 263.1 + 263.2 + 263.1 + 263.1 + 262.9 + 263.0 + 263.1'' ÷ 10 = 263.02''.<-

As this value is nearly double the previous result, the tube may be said to have been capillary, according to the definition of that term given above.

The probable error of the average of the experiments above, calculated by the formula

->0.6745 \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma\epsilon^2}{n(n-1)}},<-

amounts to 0.060'' in the first series, and 0.256'' in the second. It seemed that before beginning the examination of complex organic substances, it would be better to attempt to gain some knowledge of the causes of the phenomena presented by the microrheosis of liquids. This would be done by thoroughly examining one liquid to be used as a standard and as a <term>menstruum</term>, and then examining a series of comparable inorganic salts (about whose composition a good deal is already known) dissolved in that standard menstruum. Water was the liquid chosen.

POISEUILLE had noticed that as the temperature rose, the rate of flow increased. At first, he thought the loss of density was one of the causes of this; however, upon examining water at temperatures below 4°C, he found that the retardation increased very rapidly, even though the density decreased. GRAHAM also determined the rates for water at different temperatures but offered no remarks on the phenomena observed. As neither of these researchers determined the rate above 70°C, I undertook another examination from 0°C to 100°C. The temperature was regulated by a large glass water bath, as shown in Plate 35, Figure 2; at least ten experiments were conducted at each temperature. For a pressure chamber, a large glass reservoir with a capacity of about 20 liters was used. This was placed very close to the microrheometer and connected to it with tubes of pure <term>caoutchouc</term> (the material used to make toy balloons) with only a 1/8-inch bore. By this arrangement, no leakage occurred, and only a very slight addition of air to the reservoir was required after reversing the sequence of the stopcocks. The reason for using glass as a reservoir was that it is not nearly as sensitive to slight variations in temperature as copper (which was used by POISEUILLE); this allows one time to regulate the pressure, even when the laboratory temperature is quickly rising or falling.

It becomes clearly apparent from this table, as well as from curve No. I., that the retardation increases very rapidly as the temperature approaches the freezing point; but we know that the contraction of water as the temperature falls ceases at 4°, and below that it becomes negative. It thus appears probable that we have two separate forces at work which act in the same direction in slowing the rate of flow in the microrheometer, but which act in opposite directions in the case of the thermal expansion of water: the one being due to the vibrations we call heat, and the other being due to the gradual arrangement of the water particles to form ice crystals. The thermal force is much greater if we consider the range between 0° and 100°, but we know that water remains liquid below 0° if undisturbed; and if we could cool it until its density was as low as ice, the crystallizing force would then be enormously greater than the thermal force. An attempt was made to trace the microrheometrical curve below 0°, but the motion of the water through the tube always caused freezing. Below is a formula shorter than <term>POISEUILLE’S</term>, which agrees with the curve quite well. It is quite evident, on examining the microrheometrical table, that the crystalline force has a retarding action, but what proportion of the retardation it causes could only be determined by examining several liquids and comparing the numbers obtained with their thermal expansion curves.

Having obtained some knowledge of the solvent in which the salts were to be dissolved, an examination of the following salts was then commenced. As some of the substances to be examined were only slightly soluble and could not be prepared at normal strength, the effect of the amount of salt present was first investigated. Pure dry sodium chloride was used for this purpose, and three solutions were prepared: I. normal, II. half normal, III. quarter normal. A single glance at these numbers is sufficient to show that the crystalline form has no recognizable effect on the rate. We find two cubic salts, potassium chloride and sodium chloride, acting in opposite directions: the one accelerating the flow by 2.3 seconds and the other retarding it by 9.2 seconds. These, it is true, are salts of different metals, but below we have potassium nitrate and sulfate, both <term>trimetric</term>, and yet they diverge more widely than the first two—the nitrate accelerating the flow by 4.9 seconds and the sulfate retarding it by 12.3 seconds. Solubility, too, does not account for it, because sodium chloride is more soluble than potassium nitrate, and yet it retards the flow while the nitrate accelerates it; similarly, potassium sulfate is less soluble than sodium chloride and retards the flow more than it does. In fact, some series go one way and some directly opposite. Thus, in the case of barium, strontium, and calcium, the latter flows least rapidly and is simultaneously the most soluble; while in the case of the chloride, bromide, and iodide of potassium, the first is both the least soluble and flows the slowest. So, we see that neither the crystalline form nor the solubility of a salt materially affects the <term>microrheosis</term> of its solution. Nor can the specific volume affect it, as we know that <term>isomorphous</term> compounds have equal specific volumes. 

It appeared, then, that the phenomena of microrheosis could only be affected by the mass or energy of the salt in solution. It is worth explaining here that as normal solutions are used, mass is synonymous with "atomic weight," "equivalent proportion," or other such terms. When the energy of the salt is spoken of, it means the amount of work which can be obtained from it by successive combinations until it is degraded to such a state that no more work or energy can be obtained from it, a state I describe as "exhausted." The question is: Does each metal change its value when uniting with an acid, or does each metal and each acid radical have its own constant value? To determine this, four compounds were chosen—namely, the chlorides and nitrates of potassium and sodium (three of which were already known)—and their values were found:

Two facts are revealed by these numbers: first, that the substances containing the greatest amount of energy offer the least resistance in the tube—for instance, nitrates all flow the fastest, and sulfates, which are fully exhausted compounds, flow the slowest; the second fact is that the greater the mass, the less resistance it offers. We see this in the cases of the chlorides, bromides, and iodides; the last group, having the highest combining weight and hence the greatest chemical mass, flows much more easily than either of the others. At first, one might expect that because acids are salts of the monatomic metal hydrogen, and therefore exactly comparable with potassium and sodium salts, they would show the same microrheometrical reactions. However, when we consider, first, the very weak saturation power of hydrogen (as a base), and also that the salt of hydrogen is dissolved in its own oxide, we see it is probable that the results will not agree with those of a strong monatomic base like potassium. The relationship between the acids requires a much fuller investigation, as it has recently been shown that acid which has been allowed to stand for some time does not release as much heat upon saturation with an alkali as acid which has been freshly prepared. Therefore, upon further investigation, the rates above may require alteration.

Lastly, regarding mixtures: A large number of mixtures have been tested, and as they all give exactly the calculated value, only one example needs to be quoted here by way of illustration. A solution was made by mixing equal parts of the following normal solutions:

->KNO₃, K₂SO₄, NaNO₃, NaCl.<-

Each salt, therefore, exerted only one-fourth of its influence, which results by calculation in a rate of:

->$\frac{-4.9}{4} + \frac{+12.3}{4} + \frac{+6.6}{4} + \frac{+9.4}{4} + 131.3 = 136.9''.$<-

| | Probable error of mean. | |
|---|---|---|
| Average of 10 experiments | 0.06'' | 136.85''. |

Of course, as each metal and each acid has its own value, it does not matter how they are distributed; this provides further conclusive proof that neither solubility, crystalline form, nor specific volume have any effect upon the <term>microrheosis</term> of a salt.

From the facts above, we see that the microrheometer does not merely deal with the superficial qualities of chemical matter. Instead, by bringing to light the fundamental relations of mass and energy, it is likely to become the center of a new branch of science. My next work will consist of an examination of liquid bodies whose thermal relations are known, in order to find a fundamental relationship between the energy expended by elements in forming a certain mass of substance and the resistance offered by such substances in the microrheometer.

# X. *An Experimental Determination of the Values of the Velocities of Normal Propagation of Plane Waves in different directions in a Biaxial Crystal, and a Comparison of the Results with Theory.*

->By R. T. GLAZEBROOK, B.A., Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge.<-

->Communicated by J. CLERK MAXWELL, M.A., F.R.S.<-

---

->Received June 19,—Read June 20, 1878.<-

->PART I.<-

->Preliminary.—Professor STOKES’S Report to the British Association, 1862, with Outline of the Method.<-

->Section I.—Review of Previous Experiments and Criticism of FRESNEL’S.<-

In his report to the British Association in 1862, Professor STOKES says: “The accuracy of the spheroidal form assigned by HUYGHENS to the sheet of the wave surface within Iceland spar does not seem to have been tested with the same level of rigor as the ordinary refraction of the ordinary ray. This is because the methods applied by WOLLASTON (Phil. Trans., 1802, p. 381) and MALUS (Mem. de l’Institut Sav. Étran., vol. ii., p. 303, 1811) for observing extraordinary refraction can hardly be compared for accuracy with the method of prismatic refraction adopted for the ordinary ray; furthermore, observations on the absolute velocities of propagation in different directions within biaxial crystals are almost entirely lacking.

“This has long been recognized as a need, and it has been suggested to use the displacement of interference fringes for this purpose.

“It seems to me that a slight modification of the standard method of prismatic refraction would be more convenient and accurate.

“Unless natural faces or cleavage planes serve the purpose, let the crystal to be examined be cut so as to have two planes inclined at an angle suitable for measuring refraction. At least two natural faces or cleavage planes should be left intact to permit an exact measurement of the directions of any artificial faces. Once the prism formed in this way has been mounted as usual and placed in any azimuth, let the angle of incidence or emergence (depending on whether the prism remains fixed or turns with the telescope) be measured by observing the light reflected from the surface, and likewise the deviation for several standard fixed lines in the spectrum. Each observation provides us with an angle of incidence and the corresponding angle

In accordance with these suggestions, I undertook a series of observations at the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, which I propose to describe in the present paper; I also wish to discuss the results arrived at and to compare them with those deduced from <term>FRESNEL'S</term> and some of the rival theories of double refraction.

But before this, it seems natural to devote some space to the consideration of the experiments that have already been made with the same object.

These we may divide into two classes: (1) Those which have reference to <term>Iceland spar</term> and other uniaxial crystals; (2) Those in which biaxial crystals were used.

<term>BREWSTER</term> (Thirteenth Report of the British Association) proved conclusively that one wave in Iceland spar obeys strictly the ordinary law of refraction.

<term>SWAN</term> (Edinburgh Trans., vol. xvi., p. 375) obtained, by direct measurements with prisms placed in the position of minimum deviation, values of the ordinary refractive index which differ at most by .00002.

To verify his construction for the extraordinary ray, <term>HUYGHENS</term> himself made but few experiments, and it was not until 1802 that <term>WOLLASTON</term> (Phil. Trans., 1802, p. 381) attempted to test the theory with any degree of exactness.

In 1810 <term>MALUS</term> (“Theory of Double Refraction,” Paris Memoirs of Foreign Scientists, vol. ii., p. 303) undertook a series of experiments with the same object in view.

Rather later, <term>BIOT</term> undertook the same task, while more recently <term>RUDBERG</term> (<term>POGG.</term> Ann., vol. xiv., p. 45) and <term>MASCART</term> have measured the values of the principal indices by means of prisms cut parallel to the axis.

Since 1862 Professor <term>STOKES</term> has applied the method indicated above to prisms of Iceland spar and finds the results of the experiment agree with <term>HUYGHENS'S</term> construction, with a possible difference of .0001 in the values of the refractive index. The details of the experiments are as yet unpublished.

(2) We must consider next the case of biaxial crystals. Various experimenters have determined the values of the principal refractive indices for different crystals. <term>FRESNEL</term> alone has endeavoured to verify his theory by experiment (“Complete Works of <term>FRESNEL</term>,” vol. ii., p. 415; second supplement to the “Memoir on Double Refraction”). The method adopted was to observe the displacement of the interference fringes, formed from two parallel slits, produced by introducing two plates of topaz of the same thickness, cut in different directions from the same crystal, into the paths of the light pencils proceeding from the two slits respectively, and to compare this with the displacement calculated on <term>FRESNEL'S</term> theory.

The first set of observations, combined with the angle between the optic axes, serves to determine the principal velocities *a, b, c*. *a* being assumed to be unity, let

the effects they would produce, which, though small, may be sufficient to constitute the difference between Fresnel’s and some rival theory. Moreover, the values of the principal refractive indices in topaz are so nearly equal that any conceivable wave surface will differ very little from two spheres.

To estimate, then, the weight we may attach to these results, let us see how far the experiments are consistent with one of the rival theories.

Now, the equation for the surface of wave slowness in the theories of Green and Cauchy involves more constants than the three principal refractive indices of the crystal.

To determine these, we must make the principal sections agree with experimental results at more points than just the extremities of the axes; it is probable, therefore, that they will differ very little throughout.

In fact, the existence of these unnecessary constants is a radical defect in both of these theories.

Lord Rayleigh, however, has proposed a theory in which the only constants are the principal velocities (Phil. Mag., vol. 41, series 4, 1871).

The shape of the surface of wave slowness is also considerably different from that given by Fresnel’s theory.

Its principal sections consist of a circle and the inverse of an ellipse, instead of a circle and an ellipse.

He supposes “the density of the ether in a crystal to be a function of the direction of displacement,” while the forces called into play are the same as in a homogeneous medium.

From this, he deduces the equation to determine the velocity of a wave front, for which the direction cosines of the normal are $l, m, n$:

->$\frac{a^2l^2}{\text{V}^2 - a^2} + \frac{b^2m^2}{\text{V}^2 - b^2} + \frac{c^2n^2}{\text{V}^2 - c^2} = 0$<-

$a, b, c$ being the principal velocities.

Let us find the velocity for a wave perpendicular to the $zx$ plane, making an angle $\alpha$ with $Ox$, where $l = -\sin \alpha, m = 0, n = \cos \alpha$.

->$\text{V}^2(c^2 \cos^2 \alpha + a^2 \sin^2 \alpha) = a^2c^2$<-

or since $a = 1, c^2 = 1 - \gamma$

->$\text{V}^2\{(1 - \gamma) \cos^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \alpha\} = 1 - \gamma$<-
->$\text{V}^2 = (1 - \gamma)(1 - \gamma \cos^2 \alpha)^{-1}$<-
->$\text{V} = (1 - \frac{1}{2}\gamma)(1 + \frac{1}{2}\gamma \cos^2 \alpha)$<-

neglecting $\gamma^2$, etc.

->$\text{V} = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\gamma(1 - \cos^2 \alpha)$<-
->$= 1 - \frac{1}{2}\gamma \sin^2 \alpha$<-

Thus, Fresnel’s experiments provide just as much verification for Lord Rayleigh’s theory as for his own, and they are, therefore, an insufficient test of the truth of either.

They are, however, the only attempts made to verify the theory.

### Section II.—*Description of the Apparatus Used and Method of Making the Experiments.*

My own work was undertaken in the hope of obtaining results accurate enough to decide between some of the various theories that have been proposed.

I proceed to describe the apparatus used.

The crystal itself was a piece of aragonite, very clear and of a light color, obtained from Germany by the Demonstrator at the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, through Hilger, of Tottenham Court Road, London, W.C.

Originally it was in the form of a hexagonal prism.

Four of the faces were those marked $m$ in Professor Miller's *Mineralogy*; the other two were the faces marked $a$.

The natural ends had been cut off, and the artificial ends were approximately perpendicular to the $m$ and $a$ faces.

The crystal consisted of several twins, with the twin planes being parallel to two of the $m$ faces.

At this stage, Professor Stokes kindly undertook to examine the crystal to determine which direction to cut it for the greatest advantage for the purposes of the experiment. He found that fair reflections were obtained from three of the $m$ faces and decided that they should be left untouched to determine the position of any other cut faces.

Furthermore, the mean axis of elasticity bisects the angle between the adjacent $m$ faces;

The optic axes lie in the plane perpendicular to this axis. A prism formed with its refracting edge nearly parallel to the $b$-axis would allow observations to be made in a plane passing nearly through the optic axes; it was found that, by inclining the faces so that the $a$-axis nearly bisected the angle of the prism and making that angle about 42°, light could be passed through the crystal in the direction of either optic axis. It was therefore decided that the prism should be cut in that way.

Furthermore, by polishing one of the $a$-faces and cutting a face nearly coincident with the fourth $m$-face, a second prism was formed with its refracting edge nearly parallel to the $c$-axis.

It was important to obtain observations in different zones from the same piece of aragonite, because its chemical composition is somewhat variable, and the constants—that is, the principal refractive indices—may vary in different specimens.

The cutting was successfully performed by <term>HILGER</term>, and the faces of the prisms were quite flat.

With the crystal cut, the next task was to accurately determine the position of the cut faces with reference to the crystallographic axes.

For this purpose, and throughout all observations, I used a <term>goniometer</term> made by <term>GRUBB</term>, which was kindly lent to me by <term>Professor STOKES</term>.

The collimator is fixed to a graduated circle about 9 inches in diameter. The graduations, which are in silver, are on the *flat face* rather than the outer edge of the circle, and the circle is divided into arcs of 10 minutes (10').

Attached to the reading telescope are two verniers; *the graduations on the verniers are in the same plane as those of the circle*; by using these, the circle can be read to angles of 10 seconds (10").

At the center of this circle is a table to hold the prism; the table is attached to a second graduated circle with verniers that can be read to half-minutes.

Throughout the experiments, it was necessary to keep the edge of the prism parallel to the telescope's axis of revolution.

To achieve this, the prism was attached to a stand, adjustable with set screws, which rested in slots on the goniometer table.

The reading telescope was fitted with a needle point instead of the usual crosshairs.

To level the prism, I covered half of the slit so that, when viewed directly, the junction line between the covered and uncovered parts coincided with the needle point.

I then moved the telescope until the images of the slit, formed by reflection from the prism faces, were brought into the field one by one; I adjusted the leveling screws until the same coincidence was achieved.

Monochromatic light was produced using a <term>BUNSEN's burner</term> with a platinum wick, one end of which was immersed in a saturated salt-water solution.

On the advice of <term>Professor STOKES</term>, the observations were taken at angles of incidence increasing in an arithmetic progression.

The direct reading was taken several times during each day's work to avoid error. The method of observation was as follows: I set the telescope to a given scale reading and turned the prism until the image of the slit, seen by reflection at one of its faces, coincided with the needle point.

The difference between the direct reading and the known reading to which the telescope was set gave the supplement of twice the angle of incidence, from which the angle of incidence is easily obtained. I then turned the telescope until one image of the slit, seen by refraction through the prism, coincided with the needle point and took the reading.

The difference between this and the direct reading gave the deviation for that wave. The observation was then repeated for the second wave.

I then reset the telescope so that its axis made an angle of 4° with its former position and took a similar set of observations. This provided a series of deviations corresponding to angles of incidence increasing by 2°.

Near the vicinity of the optic axes, observations were made at every 1° of incidence.

For the first prism, each observation in the final set chosen was repeated three times, and the average of the results was taken.

The difference between this average and any single observation was only in a few cases as great as 10".

In the case of the second prism, the observed values of the deviation on different days for the same angle of incidence agreed so closely—rarely differing by more than 20"—that it seemed unnecessary to take a third set.

I also found that the refracted images were much more distinct for angles of incidence greater than that for minimum deviation than for angles that were less.

Upon passing through the position of minimum deviation, I therefore reversed the prism so that the face of incidence became the face of emergence.

->Fig. 1.<-

<image-desc>A scientific diagram labeled Fig. 1 showing light rays passing through a prism. The diagram features a central point C within a prism structure. Ray A B C D represents a ray undergoing minimum deviation. Ray P B Q R shows a ray with a different angle of incidence. Ray S B T U shows a third ray path. Points are labeled with letters A, B, C, D, P, Q, R, S, T, U. The background of the diagram is a dark rectangle with white lines and lettering.</image-desc>

Thus, if ABCD is the ray undergoing minimum deviation, for a ray such as PBQR, I made PB the incident ray and QR the emergent ray; while for a ray like SBTW, I reversed the prism so that UT became the incident ray and BS the emergent ray.

The cause of the increased distinctness lies in the fact that as the angle of incidence increases from the point of minimum deviation, the width of the image of the slit decreases, and *vice versa*.

Section III.—*Determination of the Position of the Principal Plane of the First Prism with reference to the Crystallographic Axes.—Values of the Quantities observed in the Experiments, and Calculation of the Reciprocal of the Wave Velocity for the First Prism.*

We now proceed to the measurements made to determine the position of the principal plane of the first prism, whose faces are P P$_1$.

->Fig. 2.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram on a black background showing a sphere with points A, B, C, M, M', and P connected by arcs representing great circles. Point C is at the top, A to the right, B and M/M' towards the bottom left, and P in the upper right quadrant.</image-desc>

Let A, B, and C be the points where the axes of the crystal intersect a sphere with its center at the origin.

Let M and M' be the poles of the $m$ faces of the crystal. M and M' lie on the great circle AB, and the angle MM' is known; also BM = BM'. Let P and P$_1$ be the poles of the cut faces of the prism.

Let
->PM = $\theta$, PM' = $\theta'$<-
->P$_1$M = $\theta_1$, P$_1$M' = $\theta'_1$<-

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles that OP makes with the axes.
Let MA = $\mu$.
From triangle PAM,
->cos PM = cos AP cos AM + sin AP sin AM cos PAM<-
or
->cos $\theta$ = cos $\alpha$ cos $\mu$ + sin $\alpha$ sin $\mu$ cos A<-

From PAM',
->cos $\theta'$ = cos $\alpha$ cos $\mu$ + sin $\alpha$ sin $\mu$ cos A<-
->$\therefore$ cos $\theta$ - cos $\alpha$ cos $\mu$ = cos $\theta'$ + cos $\alpha$ cos $\mu$<-
->$\therefore$ cos $\alpha$ = $\frac{\text{cos } \theta - \text{cos } \theta'}{2 \text{ cos } \mu}$<-
->$= \frac{\text{sin } \frac{\theta + \theta'}{2} \text{ sin } \frac{\theta' - \theta}{2}}{\text{cos } \mu}$ . . . . . . . . (1)<-

Again, from triangle P M B,
->cos PM = cos BP cos BM + sin BP sin BM cos PBM<-
or
->cos $\theta$ = cos $\beta$ sin $\mu$ + sin $\beta$ cos $\mu$ cos B<-
and from P B' M,
->cos $\theta'$ = cos $\beta$ sin $\mu$ - sin $\beta$ cos $\mu$ cos B<-
->$\therefore$ cos $\beta$ = $\frac{\cos \theta + \cos \theta'}{2 \sin \mu}$<-
->= $\frac{\cos \frac{\theta + \theta'}{2} \cos \frac{\theta' - \theta}{2}}{\sin \mu}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (2)<-

Now the angles $\theta$ and $\theta'$ were determined by observation.
Each angle was observed six times on two different days.
The mean of the results was:
->$\theta$ = 77° 18' 44"<-
->$\theta'$ = 100° 43' 30"<-

Some difficulty was experienced regarding the angle $\mu$.
Professor Miller gives it as 58° 5'; however, when substituted into the formulas above, this yields a value for P P, the supplement of the angle of the crystal, which differs considerably from the measured angle.
I therefore measured the angle $\mu$ and found it to be nearly 58° 30'.
Mr. Garnett (the Demonstrator at the Cavendish Laboratory) kindly communicated this result to the Rev. H. P. Gurney, of Clare College, who was then lecturing for Professor Miller, and he measured the angle with very nearly the same result as I had already reached. Taking, then, the value he obtained, and assuming as before that O B bisects the angle M O M', we have:
->$\mu$ = 58° 28'.*<-
From which, using formulas (1) and (2):
->$\alpha$ = 67° 10' 35" . . . . . . . . . . . . . (3)<-
->$\beta$ = 88° 52' 40" . . . . . . . . . . . . . (4)<-

For the position of P$_1$, we have similarly:
->$\theta_1$ = 80° 39'<-
->$\theta'_1$ = 101° 16' 23"<-
From which:
->$\alpha_1$ = 69° 59' 20" . . . . . . . . . . . . . (5)<-
->$\beta_1$ = 91° 6' 30" . . . . . . . . . . . . . (6)<-

We now come to the experimental determination of the deviation and the calculations of the refractive indices.
Throughout the work for this prism, $\phi$ represents the angle between the normal to the wave incident on or emerging from the face P when in air, and $\phi^\prime$ represents the corresponding angle in the crystal, while $\psi$ and $\psi^\prime$ are the angles for the face P <note>The text reads "face P," but likely refers to the second face of the prism, possibly designated P₁ in other sections</note>. I propose then to provide a table of the values of $\phi$ or $\psi$ according to whether the wave was incident on P or P.
(2.) Of D $+ i$, where $i$ is the angle of the prism. D $+ i$ is given because the expression $\frac{\phi + \psi}{2}$, which is equal to $\frac{\text{D} + i}{2}$, occurs in the formula, and it saved trouble to calculate D $+ i$ at once from the readings.
(3.) Of the values of $\phi^\prime$ deduced from the formulas

->$\tan \frac{\phi^\prime - \psi^\prime}{2} = \tan \frac{i}{2} \tan \frac{\phi - \psi}{2} \cot \frac{\phi + \psi}{2}$<-

proved in the first section, and $\phi^\prime + \psi^\prime = i$.
(4.) Of the values of $\mu$, the refractive index, as the mean of the results given by the two formulas

->$\sin \phi = \mu \sin \phi^\prime$<-
->$\sin \psi = \mu \sin \psi^\prime$<-

Any difference in the two values of $\mu$ found from these two formulas was due only to the errors necessarily arising from the use of proportional parts, and rarely exceeded $0.00001$.
I also introduce a list of errors in the calculated quantities which would occur from errors of $10^{\prime\prime}$ in each of the observed quantities, taken so as to produce the maximum effect on the result.
This list was obtained by recording from the tables the errors to which the assumed errors in D and $\phi$ would give rise.
The numbers in the table of errors for $\mu$ are the digits in the fifth decimal place.
The next page gives the complete work for one observation as a sample.

Section IV.—*Description of the Second Prism: Position of its Axes.—Observed Values of the Deviations and Angles of Incidence, and Calculation of the Reciprocals of the Wave Velocity.*

It will be remembered that, in describing the cutting of the crystal, I stated that a second prism was formed with its edge nearly parallel to *C*, and its faces not differing much from the *m* and *a* faces of the crystal.

->Fig. 4.<-

<image-desc>A diagram labeled Fig. 4 showing a cross-section of a crystal in the shape of an irregular hexagon with vertices labeled A, B, C, D, E, and F. Internal dashed lines indicate planes or zones within the crystal structure. Small triple-prime marks (''') are located near edges E, D, and F.</image-desc>

Let Fig. 4 represent a section of the crystal by a plane perpendicular to the *m* faces.
The traces of the faces of the second prism are AB and CD.
The greater part of the face AB lies in the twin crystal, so that the results for the second prism apply to that crystal.
On examination, the *m* face BC was seen to consist of two parts, which are not in the same plane.
Observation showed that the upper half (the prism being placed as in the figure) is in the same zone as the faces DE and EF, while the lower portion is considerably removed from this zone.
I also found that when the faces DE and EF were leveled, the line of junction of the dark and bright portions of the slit, when seen by reflection from AB, coincided with the needle point; so that AB is in the same zone as the *m* faces, while the reflection from CD, though in the field, was too high. Thus if *Q* and *Q1*, Fig. 5, are the points where the normal to AB, Fig. 4, and that to CD, Fig. 4, produced backwards meet the sphere of reference—with *A*, *B*, and *C*, Fig. 5, being the poles of the principal planes—*Q* lies on the great circle AMB, while *Q1* is slightly below it.
Let *M* and *M1'*, Fig. 5, be the points where the normal to EF, and that to ED produced backwards, cut the sphere. Then

->AM = AM1' = 58° 28'.<-

The mean of several observations gave for MQ = 103° 58'. Hence

->AQ = 45° 30' . . . . . . . . . (1)<-

The mean of the observations for MQ and M1' Q1 gave

->$\cos$ AQ$_1$ = $\frac{\cos \theta + \cos \theta'}{2 \cos \mu}$<-

where $\mu$ = AM = M$'$A.
From this, by substituting for $\theta$ and $\theta'$, we obtain

->AQ$_1$ = 2° 43' 20" . . . . . . . . . . . . (2)<-

->Fig. 5.<-

<image-desc>A white-on-black line diagram showing a sphere or circle with several intersecting arcs representing spherical triangles. Points are labeled C at the top, B on the left, and internal points M, A, M', Q, and Q1. The arcs connect these points to form geometric relationships on the surface of the sphere.</image-desc>

In the triangle MAQ, the three sides are known; from this, we can find the angle MAQ and obtain

->MAQ$_1$ = 76° 24' 45" . . . . . . . . . . . . (3)<-

In the triangle QAQ$_1$, the sides AQ, AQ$_1$, and the angle QAQ$_1$ are known:

->AQ = 45° 30'<-
->AQ$_1$ = 2° 43' 20"<-
->QAQ$_1$ = 103° 35' 15"<-

Thus, from the formula

->$\cos$ QQ$_1$ = $\cos$ AQ $\cos$ AQ$_1$ + $\sin$ AQ $\sin$ AQ$_1$ $\cos$ QAQ$_1$<-

we get

->QQ$_1$ = 46° 12' (or slightly less).<-

The mean of several experiments had already given a value for QQ$_1$ of

->46° 10'<-

These results, differing as they do by less than 2', provide a verification of the accuracy of the measurements.

<summary>This page uses spherical trigonometry to calculate the angular distance between two points in a biaxial crystal and compares the result to experimental data. The close agreement between the calculated value (46° 12') and the experimental mean (46° 10') verifies the precision of the author's measurements.</summary>

<page-num>304</page-num>

# MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.

The position of the plane Q Q$_1$ is completely determined by the arc A Q and the angle A Q Q$_1$; we have already found,

->AQ $= 45^\circ$ 30'<-

For the angle A Q Q$_1$, the triangle Q A Q$_1$ gives

->$\sin \text{AQQ}_1 = \frac{\sin \text{AQ}_1}{\sin \text{QQ}_1} \sin \text{QAQ}_1$<-

from which we get

->$\text{AQQ}_1 = 4^\circ$ 37' 20" . . . . . . . . . . . (4)<-

Thus, we see that the principal section of the second prism is inclined to the plane $c$ at an angle of $4^\circ$ 37' 20".

I mentioned above that the second prism lay in the twin crystal. This was proved by passing light through the crystal in a plane nearly parallel to the principal plane B C, when four images of the slit appeared. Upon cutting off the end containing the second prism, two images vanished; upon cutting off the other end, only the second pair vanished, and the first pair reappeared. The work for the first prism was conducted with the second pair, as the first pair was rarely sufficiently distinct for measurement.

Throughout the work, $\phi$ and $\phi'$ denote the angles that the normals to the incident or emergent wave and the wave in the crystal make with the normal to the face Q.

The same remarks regarding the reversal of the crystal hold true as in the case of the first prism.

### Section V.—*Determination of the Values of the Principal Indices.—Angle between the Optic Axes.*

Our next step is to determine the values of the refractive indices based on <term>FRESNEL'S theory</term>.

It has been shown (Section III) that the principal plane of the first prism intersects the plane $CAC'$ in a line inclined at an angle of $2^\circ 31' 58''$ to $OA$, and makes an angle of $1^\circ 12' 4''$ with that plane.

Let us consider the intersection of this plane and the plane $BC$, $B'C'$.

->Fig. 6.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a sphere with several intersecting great circles labeled with points A, B, B', C, C', M, M', P, and L. A central point O is indicated. The diagram illustrates the angular relationships between different planes and axes within a crystal structure.</image-desc>

It will be a line, say $MOM'$, inclined at $1^\circ 12'$, or slightly less, to $COC'$.

Take $OA$, $OB$, $OC$ as the axes of $x$, $y$, $z$, and let $\mu_a$, $\mu_b$, $\mu_c$ be the principal refractive indices, which are therefore the semi-axes of the wave-slowness surface.

The sections of the wave-slowness surface in <term>FRESNEL'S theory</term> through the plane $BOC$ are a circle of radius $\mu_a$ and an ellipse with axes $\mu_b$ and $\mu_c$ in the directions of $OC$ and $OB$ respectively.

Hence, the values of the radius vector in this direction provided by experiment—that is, the values of the refractive indices for light passing through the crystal in this direction—are $\mu_a$ and the radius vector of an ellipse with axes $\mu_b$ and $\mu_c$, inclined at about $1^\circ 12'$ to $\mu_b$.

To determine which of the experimental values of $\mu$ lies in this direction, we need to find $LM$, where $L$ is the point of intersection of $MM'$ and $AC'$.

From triangle $C'LM$, since $C'$ is a right angle:

->$\cos C'LM = \tan C'L \cot LM$<-

From which:

->$LM = 87^\circ 28' 4''$ . . . . . . . . . (1)<-

And if $OP$ is, as before, normal to the face $P$ of the first prism:

->$LP = 67^\circ 27' 25''$ [Section III. (8)].<-

From which:

->$MP = 20^\circ 0' 39''$ . . . . . . . . . (2)<-

<summary>This page describes the mathematical and geometric process for determining a crystal's principal refractive indices and the angle between its optic axes using Fresnel’s theory. It establishes the relationship between the experimental measurements and the axes of the wave-slowness surface.</summary>
<keywords>refractive indices, Fresnel's theory, wave slowness, biaxial crystal, principal plane, optic axes, trigonometry, geometry</keywords>

<page-num>308</page-num>
<header>MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.</header>

and MP measures the angle between the wave normal required in the crystal and the normal to the face P.

This is the angle we have denoted by $\phi'$.

From Tables II, III, VIII, and IX, we have corresponding values of:

| $\phi'$ | $\mu$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| 19° 32' 21'' | 1.68134 |
| 20° 34' 27'' | 1.68130 |
| 20° 28' 9'' | 1.68119 |
| 19° 29' 32'' | 1.68123 |

Other observations gave:

| $\phi'$ | $\mu$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| 19° 39' 22'' | 1.68126 |
| 20° 41' 22'' | 1.68129 |

Again, none of the experimental values of $\mu$ in Table III, lines 1 to 11, and Table IX, differ greatly from 1.68125, and this is not far from the mean of the six observations recorded above.

We take this, then, as the radius vector of an ellipse with axes $\mu_b$ and $\mu_c$, inclined at 1° 12' to $\mu_b$.

To determine $\mu_c$, we must have recourse to the second prism.

If the plane of the second prism coincided with that of $x$ and $y$, the values of $\mu$ in Table XXI would all be equal to $\mu_c$.

We shall consider later the effect of the inclination of the plane of the prism to that of $x$ and $y$, but for the present we may remark that the values in Table XXI differ little from 1.53013, the value of $\mu_c$ found by RUDBERG.

Let us take therefore:
->$\mu_c = 1.53013$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (3)<-

We then have in the plane BOC:
->$\frac{1}{\mu^2} = \frac{\cos^2 \theta}{\mu_b^2} + \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{\mu_c^2}$<-

$\theta$ being the angle between $\mu$ and $\mu_b$.

Now:
->$\mu = 1.68125$<-
->$\mu_c = 1.53013$<-
->$\theta = 1^\circ\ 12'$<-

From which:
->$\mu_b = 1.68132$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (4)<-

The value found by RUDBERG is 1.68157.

The difference is considerable, being 0.00025.

The author notes a significant discrepancy of 0.00025 between his calculated value for $\mu_b$ and Rudberg's findings.</summary>

We may note, however, that his values of $\mu_b$ deduced from two different pieces of crystal differed by 0.0004.
Now $\mu_a$ is the value of the refractive index for the first prism for wave E when

->$\phi' = 20^\circ\ 0'\ 39''$<-

The values of $\mu$ at about $30'$ on either side of this are

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| $1.68578$ | Table VI., | $1.68589$ |
| $1.68574$ | Table XII., | $1.68569$ |

The value

->$\mu_a = 1.68580$ . . . . . . . . (5)<-

seems to represent these fairly. Let us take it for now, and see how far it gives consistent results.
RUDBERG gives

->$\mu_a = 1.68589$<-

To verify these results, let us find the angle between the optic axes.
If $2\delta'$ is this angle in the crystal

->$\tan \delta' = \sqrt{ \frac{\frac{1}{\mu_b^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}}{\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_b^2}} }$<-

From which

->$\delta' = 9^\circ\ 4'\ 58''$ . . . . . . . . (6)<-

and if $2\delta$ is the angle in air as seen through a face normal to the least axis of the crystal

->$\sin \delta = \mu_b \sin \delta'$<-

from which

->$\delta = 15^\circ\ 23'\ 30''$ . . . . . . . . (7)<-

KIRCHOFF found $15^\circ\ 27'$ as the result of experiments.
The value provided by RUDBERG'S values of the indices is

->$\delta = 15^\circ\ 7'$<-

which differs from KIRCHOFF'S result by $20'$, whereas the value given above as the result of my experiments differs only by $3'\ 30''$.

Section VI.—*Calculation of the Reciprocal of the Velocity of Wave Propagation according to <term>FRESNEL'S Theory</term> for the First Prism and Comparison with Experiment.—The same for <term>Lord RAYLEIGH'S Theory</term>.*

We are now in a position to calculate the reciprocals of the velocity of wave propagation for the first prism based on the theory of FRESNEL.

->Fig. 7.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a unit sphere labeled with points A, A', B, B', O, O', L, M, N, and P. Several arcs intersect across the surface of the sphere, representing the traces of planes and optic axes.</image-desc>

Let O and O', in figure 7, be the points where the optic axes intersect a unit sphere.
Let LM be the trace of the principal plane of the prism, intersecting AC'A' at L and BC'B' at M.
Let N be any point in the plane where a wave normal meets the unit sphere.
Let
->NO=$\theta$   NO'=$\theta'$.<-
->C'LM=$\chi$=$1^\circ$ $12'$ [Section III. (9)].<-
->$\cos \theta = \cos \text{LN} \cos \text{OL} + \sin \text{LN} \sin \text{OL} \cos \chi = \frac{\cos \text{OL}}{\cos \lambda} \cos (\text{LN} - \lambda)$<-
if $\tan \lambda = \tan \text{OL} \cos \chi$.

Similarly
->$\cos \theta' = \frac{\cos \text{O'L}}{\cos \lambda'} \cos (\text{LN} - \lambda')$<-
if $\tan \lambda' = \tan \text{O'L} \cos \chi$.

Now
->AO = $90^\circ - 9^\circ$ $4'$ $58''$ [Section V. (6)].<-
->= $80^\circ$ $55'$ $2''$<-
->AL = $2^\circ$ $31'$ $58''$ [Section III. (10)].<-

->OL = $78^\circ$ $23'$ $4''$ . . . . . . . . . (1)<-

->O'L = $96^\circ$ $33'$ . . . . . . . . . (2)<-

from which

He establishes the trigonometric relationships required to apply the theories of Fresnel and Lord Rayleigh.</summary>

->$\lambda = 78^\circ\ 22'\ 55''$ . . . . . . . . . . (3)<-
->$\lambda' = 96^\circ\ 33'\ 5''$ . . . . . . . . . . (4)<-

Also, with $P_1$ being the point where the normal to the face $P_1$ meets the sphere:

->$\text{LN} = \text{LP}_1 + \text{P}_1 \text{N}$<-
->$= \text{LP}_1 + \phi'$<-
->$\text{LP}_1 = 67^\circ\ 27'\ 25''$ [Section III. (8)].<-
->$\text{LN} - \lambda = \text{LP}_1 + \phi' - \lambda$<-
->$= \phi' - 10^\circ\ 55'\ 30''$ . . . . . . . . . . (5)<-

->$\text{LN} - \lambda' = \text{LP}_1 + \phi' - \lambda'$<-
->$= \phi' - 29^\circ\ 5'\ 40''$ . . . . . . . . . . (6)<-

Again, if $v_1$ and $v_2$ are the velocities of propagation in the direction $\theta$ and $\theta'$, we know that:

->$v_1^2 + v_2^2 = a^2 + c^2 - (a^2 - c^2) \cos \theta \cos \theta'$<-
->$v_1^2 - v_2^2 = (a^2 - c^2) \sin \theta \sin \theta'$<-

Here, $a$ and $c$ have their usual meanings as the greatest and least principal velocities.
Hence:

->$2v_1^2 = a^2 + c^2 - (a^2 - c^2) \cos (\theta + \theta')$<-
->$2v_2^2 = a^2 + c^2 - (a^2 - c^2) \cos (\theta - \theta')$<-

From these formulas, we can find $v_1$ and $v_2$, and from there the values of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$, because:

->$\mu_1 = \frac{1}{v_1}$<-
->$\mu_2 = \frac{1}{v_2}$<-

Taking:

->$\mu_a = 1.68580$<-
->$\mu_c = 1.53013$<-
->$c^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} = 0.351876$<-
->$a^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} = 0.427117$<-

Tables XXV and XXVI give the results of the theory for the first prism.
Let us consider the outer sheet first.
In lines 1–12 of Table XXV and lines 1–10 of Table XXVI, the agreement between theory and experiment is fairly close, but these series of experiments overlap and are in the immediate vicinity of an axis of the section.
From this point onward, we see that the experimental curve lies entirely inside the one given by Fresnel's theory, and the difference between the two increases as we approach the vicinity of the optic axes (line 16 of Table XXV, and lines 14 and 15 of Table XXVI), while for the rest of Table XXV the differences diminish.
The tables extend from about 8° on one side of axis C to nearly 16° on the other. This is obvious, because between the optic axes $\theta - \theta'$ is used, while beyond them $\theta + \theta'$ is very approximately equal to twice NC.
Now let us consider the inner sheet. As before, in lines 1–14 of Table XXV and lines 1–11 of Table XXVI, the agreement is fairly close; however, these observations extend from about 6° on one side to 7° on the other side of the maximum radius vector of the section. As in the case of the outer sheet, the differences here increase as we approach the vicinity of the optic axes, reaching a maximum of .00044 in line 15 of Table XXVI.
After passing the optic axes, the differences decrease, and for the rest of Table XXV, they average about .00024; in this case, the curve produced by experiment lies outside the one produced by theory.
On examining the differences given in Table XXV for the outer sheet, I noticed that theory and experiment agree closely up to the immediate vicinity of the optic axis (line 16), while in the vicinity of the optic axis in Table XXVI (line 15), the increase in the differences is much more gradual.
In fact, if we compare the experimental values of $\mu_1$ in Table XXV, lines 11–14, and Table XXVI, 12–15, for roughly the same values of $\theta + \theta'$, we find considerable differences.
This led me to calculate the results of other sets of experiments covering the same ground that had been already conducted.
The following table gives the results of one such set, taken about two months previously; during that interval, the goniometer had been partially taken apart and was afterwards refocused and set again.
It seems worthwhile to provide the entire set of observations, which cover nearly the same ground as Table II and therefore serve as a test of the degree of accuracy of the results.
The measurements were made at angles of incidence that were nearly, but not quite, identical to those in Table II.
Therefore, in order to compare results as far as wave E (inner sheet) is concerned, a correction by interpolation is necessary.
The values of $\phi'$, it will be observed, differ by about 5' from those in Table II.
In the table, the first column gives the values of $\phi'$, and the second gives the values of $\mu$;

Let us now consider the results given in the latter part of the table for wave E. The two sets of observations recorded there were made under entirely different circumstances. The telescope and collimator of the goniometer were removed in the interval between them, and both were reset and refocused; and yet in only one case is the difference between the results of the two observations as great as 0.0001, while the average difference, regardless of sign, is about 0.00005.

This comparison serves as a strong test of the experiments' accuracy, and the close agreement of the results seems to show that the error in them is, at any rate, no greater than 0.00005.

It appears that more reliable results might have been obtained by combining the series of results recorded in this last table with those discussed throughout.

However, experiments covering the entire range included in the series we have chosen had not been performed at the same time previously.

Furthermore, we must remember that each value of $\phi$ and D + $i$, given in Tables I, IV, etc., is the mean of three measurements for the first prism and two for the second.

And, again, this comparison confirms that the difference between the experimental and theoretical results—amounting, as it does in some cases, to 0.0005 in the value of $\mu$—is far too great to have resulted from experimental errors or errors of observation.

It seems, then, that assuming the position of the prism's plane and the values of the principal axes are accurately determined, we may assert that in a central section of the wave surface inclined at a small angle to the plane of the optic

Near the axes, there is a considerable difference between Fresnel’s theory and experiment: the differences between the two are most marked in the neighborhood of the optic axes and amount to about 0.0005 there. For the outer sheet of the surface (except just in the neighborhood of the principal axes), the theoretical values of the radius vector are uniformly greater than the experimental values, while for the inner sheet, the reverse is the case.

In fact, the curves of the section of the surface, as given by experiment, approach one another more closely than those of the surface of wave slowness in Fresnel’s theory.

->Fig. 8.<-

<image-desc>A diagram labeled Fig. 8 showing a set of curved lines on a dark background. There are two solid white parabolic curves and two corresponding dotted white curves nested together, illustrating the comparison between theoretical and experimental wave surfaces.</image-desc>

In Figure 8 above, the dotted line shows the result of experiments, while the solid line shows the form of the section according to Fresnel’s theory.

To compare the results with those given by Lord Rayleigh’s theory, we have the equation to the surface, where $a, b, c$ are the principal velocities:

$$\frac{l^2}{\frac{V^2}{a^2}-1} + \frac{m^2}{\frac{V^2}{b^2}-1} + \frac{n^2}{\frac{V^2}{c^2}-1} = 0$$

Let $V = \frac{1}{r}$, where $r$ is a radius vector of the surface of wave slowness:

$$\frac{a^2l^2}{1-a^2r^2} + \frac{b^2m^2}{1-b^2r^2} + \frac{c^2n^2}{1-c^2r^2} = 0$$

Let us suppose as a first approximation that $m=0$; that is, that the plane of the prism coincides with a principal plane of the crystal:

$$a^2l^2(1-c^2r^2) + c^2n^2(1-a^2r^2) = 0$$
$$r^2a^2c^2 = a^2l^2 + c^2n^2$$
$$r^2 = \frac{l^2}{c^2} + \frac{n^2}{a^2}$$

Also $l = \cos \theta$ and $n = \sin \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $r$ and the maximum radius vector.

<summary>This page describes the discrepancies between Fresnel’s theoretical wave surface and experimental observations, particularly near the optic axes, and introduces Lord Rayleigh’s theory as an alternative mathematical framework for comparison.</summary>

->$$r^2 = \frac{1}{c^2} - \left( \frac{1}{c^2} - \frac{1}{a^2} \right) \sin^2 \theta$$<-

->$$\frac{1}{c^2} = 2.84192$$<-

->$$\frac{1}{c^2} - \frac{1}{a^2} = 0.50062$$<-

From these and the known values of $\theta$, $\mu$ or $r$ can be calculated. The table gives the result.

### Comparison between Lord Rayleigh’s Theory and Experiment.

| $\theta$ | $\mu$ Theory | $\mu$ Experiment | Excess of Theory over Experiment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1° 31' 10" | 1.68570 | 1.68568 | 0.00002 |

The differences between theory and experiment are so marked that it seems unnecessary to calculate the values of $\mu$ for smaller intervals in the values of $\theta$.

And although some of the apparent difference may be due to the error made in assuming the principal plane of the prism coincides with one of the crystal axes, that cannot account for the whole; for we have seen that in <term>Fresnel’s surface</term> the error made by the same assumption appears only in the fourth decimal place in the value of the <term>refractive index</term>, while the differences between <term>Lord Rayleigh’s theory</term> and experiment show themselves in the third place and tend to increase with $\theta$.

Thus, it seems clear that <term>Lord Rayleigh’s theory</term> does not account for the phenomena of <term>double refraction</term> in <term>aragonite</term>. This result agrees with that reached by <term>Professor Stokes</term> for <term>Iceland spar</term>.

### Section VII.—Effect of Varying Constants of Theory and Position of Plane of Prism with reference to Axes of Crystal.

It remains now to discuss the effects of variations in the values of the axes $a, b, c$. The values of $c$ and $b$ are determined directly from observation, and the agreement is closest in the neighborhood of these axes. Any alteration in them would especially affect that part of the section which lies between the optic axes, and for which the differences between theory and experiment are smallest; let us consider, therefore, a variation in the value of $a$.

<summary>This page compares Lord Rayleigh’s theory of double refraction with experimental data for aragonite, concluding that the theory's predictions are significantly less accurate than Fresnel’s theory. The author notes that the discrepancies are too large to be explained by minor orientation errors and matches observations previously made regarding Iceland spar.</summary>
<keywords>Lord Rayleigh, double refraction, aragonite, refractive index, Fresnel surface, Professor Stokes, Iceland spar, biaxial crystal</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical and experimental analysis of light waves in biaxial crystals, specifically examining the discrepancies between calculated theoretical values and experimental observations for the refractive index.</meta>

<page-num>319</page-num>
<header>MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.</header>

Such a variation would produce an alteration in the angle between the <term>optic axes</term>, and therefore in the values of $\theta$, $\theta'$ for any <term>wave normal</term>.

If, however, we take a wave normal at some distance from the optic axes, the values of $\theta$, $\theta'$ will be altered by nearly equal amounts in opposite directions, and $\theta + \theta'$ will remain nearly constant.

Let us then find the value for $a$ in order that the experimental value in line 29 of Table XXV may agree with theory.

We have
->$2v_1^2 = a^2 + c^2 - (a^2 - c^2) \cos (\theta + \theta')$<-
->$= a^2 \{ 1 - \cos (\theta + \theta') \}$<-
->$+ c^2 \{ 1 + \cos (\theta + \theta') \}$<-
->$\therefore a^2 = \frac{v_1^2 - c^2 \cos^2 \frac{\theta + \theta'}{2}}{\sin^2 \frac{\theta + \theta'}{2}}$<-
->$v_1 = \frac{1}{\mu_1}$<-
->$\mu_1 = 1.67274$<-
->$\theta + \theta' = 31^\circ \ 45' \ 40''$<-
->$c^2 = 0.351876$<-

From these we get
->$a^2 = 0.447553$<-
as against $0.427117$, and the value of $\mu_c$ is
->$\mu_c = 1.49478$<-
instead of ->$1.53013$<-

A reference to the tables for the second prism shows at once the impossibility of such a change.

It is true that any decrease in $\mu_c$ would produce a decrease in the angle between the <term>optic axes</term>. This would increase $\theta'$ and decrease $\theta$ by nearly equal amounts, and on the whole produce a small decrease in $\theta + \theta'$.

This change would decrease $v_1$ and therefore increase $\mu_1$, and hence to produce the required change in $\mu_1$—*i.e.*, to make $\mu_1$ equal to the experimental value in line 29—we must take a value for $\mu_c$ larger, but only slightly larger, than that given above.

There remains now for discussion the effect of a variation in the position of the plane of the prism with reference to the <term>crystallographic axes</term>.

We shall consider this by discussing separately the effect of a rotation about each of three lines through the center approximately at right angles. These lines are

<summary>Glazebrook calculates the theoretical value of the constant 'a' required to match experimental data, finding that the resulting refractive index for aragonite is physically improbable. He then shifts the investigation toward how the prism's orientation relative to the crystallographic axes might account for experimental discrepancies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into discrepancies between experimental refractive index values and theoretical calculations, specifically evaluating how adjustments to the prism's orientation or the angle $\chi$ might resolve these differences.</meta>

<page-num>320</page-num>
<header>MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.</header>

(1.) The normal to the principal plane of the prism; (2.) The intersection of this plane with the plane B C B'; (3.) The intersection of the principal plane with the plane A C A'.

(1.) Rotation about a normal to the principal plane of the prism.

This cannot produce the required effect; for although we can thus decrease the differences on one side of the maximum radius vector of the section, we increase those on the other side by about the same amounts.

(2.) Rotation about the intersection with B C B'.

This is of no use, because the effects produced on opposite sides of the maximum radius vector are again of an opposite kind.

(3.) There remains, therefore, only the rotation about the line of intersection with the plane C A C', or a variation in the angle $\chi$. This change must be such that the sections of the outer and inner sheets may be brought into closer proximity; $\chi$ must therefore be decreased.

Now, by referring to the tables of the experimental results, it will be seen that none of those in Table III, lines 1–11; Table VI, lines 16–29; and Table IX, lines 1–16, differ greatly from 1.68125.

If it were then permissible to neglect the angle $\chi$, this would be the value of $\mu_b$, and the other section would be, according to <term>FRESNEL's theory</term>, an ellipse of $\mu_a$, $\mu_c$.

In the abstract published in the ‘Proceedings of the Royal Society,’ No. 188, 1878, this was done, and a limit was assigned to the error thus introduced.

Professor <term>STOKES</term> has since pointed out that near the optic axes the limit is considerably too small, and this led me to the accurate calculation of the theoretical values of $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$ given above.

The effect of a decrease in the angle $\chi$ may, therefore, be estimated by referring to the calculations for the case in which we set $\chi = 0$.

The accompanying table gives the results, where $\theta$ is the angle between the wave normal and the major axis of the ellipse, which is given by:

->$\theta = \phi' - \theta_0$<-

where $\theta_0$ is the angle between the normal to the face of the prism and the major axis, and is:

->$= 20^\circ\ 0'\ 40''$ [Section V. (2)].<-

For about 10° on either side of the major axis (the passage across which is indicated by the dark line in the table), the results of theory and experiment agree fairly well.

The average difference, regardless of sign, is 0.000047 (if we neglect the values for $\theta = 2^\circ\ 30'\ 43''$ and for $\theta = 9^\circ\ 14'\ 14''$, which give a point on the circle of radius 1.68125), and in only two cases does the difference amount to 0.0001.

But when we come to values for $\theta$ greater than 11°, we see that the experimental value of $\mu$ is, as before, always greater than the theoretical, and that the difference increases with $\theta$, and at last becomes nearly the same as in Table XXV.

Thus, this change does not produce agreement between the two.

We may, however, briefly consider what alteration in $\mu_c$ would in this case bring theory and experiment more closely into agreement.

We have

->$\frac{1}{\mu^2} = \frac{\cos^2 \theta}{\mu_a^2} + \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{\mu_c^2}$<-

->$\therefore \delta\mu = \frac{\mu^3}{\mu_c^3} \sin^2 \theta \delta\mu_c$<-

Taking the last values on Table XXVIII.

->$\delta\mu = 0.00024$<-

->$\theta = 15^\circ\ 48'$<-

->$\mu = 1.67274$<-

->$\mu_c = 1.53013$<-

From which

->$\delta\mu_c = 0.00248$<-

so that the minor axis of the ellipse, which—having the same major axis as the experimental curve—would pass through the extreme experimental point, is

->$\mu_c = 1.53261$<-

instead of ->1.53013<-

And on referring to Table XXI, which gives the values of $\mu_c$ very approximately, we see that this value is quite out of the question.

Thus, a decrease in the angle $\chi$ will not produce the required effect.

Neither will an increase. For the first part of the inner sheet in Table III, and throughout Table IX, we must have the theoretical value of $\mu_1$ and therefore of $\theta + \theta'$ nearly constant; and this is clearly impossible along a plane section inclined at a finite angle to the plane of the optic axes.
