### Section VIII.—*The Theoretical Investigations for the Second Prism on <term>FRESNEL'S</term> Theory Compared with Experiment.*

Our next step is the theoretical investigation for the second prism.

Now, experiment has shown that this prism lies in the twin crystal; we must therefore find the axes of this crystal.

->Fig. 9.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled Fig. 9 showing a hexagonal section of a crystal. It contains several intersecting lines labeled with letters A, B, A', B', m, m', Q, and O. The lines represent axes and planes of symmetry within the crystal structure.</image-desc>

Let the figure represent a section of the crystal by a plane perpendicular to the axis O C.

The twinning takes place about an axis perpendicular to $m'$, and consists of a rotation through 180° about that axis.

Its effect, therefore, is to bring O B, Figure 9, into the position O B', where

->angle $mOB = mOB'$<-

that is, to turn the axes in the direction B to A, through an angle,

->$= 2(mOB) = 2(\frac{\pi}{2} - AOm)$<-
->$= \pi - 2\mu = 180^\circ - 116^\circ\ 56'$<-
->$= 63^\circ\ 4'$<-

and if Q is the point where the perpendicular on the face Q of the second prism meets the sphere, we know that

->AQ = 45° 30' <note>See Section IV. (1)</note>.<-

Hence, since AA' = 63° 4' and Q lies in plane A O B,
->A'OQ = 17° 34'. . . . . . . . . (1)<-

Now let A' B' C', Figure 10, be the points at which the new axes intersect the sphere, and let

Considering first the inner sheet, we see that theory and experiment agree closely. The greatest difference is $0.00013$; and in this case, by referring to the adjacent experimental values, it is clear that the value $1.53003$ is too small.

We must remember, however, that the investigations are concerned with that sheet of the wave slowness surface for which the section through the $x-y$ plane is a circle, and that the section considered is inclined at an angle of less than $5^\circ$ to this plane; so that the form of the curve of section differs very little from a circle. We may therefore reasonably suppose that any theory in which one of the principal sections of the wave slowness surface is a circle would also agree fairly closely with our results.

We therefore proceed to discuss the results for the outer sheet given in the table just preceding.

And here we see at once that there is a considerable difference between theory and experiment.

Moreover, from $\phi' = 12^\circ\ 16'\ 53''$ to $\phi' = 20^\circ\ 5'\ 38''$, the theoretical values of $\mu$ are uniformly greater than the experimental ones; while from $\phi' = 20^\circ\ 35'\ 20''$ to $\phi' = 31^\circ\ 42'\ 34''$ the reverse is the case.

The difference between the two generally increases uniformly, and in the last case is as great as $0.0005$.

For the values $\phi' = 19^\circ\ 13'\ 4''$ and $\phi' = 20^\circ\ 5'\ 38''$, theory and experiment agree closely.

To find the angle between any radius vector and the minimum one of the curve, we have to add the angle MQ, which is $17^\circ\ 37'\ 14''$, to the value of $\phi'$.

Let us call the angle QOP, $\theta$.

Then we see that for the angles $\theta = 0$, $\theta = 37^\circ$ (approximately), and $\theta = 90^\circ$, the curves given by theory and experiment agree.

From $\theta = 29^\circ\ 54'\ 7''$ to $\theta = 37^\circ$ (approximately), the theoretical curve lies outside the experimental one.

From $\theta = 37^\circ$ (approximately) to $\theta = 49^\circ\ 19'\ 48''$ the reverse is the case.

In the neighborhood of the axes the two must agree more closely.

These conditions would all be satisfied by a curve which agrees with <term>FRESNEL's</term> section at the extremity of the minimum radius vector; lies inside it for about $40^\circ$; then cuts <term>FRESNEL's</term> curve again, and lies outside for the rest of the quadrant, agreeing again at the extremity of the maximum radius vector.

At first sight there seems to be some discrepancy between this result and that already arrived at in Table XXV for the first prism.

But closer examination shows that the two results are corroborative.

For, in the first place, the observations tabulated there apply to the neighborhood of the major axis of the elliptic section.

For about $6^\circ$ on either side of this principal axis, the differences between theory and experiment are sometimes positive and sometimes negative; that is, within these limits <term>FRESNEL's</term> section satisfies the results of experiment; but in the last eighteen observations recorded there, the experimental value of $\mu_1$ is always greater than the theoretical.

Thus, the experimental results are represented by a curve that agrees with <term>Fresnel's</term> section near the major axis but, as we move 6° to 16° away from that axis, differs from that section and lies outside it.

This result—namely, that when moving away from the maximum radius vector, the curve produced by experiment lies outside the one predicted by theory—is exactly what we were led to by the work on the second prism.

The way the crystal was cut did not allow for observations to be taken near the minor axis of the ellipse in the case of the first prism.

Of course, it has been assumed here that the sections of the wave slowness surface made by the principal planes are curves of the same kind; or rather, the results of the experiment lead to this as a fact.

Lord <term>Rayleigh's</term> theory needs no further discussion here, because his curve, being the inverse of an ellipse, always lies outside the ellipse with the same axes and therefore cannot agree with the experiment.

### Section IX.—*Possibility of an Error in the Position of the Crystallographic Axes discussed.—No Section of the Wave Slowness Surface in <term>Fresnel's</term> Theory can agree with the experimental Results.*

However, the possibility remains that there is an error in determining the position of the prism faces, especially in the second case, with respect to the crystallographic axes.

The probability of any error is small, as the observations were repeated on several different occasions with nearly identical results.

To be certain, however, let us solve the inverse problem: given the two values, $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$, of the radii vectores of the wave slowness surface drawn in the same direction $l, m, n$ in the crystal, find $l, m, n$.

We have, as the equation to find $v$ in <term>Fresnel's</term> theory:

->$\frac{l^2}{v^2-a^2} + \frac{m^2}{v^2-b^2} + \frac{n^2}{v^2-c^2} = 0$<-

From which:

->$v^4 - v^2 \{ l^2(b^2+c^2) + m^2(c^2+a^2) + n^2(a^2+b^2) \} + l^2b^2c^2 + m^2c^2a^2 + n^2a^2b^2 = 0$<-

Therefore, if $v_1$ and $v_2$ are the roots of this equation (that is, the velocities for the same wave front):

->$v_1^2 v_2^2 = l^2b^2c^2 + m^2c^2a^2 + n^2a^2b^2$<-
->$v_1^2 + v_2^2 = l^2(b^2+c^2) + m^2(c^2+a^2) + n^2(a^2+b^2)$<-

but $n^2 = 1 - m^2 - l^2$

From which we get:

->$b^2l^2(c^2-a^2) + a^2m^2(c^2-b^2) = v_1^2 v_2^2 - a^2b^2$<-
->$l^2(c^2-a^2) + m^2(c^2-b^2) = v_1^2 + v_2^2 - a^2 - b^2$<-

From this,
-> $l^2(a^2 - c^2)(a^2 - b^2) = (a^2 - v_1^2)(a^2 - v_2^2)$ <-
-> $m^2(b^2 - c^2)(b^2 - a^2) = (b^2 - v_1^2)(b^2 - v_2^2)$ <-
-> $n^2(c^2 - a^2)(c^2 - b^2) = (c^2 - v_1^2)(c^2 - v_2^2)$ <-

From the tables for the second prism, we see that for the inner sheet for
-> $\phi' = 28^\circ\ 11'\ 21''\ \frac{1}{v_1} = 1\cdot53021$ <-

For the outer sheet,
-> $\phi' = 28^\circ\ 1'\ 21''\ \frac{1}{v_2} = 1\cdot68391$ <-

Since the value of $v_1$ changes very slowly, we can reasonably treat these two values for $\phi'$ as identical and substitute them into the formulas above.
We find
-> $\cos^{-1} n_1 = 49^\circ\ 35'$ <-
-> $\cos^{-1} m_1 = 40^\circ\ 27'$ <-

Again, for the inner sheet for
-> $\phi' = 38^\circ\ 2'\ 41''\ \frac{1}{v_1} = 1\cdot53037$ <-

For the outer sheet
-> $\phi' = 31^\circ\ 42'\ 34''\ \frac{1}{v_2} = 1\cdot68437$ <-

Treating these two as identical, we find
-> $\cos^{-1} n_2 = 55^\circ\ 44'$ <-
-> $\cos^{-1} m_2 = 34^\circ\ 23'$ <-

For the inner sheet for
-> $\phi' = 26^\circ\ 5'\ 11''\ \frac{1}{v_1} = 1\cdot53028$ <-

For the outer sheet
-> $\phi' = 26^\circ\ 19'\ 10''\ \frac{1}{v_2} = 1\cdot68378$ <-

From this,
-> $\cos^{-1} n_3 = 47^\circ\ 56'$ <-
-> $\cos^{-1} m_3 = 42^\circ\ 8'$ <-

We can justify treating the two values of $\phi'$ as the same by considering that $\mu_1$ varies at a rate of about $0.00001$ for $1^\circ$; therefore, the difference for $20'$ is negligible.

Now, the angle between the radius vectors in the first and second case cannot be less than

<summary>This page presents mathematical calculations using experimental data to determine the direction cosines of waves in a biaxial crystal. The author justifies treating slightly different refraction angles as identical due to the slow rate of change in the refractive index.</summary>
<keywords>biaxial crystal, plane waves, prism, inner sheet, outer sheet, radius vectors, refraction angle, direction cosines, Glazebrook</keywords>

--- Page 376 ---
<meta>This page concludes the comparison between experimental results and theoretical predictions for the wave slowness surface in a biaxial crystal, specifically focusing on the discrepancies found in Fresnel's theory.</meta>

<page-num>330</page-num>
<header>MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.</header>

->$\cos^{-1} n_2 - \cos^{-1} n_1$<-
*i.e.*,
->not less than $55^\circ\ 44' - 49^\circ\ 35'$<-
->or $6^\circ\ 9'$<-

But the angle between these radii is the difference between the two corresponding values of $\phi'$, or
->$= 31^\circ\ 42'\ 34'' - 28^\circ\ 1'\ 21''$<-
->$= 3^\circ\ 41'\ 13''$<-

Again, taking the second and third, the angle deduced from theory is not less than
->$\cos^{-1} n_2 - \cos^{-1} n_3$<-
->or $55^\circ\ 44' - 47^\circ\ 56'$<-
->or $7^\circ\ 48'$<-
but from experiment it is
->$31^\circ\ 42'\ 34'' - 26^\circ\ 19'\ 10''$<-
->$= 5^\circ\ 23'\ 24''$<-

In both these cases the angle, as given by theory, must be very much larger than that given by experiment. Thus, in order that the three pairs of values of $\mu_1, \mu_2$ may correspond to three radii of the surface of wave slowness on <term>Fresnel's theory</term>, the angles between them must be half as large again as they are found to be. Hence no section of the surface of wave slowness on <term>Fresnel's theory</term> can agree with the results of the experiments. We may remark, in addition, that the differences between consecutive values of $\mu$ for the outer sheet given by experiment are about double those given by theory.

After this investigation it seems unnecessary to discuss possible alterations in the position of the plane of the second prism, with a view to bringing the results of experiment more nearly into accordance with theory. While as regards the constants $a, b, c$, it has already been seen that they have received their most probable values.

Thus our results, so far as they go, point to the fact that <term>Fresnel's construction</term> does not represent Nature, and that some other theory must be sought to explain the phenomena of <term>double refraction</term>.

And as regards the rival theories already proposed, <term>Lord Rayleigh's</term>, we have seen, is even more at variance with observed appearances than <term>Fresnel's</term>, while I can hardly think that sufficient data have yet been collected to repay the labor of comparison with the theories of <term>Green</term> and <term>Cauchy</term>; for on account of the undetermined constants it would be necessary to force theory and experiment to agree in so many points that they must, of necessity, almost agree exactly along the small arcs investigated.

<summary>Glazebrook demonstrates that experimental measurements of wave angles in crystals significantly deviate from the predictions of Fresnel's theory. He concludes that neither Fresnel's nor Lord Rayleigh's theories accurately represent double refraction, though more data is needed to evaluate the theories of Green and Cauchy.</summary>

<keywords>R. T. Glazebrook, Fresnel's theory, wave slowness, double refraction, Lord Rayleigh, Green, Cauchy, biaxial crystal, refractive index, experimental physics</keywords>

### PART II.

### Section I.*—*Description of a Second Crystal and Results of Experiments.*

Before requesting permission to present the results obtained in the previous part of the paper to the Society, I thought it would be better, if possible, to repeat the investigation using a second piece of the crystal. With some difficulty, I obtained a suitable piece last February from A. Hilger, of Tottenham Court Road.

Like the previous piece, it was shaped as a hexagonal prism, but with a considerably smaller cross-section.

->Fig. 1.<-

<image-desc>A white-line diagram on a black background showing a three-dimensional hexagonal prism. The vertices and faces are labeled with letters: m, m', a, a', and c. Dotted lines indicate the internal structure and axes of the crystal.</image-desc>

The axis of the prism was parallel to the axis of *c*, with the base being perpendicular to the axis, while the top was broken off at an angle.

The planes *m* and *m'* provided the best reflections and were therefore chosen to determine the position of the artificial faces.

My main goal in having the prism cut was to obtain as long a continuous arc on the wave surface as possible. To achieve this, I had a face R (Fig. 2) polished to be as nearly aligned with *c* as possible.

->Fig. 2.<-

<image-desc>A white-line diagram on a black background showing a more complex crystal shape with an oblique cut. The diagram includes labels for faces and directions: P, Q, R, m, m', a, and a'. Dotted lines show the internal geometry and the orientation of the cut face P relative to face R.</image-desc>

The angled end was cut (P, Fig. 2) so as to be inclined at about 37° to R; the edge of the prism thus formed between P and R was nearly parallel to the intersection of *m* and *c*.

<margin>
\* Note: Because the two parts are entirely distinct, the numbering of the sections and figures begins again in Part II.
</margin>

The face $m_1$ was cut so as to be inclined at about 35° 20' to P. The line of intersection of this face (Q, fig. 2) and P was also nearly parallel to the intersection of P and R.

Consequently, the principal planes of the prisms formed by P and R, and P and Q respectively, were nearly coincident. Since my observations extended from almost perpendicular incidence on Q to perpendicular incidence on R, they covered an arc of over 70°.

The instrument used and the methods adopted for leveling, reading, etc., were fully described in the previous part of the paper.

The results of the experiments are contained in Tables I, II, III, and IV.

Tables I and II refer to the prism RP.

$\phi$ is the angle formed by the wave normal in air with the normal to P.

$\phi'$ is the corresponding angle in the crystal.

D is the observed deviation.

$i$ is the angle of the prism.

D + $i$ is provided because it was used in the calculation and was as easily determined as D.

The value used for $i$ is

->$i = 37^\circ\ 2'\ 56''$<-

This value is the average of twelve observations, none of which differed from the average by more than 10".

$\phi'$ is determined from the formulas $\phi' + \psi' = i$

->and $\tan \frac{\phi' - \psi'}{2} = \tan \frac{i}{2} \cot \frac{\phi + \psi}{2} \tan \frac{\phi - \psi}{2}$<-

which was already proven in Part I, Section I.

In Table I, $\phi$ is the same for both the outer and inner sheets, as it is the angle of incidence.

In Table II, $\phi$ has different values for the two sheets because it is the angle of emergence; as previously explained, upon passing through the position of minimum deviation, the prism was reversed so that the face of incidence became the face of emergence.

Throughout this work, $\mu_1$ refers to the inner sheet and $\mu_2$ to the outer sheet.

The values of $\delta\phi'$ and $\delta\mu$ are calculated as before, assuming errors of 10" in $2\phi$ and D + $i$, which were the observed quantities; these errors were combined to produce the greatest possible effect on the result.

Tables III and IV refer to PQ, for which $i = 35^\circ\ 18'\ 50''$.

The symbols have the same meanings, but whereas in Tables I and II the wave normal falls on the same side of the normal to P as the axis OC, in Tables III and IV it falls on the other side of OP.

In Table III, $\phi$ is the angle of emergence and is therefore different for the inner and outer sheets; in Table IV, it is the angle of incidence and is the same for both.

Each observation was repeated twice on different occasions; the results of the two measurements rarely differed by more than 20'.

### Section II.—*Determination of the Position of the Planes of the Prism P R with reference to the Axes of Elasticity.*

To compare these results with theory, we must accurately determine the position of the principal planes of the two prisms. We will consider the prism with faces P and R first.

Let OA, OB, and OC be the directions of the principal axes of the wave surface. OB bisects the angle between the faces $m$ and $m'$, and OC is parallel to the intersection of these faces.

Let the normals to the faces $m$ and $m'$ intersect a unit sphere, with center O, at points M and M'. Let the normal to face P be at P, and the normal to face R be at R.

Let the direction angles of P and R with reference to A, B, and C be $\alpha_1, \beta_1, \gamma_1$ and $\alpha_2, \beta_2, \gamma_2$, respectively.

[P lies in quadrant ABC, and R lies in A'BC'.]

->Fig. 3.<-

<image-desc>A spherical projection diagram labeled Fig. 3. It shows a circle representing a unit sphere with axes A, A', C, and C'. Points P, R, M, M', and B are plotted on the surface of the sphere, connected by various arcs representing great circles. Point P is in the upper right quadrant, R is in the lower left quadrant.</image-desc>

Let
->$\text{PM} = \theta_1, \text{PM}' = \theta_1'$<-
->$\text{RM} = \theta_2, \text{RM}' = \theta_2'$<-

Observations of the angles between P and $m$, and between P and $m'$, provide $\theta_1$ and $\theta_1'$, respectively. Similarly, observations of the angles between R and $m$, and between R and $m'$, provide $\theta_2$ and $\theta_2'$, respectively.

Let
->$\text{MM}' = 2\mu = 2\text{MB}.$<-

Then, as in the first part, from triangles M'BP and MPB, we obtain:

$$\cos \beta_1 = \frac{\cos \frac{\theta_1' + \theta_1}{2} \cos \frac{\theta_1' - \theta_1}{2}}{\cos \mu} \text{ . . . . . . . (1)}$$

$$\cos \alpha_1 = \frac{\sin \frac{\theta_1' + \theta_1}{2} \sin \frac{\theta_1' - \theta_1}{2}}{\cos \mu} \text{ . . . . . . . (2)}$$

with similar formulas for $\beta_2$ and $\alpha_2$.

The mean of the observations gives:

->$\theta_1 = 54^\circ\ 17'\ 6''$. . . . . . . . . . . . (3)<-
->$\theta_1' = 75^\circ\ 16'\ 20''$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (4)<-
->$\theta_2 = 88^\circ\ 40'\ 35''$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (5)<-
->$\theta_2' = 88^\circ\ 20'\ 20''$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (6)<-
->$\mu = 31^\circ\ 53'\ 30''$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (7)<-

In no case was the difference between the mean and any one of the observations greater than $20''$.

Substituting these values, we find:

$\left. \begin{aligned} \alpha_1 &= 71^\circ\ 49'\ 30'' \\ \beta_1 &= 60^\circ\ 25'\ 49'' \end{aligned} \right\}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (10)

$\left. \begin{aligned} \alpha_2 &= 90^\circ\ 19'\ 10'' \\ \beta_2 &= 88^\circ\ 14'\ 32'' \end{aligned} \right\}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (11)

Also,
->$\sin^2 \gamma_1 = \cos^2 \alpha_1 + \cos^2 \beta_1$<-
->$\sin^2 \gamma_2 = \cos^2 \alpha_2 + \cos^2 \beta_2$<-

from which:
->$\gamma_1 = 35^\circ\ 42'\ 57''$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (12)<-
->$\pi - \gamma_2 = 1^\circ\ 47'\ 11''$ . . . . . . . . . . . . (13)<-

Let RO meet the sphere again at R', and let the figure represent the sphere as seen by an eye looking along OC extended.

We now have sufficient data to calculate the angle R'P.

->CP = $\gamma_1$<-
->AP = $\alpha_1$<-
->BP = $\beta_1$<-
->CR' = $\pi - \gamma_2$<-
->AR' = $\pi - \alpha_2 = 89^\circ\ 40'\ 50''$<-
->B'R' = $\beta_2$.<-

From triangle B'AR'

->cos B'R' = cos B'AR' sin AR'<-
->Therefore, cos B'AR' = $\frac{\text{cos B'R'}}{\text{sin AR'}}$<-
->= $\frac{\text{cos }\beta_2}{\text{sin }\alpha_2}$<-

from which

->B'AR' = $88^\circ\ 14'\ 32''$<-
->Therefore, R'AC = $1^\circ\ 45'\ 28''$<-

From triangle CAP

->cos CP = cos CAP sin AP<-
->Therefore, cos CAP = $\frac{\text{cos CP}}{\text{sin AP}}$<-
->Therefore, CAP = $31^\circ\ 17'\ 20''$<-
->Therefore, R'AP = $33^\circ\ 2'\ 48''$<-

From triangle R'AP

->cos R'P = cos R'A cos AP + sin R'A sin AP cos R'AP<-
->= cos ($\pi - \alpha_2$) cos $\alpha_1$ + sin ($\pi - \alpha_2$) sin $\alpha_1$ cos R'AP<-

from which

->R'P = $37^\circ\ 2'\ 53''$<-

But R'P can be measured directly; the mean of twelve observations, none of which differed from the mean by more than $10''$, gave

->R'P = $37^\circ\ 2'\ 56''$<-

The close agreement between these results confirms the accuracy of the values of $\alpha_1, \beta_1,$ etc.

Let PR' intersect CA at L; we proceed to determine CL, R'L, and the angle ALP.

From triangle AR'L

->cot AL sin AR' = cot AR'P sin R'AC + cos AR' cos R'AC<-
->Therefore, cot AL sin $\alpha_2$ = cot AR'P sin R'AC + cos $\alpha_2$ cos R'AC<-

### Section IV.—General Theory.

To apply these results to the theoretical calculation:
Taking the same figure,

->Fig. 7.<-

<image-desc>A white-on-black geometric diagram showing a quadrant of a circle or sphere. A vertical line AC contains points O', L, C, and O. A horizontal line CB meets it at C. A curved arc connects A and B. A point N is plotted on the arc, with lines connecting it to points on the vertical axis, forming angles and spherical triangles.</image-desc>

Let the optic axes cut the sphere at O and O'; consider a plane cutting the plane AOC between C and O' at a point, let us say L; let N be any point on it; let angle NLA = $\chi$, NO = $\theta$, and NO' = $\theta'$.
Then we know that if $v_1$ and $v_2$ are the velocities along the wave normal through N, and $a$, $b$, and $c$ are the principal velocities, with $a$ being the greatest:

$v_1^2 - v_2^2 = (a^2 - c^2) \sin \theta \sin \theta'$
$v_1^2 + v_2^2 = (a^2 + c^2) - (a^2 - c^2) \cos \theta \cos \theta'$
$2v_1^2 = (a^2 + c^2) - (a^2 - c^2) \cos (\theta + \theta') \dots \dots \dots \dots (1)$
$2v_2^2 = (a^2 + c^2) - (a^2 - c^2) \cos (\theta - \theta') \dots \dots \dots \dots (2)$

We therefore require the values of $\theta$ and $\theta'$.
Now,
$\cos \theta = \cos \text{OL} \cos \text{LN} - \sin \text{OL} \sin \text{LN} \cos \chi$
$= \cos \text{OL} (\cos \text{LN} - \tan \text{OL} \sin \text{LN} \cos \chi)$
$= \frac{\cos \text{OL}}{\cos \lambda} \cos (\text{LN} + \lambda) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3)$

if
$\tan \lambda = \tan \text{OL} \cos \chi$

Similarly,
$\cos \theta' = \frac{\cos \text{O'L}}{\cos \lambda'} \cos (\text{LN} - \lambda') \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4)$

where
$\tan \lambda' = \tan \text{O'L} \cos \chi$.

Thus, to use the formulas for $v_1$ and $v_2$, we require to know the position of the optic axes accurately.

<summary>This section establishes the general theoretical formulas for calculating wave velocities in a biaxial crystal based on the positions of the optic axes. It utilizes spherical trigonometry to relate the wave normal's position to the principal velocities of the crystal.</summary>

<keywords>optic axes, wave normal, principal velocities, biaxial crystal, Glazebrook, wave velocity, spherical trigonometry</keywords>

--- Page 390 ---
<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of wave velocities in a biaxial crystal, shifting from the general formulas to the specific calculation of principal refractive indices based on experimental data.</meta>

<page-num>344</page-num>
<header>MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.</header>

These can only be determined by finding the values of $a, b, c$.
The results of the experiments enable us to do this with considerable accuracy.
Let $\mu_a, \mu_b, \mu_c$ be the principal refractive indices, with $\mu_a$ being the greatest and $\mu_c$ the least:

->$\mu_a = \frac{1}{c}$<-

->$\mu_b = \frac{1}{b}$<-

->$\mu_c = \frac{1}{a}$<-

### Section V.— *Values of the Principal Refractive Indices.*

We are now in a position to determine the values of the principal velocities $a, b, c$ from our experimental results.
The plane $PR'$ cuts the plane $AC$ at a short distance from $C$.
The section of the wave-slowness surface by the plane $AOC$ consists of a circle of radius $\mu_b$ and an oval curve with axes $\mu_a$ and $\mu_c$ in the directions $OC$ and $OA$ respectively, which for a small distance on either side of a principal axis may be treated as an ellipse, as in Fresnel's theory.
Also, if $L$ is the point where $PR'$ cuts the plane $AOC$:

->LP $= 35^\circ\ 0'\ 19''$<-

<note>See Section II (16).</note>
The value of $\mu$ corresponding to a value of $\phi' = 35^\circ\ 0'\ 19''$ in Table I for the inner sheet will thus be the value of $\mu_b$.
However, we have the following corresponding values:

| $\phi'$ | $\mu$ |
|---------|-------|
| $34^\circ\ 28'\ 43''$ | $1.68115$ |
| $34^\circ\ 53'\ 57''$ | $1.68114$ |
| $35^\circ\ 16'\ 20''$ | $1.68115$ |

we may therefore take:

->$\mu_b = 1.68115.$<-

The values of the radius vector to the outer sheet in the same neighborhood are, from Table I, lines 4 and 5:

We know that if O and O' are the points where the optic axes intersect the unit sphere K, then the point where any wave normal meets the sphere is defined by:

->KO = $\theta$<-
->KO' = $\theta'$<-

->$$2v^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} \right) \cos (\theta - \theta')$$<-

->$$\therefore \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} (1 + \cos (\theta - \theta'))$$<-

->$$= \frac{2}{\mu^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} (1 - \cos (\theta - \theta'))$$<-

->$$\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} \cos^2 \left( \frac{\theta - \theta'}{2} \right) = \frac{1}{\mu^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \sin^2 \left( \frac{\theta - \theta'}{2} \right) . . . . . . . (4)$$<-

If we can then determine $\theta - \theta'$, since $\mu$ is provided by experiment, this formula determines the value of $\mu_c$.

Now along the plane XY, $\theta - \theta'$ is very small, and a considerable change in the positions of O and O' will produce only small variations in the value of $\theta - \theta'$ and therefore in the value of $\mu_c$.

->$\mu_c = 1.53013$<-

Let us first consider the inner sheet.

In Table V, we see that the differences are small at the beginning and increase fairly regularly throughout the whole table, with the experimental value being almost always less than the theoretical one.

Lines 4, 5, and 6 were chosen to determine the value of $\mu_b$, which explains why the two curves coincide in that neighborhood. The table covers an arc of the surface of nearly 20°, as seen by referring to the values of $\phi'$ in Table I.

Throughout this arc, the theoretical section lies outside the experimental one, with the difference between the two increasing as we proceed from the $\mu_b$ axis.

This continues throughout Table VI.

The first three lines of Table VI just overlap the last three of Table V. The difference reaches a maximum value toward the end of Table VI at a point where $\phi' =$ 1° 19' 54'' (see Tables II, 21, and VI, 21), which is about 34° away from the $\mu_b$ axis.

After this, the difference begins to decrease—slowly at first—throughout Table VII, which refers to the other prism, PQ. Thus, the arc of the section has changed slightly between Tables VI and VII, though both arcs pass through point P.

Table VII covers an arc of 22° (Table III).

The first two lines in Table VII refer to a wave normal lying on the same side of P as L. In the rest of the table, the wave normal is on the side of P far from L.

This arc continues throughout Table VIII; the theoretical values of $\mu$ are still greater than the experimental values, but the difference diminishes as we proceed along the arc.

The last three observations in Table VII and the first three in Table VIII overlap.

Table VIII covers an arc of 20°.

Thus, the observations extend over two arcs, each passing through point P and inclined toward each other at that point at such a small angle as to be almost continuous; one arc is 35° 40' and the other is 40° 40' in length.

The results of theory and experiment agree at the end of the first arc, differ most widely in the neighborhood of the point where the two arcs meet, and tend toward equality again throughout the second arc.

It is worth noting that the experimental results at the end of Table VI (the end of the first arc) agree closely with those at the beginning of Table VII (the beginning of the second arc).

The experimental results for the inner sheet are therefore represented by a curve that coincides with <term>FRESNEL's curve</term> at the end of one axis and lies inside it throughout the next 75° of its length.

For the outer sheet, the differences are less than for the inner sheet.

$\theta - \theta'$ varies so slowly that it seemed sufficient for comparison purposes to calculate every fifth theoretical value, with the exception of that portion of Table V for which the variations of $\theta - \theta'$ are noticeable.

### Section VII.—*Effect of Possible Errors in the Values of $\mu_a, \mu_b, \mu_c$ Discussed.*

The next task will be to determine the effect of any small errors which may have occurred:
(1) In the determination of $\mu_a, \mu_b, \mu_c$;
(2) In the angles which fix the position of the planes PR and PQ relative to the axes of the surface.

(1) $\mu_a$. To determine $\mu_a$, we considered the length of the radius vector common to the principal section AOC and the section by the plane PR. This radius vector is fixed in length, and is, according to <term>Fresnel’s theory</term>, the radius vector of an ellipse with axes $\mu_a$ and $\mu_c$, inclined at a small angle to $\mu_a$.

An increase in the value of $\mu_a$ will therefore increase the value of this angle; that is, it will alter the position of the plane PLR' and be more properly considered under (2).

$\mu_b$ is determined by the intersection of the section of the inner sheet by the plane PR with a circle of radius $\mu_b$, and is therefore fixed, at least within the limits of experimental error.

$\mu_c$ is found from an independent and, on the whole, less trustworthy series of observations—less trustworthy because the faces were much less flat than P, Q, and R.
Let us consider the effect of decreasing the value of $\mu_c$.
If $\epsilon$ is the angle between the optic axes:

<image-desc>A mathematical formula for the tangent of epsilon. It shows tan epsilon equals the square root of a fraction. The numerator is (1 over mu_b squared) minus (1 over mu_a squared). The denominator is (1 over mu_c squared) minus (1 over mu_b squared).</image-desc>

$$\tan \epsilon = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{\mu_b^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}}{\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_b^2}}}$$

As $\mu_c$ decreases, $\tan \epsilon$ decreases; therefore, $\epsilon$ decreases.
Let us consider how this affects $\theta$ and $\theta'$.

<summary>Glazebrook compares the experimental results of the outer wave sheet with theoretical predictions and begins evaluating how potential errors in the refractive indices affect these calculations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the geometric and mathematical analysis of the propagation of plane waves in a biaxial crystal, specifically examining how changes in specific parameters like refractive indices affect the wave's properties.</meta>

<page-num>360</page-num>
<header>MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.</header>

Taking the same figure as previously.

->Fig. 12.<-
<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled Fig. 12 showing a vertical line AC with points O, O', L, R, C, and O_1. Arcs and lines connect these points to points N, P, K, m, and n on the right side of the vertical axis. The background of the diagram is dark with white lines and lettering.</image-desc>

Let O' K be an arc perpendicular to AC.
Let O, $O_1'$ be the new positions of O, O'.
Then
->$\text{O}_1\text{O} = \text{O}_1'\text{O}' = \delta\epsilon$<-

Let O, $m$, and O' $n$ be perpendicular to NO and $NO_1'$ respectively.

->O'L = 7° approximately<-
->O'LP = 60° approximately<-
->$\therefore$ LK = 14° approximately<-

Let N fall between P and K.

->$\delta\theta = -Om = -\delta\epsilon \cos \text{NOL}$<-
->$\delta\theta' = \text{O}_1'n = \delta\epsilon \cos \text{NO}_1'\text{A}$<-
->$\delta(\theta + \theta') = -\delta\epsilon (\cos \text{NOL} - \cos \text{NO}_1'\text{A})$<-

Thus $\delta(\theta + \theta')$ is negative and decreases numerically as we approach P; for angles NOL and $NO_1'A$ become more nearly equal.
Thus, between K and P, $\theta + \theta'$ decreases with $\epsilon$.
Between L and K, both $\theta$ and $\theta'$ decrease; therefore, $\theta + \theta'$ decreases *a fortiori*; but $\delta(\theta + \theta')$ is always numerically less than $2\delta\epsilon$.
Let us see how these changes affect $\mu_1$.
We have [Section IV. (1)]

->$\frac{2}{\mu_1^2} = \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta + \theta').$<-

If $\mu_c$ is decreased, $\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}$ is increased, $\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}$ is increased, and $\theta + \theta'$ is decreased.
Therefore $\cos (\theta + \theta')$ is increased so long as $\theta + \theta'$ is less than 90°.

<meta>MDCCCLXXIX.</meta>

Therefore, $(\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}) \cos (\theta + \theta')$ increases as long as $\theta + \theta'$ is less than 90°.

And the increase in $(\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}) \cos (\theta + \theta')$ is greatest when $\theta + \theta'$ is smallest.

Also, the increase in $(\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}) \cos (\theta + \theta')$ is less than the increase in $(\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_a^2})$.

Therefore, $\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} - (\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}) \cos (\theta + \theta')$ increases, and this increase is greatest when $\theta + \theta'$ is largest.

Therefore, as $\theta + \theta'$ increases up to 90°, $\mu_1$ decreases.

When $\theta + \theta'$ is greater than 90°, $\cos (\theta + \theta')$ is negative.

As $\theta + \theta'$ increases, $\cos (\theta + \theta')$ increases in magnitude.

Therefore, $(\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}) \cos (\theta + \theta')$ increases in magnitude and is negative.

Therefore, $\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} - (\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2}) \cos (\theta + \theta')$ increases all the more.

Therefore, $\mu_1$ decreases.

Thus, the effect of decreasing $\mu_c$ is to cause a decrease in the value of $\mu_1$, and this decrease continually grows as we move from L to Q.

Now, if we compare the differences between the theoretical and experimental values of $\mu_1$ given in Tables V and VI, we see that they increase with $\theta + \theta'$, where the theoretical value exceeds the experimental one.

The effect of the assumed change in the value of $\mu_c$ would be to decrease the theoretical value of $\mu_1$ by an amount that constantly increases; that is, to bring it into closer agreement with experiment.

But the effect in Tables VII and VIII would be the opposite.

On referring to them, we see that the differences between theory and experiment continually decrease.

The effect of the proposed change would be to subtract a quantity from the theoretical value of $\mu_1$ given in those tables—a quantity that increases rapidly as we move further from L.

The result would be that the theoretical value would soon become less than the experimental value, and the difference between the two would continually increase.

It is true that we could choose the decrease of $\mu_c$ so as to make the ends of the arcs under consideration coincide; the differences would then be reduced throughout. The effect of this would be to cause the theoretical section to lie outside the experimental one for about 75°, then cross it and lie inside it.

Whether the two could again be made to coincide when intersecting the plane A O B, only experiment could determine.

Let us now consider the effect of the supposed change on $\mu_2$.

We have:

->$\frac{2}{\mu_2^2} = \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta - \theta')$.<-

We have seen that $\theta$ is decreased by the change. $\theta'$ is at first decreased, though by less than $\theta$; afterward, it is increased. Therefore, for any point on the curve LP, the value of $\theta - \theta'$ is decreased by this alteration. Therefore, $\cos (\theta - \theta')$ is increased. 

The value $\left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta - \theta')$ is increased, though by less than the increase in $\left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right)$. In other words, the variation in $\mu_2$ is in the same direction as the variation in $\mu_1$. But since $\theta - \theta'$ is less than $\theta + \theta'$, then $\left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta - \theta')$ is greater than $\left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta + \theta')$.

And the total change in

->$\frac{1}{\mu_c^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta - \theta')$<-

is much less than the total change in

->$\left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta + \theta')$.<-

In other words, the decrease in $\mu_2$ is small compared with the decrease in $\mu_1$. Again, as the variation in $\theta - \theta'$ varies from zero at L to a maximum near K, while $\cos (\theta - \theta')$ also varies considerably, the variation in $\mu_2$ will be considerably different for different points between L and K.

After passing K, however, $\theta - \theta'$ is nearly constant all along the curve. The change in the value of $\mu_2$, therefore, will not differ much for different points—that is, for different waves. The overall effect of the alteration, therefore, will be to decrease the theoretical value of $\mu_2$ throughout; this decrease is greatest around Table V, line 23.

In the greater part of Table V, the result will be a closer agreement between theory and experiment. But in the remainder of the work, since the theoretical value of $\mu_2$ is less than the experimental value, the effect will be to increase the difference between the two and thus widen the discrepancy between theory and experiment.

Thus, considering both sheets, we cannot produce a closer overall agreement between theory and experiment by decreasing the value of $\mu_c$. Nor can we do so by increasing it. For although we might produce closer agreement for the outer sheet by increasing it in this way...

### Section VIII.—*Effect of Change in Position of Planes of Prisms with reference to the Principal Planes of the Crystal.*

We have now to discuss the effect of small variations in the position of the planes PR and PQ.

We take PR first, and we consider its position as determined by CL and the angle ALP, while the position of the normals to P and R is fixed by PL (<note>see Section II.</note>).

->Fig. 13.<-

Now variations in CL and ALP produce variations in OL, O'L, $\lambda$, $\lambda'$, etc., and hence in $\theta$ and $\theta'$, while variations in LP only change $\theta$ and $\theta'$, with OL, O'L, $\lambda$, and $\lambda'$ remaining constant.

Let us consider, therefore, the variations of LP first.

A reference to our tables shows us that through the greater part of the arcs LP, PQ', $\theta - \theta'$ is constant, so that $\delta\theta$ considered as dependent on LP is nearly equal to $\delta\theta'$.

Again,

$$\frac{2}{\mu_1^2} = \left( \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} \right) - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta + \theta')$$

$$\frac{2}{\mu_2^2} = \left( \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} \right) - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta - \theta')$$

and since the change in $(\theta - \theta')$ due to a small increment of LP is very small, such an increment will not alter the value of $\mu_2$.

But if $\theta - \theta'$ is nearly constant for a small motion along LP, then $\theta + \theta'$ will be nearly constant for a small motion perpendicular to LP.

Thus, a small motion perpendicular to PL will not appreciably alter the value of $\mu_1$;

We may therefore obtain corrections to $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ independently: to $\mu_1$ by assuming an increase in the value of LP, and to $\mu_2$ by assuming that the planes PR and PQ turn through a small angle about some line within them.

To find the variation we must assume in LP to bring the theoretical and experimental results into closer agreement for the inner sheet, we proceed as follows:

If in the equation

->$$\frac{2}{\mu_1^2} = \left( \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} + \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} \right) - \left( \frac{1}{\mu_c^2} - \frac{1}{\mu_a^2} \right) \cos (\theta + \theta')$$<-

we substitute an experimental value for $\mu_1$, we can determine a value of $(\theta + \theta')$. By subtracting this from the calculated value, we obtain $\delta(\theta + \theta')$.

Hence we have found $\delta\theta$; but $\cos (\text{LN} - \lambda) = \frac{\cos \lambda}{\cos \text{OL}} \cos \theta$. Since OL and $\lambda$ are unaltered by the assumed displacement, we obtain $\delta(\text{LN})$, and since $\text{LP} = \text{LN} + \phi'$ and $\phi'$ is constant, we have therefore found $\delta \text{LP}$.

->70° 57' 20"<-

->70° 16' 40"<-

->0° 40' 40"<-

Thus, we have found a plane section of the surface which agrees closely with the results of the experiment.

This section passes through L, a point on the principal section AC at an angular distance of 1° 21' 42'' from C. It is inclined to that section at an angle of 60° 20', while the normal to the face P lies at an angular distance from L equal to

->35° 0' 19'' + 0° 17' 15'' = 35° 17' 34''<-

Under these circumstances, it will be necessary to consider the probability of making an error such as this result indicates in the position of the normal to P with reference to the principal axes.

But before doing this, we must say a few words about the variations in the values of $\mu_2$ produced by the correction currently being considered.

The final correction will not affect any of them except the first, which will be slightly increased by it.

This follows from the fact that between lines 1 and 2 of Table IX, $\theta - \theta'$ varies considerably and increases or decreases with $\theta + \theta'$, so that $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ increase or decrease together.

The change under consideration has increased $\mu_1$; it will, therefore, increase $\mu_2$.

The difference in line 2 is considerable, but it may be noticed that the experimental value is clearly too small, falling as it does (Table I, line 18) between two considerably larger values. In the other cases, the differences between theory and experiment have been reduced but remain the same sign as before.

A further displacement in the same direction would, therefore, produce even greater agreement.

We must now consider the effect of varying CL.

Let us trace the effect of increasing CL by 10'.

The value of $\mu_a$ depends on that of CL, being found from it by the formula (Section V):

->$\frac{1}{\mu_a^2} = \sec^2 \text{CL} (\frac{1}{r^2} - \frac{\sin^2 \text{CL}}{\mu_c^2})$<-

where

->$\mu_c^2 = 1.53013$<-

and $r$ is given from experiment:

->$r = 1.68550$<-

The new value of $a$ will be found to be

->$\mu_a = 1.68571$<-

instead of ->$1.68560$<-

This increase in the value of $a$ will increase the angle between the optic axes from 9° 4' 5'', the value already found, to 9° 9' 20''.

We may suppose either that, while the axes of elasticity retain their position with

But there remains the supposition that the axes of elasticity do not have exactly the same position in all crystals of aragonite. Thus, the displacement of PR relative to the axes might be effected by slightly changing their position with reference to the faces of the crystal, while PR retains its position relative to those faces unchanged. The possibility of this is a question for the mineralogist. I have as yet been unable to find data for a satisfactory answer. It seems, however, plausible to suppose that in a substance like aragonite—which is not chemically pure but contains foreign substances to a varying degree in different specimens—some slight variation such as the one indicated might occur.

### Section X.—*General Results of the Investigation.*

Combining the results of the two series of experiments, it seems most probable to me that <term>FRESNEL'S</term> theory is true only as a first approximation.

Both series of observations have led to the discovery of considerable deviations from the theory, unless we assume errors in the experiments—especially in determining the position of the planes of the prisms with reference to the axes of the crystals—which are far in excess of the amounts we can reasonably expect.

It will be noticed that the values taken for the constants $\mu_a$ and $\mu_b$ in the two parts of the paper differ by 0.0002 and 0.00017, respectively. This is due to the fact that the two crystals used were different. <term>RUDBERG</term> (POGG. Annalen, vol. xvii., p. 1) found differences as great as 0.0004 in the values of $\mu_b$ derived from two specimens of aragonite.

It may be objected that the variations between theory and experiment do not follow exactly the same direction in the two parts; but we must remember (1) that the arcs investigated are taken from entirely different portions of the surface; and (2) in the first part, the approximately elliptical section belongs to the outer sheet, while in the second part, it belongs to the inner sheet of the wave surface.

MON is the principal plane of the first prism, nearly coincident with the plane through the optic axes AOC.

### Section XI.—*Effect of Dispersion Considered.*

The theory of dispersion appears to me to afford a more probable explanation of these small variations from <term>Fresnel’s construction</term>.

<term>Fresnel</term> himself remarked (‘Second Supplement to the first Memoir on double refraction,’ *Complete Works of Fresnel*, vol. ii.) that, in the case of the vibrations which constitute light, the radius of the sphere of action of the molecular forces brought into play by the vibration is not necessarily very small compared with the wavelength.

Consequently, it is incorrect to suppose that the propagation of each of the disturbances that compose a vibration is uninfluenced by the disturbances preceding and following it, or that the velocity of propagation is independent of the manner in which they precede and follow it.

This supposition is the basis of <term>Fresnel’s</term> work on <term>double refraction</term>.

Let us consider the effect of dispersion in a doubly refracting medium.

In an <term>isotropic medium</term>, the relation between V, the velocity of wave propagation, and $\lambda$, the wavelength, is generally accepted to be:

->$\frac{1}{\text{V}} = a + \frac{b}{\lambda^2} + \frac{c}{\lambda^4} + \text{, etc.,}$<-

where $a, b, c$, etc., are constants. The values of the terms decrease continually, so that, except in highly dispersive media, we may use $\frac{1}{\text{V}} = a + \frac{b}{\lambda^2}$ with sufficient accuracy.

<summary>Glazebrook describes the geometric orientation of crystal prisms used in his experiments and suggests that deviations from Fresnel's theory may be explained by dispersion. He challenges the assumption that molecular forces' sphere of action is negligible compared to the wavelength, which is a foundational premise of Fresnel's work.</summary>
<keywords>R. T. Glazebrook, Fresnel's surface, dispersion, double refraction, isotropic medium, wavelength, velocity of wave propagation, biaxial crystal, crystal optics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the theory of dispersion as an explanation for the small variations from Fresnel's construction in biaxial crystals, moving into the mathematical verification using experimental data.</meta>

<page-num>377</page-num>
<header>MR. R. T. GLAZEBROOK ON PLANE WAVES IN A BIAXIAL CRYSTAL.</header>
<sig>3 C</sig>
<meta>1879.</meta>

Let us suppose that an equation of this form holds in crystalline media as well, except that $a, b, c,$ etc., instead of being constants, are functions of the directions of propagation and vibration; and, furthermore, let us suppose that Fresnel’s construction is true for waves of infinite length, so that the equation $\frac{1}{v}=a$ gives us a Fresnel’s wave surface.

From the known values of the constants of the wave surface for different rays of the spectrum, the constants of the surface for infinite wavelengths can be found, and therefore the value of $a$ can be calculated in any given direction.

If from experiment we find the value of $\frac{1}{v}$ or $\mu$ for any wavelength, the difference $\mu - a$ should, according to this theory, be equal to $\frac{b}{\lambda^2}$.

And if we find the values of $\mu$ for different wavelengths (say $\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3$) in the same direction, we have

->$\mu_1 - a = \frac{b}{\lambda_1^2}$<-
->$\mu_2 - a = \frac{b}{\lambda_2^2}$<-
->$\mu_3 - a = \frac{b}{\lambda_3^2}$<-

from which it follows that

->$\frac{\mu_1 - a}{\mu_2 - a} = \frac{\lambda_2^2}{\lambda_1^2}$<-
->$\frac{\mu_2 - a}{\mu_3 - a} = \frac{\lambda_3^2}{\lambda_2^2}$<-

To verify this, I observed the values of $\mu$ in two directions for the rays C, D, and F, with the following results:

->$(\frac{\lambda_C}{\lambda_D})^2 = 1.2403$<-
->$\frac{\mu_D - a}{\mu_C - a} = 1.2875$ (first experiment)<-
->$1.2770$ (second experiment)<-
->$(\frac{\lambda_D}{\lambda_F})^2 = 1.46978$<-
->$\frac{\mu_F - a}{\mu_D - a} = 1.47208$ (first experiment)<-
->$= 1.47348$ (second experiment).<-

The numbers, especially in the last case, are close enough to make continuing the investigations seem worthwhile.

<summary>Glazebrook proposes a mathematical model to account for dispersion by assuming Fresnel's construction holds for infinite wavelengths and tests this against experimental data for specific spectral rays. The resulting experimental values closely align with the theoretical ratios, suggesting the validity of the approach.</summary>

### XI. *On certain Definite Integrals occurring in Spherical Harmonic Analysis and on the Expansion, in Series, of the Potentials of the Ellipsoid and the Ellipse.*

### *By* W. D. NIVEN, *M.A., Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge.*

### *Communicated by* J. W. L. GLAISHER, *M.A., F.R.S.*

->Received April 3,—Read May 1, 1879.<-

---

§ 1. THE purpose of this paper is to explain a method for handling a class of results—some of which occur frequently and others being of considerable importance—in the solution of LAPLACE’S equation in series.

The fundamental theorem on which the method relies is expressed by the integration of

->$\iint e^{\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z} dS$<-

over a sphere whose center is the origin of coordinates and whose radius is R. We shall call this the sphere of reference.

By changing the axes, the integral above takes the form

->$2\pi R \int_{-R}^{R} e^{x \sqrt{(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2)}} dx$<-

and its value is

->$2\pi R \frac{e^{R \sqrt{(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2)}} - e^{-R \sqrt{(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2)}}}{\sqrt{(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2)}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1)$<-

or, in series,

->$4\pi R^2 \left\{ 1 + \frac{R^2}{3!} (\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2) + \dots + \frac{R^{2i}}{(2i+1)!} (\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2)^i + \dots \right\} \dots \dots (2)$<-

It follows that if V is any function whose value may be expressed for all points within the sphere by a convergent series, according to TAYLOR’S theorem, or by the symbolic form

->$e^{x \frac{d}{dx} + y \frac{d}{dy} + z \frac{d}{dz}} V_0$<-

then the integral $\iint V dS$ taken over the surface of the sphere is

->$4\pi R^2 \sum_0^\infty \frac{R^{2i}}{(2i+1)!} \left( \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2}{dz^2} \right)^i V_0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3)$<-

<summary>W. D. Niven introduces a method for solving Laplace's equation in series by integrating an exponential function over the surface of a sphere. This fundamental theorem relates the surface integral of a function to its values and derivatives at the center of the sphere using Taylor's theorem.</summary>

<keywords>Definite Integrals, Spherical Harmonic Analysis, Potentials, Ellipsoid, Ellipse, Laplace's equation, Taylor's theorem, surface integral, sphere of reference</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of definite integrals, moving from three-dimensional surface integrals on a sphere to the corresponding theorem for a circle in two dimensions. It also defines the specific notation and coordinate systems—including Legendre coefficients and Maxwell's theory of poles—that will be used for spherical harmonic analysis throughout the paper.</meta>

<page-num>380</page-num>
<header>MR. W. D. NIVEN ON CERTAIN DEFINITE INTEGRALS</header>

The corresponding theorem in two dimensions, which we shall also employ, is this:—
The integral
->$\int e^{\alpha x + \beta y} ds$<-
taken around the circumference of a reference circle, is
->$2\pi R \sum_{0}^{\infty} \frac{R^{2i}}{2^{2i} i! \ i!} (\alpha^2 + \beta^2)^i$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (4)<-

Hence it follows that
->$\int V ds,$<-
taken around the same circumference, is
->$2\pi R \sum_{0}^{\infty} \frac{R^{2i}}{2^{2i} i! \ i!} \left( \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2}{dy^2} \right)^i V_0$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (5)<-

The theorems expressed by (3) and (5) are used below in various cases involving spherical harmonics. It is therefore necessary to specify the notation to be used at the outset.

We denote, as is customary, the colatitude and longitude of a point relative to the reference axes by $\theta$ and $\phi$: $\cos \theta$ and $\sin \theta$ by $\mu$ and $\nu$ respectively. We denote the <term>Legendre’s coefficient</term> or <term>zonal harmonic</term> of the $i^{th}$ degree by the symbol $\text{P}_i$ so that $\text{P}_i$ is defined by the equation
->$i! \ \text{P}_i = (-1)^i r^{i+1} \frac{d^i}{dz^i} \frac{1}{r}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (6)<-
<note>In modern notation, the $i$-th derivative with respect to $z$ is written as $\frac{d^i}{dz^i}$.</note>

According to <term>Clerk Maxwell’s</term> theory of poles, the general expression for the harmonic of the $i^{th}$ degree is given by the equation
->$i! \ \text{Y}_i = (-1)^i r^{i+1} \frac{d^i}{dh_1 dh_2 \dots dh_i} \frac{1}{r}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (7)<-
where $\frac{d}{dh}$ means differentiation with respect to an axis $h$.

In the harmonic (7), the $i$ poles are the points where the $i$ axes of differentiation intersect the sphere of reference. In the harmonic (6), the $i$ poles all coincide with the point where the $z$-axis intersects the sphere. If the $i$ poles coincide at any other point, the harmonic will be denoted by $\text{Q}_i$.

In the tesseral and sectorial system, we have ventured to depart from the usual notations by defining them as follows:—
->$i! \ (i, \sigma) = (-1)^i r^{i+1} \left( \frac{d^\sigma}{d\xi^\sigma} + \frac{d^\sigma}{d\eta^\sigma} \right) \frac{d^{i-\sigma}}{dz^{i-\sigma}} \frac{1}{r}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (8)<-
->$i! \ [i, \sigma] = (-1)^i r^{i+1} j \left( \frac{d^\sigma}{d\xi^\sigma} - \frac{d^\sigma}{d\eta^\sigma} \right) \frac{d^{i-\sigma}}{dz^{i-\sigma}} \frac{1}{r}$ . . . . . . . . . . . . . (9)<-

Regarding the name Spherical Harmonic introduced by <term>THOMSON</term> and <term>TAIT</term>, it seems desirable that the names of <term>LEGENDRE</term> and <term>LAPLACE</term> should be retained in some way in connection with the different kinds of harmonics with which they are associated. that the same method might be applied in cases of greater complexity. Accordingly, cases (5) and (6) have been dealt with, but they have not been solved with the completeness of case (4), the results being effectively expressed in the form of series.

The most interesting as well as the most important applications of the present method are connected with ellipsoids and ellipses. We have through this obtained, in series of harmonics, the potentials of:
(1) An ellipsoidal shell.
(2) A solid ellipsoid.
(3) An elliptic plate of uniform density.
(4) An electric current in an elliptic circuit.
Of these, case (2) leads to the approximate determination of the forces expressing the mutual action between two solid ellipsoids or uniformly magnetized ellipsoids, and case (4) leads, in certain instances, to the forces between two currents in elliptic circuits, the particular case of circular circuits being completely determinate.

Similar results also hold for rectangular solids and circuits.

Case (2) derives additional interest from the fact that it engaged the attention of LAGRANGE, who obtained the expansion as far as the first four terms. The same four terms have also been worked out in a very interesting paper on the potential of an ellipsoid at an external point by Colonel A. R. CLARKE (‘Philosophical Magazine,’ 1877, vol. ii., pp. 458-461).

In regard to case (3), Professor CAYLEY, in the ‘Proceedings of the Mathematical Society’ for 1875, has obtained the solution in the form of an integral, from which he derives interesting properties of the potential depending on certain particular positions of the attracted point. The expansion in harmonic series would seem, however, to be more useful in practice for determining the mutual forces between two electrical circuits.

Throughout the following investigations, the method of treating <term>Spherical Harmonics</term> introduced by THOMSON and TAIT will be almost exclusively adopted.

upon the product $z^m u$ may be written:

->$\{ \frac{d^2}{dx_2^2} + \frac{d^2}{dy_2^2} + (\frac{d}{dz_2} + \frac{d}{dz_1})^2 \}^i$<-

->$\displaystyle \iint \mu^m P_n dS = 4\pi R^2 \frac{2^n m! \frac{m+n}{2}!}{m+n+1! \frac{m-n}{2}!} \dots \dots \dots (11)$<-

It is obvious from the proof above that $m+n$ must be an even number and that $n$ must not be greater than $m$. In all other cases where $m$ and $n$ are integers, the integral must be zero.

### GENERAL THEOREMS IN DIFFERENTIATION.

§ 6. Before we proceed with the remaining cases, it will be convenient to state and prove various theorems in differentiation.*

Theorem i. The general operator (7) acting upon the reciprocal of $r$ may instead be made to act upon a <term>homogeneous function</term> in $x, y, z$ of the $i^{th}$ degree; this effect is expressed by the relation
->$$(-1)^i \frac{d^i}{dh_1 dh_2 \dots dh_i} \frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{r^{i+1}} \frac{d^i}{dh_1 dh_2 \dots dh_i} (r^i Q_i) \text{ . . . . . . . . (20)}$$<-
where the pole of $Q_i$ is in the direction of $r$.

---

\* Theorems i. and ii. were given in a paper by the author in the ‘Messenger of Mathematics,’ No. 73, 1877. Because of the brevity of the proofs, and to ensure completeness, it is thought best to reproduce them here.

<header>OCCURRING IN SPHERICAL HARMONIC ANALYSIS.</header>

Theorem ii. relates to the differentiation of the reciprocal of $r^{2\sigma+1}$ and may be stated as follows:

-> $(-1)^{i-\sigma} \frac{d^{i-\sigma}}{dh_1 dh_2 \dots dh_{i-\sigma}} \frac{1}{r^{2\sigma+1}} = \frac{2^\sigma \sigma!}{2\sigma!} \frac{d^{i-\sigma}}{dh_1 dh_2 \dots dh_{i-\sigma}} \left( r^{i-\sigma} \frac{d^\sigma Q_i}{d\mu^\sigma} \right) \dots$ (21) <-

Theorem iii. If $f \left( \frac{d}{dx}, \frac{d}{dy}, \frac{d}{dz} \right)$ is any homogeneous operator of the $i^{th}$ degree acting on a homogeneous expression $\phi (x, y, z)$ of the $i^{th}$ degree, then

-> $f \left( \frac{d}{dx}, \frac{d}{dy}, \frac{d}{dz} \right) \phi (x, y, z) = \phi \left( \frac{d}{dx}, \frac{d}{dy}, \frac{d}{dz} \right) f (x, y, z) \dots$ (22) <-

This theorem is obviously true; and although it is stated for only three quantities, $x, y, z$, it is true for any number of them.

Theorems i. and ii. are proved as follows: Let OP $= r$, QP $= \rho$, and O$\hat{\text{P}}$Q $= \pi - \theta$, where Q is any point near P. Then

-> $\frac{1}{\text{OQ}} = \frac{1}{r} - \frac{\rho}{r^2} Q_1 + \dots + (-1)^i \frac{\rho^i}{r^{i+1}} Q_i + \&\text{c.}$ <-

Keeping $r$ fixed, let us perform the operation (7) on both sides of this equation and then set $\rho = 0$, in which case OQ becomes $r$. It should be noted that with a homogeneous operator like (7), it does not matter which point is chosen as the origin of coordinates. If we then take P as the origin when we are dealing with the right-hand side of the expansion above, we see that the first $i$ terms will disappear through repeated differentiations, and the terms beyond the $(i+1)^{th}$ term disappear because $\rho$ is zero. The stated theorem therefore follows; substituting $r$ for $\rho$ makes no difference in a result from which $x, y, z$ are finally removed.

Theorem ii. may be proved in the same way if, instead of using the expansion for the reciprocal of OQ as shown above, we use the expansion for the reciprocal of $\text{OQ}^{2\sigma+1}$, which is found by differentiating the series above $\sigma$ times with respect to $\mu$.

->$$\frac{d^m}{d\xi_1} \frac{d^m}{d\eta_1} \frac{d^n}{dz_1}$$<-

->$$4\pi R^2 \sum_0^\infty \frac{R^{2i}}{2i+1!} \left( -v^2 \frac{d^2}{dz_1^2} - \frac{1}{v^2} \frac{d^2}{dz_2^2} + 2 \frac{d}{dz_1} \frac{d}{dz_2} \right)^i \frac{1}{\text{AO.BO}}$$<-

that is, in

that is,

->$$4\pi R^2 \sum \frac{R^{2i}}{2i+1!} \frac{2i!}{i! \ i!} \frac{d^i}{dz_1} \frac{d^i}{dz_2} \frac{1}{\text{AO.BO}}$$<-

If we now expand the reciprocals of AP and BP into harmonics, we arrive at the well-known theorems:

->$\iint P_i Q_j dS = 0$<-

->$\iint P_i Q_i dS = \frac{4\pi R^2}{2i + 1} P_i (\cos \alpha)$ . . . . . . . . . (23)<-

->$2i! \ Q_i = \rho_1^{i+1} \rho_2^{i+1} 2^i \left( \frac{d}{dx_1} \frac{d}{dx_2} + \frac{d}{dy_1} \frac{d}{dy_2} + \frac{d}{dz_1} \frac{d}{dz_2} \right)^i \frac{1}{\rho_1 \rho_2}$<-

Since the operator is an invariant, we may assume the axes to be any rectangular axes whatever.

->$2i! \ Q_i = \rho_1^{i+1} \rho_2^{i+1} (-1)^i \left( v \frac{d}{dz_1} - \frac{1}{v} \frac{d}{dz_2} \right)^{2i} \frac{1}{\rho_1 \rho_2}$<-

->$\frac{d}{d\eta_2} \div \frac{d}{d\eta_1}$<-

<margin>or</margin>

It is obvious that a term similar to this can be obtained simply by substituting $\xi_1$ for $\xi_2$ and $\eta_2$ for $\eta_1$, and by merely changing the sign of $\sigma$ in the first of the last three expressions. ### *General Method of Dealing with the Integral* $\iint Q_p Q_q Q_r \dots dS$.

§ 9. In discussing the general method of evaluating this integral, it will be convenient to limit our focus to the case of three harmonics, although the initial steps of the reasoning apply to any number.

->$\iint \frac{dS}{AP.BP.CP} = 4\pi R^2 \Sigma \frac{R^{2i}}{2i+1!} (\frac{d^2}{dx} + \frac{d^2}{dy} + \frac{d^2}{dz})^i \frac{1}{AO.BO.CO}$<-
->$= 4\pi R^2 \Sigma \frac{R^{2i}}{2i+1!} 2^i (v_{23} + v_{31} + v_{12})^i \frac{1}{AO.BO.CO}$<-

where $v_{23}$ represents

->$\frac{d}{dx_2} \frac{d}{dx_3} + \frac{d}{dy_2} \frac{d}{dy_3} + \frac{d}{dz_2} \frac{d}{dz_3}, \text{etc.}$<-

the subscripts having the same meaning as in the previous article.

The general term of $2i+2$ dimensions in R may therefore be written

->$\frac{4\pi R^{2i+2}}{2i+1!} 2^i \frac{i!}{\lambda! \mu! \nu!} v_{23}^\lambda v_{31}^\mu v_{12}^\nu \frac{1}{AO.BO.CO}$<-

Now, the general expansion of each of the operators in this expression was found in the previous article.

§ 10. If we expand each of the reciprocals of AP, BP, and CP into harmonics, we will arrive at the general term of $2i+2$ dimensions in R in a different form, namely: it will be

->$$\frac{R^{2i}}{a^{p+1}b^{q+1}c^{r+1}} \iint Q_p Q_q Q_r dS$$<-

->$\mu+\nu=p$<-
->$\nu+\lambda=q$<-
->$\lambda+\mu=r$<-

The quantities $\lambda, \mu, \nu$, as they depend on $p, q, r$, are therefore perfectly determined, and the equation expressing the identity of the general terms may, by Theorem i., be written as

->$$\iint Q_p Q_q Q_r dS = \frac{4\pi R^2}{2i+1!} 2^i \frac{i!}{\lambda! \ \mu! \ \nu!} \Sigma \Sigma \Sigma \pi (l, m, n) (Q_p r_1^p Q_q r_2^q Q_r r_3^r) \ . \ . \ . \ . \ (25)$$<-

On examining the equations determining $\lambda, \mu, \nu$, we see that for them to be positive, $p+q+r$ must be an even number, and none of the three quantities $p, q, r$ can be greater than the sum of the other two.

If these conditions are not satisfied, then $\iint Q_p Q_q Q_r dS = 0$ for integral values of $p, q, r$, regardless of where the poles of the harmonics are located.

In the general operator, by determining which terms are practically effective and discarding those which are not, we need to retain only such terms as are, for example, of the form:

->$\frac{d^\sigma}{d\xi_1} \frac{d^\sigma}{d\eta_1} \frac{d^{p-2\sigma}}{dz_1}$<-

The terms of this form are obviously obtained by setting $l=m=n = \sigma$, for example. In that case, when we omit inoperative terms, $\pi$ becomes:

->$\displaystyle 2^{6\sigma-i+1} \frac{2\lambda! \ 2\mu! \ 2\nu!}{\lambda+\sigma! \ \lambda-\sigma! \ \mu+\sigma! \ \mu-\sigma! \ \nu+\sigma! \ \nu-\sigma!}$<-
->$\displaystyle \times \left( \frac{d}{d\xi_1} \frac{d}{d\eta_1} \frac{d}{d\xi_2} \frac{d}{d\eta_2} \frac{d}{d\xi_3} \frac{d}{d\eta_3} \right)^\sigma \frac{d^{p-2\sigma}}{dz_1} \frac{d^{q-2\sigma}}{dz_2} \frac{d^{r-2\sigma}}{dz_3}$<-

that is, by virtue of LAPLACE's equation being satisfied,

->$\displaystyle (-1)^\sigma \frac{2}{2^i} \frac{2\lambda! \ 2\mu! \ 2\nu!}{\lambda+\sigma! \ \lambda-\sigma! \ \mu+\sigma! \ \mu-\sigma! \ \nu+\sigma! \ \nu-\sigma!} \frac{d^p}{dz_1} \frac{d^q}{dz_2} \frac{d^r}{dz_3}$<-

Taking all possible terms of $\pi$, such as the one just found, and performing the operation they direct, we have for $\iint P_p P_q P_r dS$ the expression:

->$\displaystyle \frac{4\pi R^2}{2i+1} \frac{2\lambda! \ 2\mu! \ 2\nu! \ i!}{\lambda! \ \mu! \ \nu!} \left( \frac{p! \ q! \ r!}{(\lambda! \ \mu! \ \nu!)^2} + 2\Sigma (-1)^\sigma \frac{p! \ q! \ r!}{\lambda+\sigma! \ \lambda-\sigma! \ \mu+\sigma! \ \mu-\sigma! \ \nu+\sigma! \ \nu-\sigma!} \right)$<-

where $\sigma$ ranges from $0$ to the smallest of the quantities $\lambda, \mu, \nu$. 
The series within the brackets is clearly the coefficient of $x^{2\lambda} y^{2\mu} z^{2\nu}$, or of $x^{\mu+\nu} y^{\nu+\lambda} z^{\lambda+\mu}$, in:

->$\displaystyle (-1)^i (y-z)^{\mu+\nu} (z-x)^{\nu+\lambda} (x-y)^{\lambda+\mu}$<-

or, again, the same series is also obviously equal to:

->$\displaystyle \frac{p! \ q! \ r!}{2\lambda! \ 2\mu! \ 2\nu!} \text{K}$<-

where K is the coefficient of $x^{\mu+\nu} \ y^{\nu+\lambda} \ z^{\lambda+\mu}$ in:

->$\displaystyle (-1)^i (y-z)^{2\lambda} (z-x)^{2\mu} (x-y)^{2\nu}$<-

that is, in:

->$\displaystyle (-1)^i x^{\mu+\nu} y^{\nu+\lambda} z^{\lambda+\mu} \left( \sqrt{\frac{y}{z}} - \sqrt{\frac{z}{y}} \right)^{2\lambda} \left( \sqrt{\frac{z}{x}} - \sqrt{\frac{x}{z}} \right)^{2\mu} \left( \sqrt{\frac{x}{y}} - \sqrt{\frac{y}{x}} \right)^{2\nu}$<-

If we now substitute here:

->$\displaystyle z = x e^{2\phi j} = y e^{\phi j}$<-

### OCCURRING IN SPHERICAL HARMONIC ANALYSIS.

We see that $K$ is the term not involving the cosine of an angle with the value $m\theta + n\phi$ in the expansion of $W$ into such cosines, where

->$\text{W} = (-1)^i \ 2^{2i} \sin^{2\lambda}\theta \sin^{2\mu}\phi \sin^{2\nu}(\theta - \phi)$<-

so that

->$\text{K} = \frac{1}{\pi^2} \int_0^\pi \int_0^\pi \text{W} d\theta d\phi$<-

Now, expanding $\sin^{2\nu}(\theta - \phi)$ in powers of sines and cosines using the binomial theorem, we observe that the odd terms in the expansion disappear upon integration; thus, the value of $K$ is given by

->$\Sigma \frac{1}{\pi^2} \int_0^\pi \int_0^\pi (-1)^i \ 2^{2i} \frac{2\nu!}{2n! \ 2\nu - 2n!} \sin^{2\lambda + 2n}\theta \cos^{2\nu - 2n}\theta \sin^{2\mu + 2\nu - 2n}\phi \cos^{2n}\phi \ d\theta \ d\phi$<-

Upon integration and reduction, this becomes

->$(-1)^i \ 2^{-2\nu} \frac{2\nu!}{\lambda + \nu! \ \mu + \nu!} \Sigma \frac{2\lambda + 2n! \ 2\mu + 2\nu - 2n!}{\lambda + n! \ \mu + \nu - n! \ \nu - n! \ n!}$<-

that is,

->$(-1)^i \ 2^{-2\nu} \frac{2\nu!}{\lambda + \nu! \ \mu + \nu!} \frac{2\lambda!}{\lambda!} \frac{2\mu + 2\nu!}{\mu + \nu!} \frac{1}{\nu!} \text{S}$<-

where

->$\text{S} = 1 + \frac{(2\lambda + 1)\nu}{2\mu + 2\nu - 1} + \frac{(2\lambda + 1)(2\lambda + 3)\nu(\nu - 1)}{(2\mu + 2\nu - 1)(2\mu + 2\nu - 3)1.2} + \text{etc.}$<-

This hypergeometric series can be summed by a method similar to that given by <term>BERTRAND</term> in '*Calcul Intégral*,' 1870, pp. 495–496. If we set

->$\lambda + \frac{1}{2} = \alpha$<-
->$\mu + \nu - \frac{1}{2} = \beta$<-

$S$ becomes

->$1 + \frac{\alpha\nu}{\beta} + \frac{\alpha(\alpha + 1)}{\beta(\beta - 1)} \frac{\nu(\nu - 1)}{1.2} + \text{etc.}$<-

->$= \frac{\Gamma(\alpha + n)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \frac{\Gamma(\beta - n + 1)}{\Gamma(\beta + 1)} \frac{\nu(\nu - 1) \dots (\nu - n + 1)}{n!}$<-

->$= \frac{\Gamma(\alpha + \beta + 1)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta + 1)} \Sigma \int_0^\infty \frac{\nu(\nu - 1) \dots \nu - n + 1}{n!} \frac{y^{\alpha + n - 1}}{(1 + y)^{\alpha + \beta + 1}} dy$<-

->$= \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta + 1)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta + 1)} \int_0^\infty \frac{y^{\alpha - 1} dy}{(1 + y)^{\lambda + \mu + 1}}$<-

->$= \frac{\Gamma(\alpha + \beta + 1)}{\Gamma(\beta + 1)} \frac{\Gamma(\mu + \frac{1}{2})}{\Gamma(\lambda + \mu + 1)}$<-

->$= 2^{2\nu} \frac{i!}{\lambda + \mu!} \frac{2\mu!}{\mu!} \frac{\mu + \nu!}{2\mu + 2\nu!}$<-

§ 12. Before leaving this case, we may remark that, as far as the preceding proof is concerned, the poles of all three harmonics are not necessarily coincident. The proof will hold when two are coincident and the third is at an angular distance, say $\alpha$, from them. In those circumstances, the value of $\iint \text{P}_p \text{P}_q \text{Q}_r d\text{S}$ will be the result found above multiplied by $\text{P}_r(\cos \alpha)$. The same is, of course, true of the integral $\iint \text{Q}_p \text{Q}_q \text{P}_r d\text{S}$, provided the two $Q$'s have the same poles. Now, let $\text{Q}_p$ and $\text{Q}_q$ be each expanded according to Laplace's Formula. Then we will have the curious result that any zonal harmonic of degree $r$ can be expanded in products of harmonics, both zonal and tesseral, of degrees $p$ and $q$, the quantities $p, q, r$ being, of course, subject to the preceding restrictions. If $q$ is less than $p$, the number of terms in such an expansion will be $2q+1$.

Suppose the differentiations are performed by the entire operator, and if one of the resulting terms is

The expression upon which the operator $\varpi$ must operate can be found by expressing $Q_p$, etc., through Laplace’s Formula and using series D: it is as follows:

->$\frac{2^{-1}p!}{\alpha! \ p-\alpha!} \{ (\xi_1^\alpha + \eta_1^\alpha)(p, \ \alpha)_a - j(\xi_1^\alpha - \eta_1^\alpha)[p, \ \alpha]_a \} z_1^{p-\alpha}$<-

->$\times \frac{2^{-1}r!}{\alpha+\beta! \ r-\alpha-\beta!} \{ (\xi_3^{\alpha+\beta} + \eta_3^{\alpha+\beta})(r, \ \alpha+\beta)_c - j(\xi_3^{\alpha+\beta} - \eta_3^{\alpha+\beta})[r, \ \alpha+\beta]_c \} z_3^{r-\alpha-\beta}$<-

->$\frac{2^{-3}p! \ q! \ r!}{\alpha! \ \beta! \ \alpha+\beta! \ p-\alpha! \ q-\beta! \ r-\alpha-\beta!} \times \{ (p, \ \alpha)_a (q, \ \beta)_b (r, \ \alpha+\beta)_c$<-
->$- (p, \ \alpha)_a [q, \ \beta]_b [r, \ \alpha+\beta]_c - [p, \ \alpha]_a (q, \ \beta)_b [r, \ \alpha+\beta]_c - [p, \ \alpha]_a [q, \ \beta]_b (r, \ \alpha+\beta)_c \}$<-
->$\times (\xi_1^\alpha \xi_2^\beta \eta_3^{\alpha+\beta} + \eta_1^\alpha \eta_2^\beta \xi_3^{\alpha+\beta}) z_1^{p-\alpha} z_2^{q-\beta} z_3^{r-\alpha-\beta}$<-

The result of the operation is accordingly

->$2^{2(\alpha+\beta)-i-2} p! \ q! \ r! \ K \{ (p, \ \alpha)_a (q, \ \beta)_b (r, \alpha+\beta)_c - \&c. \dots \}$<-

->$\frac{2^{4(\alpha+\beta)-3} p! \ p! \ q! \ q! \ r! \ r!}{p+\alpha! \ p-\alpha! \ q+\beta! \ q-\beta! \ r+\alpha+\beta! \ r-\alpha-\beta!}$<-
->$\times \iint \{ (p, \ \alpha)_a (p, \ \alpha) + [p, \ \alpha]_a [p, \ \alpha] \} \{ (q, \ \beta)_b (q, \ \beta) + [q, \ \beta]_b [q, \ \beta] \} \{ (r, \ \alpha+\beta)_c (r, \ \alpha+\beta)$<-
->$+ [r, \ \alpha+\beta]_c [r, \ \alpha+\beta] \} dS$<-

->$\frac{2^{2(\alpha+\beta)-1} p! \ q! \ r!}{p+\alpha! \ q+\beta! \ r-\alpha-\beta!} \iint (p, \ \alpha) (q, \ \beta) (r, \ \alpha+\beta) dS = \frac{4\pi R^2}{2i+1!} \frac{i! \ 2\lambda! \ 2\mu! \ 2\nu!}{\lambda! \ \mu! \ \nu!} W$<-

or finally

where $W$ is defined above in (28) as the coefficient of a term in a certain product, or as a series whose terms depend upon a single parameter.

->$\begin{aligned} (-1)^i \frac{i!}{\lambda! \mu! \nu! l! m! n!} & \times (k_2 - k_3)^{2\lambda} (k_3 - k_1)^{2\mu} (k_1 - k_2)^{2\nu} (k_4 - k_1)^{2l} (k_4 - k_2)^{2m} (k_4 - k_3)^{2n} \\ & \times \left( \frac{1}{k_1} \frac{d}{dz_1} \right)^p \left( \frac{1}{k_2} \frac{d}{dz_2} \right)^q \left( \frac{1}{k_3} \frac{d}{dz_3} \right)^r \left( \frac{1}{k_4} \frac{d}{dz_4} \right)^s \end{aligned}$<-

where

$\left. \begin{aligned} \mu + \nu + l = p \\ \nu + \lambda + m = q \\ \lambda + \mu + n = r \\ l + m + n = s \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \text{(30)}$

It transforms the general operator into an expansion that avoids specific variables, allowing for the identification of a general term defined by a system of index equations.</summary>

<sig>3 F 2</sig>

The quantities $\lambda, \mu, \nu, l, m, n$ are therefore indeterminate, and there will be a series of terms having the required indices.

The coefficient of the operator given above may be expressed in another form. Let us consider the expansion of

->$\{a(k_2-k_3)+b(k_3-k_1)+c(k_1-k_2)+d(k_4-k_1)+e(k_4-k_2)+f(k_4-k_3)\}^{2i}$<-

first in powers of $a, b, c, \dots$ and then in powers of $k_1, k_2, k_3, \dots$ We then see that the coefficient of $k_1^p\ k_2^q\ k_3^r\ k_4^s$ in $(k_2-k_3)^{2\lambda} \dots (k_4-k_3)^{2n}$ is equal to

->$\frac{2\lambda!\ 2\mu!\ 2\nu!\ 2l!\ 2m!\ 2n!}{p!\ q!\ r!\ s!} \text{W}$<-

where W is the coefficient of $a^{2\lambda}\ b^{2\mu}\ c^{2\nu}\ d^{2l}\ e^{2m}\ f^{2n}$ in

->$(-b+c-d)^p(-c+a-e)^q(-a+b-f)^r(d+e+f)^s$<-

We have, finally,

->$\iint \text{P}_p \text{P}_q \text{P}_r \text{P}_s d\text{S} = (-1)^i \frac{4\pi\text{R}^2 i!}{2i+1!} \Sigma \frac{2\lambda!\ 2\mu!\ 2\nu!\ 2l!\ 2m!\ 2n!}{\lambda!\ \mu!\ \nu!\ l!\ m!\ n!} \text{W}$<-

where $\Sigma$ denotes the sum of all such values of W multiplied by their respective coefficients corresponding to values of $\lambda, \mu, \nu, l, m, n$ determined by equations (30).

This investigation serves to show the particular practical difficulties that accompany the problem of integrating products of harmonics over the sphere of reference, if more than three harmonics are considered.

### POTENTIALS OF ELLIPSOIDS.

§ 15. Let $p$ be the perpendicular to the tangent plane at any point of an ellipsoid, and let us consider the integral

->$\iint e^{\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z} p d\text{S}$<-

taken over the surface.

By the theory of corresponding points, this integral may clearly be converted into the form of an integral taken over the surface of a sphere of radius R, namely: it is

->$\frac{abc}{\text{R}^2} \iint e^{\frac{a\alpha x' + b\beta y' + c\gamma z'}{\text{R}}} d\text{S}',$<-

the value of which, according to what we have already shown in (3), is

->$2\pi abc \frac{e^\nabla - e^{-\nabla}}{\nabla}$<-

where

->$\nabla^2 = a^2\alpha^2 + b^2\beta^2 + c^2\gamma^2.$<-

<summary>This page concludes the analysis of integrating four spherical harmonics and introduces the calculation of ellipsoid potentials. It demonstrates how to transform surface integrals over an ellipsoid into simpler integrals over a sphere using the theory of corresponding points.</summary>
<keywords>Spherical Harmonic Analysis, Potentials of Ellipsoids, integration, harmonics, tangent plane, corresponding points, surface integral</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the potentials of ellipsoids, moving from the general integral form to applications involving Taylor's Theorem and Laplace's equation.</meta>

HEADER: MR. W. D. NIVEN ON CERTAIN DEFINITE INTEGRALS

Now let V be any function of $x, y, z$ which can be expanded by <term>TAYLOR’s Theorem</term>; then
->$$\iint V p dS$$<-
taken over the surface of the ellipsoid is
->$$2\pi abc \frac{e^\nabla - e^{-\nabla}}{\nabla} V$$<-
or, in series,
->$$4\pi abc \left( 1 + \frac{\nabla^2}{3!} + \dots + \frac{\nabla^{2i}}{(2i+1)!} + \dots \right) V$$<-
where
->$$\nabla^2 = a^2 \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + b^2 \frac{d^2}{dy^2} + c^2 \frac{d^2}{dz^2},$$<-
and after the differentiations are performed, $x, y, z$ are to be set equal to zero.

§ 16. If V satisfies <term>LAPLACE’s equation</term>, then the operator $\nabla^2$ will remain unaltered if for $a^2, b^2, c^2$ we substitute $a^2 + \epsilon, b^2 + \epsilon, c^2 + \epsilon$. It follows, therefore, that the average value of V over any ellipsoid as measured by
->$$\frac{\iint \frac{V p dS}{3}}{\text{volume of ellipsoid}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (31)$$<-
is the same for that ellipsoid as for any ellipsoid confocal with it.

This theorem<note>Mathematical Tripos Solutions for 1878.</note>, which may be regarded as the analogue for ellipsoids of the corresponding theorem given by <term>GAUSS</term> for spheres, is due to Professor <term>CHARLES NIVEN</term>, who also showed that, if V is due to attracting matter E inside the surface of the ellipsoid, then the expression (31) becomes
->$$\frac{\text{E}}{2} \int_0^\infty \frac{d\psi}{\sqrt{(a^2 + \psi)(b^2 + \psi)(c^2 + \psi)}}$$<-

§ 17. As a particular case, let $\text{V} = \frac{1}{\text{QP}}$ where Q is any point outside of the ellipsoid. Then
->$$\iint \frac{p dS}{\text{QP}}$$<-
is the potential at Q due to matter of density $p$ coated over the ellipsoid. The quantity of matter is $4\pi abc$ and the potential due to it at Q, according to a well-known result, is
->$$2\pi abc \int_\epsilon^\infty \frac{d\psi}{\sqrt{(a^2 + \psi)(b^2 + \psi)(c^2 + \psi)}}$$<-
or
->$$2\pi abc \alpha$$<-
where $\alpha$ is the ellipsoidal coordinate of Q.

<summary>This page demonstrates how to expand functions over an ellipsoidal surface using Taylor’s Theorem and introduces a theorem by Charles Niven regarding average potential values over confocal ellipsoids. It concludes with an application calculating the potential at an external point due to matter distributed on an ellipsoid's surface.</summary>
<keywords>Taylor's Theorem, Laplace's equation, ellipsoid, surface integrals, potential theory, Charles Niven, Gauss, confocal ellipsoids, ellipsoidal coordinates</keywords>
